Report  of  Superintendent  Naval  Academy  of  the  location  of  that  institu¬ 
tion  at  Newport  and  making  recommendations. 

Naval  Academy, 
Newport ,  R.  I.,  May  13 ,  1861. 

Sir  :  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that,  in  obedience  to  the  order  of 
the  Department  of  the  27tli  ultimo,  the  Naval  Academy  is  transferred 
to  Fort  Adams  and  that  the  duties  of  the  institution  are  this  day 
recommenced. 

The  library  and  all  the  instruments  which  could  be  safely  trans¬ 
ported  have  been  brought  here,  and  I  have  made  a  special  report  to 
the  Bureau  of  Ordnance  and  Hydrography  in  regard  to  such  as  remain 
at  Annapolis.  I  beg  to  submit  the  following  recommendations  of  the 
academic  board  and  respectfully  ask  the  approval  of  the  Department 
of  the  same: 

1.  It  is  recommended  that  the  annual  examination  be  deferred  until 
the  25th  of  June,  aud  that  authority  be  given  to  conduct  it  by  the  aca¬ 
demic  board  without  the  presence  of  the  usual  Board  of  Visitors,  unless 
it  should  be  found  expedient  to  order  one. 

2.  That  from  the  close  of  the  examination  until  the  20th  of  September 
next,  when  the  new  appointees  will  report,  the  exercises  of  the  acting 
midshipmen  in  seamanship,  gunnery,  and  the  other  practical  branches 
of  the  profession  be  unremittingly  pursued  on  board  the  Constitution , 
and  that  the  study  of  French  be  also  pursued  by  them  during  that  time. 
I  also  propose  that  the  ship  should  be  occasionally  got  underway. 

The  fort  will  be  immediately  put  under  careful  police  and  every  pos¬ 
sible  attention  paid  to  its  preservation  and  that  of  the  public  property 
contained  in  it,  and  I  would  suggest  that  as  long  as  it  is  occupied  by 
the  Academy  it  may  be  considered  in  some  degree  garrisoned.  The 
Constitution  is  moored  near  the  fort  and  in  a  convenient  position  for 
target  practice.  The  acting  midshipmen  will  remain  on  board  of  her 
for  the  present,  where  they  Avill  be  constantly  exercised  during  the 
hours  prescribed  by  the  regulations  of  the  Department. 

With  the  exception  of  the  commandant  of  midshipmen  and  the  com¬ 
manding  officer  of  the  Constitution ,  Lieutenants  Simpson,  Buckner, 
Scott,  and  Lull  are  the  only  lieutenants  which  remain  attached  to  the 
Academy.  Their  services  are  so  very  important  in  reorganizing  the 
Academy  and  training  the  acting  midshipmen  that  I  beg  to  express 
the  hope  that  they  may  be  suffered  to  remain. 

I  also  respectfully  ask  that  the  Department  will  approve  my  retain¬ 
ing  for  the  present  three  members  of  the  first  class  named  by  the  com- 
maudant  of  midshipmen  in  his  letter  of  the  [9th]  instant.  Their  services 
are  very  important  to  the  Academy  at  this  time. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant. 

G.  S.  Blake, 

Superintendent. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy ,  Washington ,  I).  C.

Report  of  Flag -Officer  Pendergrast ,  V.  S.  Navy,  commanding  Home 

Squadron,  giving  list  of  vessels  seized  by  him  from  April  21  to  May  13, 

1861 

Flagship  Cumberland, 

Off  Fortress  Monroe ,  Va .,  May  14,  1861. 

Sir  :  I  have  the  honor  to  make  the  following  report  of  vessels  seized 
by  me,  with  their  cargoes,  viz: 

April  21,  1861. — Schooner  George  M.  Smith,  of  Brookliaven,  Long 
Island,  Captain  Mills,  from  New  York,  bound  to  Wilmington,  N.  C.; 
cargo  contraband  of  war ;  sent  by  direction  of  the  Secretary  of  the  Navy 
to  the  U.  S.  marshal  for  the  western  district  of  New  York. 

April  24. — Steam  tug  Young  America ,  of  Norfolk,  Va. ;  seized  for 
attempting  to  eaptuie  the  schooner  George  M.  Smith. 

April  28. — Schooner  Cambridge,  of  Baltimore,  Captain  Buckler,  bound 
to  Norfolk,  with  108  tons  of  coal;  now  half  unloaded. 

May  1. — Schooner  Sarah  and  Mary,  of  Plymouth,  N.  C.,  Captain  Bal- 
lance,  bound  to  Norfolk  from  Alexandria,  Ya.,  with  75  tons  of  coal;  8 
tons  taken  out.

Philadelphia,  May  14,  1861. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that  in  obedience  to  your  orders*  of 
the  22d  of  April  I  proceeded  to  Perryville  with  the  detachment  of  offi¬ 
cers  and  men  and  the  guns  placed  under  my  command,  for  the  purpose 
of  arming  the  steamer  Maryland  and  with  her  keep  open  the  commu¬ 
nication  between  that  place  and  Annapolis.  We  arrived  at  midnight, 
and  I  immediately  put  myself  in  communication  with  Colonel  Dare,  the 
commanding  officer.  From  him  I  learned  there  was  a  rumor  that 
Annapolis  had  been  seized  upon  by  the  secessionists,  the  steamer  Mary¬ 
land  aground  with  the  Massachusetts  regiment  on  board,  and  the 
steamer  Boston,  with  the  New  York  Seventh,  at  anchor  in  the  harbor 
and  unable  to  effect  a  landing.  Hearing  also  from  him  that  the  author 
of  this  was  in  his  boat  at  the  wharf  I  sent  for  and  questioned  him. 
He  corroborated  the  above  statement,  which  he  assured  me  he  had 
obtained  from  the  pilot  of  the  Constitution.  He  also  informed  me  that 
he  had  assisted  in  towing  that  vessel  into  the  outer  Eoads  of  Annapolis. 
I  immediately  telegraphed  this  information  to  Mr.  Felton,  president  of 
the  railroad  company,  with  the  request  that  General  Patterson  and 
yourself  should  be  informed. 

After  much  difficulty  with  the  parties  in  command  of  the  steamers 
(sent  there  by  the  president  of  the  railroad  company  as  transports), 


See  p.  314. 


OPERATIONS  ON  THE  ATLANTIC  COAST. 


395 


who  were  evidently  unwilling  to  risk  either  themselves  or  their  boats, 
I  succeded  in  prevailing  upon  the  captain  of  the  steamer  Wyoming  to 
place  his  vessel  at  my  disposal.  We  worked  all  night  in  getting  the 
guns  on  board,  and  having  obtained  from  Colonel  Dare  a  company  of 
the  Fourth  Pennsylvania  Regiment,  I  started  at  7  a.  m.  for  Annapolis. 
On  our  passage  we  were  employed  in  mounting  the  32-pounder,  a  work 
of  no  little  labor,  and  much  credit  is  due  to  Lieutenant  Crosby  for  the 
accomplishment  of  this  work  with  so  little  material  at  his  command. 
We  arrived  in  sight  of  Annapolis  Roads  at  noon,  and  saw  the  Constitu¬ 
tion  at  anchor.  I  stood  for  her  to  obtain  information  of  the  state  of 
affairs.  On  approaching  her  near  enough  to  be  heard  I  was  told  that 
Annapolis  was  in  possession  of  the  United  States  troops  and  General 
Butler  in  command,  with  his  regiment  and  the  New  York  Seventh.  I 
then  proceeded  to  Annapolis  and  reported  to  him  and  Captain  Blake, 
the  Superintendent  of  the  Academy,  the  object  of  my  visit. 

I  learned  from  them  that  there  was  a  great  scarcity  of  provisions, 
and  was  requested  to  report  this  fact  as  early  as  possible  to  Major- 
General  Patterson.  Remaining  only  long  enough  to  transfer  the  guns 
and  command  to  the  steamer  Maryland ,  and  leaving  the  Wyoming ,  at 
the  request  of  General  Butler,  I  returned  at  once  to  Perryville,  where 
1  arrived  at  midnight,  and  telegraphed  to  you  and  General  Patterson, 
through  Mr.  Felton,  the  state  of  affairs.  On  the  24th  Lieutenant  Wat- 
mough  and  Sailmaker  Ferguson  arrived  at  Perryville  with  two  32- 
pounders,  which  were  placed  in  battery  for  the  protection  of  that  post. 
Provisions  having  arrived  I  took  them  on  board  and,  with  several 
bearers  of  dispatches  for  the  Government,  left  for  Annapolis,  leaving 
Passed  Midshipman  White  to  follow  in  the  Wyoming  (just  returned) 
with  provisions  and  stores.  I  found  upon  my  arrival  at  Annapolis  on 
the  morning  of  the  25th  instant  [ultimo]  that  several  transports  had 
arrived  during  my  absence  with  troops  and  an  ample  supply  of  provi¬ 
sions.  This  was  unexpected,  as  they  had  been  ordered  to  proceed  to 
Washington  by  way  of  the  Potomac,  but  had  changed  their  route  on 
hearing  that  obstructions  had  been  placed  in  the  river  to  prevent  their 
ascent. 

From  Captain  Blake  I  procured  two  6-pounder  howitzers  and  neces¬ 
sary  ammunition  and  returned  to  Perryville,  when  the  communication 
from  the  Secretary  of  War  (a  copy  of  which  I  herewith  send)  was 
handed  me,  also  a  letter  from  Major-General  Patterson  on  the  same 
subject.  I  thereupon  caused  to  be  fitted  out  and  armed  two  tugboats, 
placing  them  under  the  command  of  Lieutenants  Crosby  and  Wat- 
mough,  and  requesting  of  you  fourteen  more  men,  which  were  immedi¬ 
ately  sent.  The  services  of  those  two  boats  were  of  much  importance 
(the  reports  of  their  commanders  are  herewith  transmitted)  and  I  take 
this  occasion  to  bring  to  your  notice  the  zeal,  energy,  and  ability  which 
these  officers  and  Passed  Midshipman  White  displayed  in  the  perform¬ 
ance  of  their  various  duties,  of  which  I  respectfully  request  the 
Department  be  informed. 

From  the  25th  of  April  until  the  1st  of  May  I  was  engaged  in  the 
transportation  of  troops,  munitions  of  war,  and  provisions  from  Perry¬ 
ville  to  Annapolis.  On  the  3d  of  May  Major  Devins’s  Battalion  Massa¬ 
chusetts  Rifles  were  conveyed  in  the  Maryland  to  reenforce  Fort 
McHenry.  On  the  8th  of  May  the  Maryland ,  with  Sherman’s  battery 
on  board,  and  accompanied  by  four  other  steamers  with  the  United 
States  troops  and  Colonel  Patterson’s  regiment  of  Pennsylvania  vol¬ 
unteers,  proceeded  to  Baltimore  and  landed  them  at  Locust  Point. 
On  my  return  to  Perryville,  deeming  it  no  longer  necessary  to  continue 
on  this  service,  as  there  was  not  the  slightest  probability  of  the  com- 


396  OPERATIONS  ON  THE  ATLANTIC  COAST. 

munication  being  interrupted  from  Perry ville,  I  availed  myself  of  tbe 
discretionary  orders  you  had  given  me  to  withdraw  on  the  11th  instant. 
I  returned  to  the  city  and  had  the  men  and  guns  (with  tbe  exception 
of  the  three  32-pounders,  which  were  for  the  present  left  at  Perryville) 
sent  to  the  navy  yard.  It  gives  me  pleasure  to  say  the  conduct  of  the 
men  was  most  satisfactory.  I  found  Sailmaker  Ferguson  very  atten¬ 
tive  to  his  duties. 

I  must  bring  to  your  notice  the  enclosed  passes,*  issued  by  a  Mr. 
Trimble,  which  were  taken  by  Lieutenant  Crosby  from  the  master  of 
the  steamer  Lioness  when  he  captured  her. 

Before  concluding  I  wish  to  express  my  appreciation  of  the  great 
assistance  I  received  from  Colonel  Dare  and  his  command;  also  the 
untiring  zeal  of  officers  and  employes  of  the  railroad  company  and 
their  efforts  to  carry  out  the  orders  of  the  Government. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Ciias.  Steedman, 

Commander. 

Captain  S.  F.  Du  Pont,  U.  S.  Navy, 

Commandant  TJ.  S.  Navy  Yard ,  Philadelphia ,  Pa.

Philadelphia,  May  11, 1861. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  submit  the  following  report  of  my  opera¬ 
tions  while  in  charge  of  the  steam  propellers  J.  B.  Thompson  and 
Thomas  Sparks ,  cruising  between  the  points  Annapolis  and  Perryville. 
On  the  27th  of  April,  took  command  of  the  J.  B.  Thompson,  with  ten 
seamen  and  two  guns,  making  one  trip  to  Annapolis  and  back  to  Perry¬ 
ville,  carrying  mails  and  passengers.  On  28tli,  transferred  command 
to  Sparks ,  making  daily  trips  to  and  from  above  point  with  mails  and 
passengers  or  special  messengers  till  the  30th  of  April.  May  1,  trans¬ 
ferred  command  to  the  propeller  Shriver  for  the  purpose  of  landing 
Major  Morris  and  command  (of  the  Fourth  [J.  S.  Artillery)  at  Fort 
McHenry,  Baltimore.  On  the  2d  of  May,  returned  to  the  Sparks  and 
continued  trips  with  mails  and  passengers,  or  as  convoy  to  them  and 
treasure,  till  the  5th  instant.  On  afternoon  of  5th.  sailed  in  company 
with  the  tug  Beamy ,  Lieutenant  Crosby,  on  an  expedition  in  search  of 
light-boats  removed  from  Smith’s  and  Windmill  points  south  of  the 
Potomac.  On  same  night  made  harbor  in  the  Patuxent,  in  consequence 
of  bad  weather.  At  3  a.  m.  same  night,  Beaney’ s  boiler  exploded, 
disabling  her.  Lieutenant  Crosby  transferred  men  and  guns  to  the 
Sparks.  Lieutenant  Danels,  of  the  Navy,  with  a  detachment  of  sea¬ 
men  from  the  Alleghany  at  Annapolis,  and  Lieutenant  Morton,  with  a 
detachment  of  soldiers  from  the  Thirteenth  New  York  Eegiment  and 
one  fieldpiece  (6-pounder),  had  also  joined  the  Sparks  at  Annapolis, 
On  the  7th  May  at  3  a.  m.,  started  for  the  Great  Wicomico.  Leaving 
Beaney  at  anchor,  succeeded  in  entering  the  inlet  over  the  flats  and 
seized  the  Windmill  Point  boat  snugly  moored  a  few  miles  inland; 
towed  her  out  and  same  evening  on  return  north  picked  up  the  Beaney, 
arriving  at  Annapolis  on  the  8th  May  at  5  a.  m.  The  same  evening- 
towed  the  Beaney  up  to  Perryville.  On  the  10th  instant,  by  your  order, 
brought  men  and  armament  in  the  cars  to  Philadelphia  and  delivered 
the  men  to  the  receiving  ship  on  this  station. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  sir,  your  obedient  servant, 

Pend.  G.  Watmough, 
Lieutenant,  TJ.  S.  Navy. 

Commander  Charles  Steedman,  TJ.  S.  Navy.

Philadelphia,  May  13,  1861. 

Sir  :  In  obedience  to  your  order  of  the  26th  ultimo,  I  took  command 
of  the  steamer  Commerce ,  with  a  detachment  of  twelve  men,  with  two 
guns,  one  a  12-pounder  boat  howitzer,  and  one  a  6-pounder  field  piece; 
went  over  to  Havre  de  Grace  and  seized  the  steamer  Lancaster ,  from 
Baltimore;  put  her  in  charge  of  Sailing  Master  George  B.  White,  who 
brought  her  over  in  company  with  the  Commerce  to  Perry  ville.  On  the 
afternoon  of  the  same  day  I  left  for  Annapolis  to  convoy  the  steamers 
Whildin  and  Wyoming.  On  our  way  down  discovered  a  steam  tug  tow¬ 
ing  a  ship  down  the  Patapsco;  went  in  pursuit  of  the  steam  tug,  in 
obedience  to  the  written  orders  that  I  had  received  from  you  to  seize 
all  tugs  south  of  Havre  de  Grace.  The  tug  cast  off  her  tow  and  imme¬ 
diately  ran  away  from  us.  I  tired  a  shot  across  her  bow,  but  she  con¬ 
tinued  her  course.  I  then  fired  several  shots  at  her,  but  being  much 
faster  than  the  Commerce  she  was  soon  out  of  the  range  of  our  guns 
and  escaped.  We  then  resumed  our  course  and  anchored  off  Annap¬ 
olis  in  company  with  the  convoy.  On  the  27tli  ultimo  we  returned  to 
Perry  ville  with  the  mail  and  passengers;  boarded  a  Baltimore  bark. 
On  our  arrival  we  transferred  the  guns  and  crew  to  the  William  B. 
Reaney.  On  the  28th  ultimo,  at  2.30  a.  m.,  convoyed  the  steamer  Com¬ 
merce  to  Annapolis.  At  1  p.  m.  left  for  Perry  ville.  On  the  29th  trans¬ 
ferred  the  guns  and  crew  to  the  steamer  Thomas  Sparks  and  carried 
mail  and  passengers  to  Annapolis  and  convoyed  two  steamers.  Returned 
on  the  30th  with  mail  and  passengers  to  Perry  ville;  transferred  the 
guns  and  crew  to  the  William  B.  Reaney.  On  the  31st  [sic],  employed 
in  convoying  vessels  to  Annapolis.  On  the  1st  left  for  Perry  ville; 
seized  the  steam  tug  Lioness  off  the  mouth  of  the  Patapsco  and  took 
her  to  Perryville.  The  captain  of  the  Lioness  delivered  to  me  the 
papers*  signed  by  one  Trimble,  of  Baltimore,  which  were  necessary  for 
him  to  have  in  order  to  pass  in  and  out  of  the  port  of  Baltimore,  all  of 
which  I  handed  over  to  you.  On  the  2d,  3d,  4th,  and  5th  instant, 
employed  in  convoying  vessels  between  Annapolis  and  Perryville.  On 
the  6th  [5th]  instant  at  8  a.  m.,  received  orders  from  General  Butler  to 
fit  out  an  expedition  to  go  in  search  of  the  Smith’s  Point  light-boat, 
said  to  be  in  Dividing  Creek,  between  the  Potomac  and  Rappahannock 
rivers.  Received  a  detachment  of  thirty  recruits  from  the  U.  S.  receiv¬ 
ing  ship  A  lleghany,  under  command  of  Lieutenant  Danels,  and  thirty  New 
York  State  Militia,  Lieutenant  Morton  commanding;  placed  them,  with  a 
fieldpiece,  on  board  the  Thomas  Sparks.  At  meridian  the  steamer  Thomas 
Sparks ,  Lieutenant  Watmough  commanding,  left  in  company  with  the 
William  B.  Reaney  with  a  launch  in  tow.  At  8:30  anchored  in  the 
mouth  of  the  Patuxent  River  on  account  of  bad  weather.  At  3  a.  m. 
eighty  stay  bolts  of  the  Reanexfs  boiler  blew  out,  scalding  James 
McDevitt,  landsman,  seriously.  I  discovered  that  the  accident  was 
occasioned  by  the  neglect  of  the  fireman,  who  left  his  post  and  turned 
in  without  waiting  for  the  second  engineer  to  relieve  him,  in  conse¬ 
quence  of  which  I  placed  them  both  on  board  the  Thomas  Sparks  under 
the  sentry’s  charge.  I  then  transferred  my  gun,  men,  and  launch  to 
the  Thomas  Sparks,  boarded  an  oyster  boat,  and  sent  a  bearer  of  dis¬ 
patches  to  General  Butler,  informing  him  of  the  accident  and  of  the 
disabled  condition  of  the  Reaney.  The  captain  of  the  oyster  boat 
informed  me  that  the  Smith’s  Point  light-boat  was  anchored  up  the 
Wicomico  River  [Ya.].  Owing  to  the  stormy  weather  we  were  obliged 
to  remain  at  anchor  until  2  a.  m.  the  following  morning.  The  wounded 


Not  found.

man  was  carefully  attended  to  by  Dr.  Gallagher,  who  volunteered  his 
services  for  the  expedition.  On  the  9th  [7th]  instant  at  2:30  p.  in. 
[a.  in.],  took  the  Thomas  Sparks  and  launch  and  ran  down  to  the 
Wicomico,  where  we  arrived  about  8  a.  m.  Our  pilot,  who  was  sup¬ 
plied  for  the  occasion,  proved  to  be  of  little  service  to  us,  and  we 
were  obliged  to  pilot  ourselves  in,  whereupon  we  discovered  a  light- 
boat  at  the  source  of  a  creek.  As  we  approached  her  the  lookout  at 
our  masthead  observed  her  crew  leaving  in  great  haste  with  their  boats; 
we  ran  up,  took  possession  of  her,  found  that  her  moorings  had 
been  slipped  and  that  her  light  apparatus  had  been  dismantled  and 
her  rudder  wedged  (she  proved  to  be  the  Windmill  Point  light-boat 
instead  of  the  Smith’s  Point  light-boat),  in  consequence  of  which  we 
found  it  necessary  to  tow  her  back  to  Annapolis,  and  owing  to  the 
crippled  condition  of  the  Heaney  was  obliged  to  forego  further  search. 
Hove  up  her  anchor  and  knocked  the  wedges  from  the  rudder  and  the 
Sparks  took  her  in  tow.  Afterwards  I  took  the  launch  to  reconnoiter 
and  discovered  a  number  of  armed  men,  horse  and  foot.  Returned  and 
made  the  launch  fast  to  the  light-boat  and  ran  up  to  the  mouth  of  the 
Patuxent  River  in  tow  of  the  Sparks.  At  9  p.  m.  the  Sparks  cast  off 
the  light-boat  and  ran  in  and  brought  out  the  Heaney  and  took  the 
liglit-boat  in  tow.  Ran  up  and  anchored  at  Annapolis  on  the  8th 
instant  at  5  a.  m.  and  turned  over  the  light-boat  and  public  books 
found  on  board  her  to  Colonel  Smith,  commanding  officer  of  the  station. 
I  found  by  the  log  of  the  light-boat  that  she  had  been  seized  by  three 
armed  vessels  under  the  command  of  the  colonel  of  Lancaster  County 
and  anchored  in  Indian  Creek,  there  to  await  the  orders  of  the  gov¬ 
ernor  of  Virginia.  Sent  Lieutenant  Panels  and  his  men  on  board  the 
Alleghany ,  Lieutenant  Morton  and  his  men  on  shore,  the  launch  to  her 
moorings,  and  landed  the  fieldpiece;  sent  the  fireman  and  second  engi¬ 
neer  to  the  guardhouse,  and  James  McDevitt  to  the  hospital.  At  3 
p.  m.  ran  over  to  Perryville  in  tow  of  the  Sparks,  where  we  arrived  at 
10:30  p.  m.  During  the  9th  we  remained  at  Perryville  according 
to  orders,  and  on  the  10th  instant  transferred  the  men  and  guns  to 
Philadelphia. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Peirce  Crosby, 

Lieutenant ,  TJ.  S.  Wavy. 

Commander  Charles  Steedman,  TJ.  S.  Havy. 


Abstract  Log  of  the  TJ.  S.  Ship  Constitution ,  April  21-May  9,  1861. 

April  21, 1861. — Harbor  of  Annapolis,  Md.  At  6  a.  m.  received  orders 
from  the  Superintendent. to  slip  and  get  the  ship  in  the  Roads  as  soon 
as  possible.  At  6:30  the  steamer  Maryland  from  Havre  de  Grace 
came  alongside  with  the  Eight  Regiment  of  the  Third  Brigade  Massa¬ 
chusetts  Volunteer  Militia  on  board  under  command  of  Brigadier- 
General  Butler.  Received  three  companies  on  board  from  her.  Slipped 
our  moorings  and  began  towing  out  by  the  Maryland.  At  11:30  got  in 
the  mud ;  cleared  and  got  as  far  as  Greenbury  Point  light,  when  we  took 
the  mud  again.  At  10  p.  m.  piped  down  to  wait  for  the  tide. 

April  22. — At  12:30  a.  m.  received  a  message  that  the  channel  out¬ 
side  of  us  would  probably  be  obstructed  that  night;  the  tide  falling 
rapidly  and  the  ship  setting  in  the  mud  in  the  left  bank  of  the  channel, 


United  States  Ship  Constitution.

called  all  hands  and  commenced  to  hedge  ship  ont  into  deep  water. 
A  heavy  squall  drove  us  into  the  mud  again.  Several  vessels  at  this 
time  appearing  in  the  offing,  we  went  to  general  quarters  and  prepared 
for  an  attack.  After  remaining  there  nearly  an  hour  we  commenced 
heaving  again.  At  4:30  the  steamer  Boston  with  the  Seventh  Regi- 
ment  Few  York  Volunteer  Militia  came  in.  About  the  same  time  a 
tug  from  Havre  de  Grace  came  alongside  and  towed  us  out  of  the 
Roads,  where  we  anchored.  At  7  p.  m.  steamer  Boston  disembarked 
her  troops  at  the  Academy  and  then  those  of  the  Maryland,  which  was 
aground. 

April  23. — At  10  a.  m.  a  steam  tug  hove  in  sight  with  a  mounted  gun 
forward;  beat  to  quarters,  and  as  she  came  up  her  commander  hailed 
us.  She  was  from  Philadelphia  and  went  in  the  harbor.  At  12:30 
p.  m.  the  steamer  Maryland  came  alongside ;  received  from  her  our  guns, 
that  had  been  placed  on  board  of  her  to  lighten  the  ship.  At  10  p.  in. 
five  steamers  arrived  from  Few  York  with  troops  convoyed  by  the 
Harriet  Lane. 

April  26. — Prom  8  to  meridian  got  underway  in  tow  of  the  steamer

April  29. — At  12:30  p.  m.  off  the  buoy  navy  yard,  Few  York. 

May  8. — At  0:30  a.  m.  got  underway  in  tow  of  two  steamers  and  at 
7  passed  through  Hell  Gate. 

May  9. — At  3  p.  m.  anchored  off  Fort  Adams,  [Fewport,  R.  I].  At 
5:15  the  steamer  Baltic  arrived  from  Annapolis,  Md.,  with  the  com¬ 
mandant  of  midshipmen,  O.  R.  P.  Rodgers,  professors,  and  attaches  of 
the  Academy.

The  following  order  was  issued,  through  the  adjutant-general,  to 
Major-General  William  B.  Taliaferro: 

You  will  forthwith  take  command  of  the  State  troops  which  are  now  or  may  he 
assembled  at  the  city  of  Norfolk.  Your  immediate  presence  there  is  necessary. 

The  governor  appointed  and  commissioned  the  following  officers  for 
the  State  navy : 

Robert  B.  Pegram,  captain,  to  rank  as  such  from  18th  of  April,  1861. 

George  T.  Sinclair,  captain,  to  rank  as  such  from  19th  of  April,  1861. 

Catesby  ap  It.  Jones,  captain,  to  rank  as  such  from  20th  of  April,  1861. 

James  H.  Rochelle,  lieutenant,  to  rank  as  such  from  the  18th  of  April,  1861. 

The  following  order  was  issued  to  Captain  Robert  B.  Pegram : 

Sir:  You  will  proceed  to  Norfolk  and  there  assume  control  of  the  naval  station 
with  authority  to  organize  naval  defenses,  enroll  and  enlist  seamen  and  marines, 
and  temporarily  to  appoint  warrant  officers,  and  do  and  perform  whatever  may  be 
necessary  to  preserve  and  protect  the  property  of  the  Commonwealth  and  of  the  citi¬ 
zens  of  Virginia. 

Cooperate  with  the  land  forces  under  the  command  of  Major-General  William  B. 
Taliaferro  and  report  all  importaut  acts  which  may  be  done  or  performed  under 
your  orders  promptly  to  the  executive  through  the  general  iu  command.

Letter  from  Messrs.  Peters  &  Peed  to  Captain  Herriman,  commanding 
schooner  A.  Colby,  transmitting  guarantee  of  safe  conduct  to  his  vessel. 


Portsmouth  [Va.],  April  23,  1861. 

Dear  Sir:  We  have  received  your  letter  of  to-day  with  the  letter 
for  Mr.  Churchill.  We  send  a  tug  to  bring  you  up,  and  also  a  guarantee 
of  safe  conduct  of  your  vessel  up  and  back  to  sea  without  molestation. 
There  can  be  no  possible  difficulty  with  you  or  your  vessel.  Were  it 
otherwise  we  need  not  say  we  would  at  once  instruct  you  to  proceed  to 
some  other  port.  We  trust  you  know  us  sufficiently  well  to  believe  that 
w'e  would  not  advise  you  to  any  course  that  could  possibly  bring  you 
into  difficulty.  You  will  see  that  the  guarantee  of  safe  conduct  is 
signed  by  the  commanders  in  chief  of  both  tbe  naval  and  military 
forces.  The  Harriet  Lane  was  towed  up  yesterday  under  a  like  guar¬ 
antee,  and  will  be  discharged  to-morrow.  We  hope  to  see  you  here 
to-morrow  evening  and  have  the  pleasure  of  handing  you  several  let¬ 
ters  we  have  for  you. 

Very  truly,  yours, 

Peters  &  Reed. 


Captain  Dearborn  Herriman. 


[Enclosure.] 

Naval  Station,  Norfolk,  April  22, 1861. 

We  hereby  guarantee  safe  conduct  to  the  schooner  A.  Colby,  laden 
with  sugar  and  molasses,  up  to  the  port  of  Norfolk  and  Portsmouth, 
and  the  safety  of  the  vessel  after  discharge  of  cargo  back  to  Hampton 
Roads  and  to  sea,  without  molestation  from  the  forces  under  my 
command. 

F.  Forrest, 

Commanding  Naval  Forces. 

Approved : 

Walter  G-wynn, 

Major-General ,  Commanding  Forces  in  Norfolk  Harbor.

Sir  :  You  will  proceed  with  the  steamer  Arrow  to  cruise  in  the  neigh¬ 
borhood  of  Craney  Island  and  observe  closely  the  enemy’s  skips  by

against  surprise. 

By  order: 

W.  F.  Lynch, 

Adjutant.

Order  of  Major-General  Lee ,  commanding  Virginia  forces ,  to  Colonel 
Talcott,  relative  to  the  fortification  of  James  River. 


Headquarters  Virginia  Forces, 

Richmond ,  Va.,  April  29,  1861. 

Sir:  You  will  proceed  up  James  Fiver  to  the  viciuity  of  Burwell’s 
Bay  and  select  the  most  suitable  point  which,  in  your  judgment,  should 
be  fortified  in  order  to  prevent  the  ascent  of  the  river  by  the  enemy. 
Lay  off  the  works  and  leave  their  construction  to  Lieutenant  C.  ap  R. 
Jones,  Virginia  navy,  who  will  accompany  you.  You  will  then  proceed 
to  the  mouth  of  the  Appomattox  and  there  perform  the  same  service, 
selecting  some  point  below  the  mouth  of  that  river,  supposed  to  be  old 
Fort  Powhatan.  Captain  Cocke  will  take  charge  of  the  construction 
of  this  work.  Be  pleased  to  give  the  above-mentioned  officers  such 
instructions  as  they  may  require  in  the  construction  of  these  works 
and  report  what  you  shall  have  done. 

Respectfully,  etc., 


E,  E.  Lee, 

Major-  General,  Commanding. 


Andrew  Talcott,  Esq., 

Colonel,  Engineers.

Instructions  from  Major-General  Lee ,  commanding  Virginia  forces ,  to 
Colonel  Taliaferro ,  commanding  at  Gloucester  Point ,  Fa.,  relative  to 
defense  of  that  place. 

Headquarters  Virginia  Forces, 

Richmond ,  Fa.,  May  8,  1861. 

Colonel:  In  reply  to  your  letter  of  the  Gth  instant,  asking  instruc¬ 
tions  as  to  the  course  to  be  pursued  in  the  event  of  an  attempt  on  the 
part  of  the  enemy  to  pass  the  battery  at  Gloucester  Point,  you  are 
directed,  on  the  approach  of  a  vessel  of  the  enemy  and  when  she  shall 
have  gotten  within  range,  to  lire  a  shot  across  her  bows.  Should  this 
not  deter  her  from  proceeding  on  you  will  fire  one  over  her,  and  if  she 
still  persist  you  will  fire  into  her.  Should  the  fire  be  returned  you 
will  capture  her  if  possible.  Similar  orders  have  been  issued  to  the 
naval  officer  commanding  battery. 

Respectfully,  etc., 


R.  E.  Lee, 

Major-  General ,  Commanding. 


Colonel  William  B.  Taliaferro, 

Commanding ,  etc .,  Gloucester  Point ,  Va. 


Report  of  Captain  Cabell ,  Virginia  forces ,  of  the  movements  of  United 
Stales  vessels  near  Gloucester  Point ,  Fa.,  and,  calling  attention  to 
importance  of  defending  that  place. 

Headquarters  Cabell’s  Battery, 

Gloucester  Point ,  May  10,  1861 — 9:30  a.  m. 
Sir:  Yesterday  about  1  o’clock  p.  m.  an  armed  steamer  approached 
our  battery,  coming  within  the  range  of  2  or  3  miles.  We  sprang  to 
our  guns  and  were  ready  for  action  as  soon  as  it  was  manifest  that  the 


OPERATIONS  ON  THE  ATLANTIC  COAST. 


407 


steamer  was  coining  up  the  river.  We  all  expected  an  attack,  but  sbe 
turned  and  proceeded  down  tbe  river  and  dropped  anchor  near  its 
mouth.  Another  ship  or  steamer  was  also  in  the  distance.  During  the 
night  there  was  a  vigilant  lookout.  This  morning  four  skips  or  steam¬ 
ers  passed  beyond  the  first  steamer,  proceeding  rapidly  from  north  to 
south.  About  8  o’clock  this  morning  the  attacking  steamer  weighed 
anchor  and  left  the  river.  You  can  draw  your  own  conclusions  as  well 
as  I  can  of  the  purpose  of  the  enemy. 

I  regard  this  point  as  next  in  importance  to  Fortress  Monroe.  I  hope 
I  may  say  that  1  am  acquainted  at  least  with  the  commercial  wants  of 
the  State.  It  is,  in  my  opinion,  invaluable,  both  for  military  defense 
and  the  commercial  necessities  of  the  State.  Let  its  importance  not  be 
underrated.  This  point  properly  secured  and  no  effectual  blockade  can 
continue,  no  ships  can  pass  up  York  River,  no  attack  can  be  made  on 
Richmond,  except  by  long  land  marches.  If  you  could  see  the  place 
you  would  be  satisfied  of  its  great  importance.  To  allow  it  to  be  lost 
would  be  a  fatal  error.  The  force  here,  consisting  entirely  of  volunteers, 
are  prepared  to  defend  it  to  the  last  extremity.  They  are  perfectly 
aware  of  the  strangeness  and  peril  of  their  situation,  but  though  ‘‘there 
is  plenty  of  danger,  there  is  no  fear.”  But  if  I  am  correct  in  regard  to 
the  importance  of  retaining  this  position,  though  the  necessities  of  the 
State  would  not  permit  more  men  to  be  sent  for  the  support  of  the  few 
here,  yet  that  force  should  be  promptly  sent  for  the  protection  of  the 
present  and  future  fortifications  here.  Blind  as  Lincoln  and  Cabinet 
appear  to  be,  they  must  see  the  importance  of  taking  this  place.  A 
land  attack  by  a  large  force  would  probably  do  this.  We  would  dispute 
every  inch  of  ground  with  them,  but  however  valiant  our  defense,  it 
would  not  repay  the  loss  of  this  place.  I  believe  it  can  be  easily 
defended  from  a  land  attack.  Access  from  our  rear  is  over  ground 
perfectly  level  and  mostly  open.  The  enemy  must  march  through  a 
space  not  over  a  mile  or  mile  and  a  half  wide.  Defend  this  by  a  rude 
fort  of  logs  even  and  it  would  greatly  contribute  to  our  defense.  It 
will  require  a  much  larger  force  to  do  this.  But  the  plateau  iu  the  rear 
of  this  is  the  most  beautiful  as  well  as  extensive  field  for  drill  I  have 
ever  seen.  A  brigade  could  well  maneuver  upon  it.  Send  down,  there¬ 
fore,  some  of  your  raw  troops  of  infantry  and  let  a  school  of  instruction 
be  placed  here. 

The  Federal  troops  may  land  below,  but  they  must  pass  through  the 
level  interval  or  over  Sarah’s  Creek.  They  can  not  pass  Sarah’s  Creek 
without  boats  and  its  defense  is  very  easy.  I  have  not  time  to  say  more. 

Please  submit  this  to  General  Lee  and  the  governor  and  council. 
Let  the  public  not  hear  of  it  till  the  plan  is  executed. 

Excuse  haste  and  the  excitement  of  a  camp  life  and  the  errors  of 
composition  produced  by  constant  interruptions  and  camp  tables. 

Respectfully,  yours, 

H.  C.  Cabell, 

Captain ,  etc. 

Colonel  J.  B.  Magrtjder.

Report  of  Colonel  Taliaferro,  Virginia  forces,  commanding  at  Gloucester 

Point,  Va.,  of  the  movements  of  United  States  vessels  near  that  place. 

Headquarters  Gloucester  Point,  May  14, 1861. 

Colonel:  *  *  *  An  armed  vessel  of  the  United  States  steamed 
into  York  River  yesterday  and  approached  within  some  3  miles  of  our 
works.  She  did  not,  however,  venture  to  approach  nearer,  but  seemed 
to  be  engaged  in  sounding  the  channel  at  the  mouth  of  the  river.  No 
boats  were  sent  out  from  her  and  no  attempt  made  to  land  troops. 
Other  steamers  of  the  enemy  have  been  observed  in  Mobjack  Bay  and 
just  without  the  mouth  of  York  River. 

Our  water  battery  is  now  armed  with  three  9-inch  guns,  and  the  men 
have  been  constantly  instructed  in  the  working  of  the  guns  by  Captain 
T.  J.  Page,  of  the  Navy. 

Should  the  enemy  land  in  force  on  this  side  of  York  River,  either  on 
the  York  or  the  waters  of  Severn,  it  would  be  necessary  to  resist  them 
with  a  much  larger  force  of  infantry  than  that  now  at  this  post. 

*  *  *  #  *  #  # 
Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

W.  B.  Taliaferro, 

Colonel,  Commanding  Post. 

Lieutenant-Colonel  R.  S.  Garnett, 

Adjutant-  General.

Strictly  confidential.]  Navy  Yaed,  Washington,  January  8 , 1861. 

Sir:  Various  rumors  are  in  circulation  that  a  mob  will  attempt  to 
possess  themselves  of  this  yard  between  this  and  the  4th  of  March 
next  for  the  purpose  of  securing  the  arms  and  ammunition  now  in  the 
armory  and  magazine,  to  be  used  in  preventing  the  inauguration  of  Mr. 
Lincoln,  the  President-elect.  You  will  therefore  prepare  for  the  defense 
of  the  yard  all  the  howitzers  now  available  in  the  Ordnance  Depart¬ 
ment  with  as  much  secrecy  as  possible;  this  yard  shall  not  be  surren¬ 
dered  to  any  person  or  persons  except  by  an  order  from  the  honorable 
Secretary  of  the  Navy,  and  in  the  event  of  an  attack  I  shall  require 
all  officers  and  others  under  my  command  to  defend  it  to  the  last 
extremity,  and  should  we  be  overpowered  by  numbers  the  armory  and 
magazine  must  be  blown  up.  You  will  therefore  make  all  necessary 
arrangements  for  the  execution  of  this  order  and  submit  to  me  the  plan 
you  propose.  At  the  proper  time  the  officers  will  be  designated  by  me 
to  apply  the  match.  Precautionary  arrangements  will  be  made  in  time 
to  prevent  the  seizure  of  the  main  magazine  up  the  river.  You  will 
make  to  me  such  suggestions  to  carry  out  these  arrangements  as  your 
judgment  may  dictate. 

Kespectfully,  etc., 

Frankn.  Buchanan, 

Commandant. 

Commander  Dahlgren, 

Ordnance  Department. 


Ordnance  Department, 

Washington,  January  14,  1861. 

Sir:  Your  letter  of  the  8tli,  marked  “strictly  confidential,”  was 
received  on  the  11th  instant  and  has  received  my  careful  consideration. 

In  compliance  with  the  directions  therein  contained  to  make  sug¬ 
gestions  in  relation  to  the  defense  of  the  yard  against  the  anticipated 
attack  of  a  mob,  I  have  to  remark  that  it  is  merely  a  collection  of 
buildings  open  to  the  water  on  nearly  one-half  of  its  outline,  and  on 
the  land  side  enclosed  by  a  wall,  easy  of  escalade;  it  could  only  be 
held  with  certainty  in  its  whole  extent  by  occupying  it  in  force,  with 
detachments  in  every  building.  The  northwest  angle  is  entirely  open 
to  attack,  as  nothing  but  a  slight  board  fence  is  erected,  and  just  here 
are  the  most  important  objects  to  defend — light  cannon,  rifles,  and 
ammunition. 

As  the  ordnance  buildings  have  been  built  without  reference  to  any 
defense,  they,  like  all  the  buildings  of  the  yard,  will  require  more  men. 
I  think  200  men  would  make  good  the  defense  of  the  department  and 
500  or  600  men  the  rest  of  the  yard. 


412  OPERATIONS  ON  THE  POTOMAC  AND  RAPPAHANNOCK. 


It  may  not  be  easy  to  procure  tliis  force,  and  lienee  such  as  can  be 
had  should  be  concentrated  as  much  as  possible  on  the  most  important 
points. 

To  this  end  I  have  nearly  completed  the  withdrawal  from  the  yard 
magazine  of  the  ammunition  thereto  the  attic  of  the  main  buildings, 
which  also  contains  the  cannon  and  rifles,  of  which  there  are  available, 
howitzers,  five  12-pounder  smooth,  three  12-pounder  rifled,  and  about 
800  muskets  and  rifles.  I  would  suggest,  therefore — 

1.  Withdrawal  from  general  magazine  of  all  the  powder  and  trans¬ 
ferred  to  Fort  Washington,  the  magazine  being  too  far  from  the  yard 
and  not  easy  of  defense. 

2.  Patrol,  by  day  and  night,  about  the  northwest  angle,  by  marines. 
A  few  of  the  trusty  ordinary  men  to  sleep  in  the  main  ordnance 
building. 

3.  Require  200  able  seamen  from  the  receiving  ships  to  man  the  how¬ 
itzers  and  handle  the  rifles.  I  have  the  means  of  drilling  them ;  they 
can  be  messed  and  lodged  in  the  yard. 

4.  In  the  event  of  an  actual  attack  by  a  mob,  volunteers  can  be  had 
from  the  mechanics,  which  1  can  arm. 

5.  The  marines  at  the  headquarters  should  secure  the  streets  leading 
to  the  yard,  using  a  night  patrol;  if  forced  back  they  should  retire 
upon  the  yard  and  not  on  their  barracks.  There  is  much  of  detail  that 
can  be  arranged  at  the  time  and  which  I  therefore  omit  now. 

I  am,  most  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

John  A.  Dahlgren, 

Commander. 

Captain  Bitch anan, 

Commandant. 


Ordnance  Office,  U.  S.  Navy  Yard, 

Washington ,  January  23,  1861. 

Sir  :  In  furtherance  of  your  instructions,  I  have  caused  to  be  removed 
the  contents  of  the  yard  magazine  to  the  attic  of  the  main  building, 
together  with  the  best  arms  in  the  armory,  so  they  can  not  be  reached 
by  force  until  the  defense  of  the  building  is  overpowered.  The  oper¬ 
ation  has  been  conducted  secretly  by  two  trusty  men  at  dinner  hours 
when  the  other  men  are  absent,  and  I  believe  the  knowledge  is 
limited  to  them  and  the  two  clerks.  Whatever  small  amount  of  ammu¬ 
nition  may  accumulate  from  the  product  of  the  laboratory  can  easily 
be  wetted  at  short  notice,  which  is  better  than  firing  it,  as  the  explo¬ 
sion  might  damage  the  defense  of  the  main  building,  which  is  very 
near  it. 

I  now  only  need  about  100  good  men  (prefer  seamen)  to  hold  this 
building,  but  they  should  have  some  drill. 

Whenever  you  direct  me  to  lay  communications  for  blowing  up  the 
main  magazine  I  shall  begin  to  do  so,  though  the  distance  from  the 
yard  will  render  the  success  very  doubtful. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Jno.  A.  Dahlgren, 

Commander. 

Captain  F.  Buchanan, 

Commandant.

General  Order: 


U.  S.  Navy  Yard, 
Washington ,  February  1 ,  1861. 


In  the  event  of  an  attack  upon  this  navy  yard  by  a  mob,  the  follow¬ 
ing  order  will  be  observed  by  the  officers  and  employes  connected 
with  it: 

The  main  entrance  to  the  yard  will  be  defended  by  Lieutenant  II.  H. 
Lewis,  in  charge  of  a  12-pounder  howitzer  and  the  marine  guard. 

The  east  entrance  will  be  defended  by  Lieutenant  Simms,  in  charge  of 
a  12-pounder  howitzer. 

The  west  entrance  will  be  defended  by  Lieutenant  Russell,  in  charge 
of  a  12-pounder  howitzer. 

Three  howitzers,  under  command  of  Lieutenants  Wainwright  and 
Nelson  and  Gunner  Clapham  wdl  defend  the  ordnance  buildings  and 
west  side  of  the  yard,  all  under  command  of  Commander  Dahlgren. 

Lieutenant  Commanding  Fillebrown,  with  the  howitzer  of  the  Ana- 
costia ,  assisted  by  Carpenter  Rainbow  and  Boatswain  Willmuth,  each 
in  charge  of  a  howitzer  will  defend  the  lower  part  of  the  yard. 

The  marines  and  howitzers  will  be  concentrated  as  necessary  at  any 
point  where  their  services  may  be  required. 

Commander  McBlair  will  see  this  order  executed  and  superintend 
generally,  under  my  directions,  the  defense  of  the  yard. 

Frankn.  Buchanan, 

Commandant.

Report  of  Commander  Dahlgren ,  TJ.  S.  Navy ,  in  charge  Ordnance  Depart¬ 
ment ,  navy  yard ,  Washington ,  relating  to  the  decreased  force  in  that 
department. 

Ordnance  Office,  II.  S.  Navy  Yard, 

Washington ,  April  15 , 1861. 

Sir:  There  are  twenty-six  persons  in  this  department  absent  this 
morning.  I  understand  that  this  arises  from  the  most  of  them,  if  not 
all,  having  been  mustered  into  military  service. 

It  is  with  no  little  difficulty  that  I  have  been  able  hitherto  to  supply 
with  howitzers,  etc.,  the  current  wants  of  the  service;  and  the  with¬ 
drawal  of  so  many  of  the  best  hands  at  this  time,  when  I  am  actually 
preparing  to  increase  the  number  in  order  to  meet  contingencies,  will 
be  almost  equivalent  to  a  suspension  of  the  work.

I 

It  will  therefore  be  necessary  to  excuse  from  military  duty  all  the 
men  employed  in  this  department  who  may  prefer  this  duty  if  the 
usual  supplies  for  our  ships  of  war  are  to  be  furnished,  and  in  this 
respect  1  would  request  prompt  action. 

I  remain,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Jno.  A.  Dahlgren, 

Commander,  in  charge  of  Ordnance  Department  in  Yard. 

Captain  Franklin  Buchanan, 

Commandant  U.  S.  Navy  Yard ,  Washington.

Report  of  commandant  navy  yard,  Washington,  regarding  cause  of  delay  in 

work  of  Ordnance  Department. 

Commandant’s  Office,  Navy  Yard, 

Washington,  April  19,  1861. 

SIR:  I  beg  leave  to  call  your  attention  to  the  communication  I  laid 
before  you  a  day  or  two  since  in  reference  to  the  mechanics  of  this  yard 
serving  in  the  Army.  Very  important  work  is  delayed  in  consequence, 
particularly  in  the  Ordnance  Department.  An  act  of  Congress  dated 
September  30,  1850,  prohibits  a  person  from  receiving  the  pay  for  per¬ 
forming  two  duties  for  the  Government,  conspquenily  I  can  not  pay  the 
men  as  mechanics  while  they  receive  their  pay  as  soldiers. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Frankn,  Buchanan, 

Commandant. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy.

Report  of  acting  commandant  navy  yard,  Washington ,  regarding  equip¬ 
ment  of  vessels  for  tear  service. 

U.  S.  Navy  Yard,  Washington,  April  22, 1861. 

Sir:  In  the  absence  of  the  commandant  of  the  yard,  I  have  to  report 
to  you  that  I  have  prepared  the  steamer  Mount  Vernon  for  service  to 
receive  your  orders,  so  far  as  the  following  extends:  A  32-pounder  with 
appliances;  a  breech-loading  rifle  for  each  hand  on  board;  a  pilot,  six 
hands,  seamen  to  operate  the  gun. 

I  have  also  directed  Boatswain  Willmuth  to  be  ready  to  take  the 
command  of  the  vessel  in  case  the  Department  has  made  no  other 
arrangements. 

There  is  wanted  an  assistant  pilot,  a  corporal’s  guard  of  United 
States  troops  or  marines,  and  about  six  more  men  for  guard  duty  and 
defense. 

One  of  the  greatest  difficulties  will  be  to  procure  pilots.  Several 
have  already  declined,  therefore  very  liberal  compensation  is  necessary, 
and  I  have  offered  the  pilot  of  the  Mount  Vernon  $85  per  month,  Which 
is  better  than  he  can  get  from  any  other  party  and  contents  him  per¬ 
fectly. 

There  are  provisions  for  ten  days  for  50  men;  water  for  the  same 
period. 

The  deficiencies  of  tbe  yard  in  many  respects  are  so  great  that  I 
shall  be  obliged  to  supply  them  as  quickly  as  possible. 

I  am  not  yet  informed  whether  the  men  in  the  yard  are  released 
from  militia  duty.  It  is  absolutely  necessary  to  the  equipment  of  these 
steamers  and  to  the  defense  of  the  yard  that  this  should  be  done  at 
once. 

As  soon  as  I  learn  that  the  resignation  of  Captain  Buchanan  has 
taken  place  I  shall  lose  no  time  in  putting  the  yard  into  tbe  best  state 
of  defense  that  the  time  and  means  permit. 

I  shall  be  glad  to  have  your  full  directions  for  the  steamer  and  will 
proceed  to  get  ready  the  other  three. 

1  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Jno.  A,  Dahlgren, 

Acting  Commandant  of  Yard. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy.

Report  of  Commander  Gillis ,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  TJ.  S.  S.  Pocahontas , 
of  the  cruise  of  that  vessel  from  New  Yorlc  to  Washington. 

U.  S.  S.  Pocahontas, 

Potomac  River ,  April  22,  1861. 

Sir  :  In  compliance  with  your  order,  through  Commandant  Breese, 
received  at  navy  yard,  New  Y^ork,  forenoon  of  the  19th  instant,  we 
hastened  some  repairs  of  damages  from  stress  of  weather  at  sea  during 
the  time  we  were  coaling  ship  and  left  evening  of  same  day  for  port  of 
destination. 

Not  findiug  a  pilot  off  or  in  the  Chesapeake  I  proceeded  on  up  the 
bay  by  soundings  and  bearings  of  lights  until  3  o’clock  a.  m.  Sunday 
morning.  After  anchoring  for  three  or  four  hours  in  the  hope  of  seeing 
or  hearing  of  the  steamer  Baltic  we  got  underway,  stood  on,  and 
entered  the  Potomac  River.  No  pilots  to  be  procured.  Anchored  at 
dark  and  again  this  morning  continued  up  the  river.  I  hove  to  a 
schooner  about  70  miles  from  Alexandria,  bound  to  Boston,  and  com¬ 
pelled  her  master  to  come  on  board  this  vessel  as  pilot.  We  will  reach 
the  arsenal  or  navy  yard  at  Washington  this  afternoon  and  I  will  report 
m  person  as  directed. 

I  forward  herewith  passed  Assistant  Surgeon  Kitchen’s  report  of  the 
decease  of  Jacob  Newhouse  (seaman). 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  sir,  your  obedient  servant, 

Jno.  P.  Gillis, 
Commander ,  U.  S.  Navy. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy,  Washington,  P.  C.

Report  of  Commander  Ward,  U.  S.  Navy ,  commanding  U.  S.  ship  North 
Carolina ,  regarding  proposed  u flying  flotilla"1"1  for  duty  in  the  Chesa¬ 
peake  Bay  and  its  tributaries. 


G.  S.  Beceiving-  Ship  North  Carolina,  April  22, 1861. 

Sir  :  I  have  the  honor  to  press  upon  your  attention  an  organization 
I  propose  of  a  flying  flotilla,  to  he  composed  of  one  larger  and  two 
smaller  steamers  and  three  light-draft  schooners,  the  larger  steamer  to 
be  commanded  by  myself  (in  charge  also  of  the  whole),  the  two  smaller 
by  Lieutenant  D.  L.  Braine,  G.  S.  Navy,  and  Mr.  Budd,  now  a  master 
in  the  G.  S.  Coast  Survey,  the  whole  to  draw  (loaded)  but  7  feet  of 
water;  to  carry  a  sufficient  armament,  and  the  steamers  to  be  very  fast. 
Every  arrangement  exists  for  immediately  chartering  and  speedily 
equipping  the  light  flying  force  with  a  view  to  service  in  the  Chesa¬ 
peake  and  its  tributaries;  to  interrupt  the  enemy’s  communications; 
assuredly  keep  open  our  own;  drive  from  those  waters  every  hostile 
bottom;  threaten  all  the  points  of  a  shore  line  accessible  to  such  a 
force  exceeding  1,000  miles  in  extent;  protect  loyal  citizens;  convoy, 
tow,  transport  troops  or  intelligence  with  dispatch ;  be  generally  useful ; 
threaten  at  all  points,  and  to  attack  at  any  desired  or  important  one. 

For  the  particulars  I  refer  you  to  Master  W.  Budd,  G.  S.  Coast  Sur¬ 
vey,  bearer  of  this,  who  is  in  full  possession  of  the  details. 

Very  respectfully, 

J.  H.  Ward, 

Commander . 


Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy ,  Washington ,  D.  C.

Report  of  commandant  navy  yard,  Washington,  of  the  departure  from  that 
station  of  steamer  Mount  Vernon,  and  regarding  measures  for  the 
defense  of  the  yard. 

Navy  Yard,  Washington,  April  23,  1861. 
Sir  :  Conformably  with  your  orders,*  the  Mount  Vernon  left  this  yard 
about  midnight.  A  32-pounder  was  mounted  forward  and  a  comple¬ 
ment  of  breech  loading  rifles  for  the  crew  were  put  on  board.  Having 
no  commissioned  officer  to  spare,  Boatswain  Willmnth  was  intrusted 
with  the  command.  Gunner  Ellis  volunteered  and  also  went.  Besides 
the  pilot.,  engineer,  firemen,  etc.,  there  were  four  marines  and  ten  men 
of  the  Ordnance  Department  sent. 

These  could  illy  be  spared  from  the  defense  of  the  yard,  but  I  had  no 
alternative,  for  the  captain  of  the  volunteer  Company  A,  Washington 
infantry,  declined  to  detail  any  of  his  men  for  this  service;  and  they 
refused  to  volunteer,  the  duty  being  out  of  the  District,  and  some  of 
the  men  considered  the  boat  unsafe  or  that  the  gun  might  burst. 

Mr.  Willmnth  was  instructed  in  writing  as  directed  by  your  order. 
I  also  told  him  to  communicate  with  Fort  Washington  and  ascertain  if 
anything  was  needed. 

A  number  of  the  people  at  work  in  the  yard  left  yesterday.  The 
force  for  the  defense  of  the  yard  last  night  consisted  [of] :

* 

This  yard  is  of  importance,  not  only  because  of  its  furnishing  the 
Navy  so  largely  with  naval  stores,  but  also  as  a  position  in  the  general 
defense  of  the  city.  Near  it  is  a  bridge  easily  reached  and  passed 
whenever  an  attack  may  be  conducted  by  crossing  from  Alexandria, 
then  over  the  low  heights  opposite  the  yard. 

I  sent  a  howitzer  with  ten  men  and  a  howitzer  and  corporal’s  guard 
of  marines  to  guard  this  bridge  and  found  there  four  dragoons. 

The  companies  were  distributed  along  the  borders  of  the  yard,  which 
were  also  patrolled  by  a  strong  body  of  marines.  Cannon  were  planted 
looking  down  the  stream,  as  well  as  several  howitzers.  In  fact,  the 
whole  "force  was  on  the  alert  for  any  contingency. 

The  Pocahontas  arrived  last  night  and  on  receiving  a  pilot  came  up 
and  anchored  off  the  yard,  as  you  are  already  aware  from  my  directing 
the  officer  with  Captain  Gillis’s  reports  to  deliver  them  to  you  in  person. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  most  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Jno.  A.  Dahlgren. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy. 


Report  of  Lieutenant  Fillebrown ,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Ana- 
costia,  regarding  a  reconnoissance  of  the  Potomac  River. 

U.  S.  S.  Anacostia,  April  23,  1861. 

Sir  :  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that  up  to  the  present  time  there  have 
been  no  obstructions  placed  in  the  channel  of  this  river  to  impede  navi¬ 
gation,  neither  can  I  discover  any  semblance  of  batteries  or  earthworks 
in  the  course  of  erection  on  either  bank  of  the  Potomac  between  the 
Lower  Cedar  Point  and  this  place.  Very  particular  attention  has  been 
paid  to  these  matters. 

The  steamer  George  Page  lies  moored  at  the  railroad  terminus  at 
Aquia  Creek.  As  there  is  not  sufficient  water  for  this  vessel  to  approach 
near  enough,  I  can  not  say  if  there  have  been  any  defenses  erected  there 
or  not. 

Yesterday,  at  the  request  of  Major  [J.  A.]  Haskin,  the  commander 
of  Port  Washington,  I  took  the  steamer  Jerome  alongside  and  convoyed 
her  to  the  Washington  Arsenal.  There  were  reasons  to  suppose  that 
she  would  be  detained  at  Alexandria.  She  had  on  freight — 144  barrels 
of  gunpowder  and  other  stores  for  the  Government.  I  also  convoyed 
a  large  schooner  laden  with  cement  and  other  matter  for  the  United 
States  Capitol. 

I  beg  leave  to  represent  that  I  have  no  pilot  that  can  carry  me  below 
the  Lower  Cedar  Point,  my  regular  pilot  having  been  transferred  to  the 
U.  S.  S.  Pawnee  for  special  and  particular  service. 

In  conclusion,  I  beg  leave  most  respectfully  to  request  that  at  least 
one  other  responsible  officer  be  ordered  to  this  vessel,  as  the  constant 
and  unremitting  attention  that  is  necessary  to  the  proper  execution  of 
my  orders  is  more  than  nature  will  stand.  I  have  not  laid  myself  down 
since  Thursday  night. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Tpios.  Scott  Fillebrown, 

Lieutenant ,  Commanding. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy.

Order  of  the  Secretary  of  the  Navy  to  Commander  Gillis ,  U.  S.  Navy , 
commanding  U.  S.  S.  Pocahontas ,  regarding  convoy  duty  in  the  Potomac 
River. 

Confidential.]  Navy  Department,  April  23 , 1861. 

Sir  :  When  your  ship  is  ready  for  service,  proceed  as  early  as  practi 
cable,  having  the  tide  m  view,  and  anchor  somewhere  a  short  distance 
below  the  White  House,  as  you  were  directed  by  my  dispatch  of  the 
22d,  and  await  the  arrival  of  troops  that  are  coming  up  the  Potomac. 

Should  they  not  arrive  before  the  steamer  Pawnee  shall  join  you,  then 
together  you  will  proceed  down  the  river  until  the  expected  transports 
shall  be  met,  not  going  so  far  in  the  bay  as  to  miss  seeing  them  in  their 
passage.  When  met,  convoy  them  to  any  convenient  point  of  landing 
so  that  they  may  reach  the  capital. 

Be  at  quarters  at  any  point  where  a  battery  may  open  and  do  your 
best  in  the  performance  of  the  duty  assigned. 

If  the  troops  do  not  appear  in  three  days  return  to  your  anchorage. 

I  am,  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant. 

Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  Navy. 

Commander  John  P.  Gillis, 

U.  S.  S.  Pocahontas.

Report  of  commandant  navy  yard ,  Washington ,  regarding  force  of  marines 

at  the  yard. 

Commandant’s  Office,  Navy  Tard, 

Washington,  April  24,  1861. 

Sir:  The  Colonel  Commandant  of  the  Marine  Corps  did  me  the  honor 
to  call  at  this  office  this  morning  in  order  to  confer  upon  measures  taken 
in  regard  to  certain  detachments  of  marines  which  I  had  detained  in 
the  yard.  I  did  this  under  the  supposition  that  I  was  authorized  so  to 
do  by  a  verbal  order  from  Commodore  Paulding.  I  learn,  however, 
from  Colonel  Harris  that  I  was  mistaken  and  that  Commodore  Pauld¬ 
ing  did  not  intend  to  give  any  such  permission. 

I  regret  having  made  this  mistake  and  lose  no  time  in  correcting  it 
by  returning  at  once  to  headquarters  the  marines  so  detained.  This 
will,  of  course,  leave  me  with  some  forty  marines,  which  will  be  totally 
inadequate  for  the  defense  of  the  yard.  Colonel  Harris  made  certain 
proposals  to  me  in  regard  to  the  disposition  of  the  guard  which  are  on 
duty  in  the  yard,  which  I  could  not  concur  with.  As  a  consequence  I 
shall  have  but  forty  marines  in  the  yard  for  its  defense. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Jno.  A.  Dahlgren. 

[Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy.}

Boatswain  Willmuth,  U.  S.  Navy ,  steamer  Mount  Vernon,  regarding 
cruise  of  that  vessel. 

Navy  Yard,  Washington,  April  25,  [1861] — 9  a.  m. 
Captain  Dahlgren  has  the  honor  to  acquaint  the  honorable  Secretary 
of  the  Navy  with  the  arrival  of  the  Mount  Vernon,  which  reports  the 
river  open  as  far  as  Cedar  Point,  the  extent  of  his  trip.  No  signs  of 
batteries  on  the  banks. 

Enclosed  is  a  copy  of  Boatswain  [George]  Willmuth’s  minutes. 

[John  A.  Dai-ilgren, 

Commandant .] 

[Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy.  \ 

[Enclosure.] 

U.  S.  S.  Mount  Yernon,  April  22, 1861. 
At  11 :  30  left  the  wharf  at  navy  yard.  In  winding  steamer  our  stem 
struck  the  wharf,  damaging  rudder;  proceeded  down  river.  At  1:30 
a.  m.  made  fast  to  wharf  at  Fort  Washington.  At  G:30  a.  m.  left  the 
wharf  and  steamed  down  the  river.  At  9  a.  m.  fell  in  with  U.  S. 
steamers  Pawnee,  Keystone  State ,  and  Anacostia,  under  command  of 
Commodore  Paulding.  Boarded  Keystone  State  and  reported.  Returned 

on  board  and  steamed  down  river.  At  12:30  p.  m.  came  to  anchor - 

miles  from  Lower  Cedar  Point  light-ship,  light-sliii)  bearing  N.  E.  by  E. 
by  compass.  Shortly  after  coming  to,  saw  smoke  in  direction  of  light¬ 
ship.  In  a  short  tune  saw  a  boat  with  twenty  men  leave  the  light  ship. 
Shortly  after  the  boat  left  discovered  light  ship  on  fire.  Fired  ten 
rounds  from  muskets  to  bring  boat  to;  boat  took  no  notice  of  the 
musketry;  fired  a  shell  across  his  bow,  but  they  proceeded  on  and 
effected  a  landing.  Meantime  steamer  James  Guy,  maneuvering  in  a 
suspicious  manner  and  communicating  with  the  shore,  steamed  along¬ 
side  and  hailed  her;  having  lady  passengers  on  board,  allowed  her  to 
proceed.  We  then  returned  to  light  ship,  lowered  a  boat  and  went 
alongside,  but  finding  her  a  perfect  wreck,  returned  to  steamer  and 
proceeded  to  Fort  Washington.  Commander  of  fort  expecting  an 
attack,  concluded  to  remain  all  night.  During  the  night,  steamer  leak¬ 
ing  badly,  kept  the  watch  at  the  pumps  all  night.  At  5  a.  m.  lit  fires, 
ready  for  a  start.  At  7 : 30  a.  m.  (J.  S.  S.  Anacostia  hove  in  sight.  At 
8:20  boarded  Anacostia  and  received  orders  from  captain  of  Anacostia 
to  proceed  down  the  river.  Followed  instructions,  and  scrutinizing 
the  shore  ou  both  sides  saw  no  signs  of  batteries.  At  11  a.  m.  passed 


426  OPERATIONS  ON  THE  POTOMAC  AND  RAPPAHANNOCK, 


wreck  of  Lower  Cedar  Point  light- ship;  proceeded  on;  ascertained  that 
buoys  had  not  been  removed.  At  12:30  turned  the  steamer’s  head  up 
river.  At  2: 30  mustered  the  crew  for  drill  and  small  arm  exercise,  also 
target  exercise.  At  3  p.  m.  beat  the  retreat.  At  5 : 30  p.  m.  made  fast 
to  wharf  at  Fort  Washington.  Steamer  still  leaking  badly.  At  11 :30 
p.  m.  boarded  a  suspicious  schooner,  but  found  her  to  be  coal  loaded 
and  twenty-five  passengers  on  board,  bound  for  Philadelphia.  Allowed 
her  to  proceed.  At  5  a.  m.  started  fires.  At  7  a.  m.  cast  off'  from  wharf 
and  steamed  up  river.  At  7 : 30  passed  the  IT.  S.  S.  Pocahontas ;  gave 
her  instructions  concerning  light  ship,  buoys,  etc.  At  8:  30  a.  m.  made 
fast  alongside  U.  S.  S.  Powhatan.

Report  of  Commander  Gillis ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Pocahon¬ 
tas ,  regarding  the  movements  of  that  vessel  in  the  Potomac  River  and 
Chesapeake  Bay. 

U.  S.  S.  Pocahontas, 

Off  the  Mouth  of  Potomac ,  April  26 ,  1861. 
Sir:  On  receipt  of  your  order  on  the  evening  of  the  24tli  we  left  in 
thirty  minutes  the  navy  yard,  Washington,  and  owing  to  the  stupidity 
of  the  pilot  (whom  1  had  cautioned  before  leaving)  grounded  hard  oppo¬ 
site  the  arsenal.  I  sent  to  commandant  of  navy  yard,  requesting  the 
Powhatan  sent  to  our  assistance  by  high  tide  on  the  following  morning, 
having  used  all  exertions  with  our  crew,  which  had  been  hard  worked 
since  4  o’clock  a.  m.  of  same  day.  With  the  assistance  of  the  Powhatan 
at  G  a.  m.  25tli  we  got  afloat  and  proceeded  down  the  river,  closely 
observing  its  banks;  no  offensive  demonstrations  were  seen.  Light- 
boats  on  the  river  P.  [ Potomac J  and  at  Smith’s  Point  taken  away;  a 
number  of  the  buoys  gone. 

Got  underway  at  daylight  (26th)  and  ran  down  the  Chesapeake  Bay 
to  opposite  Windmill  Point,  where  we  boarded  the  ship  Martha  Whit¬ 
more ,  from  Baltimore,  bound  to  Liverpool.  Her  master  informed  me 
that  three  large  sea  steamers  and  a  brig  of  war  in  tow  were  at  anchor 
off  the  Potomac  yesterday  (25th)  at  noon;  that  they  contained  troops 
and  passed  on  up  toward  Annapolis.  A  large  sea  steamer  passed  down 
the  bay  on  the  24th ;  another  yesterday  about  3  p.  in. 

Upon  receiving  this  information  I  immediately  stood  up  the  Chesa¬ 
peake,  intending  to  proceed  as  far  as  Annapolis,  trusting  to  your 
approval  of  my  course,  believing  it  the  desire  of  the  Government  to 
have  the  troops  brought  to  Washington  by  way  of  the  Potomac  River. 

At  meridian,  26th,  received  your  order  of  the  25th  by  Lieutenant 
Sproston,  of  Powhatan,  as  we  were  passing  the  Potomac,  and  to  fulfill 
the  spirit  of  your  instructions  will  proceed  to  Annapolis  to  communi¬ 
cate  with  the  commanding  officer  of  the  troops  if  there. 

I  am,  respectfully,  sir,  your  obedient  servant, 

Jno.  P.  Gillis, 
Commander,  U.  S.  Navy. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy,  Washington,  D.  C.

Report  of  Lieutenant  Fillebrown ,  TJ.  8.  Navy ,  commanding  TJ.  8.  8. 
Anacostia ,  o/  f/ie  cruise  of  that  vessel  in  the  Potomac  River. 

U.  S.  S.  Anacostia, 

Washington ,  April  26 ,  1<9W. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that  yesterday  afternoon  I  proceeded 
down  the  Potomac  under  slow  steam  as  far  as  Occoquan,  keeping  a 
strict  lookout  to  both  sides  of  the  river.  I  could  not  discover  that  any 
earthworks  were  being  thrown  up  or  batteries  erected,  neither  could  I 
detect  any  suspicious  movements  on  the  part  of  vessels  or  persons  on 
shore. 

This  morning  at  daylight  I  proceeded  down  to  about  5  miles  below 
Maryland  Point  (50  miles  from  this)  without  discovering  anything  to 
attract  my  attention,  except  that  on  passing  Aquia  Creek  I  noticed 
that  the  steamer  George  Page  had  left  her  moorings  at  the  wharf.  My 
impression  is  that  she  has  proceeded  up  the  creek  to  avoid  seizure. 

On  my  return  I  dispatched  a  reliable  person  to  the  White  House 
Bluff  to  ascertain  if  any  fortifications  were  in  progress  at  that  point. 
After  a  careful  reconuoissance  he  reports  none  whatever.  A  battery 
on  this  point  would  command  the  approach  to  it  for  more  than  3  miles, 
and  vessels  of  more  than  12  feet  draft  can  not  pass  more  than  three- 
eighths  of  a  mile  from  it.  The  deepest  water  is  near  the  bluff. 

On  passing  Fort  Washington  I  have  deemed  it  advisable  to  commu¬ 
nicate  with  the  commander  thereof  with  the  view  of  conveying  such 
dispatches  or  information  as  he  may  wish  to  transmit  to  the  Govern¬ 
ment. 

On  passing  Glymont  I  was  boarded  by  Captain  [D.]  Pierson,  of  the 
schooner  John  McAdam ,  of  St.  George,  Me.,  who  claimed  my  protection. 
He  reports  that  he  was  ordered  by  citizens  of  Charles  County,  Md.,  to 
leave  that  place  or  his  vessel  would  be  burned  to-night.  His  cargo 
consisted  of  timber  destined  for  the  U.  S.  navy  yard,  Charlestown, 
Mass.,  and  has  other  freight  to  take  from  the  navy  yard  here.  I  took 
him  in  tow  and  anchored  him  under  the  guns  of  the  fort. 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Thos.  Scott  Fillebrown, 

Lieutenant ,  Commanding. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy ,  Washington,  D.  C.

U.  S.  S.  Pocahontas, 

Off  Mouth  of  Potomac,  April,  27,  1861 — 12:30  p.  m. 

Sir:  After  a  short  chase  and  firing  two  guns  we  have  intercepted 
the  transport  Bienville  with  550  Rhode  Island  troops  on  board  for 
Washington. 

Directed  her  to  proceed  up  the  Potomac  to  navy  yard.  Two  of  the 
pilots  we  received  from  Powhatan  proving  inefficient,  and  admitting, 
they  were  only  capable  for  vessels  of  10  or  12  feet  from  Maryland  Point 
up,  I  took  the  lead  in  this  vessel  and  will  convoy  the  transport  to 
Washington. 

Communicated  this  forenoon  with  U.  S.  S.  Monticello ,  Lieutenant 
Braine,  [and]  Captain  Eagle,  U.  S.  Navy,  on  board  with  dispatches  for 
Washington  via  Annapolis.  Continued  on  up  the  Potomac  until  dark, 
when  we  anchored  for  the  night,  Bienville  in  company;  had  an  inter¬ 
view  with  Lieutenant-Colonel  [J.  T.]  Pitmau,  commanding  the  troops 
on  board  transport,  and  learned  that  4,000  volunteers  in  New  York 
await  transportation. 

The  Parlcershurg  sailed  on  Wednesday  with  Albany  troops,  the  Kill 
von  Kull  on  Thursday,  in  company  with  the  Monticello.  She  had  sup¬ 
plies  and  material  for  repairing  railroad  from  Annapolis. 

April  28, 10  a.  m. — Having  overhauled  the  Daylight  near  Alexandria, 
I  have  the  honor  to  report  my  arrival  off  the  arsenal,  Washington,  con¬ 
voying  the  two  transports  mentioned,  with  about  800  troops.  In  a 
former  letter  I  advised  you  of  having  directed  the  Daylight  to  proceed 
up  the  Potomac  with  the  recruits  for  Seventh  Regiment,  New  York 
State  Militia. 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Jno.  P.  Gillis, 
Commander,  U.  S.  Navy. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy.

U.  S.  S.  Powhatan,  April  27 , 1861. 

Sir  :  I  have  the  honor  of  reporting  the  arrival  of  the  Powhatan  at  the 
navy  yard,  having  left  the  same  in  obedience  to  instructions  on  the  even¬ 
ing  of  t  he  25tli  instant.  Steamed  down  the  Potomac,  speaking  the  Ana- 
costia  oil  Freestone  Point,  and  anchored  at  midnight  below  Maryland 
Point.  It  was  here  that  I  discovered  having  in  my  possession  orders 
for  the  Anacostia ,  which  I  much  regretted,  as  distance  and  time  pre¬ 
cluded  iny  steaming  back  to  deliver  them. 

At  daylight  weighed  anchor  and  continued  down  stream,  noting  the 
condition  of  the  channel  buoys,  more  especially  in  that  section  of  the 
stream  styled  Kettle  Bottom.  Both  light-boats  had  been  destroyed, 
the  stem  piece  of  one  being  visible  above  water.  The  lower  can  buoy 
and  stakes  in  position ;  those  above  gone.  Neither  going  nor  returning 
were  there  any  appearances  of  batteries  being  erected  at  Cedar  or 
other  points;  found  also  the  light-boat  missing  off  Smith’s  Point  and 
learned  from  a  schooner  master  that  it  had  been  towed  inshore.  When 
5  miles  beyond  the  mouth  of  the  river  made  out  the  U.  S.  S.  Pocahontas 
steaming  up  from  the  southeast;  stood  for  her  and  communicated  with 
Captain  Gillis,  delivering  to  him  the  three  pilots  sent  down  in  my  charge 
as  directed. 

The  expected  transports  having  proceeded  up  the  bay,  even  before 
the  arrival  of  the  Pocahontas ,  I  suggested  to  Captain  Gillis  the  utility 
of  the  Powhatan  accompanying  him  to  Annapolis,  to  which  he  assented, 
but  on  a  comparison  of  coal  and  distance  it  was  doubtful  if  the  former 
would  hold  out  the  required  time.  Since  then  by  experimenting — i.  e., 
working  expansively  in  connection  with  the  cut-off- — a  much  less  con¬ 
sumption  of  coal  has  been  obtained  and  a  fair  rate  of  speed  maintained. 

While  in  company  with  the  Pocahontas  a  bay  steamer  appeared  in 
sight  standing  to  the  northward.  In  obedience  to  orders  from  Captain 
Gillis,  I  steamed  down  to  her.  She  proved  to  be  the  Belvidere ,  from 
Richmond,  bound  to  Baltimore,  cotton  and  tobacco  as  freight.  Ordered 
the  captain  to  hoist  his  colors  and  follow  in  my  wake.  A  boarding  offi¬ 
cer  was  sent  to  her  from  the  Pocahontas  and  she  soon  after  kept  on  her 
course. 

Stood  in  for  the  Potomac,  passing  Point  Lookout  at  4  p.  m.;  Poca¬ 
hontas  when  last  seen  standing  up  the  bay. 

Reached  the  Kettle  Bottom  Channel  after  dark,  but  the  pilot  (Cap¬ 
tain  Walter)  took  the  steamer  through  safely  and  I  reached  the  navy 
yard  at  2 :  30  a.  m. 

Enclosed  are  the  dispatches  of  Captain  Gillis;  also  the  orders  for  the 
Anacostia.

was  desirous  of  reaching  Washington  if  the  Government  would  allow

II.  S.  S.  Anacostia, 

Washington ,  April  28,  1861. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  inform  you  that  your  order  of  yesterday 
has  been  strictly  obeyed. 

At  daylight  this  morning  I  sent  an  officer  on  shore  to  make  a  careful 
examination  of  White  House  Bluff  and  vicinity.  On  his  return  he 
reported  that  he  had  carefully  examined  the  whole  length  of  the  bluff, 
including  the  site  of  the  old  works,  and  saw  no  signs  of  any  force 
having  been  there.  There  were  no  hoof  marks  in  the  clay  or  tracks  of 
wheels. 

He  ascertained  from  persons  on  the  beach  that  about  fifty  men  from 
the  back  country  had  been  there  last  week,  but  they  had  no  implements 
for  throwing  up  breastworks,  and  after  a  short  stay  they  disappeared. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Thos.  Scott  Fillebrown, 

Lieutenant ,  Commanding . 

Commander  John  A.  Dahlgren, 

Commandant  Wavy  Yard ,  Washington,  D.  C.

Sir:  You  will  take  charge  of  the  steamboat  Powhatan  and  proceed 
down  the  Potomac  in  order  to  replace  and  protect  the  buoys  at  the 
Kettle  Bottom  Shoals,  which  have  been  removed.  If  light-boats  are 
no  longer  of  service  in  distinguishing  the  dangers  for  which  they  were

Messrs.  Stephens  and  Walter,  are  sent  with  you  for  this  duty. 

You  will  observe  closely  the  bank  of  the  river  so  as  to  notice  any 
battery  that  may  exist,  particularly  the  bluff  near  the  White  House. 

Respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

J.  A.  Dahlgren.

Letter  from  Major  Ramsay ,  U.  S.  Army ,  to  commandant  navy  yard , 

Washington ,  giving  information  regarding  suspicious  movements  of  a 

steamer. 

Washington  Arsenal, 

Sunday  [April  28,  1861.} 

Captain  :  The  steamer  which  passed  down  from  the  yard  this  even¬ 
ing,  when  abreast  of  Alexandria,  was  seen  by  my  orderly  and  the  sen¬ 
tinel  on  the  wharf  to  be  bows  on  to  the  town.  The  orderly  came  to 
call  me  when  it  was  too  dark  to  discern.  The  sentinel  is  certain  that 
the  boat  went  in  to  the  wharf.  There  has  been  no  bring  heard. 

I  think  it  proper  to  give  you  the  information  for  what  it  is  worth,  as 
the  destination  of  the  steamer  is  doubtless  by  your  order.  The  boat 
was  not  seen  to  go  out  from  the  town.  The  twilight,  however,  rendered 
objects  so  indistinct  that  with  a  glass  I  could  only  recognize  the  light¬ 
house. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Geo.  D.  Eamsay, 

[Major  Ordnance.] 

Captain  Dahlgren,  or 

Commanding  Ofeicer,  Washington  Navy  Yard.

Report  of  Lieutenant  Trenchard,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Key 
stone  State ,  of  the  cruise  of  that  vessel  to  New  York  and  return. 

U.  S.  S.  Keystone  State, 

U.  S.  Navy  Yard,  Washington,  May  1,  1861. 

Sir  :  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that,  in  conformity  with  the  order 
of  the  Department  of  the  24tli  ultimo,  having  proceeded  to  New  York, 
arriving  there  on  the  26th  ultimo,  and  having  received  on  board  the 
provisions,  have  returned  with  all  possible  dispatch  to  this  place.  This 
duty  was  delayed  some  twenty  hours  in  consequence  of  the  light-boats 
in  the  Potomac  and  off  Smith’s  Point  being  burned. 

The  mails  received  on  board  at  Washington  were  landed  at  New 
York  and  dispatched  to  the  post-office  in  that  city  immediately  after 
our  arrival,  and  the  dispatches  from  the  War  and  Navy  Departments 
were  forwarded  at  once  in  charge  of  an  officer  in  advance  of  the  mail.
