Report  of  commandant  navy  yard,  Washington,  transmitting  report  of 

Lieutenant  Sproston,  U.  S.  Navy ,  commanding  steamer  Powhatan,  of 

the  replacing  of  buoys  in  the  Potomac  River. 

TJ.  S.  Navy  Yard,  Washington,  May  1,  1861. 

Sir:  I  enclose  herewith  the  report  of  Lieutenant  Sproston,  just 
returned  from  replacing  the  buoys  that  had  been  removed  from  the 
Kettle  Bottoms.  He  also  marked  the  dangers  formerly  indicated  by 
the  light-boats  that  were  burned. 

There  is  not  the  least  evidence  of  any  attempt  yet  to  fortify  the  bluff 
near  the  White  House,  but  all  that  is  necessary  could  be  done  in  a 
night,  so  that  continued  observation  is  requisite.  It  may  be  well  occa¬ 
sionally  to  send  a  steamboat  to  look  at  the  buoys  which  have  been  just 
replaced. 

The  duty  assigned  to  Lieutenant  Sproston  appears  to  have  been  exe¬ 
cuted  intelligently. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Jno.  A.  Dahlgren, 

Commandant. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy. 

[Enclosure.] 

TJ.  S.  S.  Powhatan, 
Washington  Navy  Yard ,  [May  1,  1861.] 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  inform  you  of  the  return  of  the  Powhatan 
and  to  submit  a  report  of  the  duties  performed  under  instructions. 

Having  got  on  board  the  number  of  buoys,  sinkers,  and  spars 
required,  I  left  the  navy  yard  on  the  alteruoon  of  the  28th  and  pro¬ 
ceeded  down  the  river,  running  close  in  to  Alexandria,  communicating 
with  Fort  Washington,  and  taking  the  inshore  channel  past  White 
House  Point.  Too  dark  to  make  observations.  At  11:30  anchored 
below  Freestone  Point.  As  usual,  an  armed  watch  and  sentries  posted; 
banked  fires.  During  the  night  heard  in  the  distance  the  sound  of 
wheels,  as  if  a  steamer  had  gone  up  Aquia  Creek.  At  5  a.  in.,  underway; 
passed  Maryland  Point  and  prepared  buoys  and  spars  for  launching. 
Commencingofif  Upper  Cedar  Point  planted  buoys  in  the  following  order: 

Upper  Cedar  Point,  small  red  buoy;  Yates  Bar,  large  black  buoy; 
Montgomery  Bluff  Pjoint],  Virginia  side,  large  black  and  white  buoy 
(charred  stem  of  light-boat  close  to  this  buoy);  Swan  Point,  spar  buoy; 
Kettle  Bottom  No.  1,  spar  buoy;  Kettle  Bottom  No.  2,  spar  buoy. 
Found  the  three  buoys  below  this  in  position. 


442  OPERATIONS  ON  THE  POTOMAC  AND  RAPPAHANNOCK. 

At  low  water  steamed  up  the  channel  again  and  sounding  found  nothing 
less  than  22  feet  G  inches.  At  2  p.  m.  anchored  off  Montgomery  Bluff' 
(one-third  of  a  mile).  .During  the  forenoon  obtained  fish  from  the 
fishermen  and  threatened  to  stop  fishing  on  the  river  if  the  buoys  were 
cut  away.  At  sunset  steamed  up  and  anchored  in  Machodoc  Creek. 
The  men  who  burned  one  of  the  light-boats  reside  in  this  neighborhood. 
At  daylight  weighed  anchor  and  steamed  down  along  the  settlement  of 
Madrick.  At  the  point,  seeing  the  people  seining,  pulled  on  shore, 
bought  fish  of  them,  and  held  a  conversation  of  a  civil  character.  A 
friend  of  the  pilot’s  went  on  board  and  we  learned  that  two  schooners 
that  we  had  seen  the  day  previous  up  a  creek,  but  had  now  left,  had 
bodies  of  armed  men  on  board.  Steamed  to  the  opposite  side  of  the 
river  and  anchored  off  Ludlow’s  Ferry,  inside  of  Lower  Cedar  Foint. 
In  a  little  inlet  nearby  discovered  one  of  the  channel  buoys  and  the 
longboat  of  the  light-ship.  Went  on  shore  with  an  armed  boat’s  crew 
and  towed  them  off.  Found  the  people  rank  secessionists.  They  had 
not  received  a  mail  for  two  weeks  in  this  part  of  the  country.  This 
day  spoke  a  store  steamer  bound  up  arid  informed  them  of  the  buoys 
being  placed.  A  steamer  passed  down  also.  At  noon  a  heavy  squall 
of  wind  and  rain  coming  up  from  the  northeast,  was  obliged  to  get 
underway  and  steam  to  the  lee  of  Upper  Cedar  Point  for  shelter.  At 
4  ii.  m.  the  U.  S.  S.  Pocahontas  passed  down,  also  the  Erickson ,  canal 
steam  packet  between  Philadelphia  and  Baltimore,  with  deck  freight 
visible.  In  coining  up  the  channel  sighted  all  the  buoys.  Within  these 
limits  channel  passes  a  half  mile  from  Montgomery  Bluff  and  close  to 
Upper  Cedar  Point;  all  other  points  are  distant  more  than  a  mile. 
From  Lower  Cedar  Point  to  the  mouth  of  the  river  ships  are  entirely 
out  of  range.  No  signs  of  batteries  in  contemplation  have  yet  been 
seen. 

May  1,  got  underway  at  5  a.  m.  and,  steaming  up  to  Tompkin 
[Matomkin]  Point,  planted  a  spar  buoy  in  4  fathoms.  Keystone  State , 
Boston ,  and  tug  passed  up.  Steamed  along  the  beach  of  Sandy  Point 
and  anchored  off  Stump  [Neck]  Point;  went  on  shore,  communicated 
with  the  people,  and  bought  fish.  But  little  provision  in  the  county. 
Boatmen  afraid  to  bring  it  over.  At  11:30  anchored  off  the  White 
House  Bluff;  landed  with  an  armed  boat’s  crew;  divided  and  ranged 
the  heights;  saw  no  one  but  fishermen  and  negroes.  While  on  the 
summit  of  the  hill  the  troopship  Daylight  passed  in  the  regular  ship 
channel,  well  outside  of  the  Powhatan.  The  altitude  was  such  as  to 
enable  me  to  look  directly  down  on  her  deck.  The  land  opposite  is  low 
and  sandy,  distant  a  mile. 

Provisions,  more  than  a  week’s  supply,  excepting  butter,  of  which 
five  days  remaining.

Report  of  commandant  navy  yard ,  New  York,  regarding  purchase  of  two 

vessels  for  the  u  flying  flotilla  fl 

Navy  Yard  [New  York],  May  1, 1861. 

Sir:  In  compliance  with  your  order  to  forward  tlie  fitting  [of]  the 
flotilla  to  be  in  charge  of  Commander  Ward,  I  have  this  day  agreed  to 
purchase  two  very  fast  screw  steamers  selected  by  Commander  W[ard] 
as  adapted  to  his  purpose.  They  are  entirely  new  and  will  mount  a 
24  pounder  howitzer.  One  larger  is  being  sought  for.  The  price  of 
those  purchased  is  $15,000  each,  some  six  or  eight  [thousand],  I  under¬ 
stand,  less  than  the  cost.  I  will  give  acting  appointments  to  their 
commanders  as  masters,  also  to  their  engineers,  as  I  have  done  with 
the  others.  Shall  I  place  them  on  the  books  of  the  receiving  ship  for 
pay?  As  the  purser  of  the  receiving  ship  is  now  removed,  I  may  be 
excused  if  I  apprise  the  Department  that  Paymaster  Cahoone  is  in 
this  city. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant,

Report  of  Lieutenant  Fillehroicn ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  commanding  U.  S.  S. 

Anacostia,  of  a  reconnoissance  in  the  Potomac  River. 

U.  S.  S.  Anacostia, 
Washington  Navy  Yard ,  May  3,  1861. 

Sir:  1  have  the  honor  to  inform  the  Department  that,  in  obedience 
to  instructions  received  yesterday  afternoon,  I  proceeded  down  the  river 
as  far  as  Aquia  Creek  and  executed  my  orders. 

On  my  arrival  there  I  sent  a  boat  with  a  reliable  officer  to  make  a 
careful  examination  of  that  locality,  and  he  reports  that  there  were  no 
evidences  of  any  batteries  in  the  course  of  erection ,  nor  could  he  per¬ 
ceive  any  hostile  gatherings.  There  were  very  few  persons  to  be  seen, 
no  persons  in  uniform,  or  indications  of  troops  thereabouts. 

Just  as  I  anchored  I  observed  a  train  of  cars,  three  in  number, 
arrive  and  after  a  stay  of  about  fifteen  minutes  they  departed,  accom¬ 
panied  by  another  train  of  eight  or  ten  platform  or  dirt  cars. 

The  White  House  Bluff  remains  the  same  as  indicated  in  my  last 
report. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Thos.  Scott  Fillebrown, 

Lieutenant ,  Comm anding. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy.

Letter  from  the  Secretary  of  the  Navy  to  the  Secretary  of  State,  regarding 
allowance  of  time  for  departure  of  neutral  and  foreign  vessels. 

Navy  Department,  May  3 , 1861. 

Sir  :  In  answer  to  your  letter  of  yesterday,  suggesting  a  compliance 
witli  tlie  application  of  the  minister  of  Bremen  concerning  the  Bremen 
bark  Admiral  Bromney,  now  loading  at  the  port  of  Alexandria,  Va.,  I 
have  the  honor  to  state  that  the  commandant  of  the  blockading  squad¬ 
ron,  Captain  Stringhain,  has  not  yet  arrived  at  his  station.  After  he 
reaches  it  and  the  blockade  is  established  with  a  force  sufficient  to 
close  the  ports,  his  instructions  are  “  to  neutral  or  foreign  vessels  that 
are  already  in  the  port  you  will  allow  a  reasonable  number  of  days  to 
leave  them.”  He  will  be  instructed  to  give  at  least  fifteen  days’  notice 
for  vessels  to  leave,  with  or  without  cargoes. 

The  Bremen  vessel,  therefore,  will  have  ample  time  to  depart  without 
molestation  if  her  captain  exercises  ordinary  vigilance. 

I  am,  sir,  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  Navy. 

Hon.  William  H.  Seward, 

Secretary  of  State. 


Report  of  Commander  Oillis,  U.  S.  Navy ,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Pocahon¬ 
tas,  of  the  cruise  of  that  vessel  in  the  Potomac  River  from  April  30  to 
May  4,  1861. 

H.  S.  S.  Pocahontas, 

Off  Entrance  [to]  Potomac  River,  May  1,  1861. 
Sir  :  In  obedience  to  your  order  of  the  29th  ultimo,  we  left  the  navy 
yard  on  the  30th  April,  9:  30  a.  m.,  and  proceeded  down  the  Potomac; 
no  evidence  of  offensive  demonstrations  on  its  shores.  Spoke  the  Ana- 
costia  bound  up  and  the  river  steamer  Powhatan  at  anchor. 

After  dark  we  came  to  at  the  entrance  of  the  river  off  Point  Lookout 
light-house.  At  midnight  a  large  steamer  passed  up  the  Potomac,  too 
distant  to  hail;  we  burned  blue  light;  supposed  her  to  be  the  Baltic. 
At  daylight  two  steamers  were  discovered  standing  up  the  Chesapeake 
too  far  off  to  be  made  out. 

As  we  stood  into  the  bay,  fell  in  with  and  boarded  a  small  schooner. 
Her  crew  anchored  her  and  fled  in  their  boat  to  the  shore.  She  proved 
to  be  an  empty  lime  vessel.  Continuing  down  the  bay,  so  as  to  inter¬ 
cept  any  vessels  coming  up,  spoke  the  ship  Heloise,  one  hundred  and 
two  days  from  Y alparaiso,  bound  to  Baltimore.  She  reports  no  steamers 
outside. 

Being  off  Windmill  Point,  we  now  stood  up  the  Chesapeake.  Spoke 
bark  [ - ],  from  Baltimore,  bound  to  New  York.  She  reports  pass¬ 

ing  last  night  at  9  o’clock  (about  the  time  we  reached  the  mouth  of  [the] 
Potomac)  a  steamer  at  anchor  off  the  Patuxent  with  troops  on  board; 
all  quiet  in  Baltimore  and  generally  in  the  State.  Spoke  Bremen  ship 
from  Baltimore,  bound  to  Bremen;  stood  down  the  bay  and  spoke 
steamer  Adelaide,  from  Old  Point  for  Baltimore;  no  news.  She  has  not 
seen  any  sea  steamers.  We  then  stood  up  the  bay;  fresh  gales  from 
northwest;  anchored  for  the  night  to  the  southward  of  Smith’s  Point, 
off  Bluff  Point;  heavy  squalls  of  wind  through  the  night.  At  daylight 
steamed  up  to  Point  Lookout,  Potomac,  thence  out  into  the  Chesa¬ 
peake.  Several  river  steamers  passed  up.  Running  off  and  on  in  track 
of  vessels,  and  at  sundown  anchored  in  the  bay  off  Point  Lookout. 
Fresh  breezes  from  northwest.  Weighed  anchor  at  8  p.  m.  and  chased.

\ 

a  steamer  bound  up ;  fired  a  sliot ;  could  not  overhaul  her ;  supposed 
her  to  be  a  river  steamer.  Anchored  in  the  bay.  At  daylight  steamed 
out  and  spoke  ship  Neptune ,  from  Bremen,  bound  to  Baltimore.  She 
reports  two  steamers  with  troops  gone  into  Fortress  Monroe  yesterday 
(2d  May)  and  the  Quaker  City  cruising  at  entrance  of  Chesapeake  Bay. 
Exercised  the  crew  daily  at  the  great  guns  and  small  arms.  Blowing 
fresh  from  southward  and  eastward.  Kept  in  the  bay  until  near  dark, 
then  ran  into  mid-channel,  entrance  of  Potomac. 

At  daylight,  4tli  May,  got  underway  and  stood  out;  spoke  brig  Trial , 
from  St.  Johns  [San  Juan],  Port  [Puerto]  Rico,  bound  to  Baltimore. 
Ship  John  Clark ,  from  Liverpool  for  Baltimore,  reports  no  steamers 
down  the  bay  except  Quaker  City ,  lying  off  and  on  the  entrance.  Spoke 
steam  tug  Commerce ,  from  Washington  for  Philadelphia,  via  canal. 
Vessels  generally  seeking  a  harbor,  owing  to  rough  and  thick  weather, 
with  strong  breezes  from  northward  and  westward.  Anchored  off  Point 
Lookout ;  raining ;  thermometer  42°  F. 

I  have  written  in  detail,  showing  that  we  have  been  actively  employed. 
About  6:20  p.  m.  discovered  two  steamers  standing  up  the  bay;  made 
chase,  firing  guns,  and  after  dark  sent  up  rockets  to  bring  them  to ; 
overhauled  them  off  the  Patuxent;  they  proved  to  be  the  Harriet  Lane, 
in  company  with  the  transport  Star  of  the  South,  having  on  board  600 
troops,  Brooklyn  regiment,  Lieutenant- Colon  el  [Michael  W.]  Burns, 
commanding.  Communicated  with  him  and  directed  her  to  follow  the 
Pocahontas  to  the  Potomac.  They  report  the  U.  S.  steam  frigate  Niag¬ 
ara  to  leave  New  York  to-day  (Saturday,  4th  May)  for  Chesapeake  Bay; 
transport  Columbia  to  leave  with  Maine  regiment.  I  learn  also  that 
Colonel  Ellsworth,  with  Firemen  Zouaves,  is  at  Annapolis;  the  Ulster 
County  Guards  left  in  barracks  in  park,  New  York.  Star  of  the  South 
waited  in  New  York  until  4: 30  p.  m.  on  Thursday  for  Columbia ;  Har¬ 
riet  Lane  has  orders  to  proceed  to  mouth  of  Patapsco  River,  there  to  lie 
off  and  on  until  further  orders.  I  will  convoy  the  transport  to  Wash¬ 
ington  5th  May.  Troops  will  debark  at  Arsenal  [Greenleaf]  Point. 
The  motion  of  propeller  almost  prevents  writing. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Jno.  P.  Gillis, 

Commander ,  U.  S.  Navy. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy,  Washington.

Letter  from  the  Secretary  of  the  Treasury  to  the  Secretary  of  the  Navy , 
regarding  reconnoissance  in  the  Potomac  River. 


Treasury  Deparment,  May  4, 1861. 

Sir  :  In  order  to  have  made  at  once  a  reconnoissance  of  the  Potomac 
River,  I  would  respectfully  request  that  the  steamer  Mount  Vernon ,  now 
at  the  Washington  navy  yard,  with  her  present  force  and  four  good 
landsmen,  and  the  steamer  Anacostia,  with  her  present  force,  as  a  guard 
vessel,  be  placed  at  the  disposal  of  this  Department,  which  has  directed 
the  Superintendent  of  the  Coast  Survey  to  make  this  reconnoissance. 
Not  more  than  three  working  days  will  probably  be  required  for  this 
purpose,  and  it  is  important  that  the  work  should  be  done  at  once. 

Very  respectfully, 


Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy. 


S.  P.  Chase, 
Secretary  of  the  Treasury. 


Report  of  Lieutenant  Fillebrown ,  TJ.  S  Navy ,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Ana¬ 
costia ,  regarding  reconnoissance  in  the  Potomac  River. 

IJ.  S.  S.  Anacostia, 

Washington ,  May  5,  1861. 

Sir  :  I  have  the  honor  to  inform  the  Department  that  yesterday  and 
to-day  I  proceeded  down  the  Potomac  as  far  as  Aquia  Creek,  keeping 
a  strict  lookout  on  both  banks  of  the  river  for  any  suspicious  move¬ 
ments  or  hostile  gatherings,  and  have  to  report  that  none  could  be 
detected. 

The  foliage  at  the  White  House  Bluff  is  getting  quite  thick,  but  as 
far  as  I  could  observe  there  was  nothing  to  indicate  its  being  occupied 
by  any  military  or  other  force. 

At  Aquia  Creek  everything  seemed  quiet;  but  very  few  persons  to 
be  seen. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Thos.  Scott  Fillebrown, 

Lieutenant ,  Commanding. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy ,  Washington ,  l).  C.

Commandant’s  Office,  Navy  Yard, 

Washington ,  May  8 ,  1861. 

Sir:  You  will,  at  the  earliest  time  of  the  morning  when  the  light  is 
sufficient,  proceed  with  the  Pawnee  under  your  command  to  convoy  a 
schooner  as  far  as  Old  Point,  now  lying  at  the  navy  yard  and  having

Please  deliver  the  dispatches  and  letters  herewith  sent  you  to  the 
senior  naval  officer  in  the  vicinity  of  Fortress  Monroe,  and  receive  any 
communications  which  the  commandant  of  the  fortress  may  desire  to 
transmit. 

You  will  observe  the  condition  of  the  commanding  points  on  the  river.

Report  of  Lieutenant  Jeffers,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  commanding  steamer  Philadel¬ 
phia,  regarding  duty  executed  by  that  vessel. 

Steamer  Philadelphia, 

Navy  Yard,  Washington,  May  9,  1861 — 6  p.  m. 
Sir:  In  obedience  to  your  order  of  the  6th  instant,  I  proceeded  to  the 
arsenal  and  conveyed  to  Fort  Washington  in  two  trips  eleven  cannon, 
with  their  carriages,  and  a  large  quantity  of  ammunition  and  other 


OPERATIONS  ON  THE  POTOMAC  AND  RAPPAHANNOCK.  451 


stores,  72  barrels  of  musket  powder  to  tlie  arsenal  from  the  fort,  and 
convoyed  a  propeller  loaded  with  powder,  and  two  other  vessels  with 
stores  to  the  city. 

Yesterday,  while  loading  at  the  arsenal  wharf,  the  steamship  Colum¬ 
bia  ran  into  this  vessel,  staving  the  port  wheelhouse  and  breaking  one 
ot  the  braces  of  the  framing.  I  temporarily  repaired  it  to  enable  me 
to  complete  the  service  upon  which  I  was  engaged,  but  some  further 
work  will  be  required. 

Respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

W.  R.  Jeffers, 
Lieutenant ,  Commanding .

Ravy  YArd,  Washington,  May  9 , 1861. 

Sir  :  I  enclose  herewith  report  of  Lieutenant  Sproston,  of  the  Poiv- 
hatan ,  returned  last  night  about  3:30  a.  m.  from  below. 

The  Baltimore  left  last  night  to  assist  the  propeller  ashore,  with 
orders  to  recapture  if  taken.  The  accidental  presence  of  the  other 
steamers  probably  prevented  this. 

The  Pawnee  left  early  this  morning  with  schooner  under  convoy. 

I  have  received  and  will  deliver  the  detachment  of  Lieutenant 
Sproston,  which  will  be  an  inconvenience  to  the  service  here  at  this  time.

[Enclosure.] 

U.  S.  Armed  Steamer  Powhatan, 

W asliington  Navy  Yard ,  May  [ .9],  1861. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  having  left  Washington  navy  yard 
on  May  5  at  11:30  a.  m.,  in  obedience  to  instructions. 

Communicated  with  Major  Ramsay  at  the  arsenal;  he  had  no  dis¬ 
patches  to  send.  Stopped  at  Fort  Washington  and  landed  stores. 
Commandant  of  fort  was  advising  all  store  steamers  to  await  convoy 
up;  he  also  spoke  of  the  want  of  a  serviceable  battery  at  the  fort,  the 
guns  there  being  few  and  old.  Spoke  the  Pocahontas  (convoying)  and 
Anacostia.  At  4  p.  m.,  off  Lower  Cedar  Point,  found  the  store  steamer 
Cataline  aground  on  a  ledge  of  rocks  near  mid-channel  buoy,  the  buoy 
being  placed  to  indicate  their  position.  She  had  struck  at  2:  30  p.  m., 
high  water.  Anchored  near  her.  Also  anchored  the  Kill  von  Kull , 
which  was  steaming  by,  and  placed  her  in  charge  of  Mr.  Stephens, 
pilot.  Anchored  off  the  steam  tug  alongside  the  Cataline ,  a  portion  of 
the  cargo  being  transferred  to  her.  Sounding,  my  pilot  reported  2^ 
feet  forward  and  9  feet  aft.  Made  preparations  for  towing  the  Cataline 
oft.  Sent  a  midshipman  with  sixteen  soldiers  to  assist  in  transporting 
cargo  aft.  At  9:30,  hawsers  being  fast  from  this  steamer  and  the  Kill 
von  Kull ,  commenced  towing  her  off.  At  11  she  swung  into  the  channel 


452  OPERATIONS  ON  THE  POTOMAC  AND  RAPPAHANNOCK. 


and  at  12  got  clear  of  the  rocks.  Anchored  the  steamers  for  the  night, 
it  being  dark  and  rainy.  At  daylight  steamers  underway,  Cataline  and 
tug  steaming  up  the  river. 

May  6. — Rainy,  blowy  weather,  wind  S.  E.  Spoke  the  Chesapeake, 
bound  up  with  stores.  Exercised  the  crew  at  quarters,  fired  a  canister 
(300  yards),  5-second  shell,  1,600  yards.  At  1:30  p.  m.,  blowing  very 
fresh.  A  heavy  sea  on  for  the  day.  Consuming  much  coal  and  mak¬ 
ing  little  way;  stood  inshore  and  anchored  oft'  Mill  Creek  with  both 
anchors,  keeping  12  pounds  of  steam  on.  Remainder  of  the  day  blow¬ 
ing  a  S.  E.  gale.  At  sunset  saw  two  transports  in  the  bay  steaming 
up;  blowing  too  heavy  to  go  out  to  them.  At  10  p.  m.  gale  broke  up  in 
a  thunderstorm.  Lights  and  boats  collecting  from  the  shore  astern, 
hailed  the  nearest  and  fired  a  musket.  No  reply.  Went  to  quarters; 
prepared  for  slipping.  Manned  a  boat  and  pulled  in  a  circuit  of  2  miles 
round  and  inshore  of  the  steamers;  lights  out  and  boats  gone. 

May  7. — At  3  a.  m.,  underway;  afresh  S.  W.  wind.  Twelve  miles 
N.  E.  from  New  Point  passed  a  sunken  schooner;  half  of  lower  masts 
above  water;  some  rigging  still  on  topmasts.  Three  miles  below  this 
passed  another  wreck  awash;  position  dangerous  for  vessels  bound 
down.  No  masts  standing  on  the  second  wreck.  Off  New  Point  made 
a  ship  standing  up;  fired  a  blank  cartridge;  no  notice  being  taken, 
sent  a  shell  across  her  bows.  She  hove  to.  Boarded  her;  found  her  to 
be  a  Richmond  vessel  ( Cherubim )  bound  to  Baltimore,  with  a  pass  from 
Captain  Marston,  of  the  Cumberland.  At  11  a.  m.  anchored  alongside 
the  flagship  Cumberland  and  delivered  dispatches  to  the  flag-officer; 
then  steamed  to  Portress  Monroe  and  took  in  6  tons  of  coal  from  one 
of  several  prize  schooners.  Lifted  the  cylinder  head  and  repacked  the 
piston.  At  5  p.  m.  steamed  up  to  the  Cumberland ,  received  dispatches, 
and  kept  on  up  the  bay.  At  midnight  off  the  mouth  of  the  Potomac. 
Shore  lights  confusing  and  water  shoaling;  stood  out  to  4  fathoms  and 
anchored. 

May  8. — At  daylight  found  the  ship  anchored  off  Smith’s  Point.  The 
lights  seen  during  the  night,  from  bearings  taken,  must  have  been 
false  lights  on  the  Virginia  side.  Such  lights  about  Smith’s  Point  are 
very  dangerous.  Point  Lookout  light  was  not  lighted.  At  10  a.  m. 
sent  an  officer  on  board  a  schooner ;  her  deck  load  proved  to  be  hogs¬ 
heads  of  tobacco;  and  then  to  a  Bremen  bark, bound  from  Alexandria  to 
New  York  for  a  cargo.  At  11  spoke  the  Mount  Vernon  surveying.  At 
30-minutes  p.  m.  boarded  the  propeller  Octagon  [Octorara]  ashore  on  the 
Virginia  side;  found  a  guard  on  board  from  the  Anacostia,  the  pro¬ 
peller  having  fieldpieces  and  stores  on  her  decks.  Got  a  hawser  and 
kedge  from  the  Anacostia ,  steamed  into  draft,  carried  out  the  hawser, 
and  commenced  towing  off  the  tug,  when  the  hawser  parted.  Shortly 
after  the  discharge  box  of  this  steamer’s  engine  (of  cast  iron)  com¬ 
menced  leaking  badly,  and  was  obliged  to  get  underway  at  once.  Put 
on  all  steam  pumps,  stood  up  the  river,  and  kept  leak  under.  Pass¬ 
ing  a  propeller  steaming  down,  by  request  of  Lieutenant  Command¬ 
ing  Fillebrown,  ordered  her  to  pass  within  hail  of  the  Anacostia.  A 
side-wheel  steamer  of  light  draft  and  two  hawsers  are  requisite  to 
get  the  propeller'  off,  or  a  large  boat  to  discharge  portion  of  cargo  into. 
The  pilot  of  this  propeller  was  picked  up  at  the  mouth  of  the  river, 
and  was  allowed  to  leave  her  after  the  vessel  grounded,  very  improp¬ 
erly.  The  vessel  is  on  shore  nearly  a  mile  from  the  channel,  and  the 
whole  has  the  appearance  of  intention.  Her  position  is  on  Yates  Bar, 
near  wreck  of  light-boat  on  Virginia  side.  Anacostia  at  anchor  two- 
thirds  of  a  mile  off  near  white  and  black  can  buoy.  Guard  is  to  remain 
on  board  propeller  and  night  signals  are  arranged. 


OPERATIONS  ON  THE  POTOMAC  AND  RAPPAHANNOCK.  453 

While  at  Old  Point  noticed  great  activity  on  the  part  of  gunboats. 
Monticell o  came  down  from  off  Craney  Point;  had  been  well  within 
range  of  battery  withont  being  fired  at.  Tng  Neptune’s  Car  had  gone 
up  the  Virginia  side  of  the  bay  looking  for  batteries.  The  Yankee  had 
just  returned  from  off  Yorktown,  York  River,  <30  [ 6]  miles  up.  A  battery 
there  fired  ten  times  at  her;  no  shot  struck.  The  steamers  Kedar  and 
Kill  von  Kull  were  landing  ordnance  stores  and  provisions  at  the  fort, 
which  is  garrisoned  by  1,600  men.  A  schooner  loaded  with  arms  and 
clothing  for  North  Carolina  is  a  prize.  Two  little  steamboats  and  a 
dozen  schooners  are  prizes.  The  Niagara  is  expected  daily.  Saw  a 
secession  gunboat  at  the  end  of  James  River  reconnoitering.  Intelli¬ 
gence  from  the  Gosport  [Norfolk]  navy  yard  unreliable.  Quaker  City 
off  the  Horseshoe  boarding.  Soldiers  in  Portress  Monroe  mounting 
guns.  Large  gun  still  on  beach  in  front  of  fort.  Vessels  when  boarded 
are  warned  not  to  attempt  to  enter  a  Virginia  or  Southern  port.  The 
bay  boats  from  Baltimore  have  been  stopped.

Letter  from  Robert  Spear,  esq.,  to  the  Secretary  of  the  Navy,  requesting 
Government  protection  of  his  property. 

Washington,  May  10, 1861. 

Sir:  I  have  a  large  quantity  of  ship  timber  lying  on  the  banks  of 
the  Potomac  in  Maryland  cut  for  the  navy  yards.  I  had  dispatched 
vessels  to  take  the  timber  away,  but  the  crews,  warned  of  danger  when 
near  the  landing,  departed  without  attempting  to  load.  One  of  these 
vessels  now  lies  in  a  creek  on  Virginia  side  river,  the  crew  having 
abandoned  her.  The  other  has  retreated  to  some  place  of  safety  and 
suppose  her  to  be  lying  near  Fort  Monroe. 

I  respectfully  solicit  the  protection  of  the  Government  and  the  assist¬ 
ance  of  a  steam  tug  to  enable  me  in  security  to  bring  these  vessels  to 
the  landing  of  the  timber. 

With  great  respect,  your  obedient  servant, 

Robert  Spear. 

Hon.  Secretary  of  Navy.

[Telegram.] 

Navy  Yard,  May  11, 1861. 

I  have  just  been  informed  by  a  Mr.  Burch  that  two  small  vessels  were 
detained  last  evening  at  Alexandria.  One  of  them,  was  fired  at.  He 
says  also  that  some  changes  in  telegraphic  communications  are  making 
near  Alexandria.  I  have  sent  up  the  man  with  a  note. 

Jno.  A.  Dahlgren, 

Commandant. 

Navy  Department.

[Telegram.] 

Navy  Yard,  May  11, 1861. 

The  river  steamers  have  each  a  32-pounder  and  some  rifles,  but  they 
are  mere  shells  and  could  not  resist  grapeshot  from  the  wharves.  Their 
weakness  might  invite  aggression.  The  heavy  broadside  of  the  Pawnee 
is  just  suitable  for  the  case,  as  it  would  overawe  all  opposition,  and  I 
would  recommend  a  steamer  to  go  from  here  with  orders  for  the  Paionee 
to  take  position  near  Alexandria  for  the  purpose  intended. 

Jno.  A.  Dahlgren, 

Commandant. 

Secretary  Navy.

Report  of  commandant  navy  yard,  Washington ,  regarding  protection  to 

vessels  at  Alexandria,  Va. 

Commandant’s  Office,  Navy  Yard, 

Washington,  May  12,  1861. 

Sir  :  When  your  telegraphic  order  of  yesterday  was  received  in  the 
afternoon  there  was  no  armed  vessel  at  the  yard  properly  capable  of

Sir  :  Having  reported  to  you  by  the  Baltimore  last  evening,  we  pro¬ 
ceeded  down  the  Potomac,  and  this  morning,  7  a.  m.,  fell  in  with  the 


462  OPERATIONS  ON  THE  POTOMAC  AND  RAPPAHANNOCK. 

Mount  Vernon  off  Aquia  Creek.  Delivered  to  Lieutenant  Sproston  liis 
orders  with  instructions.  He  reports  to  me  an  earth  battery  with  four 
embrasures  and  one  32-pounder  mounted ;  also  one  fieldpiece,  with  about 
fifty  men.  Their  gun  was  manned,  but  no  further  aggressive  movement 
seen. 

I  directed  Lieutenant  Sproston  to  send  his  pilot  on  board  this  vessel, 
who  reports  the  channel  at  Aquia  very  narrow,  with  but  10  to  12  feet 
of  water — not  room  enough  to  turn  the  vessel  in.  My  pilot  says  there 
is  but  9  feet. 

I  conclude  it  best  under  the  circumstances  to  proceed  in  obedience  to 
your  instructions  to  the  Rappahannock. 

If  a  storming  party  were  in  an  armed  steamer  of  light  draft,  with 
boats  to  land,  the  battery  could  be  taken  and  destroyed.  Report  says 
they  have  four  32-pounders  and  two  fieldpieces. 

I  forward  this  by  the  Marion ,  transport,  bound  to  Washington  from 
Hew  York,  with  stores,  I  suppose. 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  sir,  your  obedient  servant, 

Jno.  P.  Gillis, 
Commander ,  U.  8.  Navy.

ONE  MILE . 


Mount  Yernon, 

Lieutenant  Sproston ,  Commanding, 

Off  Aquia  Creek,  May  14. 

Anchored  the  night  previous  in  position  1.  Shortly  after  heard  the  beat¬ 
ing  of  drums  at  Aquia  Creek  landing.  At  midnight  blowing  and  rainin 
let  go  the  second  anchor.  At  dayligb  t  the  reveille  was  beaten  in  the  sam'e 


OPERATIONS  ON  THE  POTOMAC  AND  RAPPAHANNOCK.  463 


quarter.  W eiglied  anchor  and  stood  in  as  indicated  by  curved  line.  Dis¬ 
covered  an  earthen  battery  inshore  of  the  end  of  wharf.  When  within 
about  a  third  of  a  mile  stopped  the  boat,  keeping  the  long  gun  trained  on 
the  battery.  Observed  with  the  glass  an  earthen  battery,  semicircular  in 
form,  having  four  embrasures ;  in  the  one  next  the  house  was  a  32-pounder 
manned  and  trained  on  the  boat,  an  officer  holding  the  lock  string.  In 
the  second  embrasure  they  were  preparing  to  mount  a  gun.  In  the 
third  was  apparently  a  fieldpiece  pointed  toward  the  opposite  side  of 
the  wharf,  at  the  end  of  which  we  supposed,  from  the  number  of  men 
gathered  there,  were  two  more  fleldpieces  concealed.  The  men,  some 
twenty  in  number,  at  first  advanced  to  the  end  of  the  wharf,  and  then, 
as  we  approached,  retired  to  the  main  fortification,  where  they  were 
now  engaged  in  cutting  down  two  trees  in  front  of  the  fort,  training 
the  large  guns  and  loading  small  arms  and  digging  out  the  interior  of 
the  fort,  most  of  which  was  visible  to  the  eye  unassisted  by  a  glass. 

WThile  steaming  into  position  noticed  the  Pocahontas  coming  down 
the  river.  Having  remained  stationary  some  ten  or  fifteen  minutes, 
making  the  above  observations,  backed  round,  steamed  out,  and  com¬ 
municated  with  the  Pocahontas. 

I  am  informed  by  my  pilot  (Captain  Walter)  that  a  young  man,  Henry 
Hainey,  who  runs  a  sloop  in  the  river  and  who  was  driven  out  of  Alex¬ 
andria  on  account  of  his  Union  sentiments,  came  up  from  Aquia  Creek 
yesterday  and  reported  having  seen  there  in  battery  four  guns  of  the 
size  of  this  steamer’s  (32-pounder)  and  two  fleldpieces.  I  noticed  about 
fifty  men  in  and  about  the  battery,  many  muskets,  and  some  in  uniform. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

J.  Glendy  Sproston, 
Lieutenant,  Commanding  Mount  Vernon. 

Commander  Gillis,  U.  S.  Navy, 

Commanding  U.  8.  8.  Pocahontas.

U.  S.  S.  Keystone  State, 

Washington ,  May  14,  1861. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  the  arrival  here  of  this  vessel, 
which  sailed  on  the  4th  instant  in  conformity  with  instructions  from 
the  Department  of  the  3d  instant. 

The  steamer  proceeded  on  the  afternoon  of  the  3d  to  the  arsenal, 
received  on  board  a  number  of  gun  carriages,  ordnance  stores,  etc., 
which  were  landed  at  Forts  Washington  and  Monroe.  Upon  arriving 
at  tbe  last-named  place  I  found  the  steamer  Cambridge  taking  in  the 
Columbiads,  shot,  and  shell  that  this  vessel  was  designed  to  convey  to 
Washington.  I  then  proceeded  with  all  possible  dispatch  to  New  York, 
arriving  there  on  the  afternoon  of  the  7th  and,  after  receiving  on  board 
from  the  navy  yard  the  provisions  and  from  the  assistant  quartermaster- 
general  three  rifled  cannon  and  two  brass  fleldpieces,  sailed  for  this 
place,  arriving  here  at  10  o’clock  this  morning.  The  vessel  was  delayed 
some  twelve  hours  in  the  Potomac,  owing  to  a  dense  fog. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Stephen  D.  Trenchard, 

Lieutenant ,  Commanding.

Report  of  Lieutenant  Fillehroivn,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  TJ.  S.  S.  Ana- 

costia,  of  information  received  during  a  reconnoissance  on  that  vessel. 

II.  S.  S.  Anacostia, 

Washington,  May  15,  1861. 

Sir  :  I  have  the  honor  to  report  to  the  Department  that  to-day  I 
made  a  trip  down  the  Potomac  as  far  as  Smith’s  Point  (about  45  miles), 
having  on  board  Lieutenant  [Thomas  S.]  Phelps,  of  the  Coast  Survey, 
now  engaged  in  making  a  reconnoissance  of  the  river. 

As  far  as  we  could  discover,  there  were  no  indications  of  batteries 
being  erected,  nor  could  we  perceive  any  hostile  gathering  or  any  assem¬ 
blage  of  persons. 

From  a  fisherman  who  was  at  Dumfries  on  Sunday  last  I  gathered 
the  information  that  there  were  no  troops  assembling  there.  He  reports 
that  a  week  previous  to  that  time  there  had  been  a  company  of  about 
one  hundred  men  there,  but  they  only  remained  one  day. 

This  man  also  informed  me  that  there  is  a  battery  being  constructed 
at  Aquia  Creek,  a  short  distance  from  the  wharf,  the  guns,  some  tenor 
fifteen  m  number,  having  been  brought  either  from  Richmond  or  Fred¬ 
ericksburg  by  rail. 

This  fisherman  obtained  his  information  from  hands  employed  by  a 
man  named  Evans,  who,  he  says,  is  engaged  in  conveying  mails  to  the 
Maryland  shore  from  a  place  known  as  Evansport,  opposite  Budd’s 
Ferry. 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Thos.  Scott  Fillebrown, 

Lieutenant,  Commanding.

IT.  S.  S.  Pocahontas, 
Chesapeake  Bay,  May  16,  1861. 

Sir  :  I  would  respectfully  state  that  this  vessel  and  the  Mount  Ver¬ 
non,  steamboat,  ran  up  the  Rappahannock  20  miles  to  the  town  of 


OPERATIONS  ON  THE  POTOMAC  AND  RAPPAHANNOCK.  465 


Urbana  without  meeting  or  seeing  any  offensive  demonstrations;  all 
peaceful  along  the  shores,  and  tlie  people  employed  [in]  farming  and 
fishing. 

We  have  some  reports,  which  may  be  of  the  sensation  order  or  very 
much  exaggerated,  circulated  possibly  by  secessionists  to  bring  on  some 
aggressive  act  which  may  be  used  politically  to  affect  the  election  soon 
to  come  off'  in  Virginia. 

I  dispatched  the  Mount  Vernon  to  overhaul  two  schooners  standing 
up  the  bay.  They  proved  to  be  from  the  Piankatank,  with  strong  Union 
passengers  on  board,  bound  to  Baltimore. 

On  the  15th  instant  sent  the  Mount  Vernon,  Lieutenant  Sproston,  to 
Indian  Creek  to  look  for  light-boat  reported  to  be  there.  His  report  is 
respectfully  submitted. 

We  have  seen  nothing  of  the  steamers  Virginia  and  Logan ,  and  prob¬ 
ably  will  not,  as  they  are  reported  to  be  at  or  near  Fredericksburg. 

Chased  to-day  the  schooner  Osprey  and  having  to  run  to  abreast  of 
Old  Point  before  overhauling  her,  1  communicated  with  the  flagship 
Minnesota.  There  has  been  captured  here  a  quantity  of  tobacco,  rumor 
says  $300,000  worth,  and  sent  North.  No  further  news. 

Left  the  Mount  Vernon  lying  off’  and  on  the  entrance  of  the  Rappa¬ 
hannock.  Met  the  river  steamer  Baltimore.  The  Osprey's  papers  were 
all  right;  her  cargo,  resin,  for  New  York.  Am  on  the  lookout  for  trans¬ 
ports  with  troops;  will  convoy  up  and  be  vigilant  in  examining  all 
vessels  of  a  suspicious  character. 

I  am,  respectfully,  sir,  your  obedient  servant, 

Jno.  P.  Gillis, 
Commander ,  TI.  S.  Navy. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  Navy,  Washington.

Sir  :  In  obedience  to  your  instructions,  proceeded  up  Indian  Creek 
in  the  Mount  Vernon  as  far  as  practicable — about  5  miles.  No  light 
vessel  to  be  seen.  Returning,  anchored  at  the  mouth;  landed  with  the 
pilot  and  called  at  the  residence  of  Judge  Carter,  who  states  that  the 
light-boat  had  been  taken  away  the  week  previous  by  a  naval  party. 
1  proceeded  then  to  steam  into  Great  Wicomico,  below  Smith’s  Point, 
and  examined  Cockle’s  [Cockrell],  the  main  branch,  and  Mill  Creek,  but 
could  see  no  light-boat.  From  what  was  said  at  Indian  River  [Creek1?], 
we  expected  to  meet  with  a  show  of  resistance  in  these  last-mentioned 
creeks,  but  none  was  made. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

J.  Glendy  Sproston,

Report  of  Lieutenant  Fillebroicn ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  commanding  TJ.  S.  S.  Ana- 
costia ,  regarding  Confederate  battery  at  Aquia  Creek. 

U.  S.  S.  Anacostia, 

Washington,  May  17,  1861. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  inform  the  Department  that  a  battery  has 
been  erected  at  Aquia  Creek  immediately  around  the  hotel  at  the  ter¬ 
minus  of  the  railroad. 

As  far  as  I  could  discover  there  are  only  four  guns  mounted,  one  of 
which  appeared  to  be  of  heavy  caliber  and  was  manned  while  I  was 
passing.  The  work  does  not  appear  to  be  completed  on  the  east  front. 

I  observed  a  number  of  men,  I  should  judge  about  200;  some  were 
armed  and  the  others  were  laboring  at  the  earthworks. 

A  small  Confederate  flag  is  hoisted  upon  the  engine  house  and  the 
steamer  George  Page  is  lying  at  anchor  in  the  creek  about  half  a  mile 
above  the  battery.  •  I  could  not  see  that  any  picket  guards  or  sentinels 
were  stationed  along  the  heights  extending  from  the  battery  toward 
the  mouth  of  Potomac  Creek. 

Yery  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Thos.  Scott  Fillebrown, 

LAeutenant,  Commanding. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy,  Washington,  D.  C.

[Enclosure.] 

TJ.  S.  Armed  Steamer  Mount  Yernon, 

Inside  Windmill  Point,  Rappahannock  River,  May  16,  1861. 

Sir:  I  have  to  report  that  during  the  day  no  vessels  have  passed  up 
or  down  the  river.  The  people  on  shore  consider  the  river  in  a  state  of 
close  blockade.  Boarded  a  schooner,  the  Falcon,  in  ballast,  belonging 
to  the  settlement  opposite,  who  stated  that  the  inhabitants  on  the 
banks  of  the  river  were  fearful  that  we  would  attack  them, 


468  OPERATIONS  ON  THE  POTOMAC  AND  RAPPAHANNOCK. 

* 

I  told  Mm  to  say  to  them  that  we  were  here  to  attack  only  those  who 
were  in  arms  against  the  U.  S.  Government  or  were  assisting  the  rebels. 
Discovering  a  pole  at  the  end  of  the  point,  went  on  shore  in  an  armed 
boat;  found  halyards  attached  to  it;  considered  it  erected  to  show  a 
false  light,  cut  it  down,  and  sent  word  to  the  people  living  in  the  neigh¬ 
borhood  the  reason  for  my  doing  so.  Learned  that  during  the  night  it 
had  been  guarded  by  a  party  of  eighteen  armed  men,  and  that  it  was 
the  first  of  a  system  of  poles  used  for  telegraphic  purposes  between  the 
point  and  Fredericksburg,  lights  being  hoisted  at  night  and  flags  by 
day.  Afterwards  noticed  similar  poles  farther  up  the  river,  time  of 
communication  with  Fredericksburg  being  from  one  to  two  hours.  A 
man  also  came  off  from  Stingray  Point  who  said  the  authorities  per¬ 
mitted  but  would  not  authorize  him  to  come.  He  said  the  residents  on 
shore  wanted  to  know  the  steamer’s  intentions;  I  replied  as  above. 

At  2  p.  m.  the  steamer  Baltimore  passed  down  the  bay.  During  the 
night  all  quiet,  no  sails  passing  up  or  down  the  river. 

Yery  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

J.  Glendy  Sproston, 
Lieutenant ,  Commanding  Mount  Vernon. 

Commander  Gillis,  U.  S.  Navy, 

Commanding  U.  S.  8.  Pocahontas.

Report  of  Brigadier- General  Butler ,  TJ.  8.  Army ,  commanding  Depart¬ 
ment  of  Annapolis ,  of  an  expedition  for  the  recapture  of  Smith’s  Point 
light-boat ,  in  Wicomico  River,  Virginia. 

Headquarters  Department  of  Annapolis, 

Washington ,  May  18,  1861. 

Sir  :  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that,  having  received  information 
that  one  of  the  light-ships  removed  from  their  stations  in  Chesapeake 
Bay  was  concealed  in  a  branch  of  the  Wicomico  River,  I  ordered  Lieu¬ 
tenant  Flusser,  of  the  U.  S.  Navy,  with  the  chartered  steamer  William 
Underwood ,  having  on  board  thirty  seamen  from  the  Alleghany  and 
Forward ,  and  a  detachment  from  the  force  at  Annapolis  to  find  and 
recapture  her.  This  service  was  successfully  performed  and  the  prize 
now  lies  in  Annapolis  Harbor.  A  force  of  about  thirty  men  disputed 
the  recapture  of  the  vessel  and  a  brisk  fire  was  kept  up  on  the  steamer 
while  she  remained  in  range.  I  am  happy  to  report  no  casualties  on 
our  side. 

Owing  to  the  concealed  position  of  the  enemy  it  is  impossible  to  say 
whether  they  incurred  any  loss.  The  detachment  composed  of  five 
men  from  the  Thirteenth  New  York,  Lieutenant  Woodward,  and  two 


OPERATIONS  ON  THE  POTOMAC  AND  RAPPAHANNOCK.  469 

guns  and  twenty  men  from  the  Eighth  New  York,  Lieutenant  Byrnes, 
the  whole  under  command  of  Captain  [R.  S.]  Fay  [jr.|,  of  my  staff, 
behaved  with  great  steadiness.  The  prize  is  the  Smith’s  Point  light¬ 
ship.  She  has  been  stripped  of  everything  which  could  be  removed, 
but  the  vessel  is  perfectly  good. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  with  much  respect,  your  obedient  servant, 

Benj.  F.  Butler, 
Brigadier-  General.  Commanding. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy.

Abstract  log  of  steamer  Mount  Vernon ,  Lieutenant  Sproston,  U.  8.  Navy , 
commanding,  from  May  13  to  19, 1861. 

May  13, 1861. — 1  p.  m.,  left  the  yard.  Communicated  with  the  Poca¬ 
hontas,  Pawnee,  and  Fort  Washington.  At  8  p.  m.,  anchored  off'  Aquia 
Creek.  Heard  the  beat  of  tattoo  and  reveille  and  standing  in. 

May  14. — This  morning  discovered  Aquia  Creek  battery.  Stood  out 
and  made  report  to  Commander  Gillis.  Pocahontas  in  compauy,  steamed 
down  the  river  and  bay  to  mouth  of  Rappahannock.  Stood  in  and 
boarded  schooners;  no  news.  Out  again  and  anchored  alongside  Poca¬ 
hontas. 

May  15. — In  company  with  Pocahontas  steamed  up  the  Rappahannock 
to  country  town  of  Urbaua  (20  miles  up  the  river).  Returned  again 
to  the  mouth.  River  deserted  by  crafts.  9  a.  m.,  parted  company 
with  Pocahontas.  Steamed  up  and  into  Indian  Creek  to  head  of  navi¬ 
gation  and  returned.  Country  quiet;  but  few  inhabitants  visible.  At 
the  mouth  anchored;  visited  a  county  judge;  learned  that  Mr.  Price’s 
property  was  held  by  the  authorities  until  he  presented  himself  for 
examination;  men  still  in  confinement.  Steamed  up  the  Virginia  side 
and  into  Great  Wicomico  Branch,  Cockle’s  [Cockrells],  and  Mill  Creek. 
From  information  received,  expected  resistance  here.  Rone  was  offered. 
Returning,  boarded  a  schooner  of  Philadelphia  from  Fredericksburg; 
had  been  detained  by  authorities  for  several  days;  wanted  him  to  con¬ 
voy  guns  to  Mathias  Point.  Reported  sending  guns  and  several  com¬ 
panies  to  Aquia  Creek.  On  Sunday,  Virginia  carrying  guns  to  Bowlers 
Rocks,  which  point,  40  miles  up  the  river,  strongly  fortified.  Did  not 
know  where  steamer  Logan  was.  With  Pocahontas,  anchored  off  mouth 
of  river. 

May  16. — At  2  a.  m.,  chased  a  passing  steamer;  did  not  come  up  with 
her;  steamer  bound  down  the  bay.  At  daylight  steamed  out  into  the 
bay  with  Pocahontas ;  blowing  fresh.  Parted  company,  returned  and 
anchored  well  inside  the  mouth  of  the  river.  2  p.  m.,  discovering  a  pole 
with  halyards  rove  at  end  of  Mill  Creek  Point,  considered  erected 
for  the  purpose  of  hoisting  a  false  light;  landed  and  cut  it  down. 
Boarded  a  schooner,  and  a  boat  from  shore  came  off.  Learned  an  armed 
guard  had  been  stationed  at  pole  night  previous ;  that  it  was  one  of  a 
chain  communicating  for  telegraphic  purposes  with  Fredericksburg. 
During  the  night  anchored  with  spring  on  cable.  During  the  day  no 
vessel  passed  up  or  down. 

May  17. — At  daylight,  Pocahontas  steaming  up  the  bay;  anchored 
during  the  forenoon,  boarding  vessels  in  the  bay;  Pocahontas  went 
down  the  bay  and  returned  in  the  evening;  no  vessels  in  the  river 
during  the  day. 

May  18. — At  daylight,  steamed  out  into  the  bay  in  company  with  the 
Pocahontas-,  left  the  Pocahontas  outside  and  returned  to  anchorage; 
visited  the  shore  in  an  armed  boat;  people  distrustful,  otherwise  civil; 


OPERATIONS  ON  THE  POTOMAC  AND  RAPPAHANNOCK.  471 

obtained  a  quantity  of  water  for  the  steamer;  was  told  anyone  who 
brought  oft  supplies  to  the  steamer  would  be  hung;  volunteers  of  county 
to  muster  on  Wednesday  next;  county  much  in  want  of  usual  supplies 
from  Baltimore;  hauled  alongside  of  Pocahontas  to  coal;  smoke  of 
steamer  seen  down  the  bay,  Virginia  side;  cast  off,  steamed  out,  met 
and  boarded  the  George  Peabody,  with  Government  stores;  communi¬ 
cated  with  the  Pocahontas;  received  orders  and  dispatches;  returned 
to  George  Peabody  and,  with  her  in  convoy,  steamed  up  the  bay  and 
Potomac  River,  speaking  and  boarding  vessels  and  propellers  on  the 
way;  anchored  at  8  p.  m.  oft'  Lower  Cedar  Point.  A  schooner  with 
Government  lumber  also  anchored  near. 

May  19.— At  daylight  got  under  way;  Peabody  and  schooner  in  com¬ 
pany;  on  Mathias  Point,  no  battery;  at  Aquia  Greek,  three  more  guns 
mounted  in  barbette  below  the  house;  steamer  Page  in  sight  below  the 
bend  of  the  creek;  no  signs  of  her  having  steam  up;  sent  Captain 
Walter  on  board  George  Peabody  to  pilot  her  up ;  lost  sight  of  schooner 
above  Aquia  Creek ;  communicated  with  Fort  Washington  and  Pawnee. 

Note. — The  residents  along  the  shore  of  Virginia  have  threatened 
Captain  Walter,  my  pilot,  through  those  Avho  have  communicated  with 
the  steamer,  his  knowledge  of  every  creek  and  inlet  on  the  coast  being 
the  cause. 

Respectfully  submitted.

Report  of  Commander  Gillis ,  TJ.  S.  Navy ,  commanding  TJ.  S.  S.  Pocahontas, 
of  the  cruise  of  that  vessel  in  the  Potomac ,  Chesapeake  Bay ,  and  Rappa¬ 
hannock  River. 

U.  S.  S.  Pocahontas, 

Potomac  River ,  May  21,  1861. 

Sir:  My  last  report  to  you  was  by  river  steamer  Mount  Vernon , 
which  vessel  I  dispatched  to  convoy  the  transport  George  Peabody  to 
Washington  with  Government  stores.  Since  then  we  have  run  up  to 
near  Urbana  (second  time)  on  the  Rappahannock,  looked  into  the 
Piankatank,  and  run  up  the  bay  alongshore.  All  quiet. 

[May]  19tli  discovered  a  steamer  ahead  and  aground  off  the  entrance 
of  the  Potomac.  Went  to  her  assistance.  She  got  off'  at  sunset  and 
was  the  Baltimore,  of  Baltimore,  laden  with  lard  and  bacon,  bound  to 
Havana. 

[May]  20th  stood  down  the  bay.  Off'  the  Rappahannock  met  trans¬ 
port  steamer  Coatzacoalcos ,  from  New  York,  with  Government  stores 
for  Washington.  Took  her  under  convoy,  directing  her  to  follow  astern. 
Blowing  fresli.  While  running  along  with  her  well  off  our  port  quar¬ 
ter  she  took  a  sheer  and  ranged  up  alongside  suddenly;  put  our  helm 
a  port,  but  could  not  prevent  the  collision.  She  struck  us  on  the  port 
quarter,  stove  in  our  quarter  boat,  bending  iron  davits,  carrying  away 


OPERATIONS  ON  THE  POTOMAC  AND  RAPPAHANNOCK.  473 


part  of  main  channels,  railing  and  stanchions  on  poop,  etc.  I  censured 
the  master  for  his  awkward,  lubberly  management.  He  replied  lie 
could  not  help  it.  Had  he  stopped  liis  engines  or  sheered  her  with 
starboard  helm  the  accident  would  not  have  occurred.  It  will  be  nec¬ 
essary  to  make  these  repairs,  as  also  to  finish  those  on  engines. 

We  had  intercourse  with  several  persons  on  the  Rappahannock  and 
have  concluded  that  the  reports  given  generally  are  for  sensational  arti¬ 
cles,  either  without  foundation  or  very  much  exaggerated,  particularly 
in  regard  to  batteries,  number  of  soldiers,  etc.;  vide  that  published  in 
connection  with  Aquia  Creek,  where  one  gun  frightened  off  three  or 
four  steamers.  The  old  Virginia,  steamboat,  is  at  Fredericksburg  and 
Logan  up  York  River,  which  is  blockaded.  One  or  two  of  the  river 
steamboats  would  be  more  efficient  off  the  Rappahannock  on  account  of 
their  speed.  At  7:30  a.  in.,  21st,  picked  up  the  steamboat  James  Guy. 
She  came  off  from  Machodoc  Creek.  Ran  in  as  far  as  water  would  per¬ 
mit  to  Aquia  landing.  The  steamboat  James  [  George)  Page  lying  in  the 
creek.  Saw  an  earth  battery  of  four  embrasures,  but  no  guns  visible; 
a  wheel  carriage  for  howitzers  on  beach;  about  100  men  seen  on  the 
wharf  and  about  dwelling  house.  We  remained  a  short  time  making 
observations,  then  proceeded  up  the  river.  Will  deliver  the  James  Guy 
at  navy  yard. 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  sir,  your  obedient  servant, 

Jno.  P.  Gillis, 
Commander ,  U.  S.  Navy. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles,

Report  of  Commander  Ward ,  TJ.  8.  Navy ,  commanding  Potomac  Flotilla , 
of  affairs  on  the  Potomac  River . 


U.  S.  S.  (Flotilla)  Freeborn, 

Potomac  River ,  May  22,  1861. 

Sir:  Steaming  down  the  river  to-day,  I  have  gone  close  in  with 
several  points  designated  as  the  White  House,  etc,,  on  the  Virginia 
shore,  but  could  discover  no  signs  of  a  hostile  nature. 

The  pilot  ran  me  fast  aground  at  a  point  5  miles  above  Mathias. 
Every  effort  to  get  afloat  having  failed,  1  have  taken  the  liberty  to 
detain  the  Philadelphia,  armed  tug,  which  conveys  this.  With  her  aid 
in  various  ways,  lightening,  etc.,  I  hope  soon  to  get  off'.  The  place  is 
rendered  dangerous  by  removal  of  the  buoy,  which  secession  parties 
have  done. 

Landing  abreast  this  place  on  the  Maryland  side,  I  found  the  inhab¬ 
itants  strongly  Union  in  sentiment.  They  had  no  intercourse  with  the 
other  shore,  knew  nothing  of  any  batteries  there;  said,  however,  that 
constant  communication  was  kept  up  between  Port  Tobacco,  a  little 
way  below,  and  Mathias  Point.  Disaffected  Marylanders,  they  say,  go 
over  that  way  to  join  the  Virginia  forces;  also  that  supplies  pass.  I 
shall  report  all  this  to  the  flag-officer  below. 

If  I  chance  to  pass  Mathias  Point  by  daylight  shall  give  it  a  critical 
inspection  and  go  so  close  as  to  tempt  their  tire,  and  know  therefore  if 
their  preparations  have  progressed  considerably. 

Possibly  the  flag-officer  may  direct  my  return  to  this  region,  in  which 
event  I  shall  be  pretty  sure  to  know  something  about  it. 

Considering  that  the  detention  of  the  tug  will  make  only  the  differ¬ 
ence  between  arriving  in  the  evening  of  to-day  and  the  morning  of 
to-morrow,  I  have  not  hesitated  in  the  matter. 

Very  respectfully,  I  am,  sir,  your  obedient  [servant], 

J.  H.  Ward, 

Commander. 


Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy,  W ashington ,  D.  C. 


p.  s. — I  open  this  to  say  that  the  shoal  is  off  Maryland  Point,  called 
Tomkins  Shoal-  [Matomkin?].  The  buoy  was  in  place  when  I  went  up 
on  Sunday  and  was  set  adrift  last  night;  hence  our  difficulty.

The  occupation  of  Alexandria,  Ya.,  May  24,  1861. 

Report  of  commandant  navy  yard,  Washington,  of  the  assistance  rendered  by  the  Navy  in  the 
occupation  of  Alexandria,  Va.,  and  of  the  killing  of  Colonel  Ellsworth. 

Commandant’s  Office,  Navy  Yard, 

Washington,  May  24,  1861. 

Sir:  Conformably  with  the  request  of  General  Mansfield,  the  steam¬ 
ers,  lighters,  and  boats  at  this  yard  were  sent  to  assist  in  the  operations 
of  last  night. 

Between  2  and  4  a.  m.  the  regiment  of  Zouaves,  commanded  by  Colo¬ 
nel  Ellsworth,  were  embarked  from  Giesboro  Point  in  the  steamers  and 
moved  to  Alexandria,  where  they  landed  and  occupied  position  about 
daylight. 

After  this  was  effected,  I  regret  to  say  that  Colonel  Ellsworth  was 
deliberately  murdered  by  one  of  the  inhabitants,  who  was  himself  killed 
instantly  by  a  private  who  was  near  the  colonel  at  the  time. 

My  short  acquaintance  with  this  officer  fully  impressed  me  with  the 
correctness  of  the  common  opinion  of  his  excellent  qualities  as  a  citizen 
and  a  soldier. 

I  conveyed  his  body  to  this  place,  where,  with  every  mark  of  respect, 
it  has  been  landed  under  the  escort  of  Zouaves,  Seventy-first  Regiment, 
and  marines,  and  deposited  in  a  suitable  place  under  a  proper  guard. 

The  remains  of  this  gallant  soldier  await  the  further  disposition  of 
the  authorities. 

The  steamers  Baltimore,  Mount  Vernon,  and  Guy  were  commanded 
respectively  by  Lieutenant  West,  Master  Morris,  and  Acting  Master 
Woods;the  creditable  performance  of  the  duty  intrusted  to  them  in  this 
case  entitles  them  to  my  thanks. 

The  presence  of  Mr.  Fox,  the  chief  clerk  of  the  Department,  was 
exceedingly  acceptable,  and  the  interest  he  manifested  during  the  whole 
affair  had  an  excellent  effect  in  impressing  all  concerned  with  a  sense 
of  the  importance  which  the  Department  felt  in  the  operation. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Jno.  A.  Dahlgren, 

Commandant. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy.

Report  of  Commander  Rowan,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Pawnee,  transmitting  report 
of  Lieutenant  Lowry,  II.  S.  Navy,  regarding  the  occupation  of  Alexandria,  Va. 

U.  S.  S.  Pawnee, 

Off  Alexandria,  May  29,  1861. 

Sir  :  In  obedience  to  your  order  of  yesterday’s  date,  to  furnish  the 
Department  with  a  minute  report  of  your  (my)  proceedings  during  the 
night  and  morning  of  the  23d  and  24th  instant,  communicating  any¬ 
thing  of  interest  or  importance  that  came  under  your  (my)  observation, 
in  reply,  I  have  the  honor  to  state  that  during  the  night  of  the  23d 
nothing  of  interest  or  importance  occurred.  On  the  morning  of  the 
24th,  about  daylight,  two  steamers  containing  the  Zouave  regiment 
approached  Alexandria  from  the  navy  yard,  for  the  purpose  of  landing 
and  occupying  that  city.  As  soon  as  the  steamers  came  in  full  view  of 
the  city,  and  so  near  as  not  to  expose  the  secrecy  of  the  expedition,  I 
sent  Lieutenant  [R.  B.]  Lowry  on  shore  to  demand  the  surrender  of  the 
town.  Lieutenant  Lowry  returned  to  the  wharf  in  time  to  meet  Colonel 
Ellsworth  as  he  landed  and  informed  him  that  no  resistance  would  be 
made — that  the  town  would  be  evacuated.  Shortly  after  Lieutenant 
Lowry  left  the  ship  I  sent  Lieutenant  [J.  C.]  Chaplin  in  the  first  cutter 
to  lie  oft' the  starting  point  of  the  railroad  cars,  and  to  jump  on  shore 
immediately  the  steamers  touched  the  wharf  and  cut  off  the  departure 
of  the  early  morning  train  then  at  that  point.  The  engine  escaped,  but 
the  burden  cars  laden  with  railroad  iron  were  captured. 

I  sent  a  cutter  in  charge  of  the  master  to  bring  out  two  steamers,  the 
Collyer  and  Gipsy ,  that  had  been  seized  by  the  secessionists.  The 
former  belongs  to  parties  in  Washington  and  the  latter  to  parties  in 
Maryland.  Both  these  vessels  have  been  turned  over  to  their  respec¬ 
tive  commanders  by  the  authority  of  the  Department  and  are  now  on 
their  routes,  the  first  between  Washington  and  Alexandria  and  the 
other  between  Alexandria  and  Port  Washington. 

I  directed  Lieutenant  Lowry  to  return  to  the  town  and  cooperate 
with  the  troops,  under  the  impression  that  Colonel  Ellsworth’s  command 
was  the  only  force  then  moving  on  Alexandria,  and  that  his  knowledge 
of  the  localities,  together  with  this  additional  force,  would,  in  case  of 
resistance,  be  valuable. 

In  demanding  the  surrender  of  Alexandria  I  was  actuated  solely  by- 
motives  of  humanity.  I  knew  the  town  to  be  full  of  helpless  women 
and  children,  mostly  of  the  middle  and  poorer  classes,  whom  I  saw 
running  frantically  through  the  streets  in  search  of  protection  as  the 
troops  landed.

[Enclosure.] 

TJ.  S.  S.  Pawnee, 

Off  Alexandria,  Va.,May  24,  1861 — 10:30  a.  m. 

Sir:  In  obedience  to  your  verbal  order  given  this  morning  about 
4:  20  a.  in.,  I  proceeded  on  shore  a  t  this  place  and  communicated  with  a 
Major  [George  H.]  Terrett,  commanding  the  Virginia  secession  forces 
at  Alexandria.  Iu  your  name  I  demanded  the  surrender  of  the  place, 
stating  that  as  we  were  prepared  to  seize  the  place,  it  would  be  useless 
to  resist,  and  that  you  were  actuated  simply  by  a  desire  to  spare  the 
shedding  of  blood  of  women  and  children. 

The  interview  was  held  in  the  open  street,  surrounded  by  excited 
soldiers.  Major  Terrett  said  he  would  not  surrender;  that  he  would 
evacuate,  or  was  about  evacuating;  that  if  hostilities  were  not  opened 
upon  him  he  would  not  use  any.  He  wanted  to  know  how  much  time 
he  could  have.  I  told  him  I  did  not  know;  I  would  return  to  the  Caw- 
nee',  that  no  time  was  to  be  lost.  He  said  he  would  require  till  8  a.  m. 
to  get  such  women,  children,  and  property  out  as  he  would  require. 
I  said,  “Very  well ;  I  will  go  at  once  to  the  Pawnee.  Should  the  troops 
land  and  you  make  no  resistance,  I  have  no  doubt  that  no  harm  will 
be  done  to  the  town  and  its  inhabitants.  Should  the  Pawnee  be 
obliged  to  open  her  batteries  no  one  knows  better  than  yourself  what 
would  be  the  result.” 

I  hastened  to  the  river  side  and  reached  the  wharf  just  in  time  to 
witness  the  first  approach  of  the  Zouaves  under  Colonel  Ellsworth. 
The  sentries  on  the  wharf  fired  their  muskets,  which  was  returned  by 
a  scattering  fire  from  the  troops  on  board  the  transports.  As  the  troops 
commenced  to  land  I  sought  out  Colonel.  Ellsworth,  told  him  iu  these 
words:  “Sir,  I  am  an  officer  of  the  Pawnee.  I  have  been  on  shore  with 
a  flag  of  truce,  demanding  the  surrender  of  the  town.  The  command¬ 
ing  officer  is  already  evacuating.  He  promises  to  make  no  resistance. 
The  town  is  full  of  women  and  children.”  Colonel  Ellsworth  replied: 
“All  right,  sir;  I  will  harm  no  one.” 

I  then  proceeded  with  a  detachment  of  men  from  the  Pawnee  under 
Lieutenant  Chaplin  and  took  possession  of  the  railroad  and  some  bur¬ 
den  cars. 

I  informed  Colonel  Ellsworth  of  the  whereabouts  of  the  telegraph 
and  other  places.  He  landed  his  regiment  with  great  rapidity.  I  pro¬ 
ceeded  to  the  Paicnee  and  reported  to  you,  when  you  sent  me  back  at 
once  to  cooperate  with  the  troops  and  to  say  that,  as  they  had  landed, 
you  had  no  further  jurisdiction,  and  that  I  should  accompany  the 
troops,  with  the  Pawnee"1  s  force,  and  take  part  in  what  should  occur. 
1  did  so;  found  Colonel  Ellsworth  was  not  at  the  head  of  his  regiment, 
which  had  marched  some  distance  up  the  street.  After  waiting  some 
time  I  advanced  through  the  upper  part  of  the  town,  hoisted  the  Amer¬ 
ican  ensign  on  a  street  flagstaff,. and  also  upon  the  custom-house,  where 
I  left  a  small  guard,  and  after  a  rapid  march  through  the  town  reached 
the  depot,  where  I  found  troops  of  the  United  States  in  possession. 


480  OPERATIONS  ON  THE  POTOMAC  AND  RAPPAHANNOCK. 

These  troops  had  advanced  by  land  from  Washington  and  were  under 
command  of  Colonel  Willcox.  I  stated  to  him  the  substance  of  the 
above  report  subsequently,  as  Colonel  [O.  B.J  Willcox  called  on  board 
this  ship  for  a  better  explanation  of  our  position.  It  is  proper  to  state 
that  your  order  to  me  was  simply  “to  demand  the  surrender  of  the 
town.”  Any  misunderstanding  which  the  rebels  may  have  had  was 
owing  to  their  excited  condition  and  exhibited  by  the  rapidity  in  which 
they  evacuated,  not  even  waiting  for  the  time  for  which  they  stipulated. 

The  spirit  of  my  language  was  intended  to  apply  only  for  the  “pro¬ 
tection  of  helpless  women  and  children,”  and  I  so  distinctly  stated  to 
Major  Terrett. 

In  passing  to  and  from  the  interview  with  Major  Terrett  I  observed 
small  bodies  of  men  in  marching  order,  hastening  out  of  the  town. 

I  am,  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

R.  B.  Lowry, 
Lieutenant ,  TJ.  S.  Navy. 

Commander  S.  C.  Rowan, 

Commanding  U.  S.  Steam  Sloop  Pawnee. 


Letter  from  the  Secretary  of  the  Navy  to  Commander  Rowan,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  S. 
Pawnee,  expressing  disapproval  of  his  course  in  connection  with  the  occupation  of  Alexan¬ 
dria,  Va. 

Navy  Department,  June  5, 1861. 

Sir  :  I  have  received  your  report  of  the  29tli  ultimo,  made  in  pursu¬ 
ance  of  the  order  sent  to  you  by  the  Department  on  the  day  preceding, 
together  with  a  copy  of  the  report  of  Lieutenant  Lowry  to  yourself  on 
the  24th  ultimo,  detailing  his  proceeding  at  Alexandria  on  the  morn¬ 
ing  of  that  day,  which  had  not  previously  been  communicated  to  the 
Department. 

It  is  stated  in  your  report  that  on  the  morning  of  the  24tli  instant, 
about  daylight,  two  steamers  containing  the  Zouave  regiment  ap¬ 
proached  Alexandria  from  the  navy  yard  for  the  purpose  of  landing  and 
occupying  that  city.  As  soon  as  the  steamer  came  in  full  view  of  the 
city  and  so  near  as  not  to  expose  the  secrecy  of  the  expedition,  1  (you) 
sent  Lieutenant  Lowry  on  shore  to  demand  the  surrender  of  the  town. 
This  portion  of  your  report,  so  manifestly  inconsistent  with  correct  dis¬ 
cipline  and  the  obligations  due  to  the  army  which  was  making  a  secret 
movement  on  Alexandria,  was  read  with  pain  aDd  surprise.  You  have 
received  no  orders  from  this  Department  to  demand  the  surrender  of 
Alexandria,  yet  when  you  became  aware  that  a  portion  of  the  army  was 
moving  on  that  place  you  volunteered  an  interference,  which  attended, 
perhaps,  by  no  serious  inconvenience  in  this  instance,  might  have 
defeated  the  object  intended  and  been  followed  by  serious  disaster.  As 
it  was,  your  demand  was  a  notice  to  the  leading  insurgents  to  escape 
capture,  and  they  availed  themselves  of  it. 

You  say  that  “In  demanding  the  surrender  of  Alexandria  I  was 
actuated  solely  by  motives  of  humanity.  I  knew  the  town  to  be  full  of 
helpless  women  and  children,  mostly  of  the  middle  and  poorer  classes, 
whom  I  saw  running  frantically  through  the  streets  in  search  of  pro¬ 
tection  as  the  troops  landed.”  While  I  will  not  question  the  humane 
motives  alleged  as  a  justification  for  interfering  in  a  manner  that  might 
have  defeated  an  expedition  planned  without  your  knowledge,  let  me 
say  to  you  that  before  arriving  at  that  conclusion  it  would  have  been 
well  to  have  considered  that  those  who  projected  and  those  who  exe- 


OPERATIONS  ON  THE  POTOMAC  AND  RAPPAHANNOCK.  481 

exited  that  expedition  were  governed  by  motives  of  humanity  also. 
They  were  not  barbarians,  unworthy  or  incapable  of  carrying  into  effect 
the  orders  [with]  which  they  had  been  intrusted,  but  your  countrymen; 
and  why  you  should  have  availed  yourself  of  the  first  intelligence  that 
came  to  you  by  giving  an  alarm,  appears  so  unaccountable  that,  after 
waiting  a  reasonable  time  for  a  report  or  explanation  and  receiving 
none,  the  order  of  the  28th  ultimo  was  issued.  In  demanding  the  sur¬ 
render  of  the  town  when  the  expedition  from  Washington  was  secretly 
approaching  it,  you  committed,  to  say  the  least,  a  grave  error.  The 
promptings  of  humanity  are  commendable,  and  the  sympathy  which  you 
felt  for  the  “women  and  children,  mostly  of  middle  and  poorer  classes, 
whom  [you]  saw  running  frantically  through  the  streets  in  search  of 
protection”  after  notice  had  been  given  them  and  as  the  troops  landed, 
may  do  credit  to  you  as  a  man,  though  having  its  origin  in  your  error 
as  an  officer. 

The  Department  deems  it  a  duty  to  express  its  disapproval  of  your 
interference  under  the  circumstances,  and  it  also  regrets  that  you  should 
have  omitted  a  prompt  and  frank  report  of  your  proceedings  on  so 
eventful  an  occasion  until  an  order  was  issued  demanding  it. 

I  am,  respectfully,  etc., 

Gideon  Welles. 

Commander  S.  C.  Rowan, 

Commanding  U.  S.  8.  Pawnee ,  Washington.

Sir  :  In  obedience  to  instructions  from  headquarters  of  this  day’s  date 
in  regard  to  the  capture  of  Captain  Ball  and  his  troops,  I  have  to  rei>ort 
that  on  the  morning  of  the  24th  instant  about  1 : 30  a.  m.,  Captain  Ball 
came  to  my  quarters  and  reported  that  one  of  the  vedettes  stationed 
at  the  Chain  Bridge,  about  3  miles  west  of  Georgetown,  D.  C.,  had 
informed  him  that  a  squadron  of  cavalry  had  crossed  over  to  the  Vir¬ 
ginia  shore.  1  immediately  ordered  my  command  under  arms  to  await 
further  orders.  About  5 : 30  a.  m.  an  officer  was  sent  from  the  steamer 
Pawnee,  Northern  Navy,  to  inform  me  that  an  overwhelming  force  was 
about  entering  the  city  of  Alexandria  and  it  would  be  madness  to  resist, 
and  that  I  could  have  until  9  a.  m.  to  evacuate  or  surrender.  I  then 
ordered  the  troops  under  my  command  to  assemble  at  the  place  desig¬ 
nated  by  me  on  assuming  command  in  Alexandria,  that  I  might  either 
resist  or  fall  back,  as  circumstances  might  require.  As  soon  as  the 
troops  were  formed,  which  was  promptly  done,  I  repaired  to  the  com¬ 
mand,  and  then,  ascertaining  that  the  enemy  were  entering  the  city  by 
Washington  street  and  that  several  steamers  had  been  placed  so  that 
their  guns  could  command  many  of  the  principal  streets,  I  ordered  the 
command  to  march,  and  proceeded  out  of  the  city  by  Duke  street. 
Captain  Ball  accompanied  me  as  far  as  his  quarters,  a  little  west  of  the 
railroad  depot,  where  he  halted,  and  I  proceeded  to  the  cars,  which 
were  about  half  a  mile  from  the  depot,  where  I  had  ordered  them  to  be 
stopped;  and,  from  orders  given  before  marching  out  of  the  city,  the 
cavalry  was  to  follow  in  my  rear  for  the  purpose  of  giving  me  inlorma-

Report  of  Lieutenant  Jeffers ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  commanding  steamer  Philadel¬ 
phia ,  of  the  cruise  of  that  vessel  to  New  York  and  return. 

H.  S.  S.  Philadelphia, 

Navy  Yard ,  Washington ,  May  24,  1861. 

Sir  :  In  obedience  to  your  order  of  May  11,  I  proceeded  to  Fortress 
Monroe,  Philadelphia,  and  New  York  and  landed  the  ordnance  stores 
destined  for  those  places. 

On  Tuesday  morning,  the  21st  ultimo  [instant],  after  being  detained 
by  bad  weather  for  several  days,  I  sailed  for  Fortress  Monroe,  which 
place  I  reached  on  Thursday  afternoon,  having  been  obliged  to  harbor 
at  the  Delaware  Breakwater  on  account  of  the  weather. 

On  the  passage  from  the  breakwater  encountered  a  heavy  swell  from 
S.  E.,  which,  coupled  with  previous  straining,  broke  the  A  frame  of  the 
port  Avheelhouse.  This  I  temporarily  secured,  but  it  will  require  a  thor¬ 
ough  repair. 

Left  Fortress  Monroe  at  8:30  p.  m.  Thursday.  This  morning,  off 
Kettle  Bottom,  fell  in  with  propeller  City  of  Neic  York ,  laden  with  army 
stores.  The  captain  desiring  convoy,  towed  her  as  far  as  Alexandria. 

On  my  way  up  carefully  examined  both  shores  of  the  river.  At  Aquia 
Creek  a  secession  flag  was  flying  over  what  appeared  to  be  a  battery 
and  the  steamboat  George  Page  lay  at  the  wharf.  No  signs  of  batteries 
at  any  other  point. 

In  conclusion  I  would  state  that  this  steamer  is  in  no  respect  suitable 
for  outside  service. 

Respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

William  N.  Jeffers, 

Lieutenant ,  Commanding , 

Commander  J.  A.  Dahlgren, 

Commandant  Navy  Yard 3  Washington ,  D.  C,

continually  at  that  part  of  the  river  in  the  hope  of  producing  a  complete

at  anchor  in  this  creek  being  laden  with  the  supplies,  which,  if  on  board

J.  H.  Ward,
