Engagements  between  vessels  of  the  Potomac  Flotilla ,  Commander  James 

H.  Ward ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  commanding,  and  the  batteries  at  Aquia  Creek, 

May  29-  June  1,  1861. 

Report  of  Commander  Ward,  IT.  S.  Navy,  commanding  Potomac  Flotilla. 

U.  S.  S.  Thomas  Freeborn, 

Off  Aquia  Creek,  Potomac ,  May  31,  1861. 

Sir  :  My  immediate  commanding  officer  (Flag-Officer  Stringham)  not 
being  present  to  receive  it,  I  communicate  directly  to  the  Department 
the  report  of  a  serious  cannonade  made  by  this  vessel,  supported  by  the 
Anacostia  and  Resolute,  steamers,  upon  the  batteries  at  Aquia  Creek 
this  morning. 

After  an  incessant  discharge,  kept  up  for  two  hours  by  both  our  32- 
pounders,  and  the  expenditure  of  all  the  ammunition  suitable  for  dis¬ 
tant  firing,  and  silencing  completely  the  three  batteries  at  the  railroad 
terminus,  the  firing  from  shore  having  been  rapidly  kept  up  by  them 
until  so  silenced,  and  having  been  recommenced  from  the  new  batteries 
on  the  heights  back,  which  reached  us  in  volleys,  dropping  the  shot  on 
board  and  about  us  like  hail  for  nearly  an  hour,  but  fortunately  wound¬ 
ing  but  one  man,  I  hauled  the  vessels  off,  as  the  heights  proved  wholly 
above  the  reach  of  our  elevation. 

Judging  from  the  explosion  of  our  10-second  shell  in  the  sand  bat¬ 
teries,  two  of  which  were  thrown  by  the  Anacostia,  it  is  hardly  possible 
the  enemy  can  have  escaped  considerable  loss.  Several  others  of  the 
Anacostia’s  shells  dropped  in  the  vicinity  of  the  battery. 

I  can  not  speak  in  too  high  terms  of  the  officers  and  men,  whose  cool¬ 
ness  and  activity  under  great  exposure  are  beyond  praise.  As  the 
former  are  all  acting,  having  volunteered  from  civil  life,  none  but  myself 
being  of  the  Regular  Navy,  I  beg  leave  to  ask  for  them  a  favorable  con¬ 
sideration  by  the  Government. 

The  long  32-pounder  in  use  is  of  the  old  pattern  cast  in  1819,  and 
can  not  be  excelled  in  precision. 

Both  the  guns  are  on  carriages  of  the  new  construction,  devised  by 
myself,  and  answered  admirably,  working  with  such  ease  that  the  crews 
came  out  of  action  wholly  unfatigued.  In  the  extreme  sweep  of  140° 
which  these  carriages  have,  together  with  their  ease  and  rapidity  of 
movement,  enabling  the  vessel  to  constantly  change  position,  yet  keep 
up  accurate  fire,  which  impaired  the  enemy’s  range  and  direction — he 
firing  always  with  rifled  cannon— is  to  be  materially  attributed  our 
escape  without  loss  of  life  or  damage  to  the  vessel  or  machinery.  The 
men  say  they  are  as  free  from  fatigue  as  when  they  entered  action. 

We  cannonaded  for  an  hour  before  the  same  batteries  the  day  before 
yesterday,  but  the  tide  being  out,  neither  party  reached  with  any  con¬ 
siderable  certainty. 


OPERATIONS  ON  THE  POTOMAC  AND  RAPPAHANNOCK.  491 


I  doubt  if  it  is  possible  to  reduce  the  batteries  now  established  on 
the  heights  from  ships ;  nor  is  it  at  all  important,  considering  that  they 
are  remote  from  the  ship  channel  of  the  river  and  command  only  the 
railroad  terminus. 

Yesterday  I  landed  in  person  with  Acting  Master  Budd  and  Master’s 
Mate  Lee  and  a  small  party  of  seamen  and  made  a  most  minute  explora¬ 
tion,  extending  over  the  whole  of  Mathias  Point.  I  am  therefore  able 
to  speak  with  ocular  certainty  and  to  say  that  not  a  sign  of  a  move¬ 
ment,  the  cutting  of  a  sapling,  driving  a  stake,  or  casting  a  shovelful 
of  earth  toward  the  erection  of  a  battery  exists.  The  jungle  is  very 
thick,  but  we  penetrated  a  belt  of  it  300  yards  wide  from  the  shore  and 
3  miles  in  length,  assuring  ourselves  of  the  facts  as  stated  in  this  report. 

I  have  especially  to  ask  for  the  steamers  Reliance  and  Resolute ,  of  the 
flotilla,  each  a  small  rifled  cannon  in  addition  to  the  smoothbored  gun 
with  which  they  are  provided.  For  the  want  of  a  rifled  gun  in  them  I 
was  obliged  to  forbid  their  coming  closely  under  a  tire  to  which  they 
could  not  reply  with  even  an  approximate  effect. 

Lieutenant  Commanding  1ST.  Collins,  of  the  Anacostia,  will  make  his 
own  report. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  sir,  your  obedient  servant, 

Jas.  H.  Ward, 

Commander ,  U.  8.  Navy ,  Commanding  Flotilla. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy ,  Washington ,  T).  C. 


Report  of  Commander  Ward,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  Potomac  Flotilla. 

Flotilla  Steamer  Freeborn, 

Potomac  River ,  June  1 ,  1861. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  a  renewal  of  the  bombardment  at 
Aquia  Creek,  commencing  11:30  a.  m.  this  day  and  terminating  from 
fatigue  of  the  men — the  day  being  very  warm  and  the  firing  on  our  side 
incessant — at  4:30  p.  in.,  making  a  duration  of  five  hours. 

The  firing  on  shore  was  scarcely  as  spirited  at  any  time  as  yesterday. 
The  heights  were  abandoned,  the  guns  apparently  having  been  trans¬ 
ferred  to  the  earthworks  at  the  railroad  terminus  iu  replacement  of 
the  battery  silenced  there  by  us  yesterday.  During  the  last  hour  of  the 
engagement  only  two  or  three  shots  were  thrown  from  the  shore,  by  a 
few  individuals  seen  stealthily  now  and  then  to  emerge  from  conceal¬ 
ment  and  hastily  load  and  fire  a  single  gun.  The  bulk  of  the  party  had 
left  a  half  hour  before,  and  squads  were  observed  from  time  to  time 
taking  to  their  heels  along  the  beach  with  a  speed  and  bottom  truly 
commendable  for  its  prudence  and  highly  amusing  to  the  seamen.  It 
did  not  seem  advisable  to  permit  so  feeble  a  fire  to  wear  out  my  men, 
therefore  discontinued  the  engagement. 

Several  shots  came  on  board  of  us,  causing  the  vessel  to  leak  badly, 
and  beside  other  injuries  crippling  the  port  wheel,  the  wrought-iron 
shaft  being  gouged  by  a  shot  which  would  have  shattered  it  if  of  cast 
iron,  a  point  considered  by  me  in  selecting  this  vessel  for  purchase. 
Fortunately,  I  have  again  neither  killed  nor  wounded  to  report,  though 
the  shot  at  times  fell  thick  among  us,  testing  the  gallantry  and  steadi¬ 
ness  of  my  people,  which  I  consider  of  standard  proof  for  any  emergency. 

I  proceed  to  Washington  to  repair  damages  and  refill  my  exhausted 
magazines.  The  Pawnee  remains  meantime  below  to  supply  my  place 
in  the  blockade.  Captain  Bowan,  of  that  ship,  joined  me  last  night, 


492  OPERATIONS  ON  THE  POTOMAC  AND  RAPPAHANNOCK. 

% 

replenishing  my  exhausted  stores,  and  most  gallantly  opened  the  lire 
this  morning,  having  followed  my  lead  inshore  toward  the  batteries. 
His  ship  received  numerous  wounds  both  below  and  aloft,  inflicted  by 
the  enemy’s  shot,  appearing  from  her  size — therefore  most  easily  hit — 
to  be  their  favorite  mark,  and  was  herself  often  a  sheet  of  flame  owing 
to  the  rapidity  of  her  discharges. 

I  have  instructed  Captain  Iiowan  to  report  circumstantially  direct  to 
the  Department. 

The  enemy  set  lire  to  the  large  passenger  and  freight  depot  on  the 
end  of  the  long  pier  as  we  were  approaching,  probably  to  remove  it  as 
an  obstruction  to  their  aim,  but  were  not  permitted  to  extinguish  the 
flames  during  the  whole  five  hours’  cannonade,  consequently  nearly 
the  whole  pier  was  destroyed,  only  the  charred  piles  remaining  above 
the  water  to  mark  its  former  position. 

My  gun  carriage  endures  its  continued  test  admirably.  The  pivoting 
arrangement  of  the  after  one  gave  out  in  the  last  hour  of  the  action, 
when  the  gun  was  fought  on  its  trucks,  which  had  neither  been  removed 
nor  in  any  manner  interfered  with  in  the  construction. 

The  recoil,  however,  became  severely  racking  to  the  vessel;  the  gun 
was  served  slower  and  with  less  accuracy,  and  Avith  greatly  increased 
awkwardness  as  well  as  fatigue  to  the  men. 

Though  not  assuming  to  be  proper  judge  of  my  own  invention,  it  is 
possible  the  officers  and  men,  especially  the  gun’s  crews,  are  competent 
to  speak  after  the  several  cannonades  in  which  we  have  been  engaged, 
amounting  altogether  in  the  two  weeks  we  are  commissioned  to  ten 
hours,  nine  of  it  under  fire  returned  upon  us  with  more  or  less  vigor 
and  effect. 

More  than  100  shots  have  fallen  aboard  and  around  us,  any  one  of 
which  would  have  struck  a  frigate.  We  have  had  more  than  1,000 
shots  discharged  at  us  within  range,  and  have  ourselves  fired  upward 
of  300  shots  and  shells,  with  1,700  pounds  of  powder.  What  damage 
we  have  inflicted  remains  to  be  seen.  That  we  have  received  none  not 
easily  repaired  is  truly  remarkable. 

The  Anacostia  and  Reliance  were  not  permitted  to  come  under  damag¬ 
ing  fire,  their  support  having  been  necessary  to  embolden  those  engaged 
by  giving  them  confidence  that  if  disabled  in  the  machinery,  assistance 
was  at  hand  to  drag  them  out. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

J.  H.  Ward, 

Commander ,  Senior  Officer  on  the  Potomac. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy. 


Report  of  Commander  Rowan,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  IT.  S.  S.  Pawnee. 

XL  S.  S.  Pawnee, 

Off  Aquia  Creek ,  Va.,  June  2,  1861. 

Sir:  In  obedience  to  an  order  received  on  the  evening  of  the  31st 
ultimo,  I  proceeded  immediately  to  join  Captain  Ward. 

In  passing  down  the  river  I  was  informed  by  Lieutenant  Mygatt,  of 
the  steamer  Reliance ,  that  Captain  Ward  had  gone  10  miles  below  Aquia 
Creek  for  the  night.  I  continued  down  the  river,  passing  the  creek 
about  3  o’clock  a.  m.  of  the  1st  of  June.  At  6  o’clock  I  joined  Com¬ 
mander  Ward.  At  9  I  stood  for  Aquia  Creek  in  company  with  the 
Freeborn  for  the  purpose  of  attacking  the  batteries.  We  arrived  off  the 


United  States  Steamer  Pawnee. 


' 

•- 


OPERATIONS  ON  THE  POTOMAC  AND  RAPPAHANNOCK.  493 


creek  at  11  o’clock  and  at  half  past  11  we  ran  m,  tlie  Freeborn  leading, 
being  of  a  lighter  draft  than  the  Pawnee ,  while  this  ship  kept  just  out¬ 
side  on  her  starboard  quarter  to  avoid  grounding.  As  we  ranged  up 
the  enemy  set  fire  to  the  buildings  on  the  end  of  the  railroad  wharf  and 
then  opened  his  fire,  which  was  promptly  returned  by  us.  Finding  my 
15-second  shell  fell  short  with  all  the  elevation  the  ports  admitted  of,  I 
ranged  ahead  of  the  Freeborn  and  edged  in  as  near  as  I  could,  feeling 
the  way  with  the  lead  till  I  got  within  range  of  the  forts  with  the  15- 
second  shell,  when  we  opened  a  heavy  fire.  1  held  this  position  as  long 
as  possible,  when  the  ship  fell  off  against  our  exertions  to  keep  her 
steady  and  [it  |  became  necessary  to  round  out  into  the  river  and  approach 
a  second  time  on  the  same  tack.  Having  got  the  ship  nearer  than  the 
first  xiosition  and  as  near  as  was  safe,  with  but  2  feet  of  water  to  spare, 
and  to  the  northward  and  westward  of  the  Freeborn ,  we  opened  a  ter¬ 
rible  fire  from  five  9-iuch  guns.  The  batteries  were  twice  silenced  under 
the  weight  of  our  fire,  but  resumed  again  when  our  fire  ceased.  The 
houses  near  the  forts  were  destroyed  and  the  southern  end  of  the 
bridge  set  on  fire  by  the  shells. 

The  wind  being  from  the  southward  the  bridge  was  destroyed.  The 
enemy’s  fire  was  almost  exclusively  directed  at  this  ship,  his  rifled  shot 
passing  constantly  over  and  around  us. 

This  ship  was  struck  nine  times  during  the  bombardment,  four  of  the 
shot  in  the  hull,  one  of  them,  passing  through  the  bulwarks,  tore  up 
the  deck  and  was  glanced  on  board  by  one  of  the  iron  straps.  Of  the 
shot  that  hit  the  ship  above  the  hull  one  passed  through  the  maintop- 
sail  yard,  another  shattered  the  mizzenmast  head  and  topmast,  and 
another  passed  through  the  smokestack. 

The  cool  and  gallant  bearing  of  the  officers  and  crew  excited  my 
warmest  admiration.  Everyman  of  the  divisions  performed  his  duties 
coolly  and  promptly  and  intelligently,  showing  the  ship  in  a  high  state 
of  training;  to  attain  this  end  I  have  been  ably  seconded  by  the  divi¬ 
sional  officers,  Lieutenant  Chaplin  and  Master  Blue,  but  above  all  by 
my  able  executive  officer,  Lieutenant  R.  B.  Lowry,  whose  fine  bearing- 
on  the  occasion  was  everything  I  could  wish. 

I  am  happy  to  inform  you  that  I  have  no  casualties  to  report;  the 
only  scratch  was  one  that  I  received  on  the  face  from  a  small  splinter. 

At  4:30  p.  in.,  having  expended  all  my  10-second  and  15-second  shell 
and  the  38  rounds  of  ammunition  for  the  rifled  cannon  and  155  hollow 
shot,  I  hauled  off  out  of  range. 

As  soon  as  I  am  relieved  by  Commander  Ward  it  will  be  necessary  to 
return  to  the  navy  yard  for  repairs  and  supplies. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

S.  C.  Rowan, 

Commander. 


Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy.

Unofficial  letter  from  Commander  Ward,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  Potomac  Flotilla,  to  the 

Assistant  Secretary  of  the  Navy. 

[U.  S.  S.]  Freeborn,  June  11, 1861. 

My  Dear  Captain  Fox:  Captain  Build,  of  tlie  Resolute ,  had  a 
conversation  with  Mr.  Goff,  agent  of  the  St.  Nicholas ,  steamer,  in  Bre¬ 
ton’s  Bay,  Maryland,  a  day  or  two  since.  Mr.  Goff  spoke  in  terms  of 
surprise  at  the  heroic  persistency  witli  which  Captain  W.  F.  Lynch, 
formerly  of  our  Navy,  who  commanded  at  Aquia  during  my  several 
attacks,  held  his  post,  glass  in  hand,  on  the  ramparts,  against  all  the 
urgency  of  his  men  to  quit  a  post  made  desperately  hazardous  by  the 
shot  and  shell  falling  thickly  and  exploding  about  him. 

Mr.  Goff,  though,  could  not  be  made  to  divulge  in  regard  to  the  exe¬ 
cution  we  did.  His  expressions  regarding  Captain  Lynch  imply,  how¬ 
ever,  that  it  was  considerable,  if  not  great.  I  would  like  you  to  talk 
with  Budd  or  set  him  in  hands  of  the  reporters.  I  am  quite  disposed 
to  have  this  thing  published. 

Very  truly, 

J.  H.  Ward.

Report  of  Captain  Lynch,  Virginia  navy,  commanding  naval  defenses  of  the  Potomac. 

Naval  Battery  No.  1, 

Aquia  Creelc ,  June  2 ,  1861. 

Sir:  On  Thursday  p.  in.,  as  my  telegram  the  next  morning  apprised 
you,  the  enemy  engaged  us  for  a  short  time  and  then  withdrew.  The 
Washington  papers  state  that  one  of  them  had  a  Massachusetts  regi¬ 
ment  on  board  for  the  purpose  of  landing.  One  of  the  steamers  was 
crowded  with  men. 

On  Friday,  at  10:30  a.  m.,  two  out  of  three  steamers  abreast;  of  the 
battery  opened  fire  upon  us  and  continued  the  cannonade  for  three 
hours,  when  they  withdrew.  The  largest  steamer  very  much  resembled 
the  Crusader.  As  they  kept  at  long  shot,  mostly  beyond  our  range,  I 
economized  ammunition  and  only  fired  fifty-six  times.  One  of  the 
steamers  had  a  rifled  gun,  the  shell  from  which  penetrated  through  the 
sand  bank,  and  one  of  them  exploded  in  and  completely  demolished  the 
room  occupied  by  the  officers  and  myself. 

Upon  our  part  no  one  was  injured,  but  lookers  on  from  the  hills  and 
opposite  shores  state  that  the  enemy  was  repeatedly  struck. 

Yesterday  the  steamers,  which  had  laid  off  during  the  night,  were 
reinforced  by  the  Pawnee ,  and  at  11:  30  a.  m.  they  commenced  a  brisk 
cannonade,  which  continued  with  little  interruption  until  about  4:30 
p.  in.,  during  which  the  Pawnee  fired  392  shot  and  shell  and  the  other 
steamer  207,  the  greater  portion  of  the  latter  being  rifled  shells. 

Our  sand  banks  not  being  en  barbette,  we  could  only  fire  as  the  enemy 
came  within  range  through  the  embrasures.  This,  added  to  the  long 
distance  at  which  he  kept,  and  the  necessity  of  occasionally  repairing 
damages  to  the  breastwork,  combined  with  my  desire  to  save  ammuni¬ 
tion,  constrained  me  to  withhold  fire  except  when  something  like  a  fair 
shot  presented.  The  houses  in  the  rear  were  very  much  knocked  about 
and  the  railroad  track  torn  up  in  three  or  four  places,  but  thanks  to  a 
kind  Providence,  who  seems  to  smile  benignly  upon  our  cause,  no  one 
with  us  was  injured. 

As  the  enemy  had  on  Friday  made  the  buildings  at  the  extremity  of 
the  wharf  his  line  of  sight  upon  the  battery,  I  had  all  the  furniture, 
etc.,  together  with  the  weatherboarding,  conveyed  to  the  rear  of  the 
battery,  and  in  the  course  of  the  forenoon  set  fire  to  and  blew  up  the 
platform  and  outer  end  of  the  bridge. 

I  have  spoken  of  Commander  Thorburn’s  zeal  in  the  first  engagement, 
and  can  not  too  highly  applaud  the  spirit  and  alacrity,  tempered  by 
deference  to  orders,  of  Commander  Cooke  and  Lieutenant  Trobel.  With 
the  exception  of  Gunner’s  Mate  Cunningham  and  Master’s  Mate  Lar- 
mour,  whose  services  were  of  inestimable  value,  our  guns’  crews  con¬ 
sisted  only  of  volunteer  militia,  who  stood  their  ground  bravely. 

We  had  yesterday,  in  addition  to  our  guns,  a  small  rifled  one  from 
Captain  Walker’s  battery,  under  the  immediate  command  of  Lieutenant 
Robertson,  of  Tennessee,  which  rendered  efficient  service. 

In  connection  with  the  transportation  of  the  Columbiads  to  the  sum¬ 
mit  of  a  lofty  hill,  I  can  not  speak  in  too  highly  commendable  terms  of 
the  zeal  and  untiring  energy  of  Lieutenant  Charles  C.  Simms. 

One  of  the  enemy’s  steamers  went  up  the  river  yesterday  afternoon, 
we  think  for  ammunition  or  additional  force.  The  Pawnee  and  another

steamer  remained  at  anchor  all  nig'lit  near  the  Maryland  shore,  and  at 
this  time,  9:15  a.  m.,  occupies  the  same  position. 

I  am,  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

W.  F.  Lynch, 
Captain ,  Virginia  Navy.

Commandant’s  Office,  Naval  Defenses  of  tiie  Potomac, 

Aquia  Creek ,  June  6 ,  1861. 

Sir:  In  my  report  of  the  engagements  with  this  battery  I  am  not 
certain  of  having  stated  that  on  Friday  Walker’s  battery  of  four  3-inch

On  Saturday  one  of  the  four  guns  was  placed  in  battery  here  and 
was  well  and  bravely  handled  under  the  immediate  command  of  Lieu¬

I  am,  very  respectfully, 

W.  F.  Lynch,

Report  of  Colonel  Ruggles,  C.  S.  Army,  commanding  Department  of  Fredericksburg,  Va. 

Headquarters  Department  of  Fredericksburg, 

Fredericksburg ,  Va.,  May  30,  1861. 

Sir  :  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that  two  small  steamers  of  the  enemy 
attacked  the  Aquia  Creek  Railroad  battery  last  evening  about  sunset 
with  twelve  shot  and  shell.  Our  battery  returned  the  lire  with  twelve 
shot  and  shell.  The  contest  terminated  about  9  o’clock,  when  the 
enemy  departed.  One  man  was  slightly  wounded  in  the  hand  by  the 
fragments  of  a  shell.  I  prepared  to  cover  our  front  with  my  whole 
force,  comprising  the  Tennessee  regiment  and  a  battalion  of  volun¬ 
teers,  assembled  at  Camp  Mercer,  and  proceeded  with  some  700  men 
to  the  point  attacked,  having  in  view  sending  back  the  train  for  the 
remaining  500.  The  conflict  having  terminated  before  we  reached  the 
scene  of  action,  I  returned  with  the  forces  above  specified,  reaching 
this  town  about  5  a.  m.  The  spirit  and  conduct  of  the  troops  have  been 
admirable  in  connection  with  this  little  affair.  Much  agitation  prevails 
along  the  Potomac  coast  from  apprehension  that  the  enemy  will  land  in 
large  and  small  numbers  to  devastate  and  plunder.  I  respectfully 
recommend  that  guns  of  heavy  caliber  be  furnished  (say  12’s,  18’s,  and 
32’s)  for  use  at  various  points  on  the  coast  for  surprising  and  harassing 
the  enemy. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Daniel  Ruggles, 

Colonel ,  Provisional  Army ,  Commanding  Forces. 

Colonel  R.  S.  Garnett, 

Adjutant- General,  Virginia  Forces.

Report  of  Colonel  Ruggles,  C.  S.  Army,  commanding  Department  of  Fredericksburg,  Va. 

Headquarters  Department  of  Fredericksburg, 

Fredericksburg ,  Va.,  June  1,  1861. 

Sir:  The  enemy  attacked  the  naval  battery  at  Aqnia  Creek  yester¬ 
day  about  10  a.  m.  The  enemy  had  three  war  steamers  and  some  small 
transports,  not  containing,  however,  many  troops.  They  had  some 
longboats,  or  launches,  but,  so  far  as  observed,  made  no  preparation 
for  landing.  The  lire  on  both  sides  was  skillfully  directed  and  contin¬ 
ued  up  to  about  1  p.  m.,  when  the  steamers  hauled  off,  and,  it  is  sup¬ 
posed,  in  a  partially  disabled  condition.  I  took  all  the  available  forces, 
comprising  the  four  companies  of  infantry  and  one  of  cavalry,  from  this 
vicinity,  and  Colonel  Date’s  Tennessee  (Walker)  Legion  with  me,  reach¬ 
ing  the  Potomac  soon  after  the  firing  ceased.  The  conduct  of  the  troops 
in  the  batteries — that  of  Captain  Walker,  with  his  G-pounder  rifle  guns, 
having  been  brought  early  into  the  action — is  represented  as  having 
been  admirable,  including  the  covering  and  protecting  force  on  the 
field.  I  have  transferred  the  Tennessee  (Walker)  Legion  to  Brooke’s 
Station,  where  I  have  reestablished  Camp  Jackson.  From  that  point 
lateral  movements  may  be  easily  made  to  cross  the  coasts  and  forward 
movements  to  cover  the  batteries  with  great  facility. 

The  ladies  are  now  making  tents,  cartridges,  and  belts,  and  I  hope 
soon  to  have  our  forces  sheltered  and  better  equipped.  I  left  Aquia 
Creek  late  last  evening  and  return  there  this  morning. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Daniel  Buggles, 

Colonel,  Provisional  Army,  Commanding  Forces. 

Colonel  R.  S.  Garnett, 

Adjutant- General,  Virginia  Forces. 


Report  of  Colonel  Ruggles,  C.  S.  Army,  commanding  Department  of  Fredericksburg',  Va. 

Fredericksburg,  Ya.,  June  1,  1861. 

Sir  :  The  report  has  arrived  this  moment  that  five  of  the  enemy’s 
steamers,  with' two  transport  ships,  one  of  which  is  of  considerable  size, 
had  appeared  off'  Aquia  Creek  battery,  with  the  evident  intention  of 
attacking  it.  When  the  train  left  (11  a.  m.)  soon  after  heavy  firing  was 
heard  from  that  point.  I  am  in  want  of  at  least  1,000  well-deciplined 
volunteers  as  soon  as  it  is  possible  to  send  them.  Twenty  thousand 
musket-rifle  caps  are  absolutely  necessary  for  the  use  of  troops  with 
percussion  arms.  I  go  to  the  battery  at  once.  Communicate  with 
Major  [W.  S.j  Barton,  acting  assistant  adjutant-general  to  this  office. 

Daniel  Ruggles, 

Colonel,  Provisional  Army. 

Colonel  R.  S.  Garnett, 

Adjutant-  General.

Report  of  Colonel  Ruggles,  C.  S.  Anny,  commanding  Department  of  Fredericksburg,  Va , 
regarding  measures  of  protection  against  further  attacks  upon  Aquia  Creek  batteries. 

Headquarters  Department  of  Fredericksburg, 

Fredericksburg ,  Va .,  June  4,  1861. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  state  for  the  information  of  the  general 
commanding,  that  since  Saturday  last  no  attack  has  been  made  on  our 
batteries  at  Aquia  Creek,  and  that  the  steamer  Pawnee  only  has  been 
lying  off  at  that  point  repairing  damages  and  in  communication  with 
various  steamers  and  other  vessels  passing  up  and  down  the  Potomac. 
It  has  just  been  reported  to  me,  however,  that  after  I  left  the  creek 
yesterday,  and  at  about  9  o’clock  at  night,  two  or  more  war  steamers, 
with  a  vessel  in  tow,  came  down  the  Potomac  and  joined  the  Pawnee. 
Thus  tar  I  have  no  report  of  the  renewal  of  the  attack  this  morning. 
It  is  my  intention  to  throw  the  Arkansas  regiment,  Colonel  Fagan,  now 
at  Camp  Jackson,  upon  the  Potomac  coast,  near  Chopawamsic,  as  soon 
as  it  is  in  condition  to  do  so. 

I  am  much  in  want  of  an  effective  battery  of  24-pounder  howitzers 
for  service  in  conjunction  with  that  force  to  prevent  the  enemy  from 
landing.  The  Fredericksburg  Artillery,  of  6-pounders,  will  be  wanted 
at  Aquia  Creek  to  prevent  landing  there  if  an  attack  is  made.  The 
movements  of  the  enemy  indicate  that  an  attempt  will  soon  be  made 
in  force  to  laud  at  or  in  the  vicinity  of  Mathias  Point  in  a  brief  period 
of  time.  I  respectfully  recommend  that  that  point  be  covered  by  a 
good  regiment  of  infantry,  with  a  good  battery  of  field  guns,  until 
measures  are  taken  to  establish  a  good  and  sufficient  battery  at  that 
point  to  command  the  channel,  for  the  establishment  of  which  i  respect¬ 
fully  renew  my  former  recommendation.  Under  authority  given  me  I 
have  fabricated  here  carriages  for  a  battery  of  6-pounder  guns,  and 
respectfully  request  that  guns  may  be  furnished  me  without  delay  for 
use  in  the  field. 

Since  it  has  become  impracticable  to  establish  a  battery  at  the  White 
House  to  command  the  Potomac,  1  respectfully  recommend  that  a  com-

petent  engineer  be  sent  me  to  examine  the  vicinity  of  Evan  sport  with 
that  view,  and,  if  found  suitable,  that  a  battery  may  be  established 
there  with  as  little  delay  as  is  practicable.  That  point  is  important  in 
connection  with  the  position  at  Manassas  Junction,  as  well  as  the  ave¬

Daniel  Ruggles,

Letter  from  Captain  Lynch,  C.  S.  Navy,  to  the  editor  of  the  Fredericksburg  News. 

Naval  Battery,  Aquia  Creek,  June  9,  1861. 

Sir:  My  official  report  of  our  recent  contest  with  the  enemy  Avas 
rendered  as  brief  as  possible,  embracing  only  the  names  of  those  who 
Avere  legitimately  engaged;  but  as  there  were  several  instances  of  indi¬ 
vidual  gallantry  by  volunteers,  some  of  whom  reside  in  this  vicinity, 
1  deem  it  proper  to  give  publicity  to  them. 

To  this  L  am  the  more  impelled  by  the  slanderous  assertion  cast  upon 
them  by  the  commander  of  the  enemy’s  flotilla. 

Had  that  officer,  whose  characteristic  traits  long  since  earned  for  him 
in  his  profession  the  cognomen  of  “  Yankee  Ward,”  for  once  violated 
his  instincts  and  been  sincere  he  Avould  have  stated  that  men  were 
seen  running  toward,  as  well  as  from,  the  batteries,  mostly  bearing 
ammunition. 

The  attack  on  Wednesday  evening  was  repelled  with  spirit  by  Com¬ 
mander  Thorburn,  as  I  did  not  reach  the  battery  until  very  near  the 
close  of  the  engagement. 

In  writing  my  official  report  I  labored  under  the  impression  that  the 
shot  from  Captain  Walker’s  battery  during  Friday’s  engagement  fell 
short,  although  it  diverted  the  Are  of  the  enemy;  but  the  admission  of 
that  enemy  proved  the  fire  of  the  rifled  battery  to  have  been  effective 
and  that  my  impression  was  an  erroneous  one. 

During  Friday’s  attack  Lieutenant  Barnes,  of  the  Stafford  Guards, 
bore  a  message  from  me  to  Captain  Walker  and  returned  with  his 
reply,  his  course  being  along  the  causeway  over  which  the  enemy’s 
shot  was  sweeping. 

On  the  same  day,  too,  if  I  remember  aright,  Lieutenant  Betts,  of  the 
Washington  Guards,  came  to  the  battery  and  tendered  his  services. 

On  Saturday  Lieutenants  Yancey  and  Eckles,  of  the  Tennessee  vol¬ 
unteers,  with  two  others,  Arhose  names  I  unfortunately  do  not  know, 
volunteered  their  services  at  the  guns  just  before  the  conflict.  I  sta¬ 
tioned  them  near  by,  to  be  ready  in  the  event  of  casualties.  One  of 
them  bore  a  note  from  me  to  the  mainland  during  the  hottest  of  the  fire 
and  tAATo  or  three  others  went  for  and  brought  ammunition. 

So  far  from  trepidation,  one  of  the  messengers  stopped  upon  the 
causeway  and  picking  up  a  shot  which  had  fallen  near  him  brought  it 
in  as  a  trophy. 

Captain  Sener,  of  the  Washington  Guards,  was  present  during  the 
day’s  conflict  and  volunteered  to  extinguish  a  fire  kindled  at  the  inner 
end  of  the  wharf,  but  I  withheld  consent. 

Captain  Wise,  of  Company  E,  Richmond  volunteers,  was  by  me 
throughout  Saturday’s  engagement,  and  while  the  enemy’s  fire  was 
hottest  volunteered  to  go  for  infantry  to  repel  an  apprehended  landing  of 


500  OPERATIONS  ON  THE  POTOMAC  AND  RAPPAHANNOCK. 


tlie  enemy  under  cover  of  tlie  smoke.  Before  recognizing  Captain  W[ise] 
I  twice  ordered  him,  the  last  time  peremptorily,  within  the  redoubt, 
for,  next  to  damaging  the  enemy,  it  was  my  duty  to  preserve  the  lives 
of  those  around  me.  These  are  all  the  individual  cases  I  can  call  to 
mind.  The  demeanor  of  the  men  at  the  battery  is  so  worthy  of  com¬ 
mendation  that  it  would  be  invidious  to  particularize,  even  if  they  were 
not  mentioned  in  my  official  report.  Being  short  of  ammunition  our 
guns  were  worked  discreetly,  but  now  we  are  prepared  to  warm  them 
thoroughly. 

Very  respectfully, 

W.  F.  Lynch. 

Editor  Fredericksburg  Yews. 


Letter  from  Colonel  Bate,  C.  S.  Army,  commanding  Walker  Legion,  to  the  Secretary  of  War. 

Camp  Jackson,  on  the  Potomac,  June  11 ,  1861. 

Dear  Sir  :  I  suppose  you  have  heard  all  the  particulars  of  the  Aquia 
Creek  fight  and  the  part  borne  by  the  Walker  Legion.  One  company 
of  it  was  in  one  of  the  batteries  and  tlie  celebrated  rifled  cannon,  so 
effective  upon  the  enemy,  was  managed  by  one  of  our  young  lieutenants. 
The  remainder  of  the  regiment  was  held  in  reserve,  though  within  range 
of  their  guns,  at  a  point  of  concealment  to  prevent  a  landing  if  such 
was  attempted.  The  boys  were  too  eager  and  courted  a  hand-to-hand 
fight.  I  made  a  report  to  Colonel  Buggies  and  forbear  further  trespass 
now.  I  want  the  Walker  Legion  to  be  in  the  column  which  advances 
upon  Washington.  I  believe  we  will  have  skirmishes  here  now,  noth¬ 
ing  more.  We  will  sink  their  ships  on  another  effort  if  they  come  in 
range.  I  had  Walker’s  rifle  battery  under  my  command  placed  with 
two  rifle  companies  to  sustain  and  one  company  of  mounted  men  with 
carbines  within  hailing  distance  on  Symmes’s  Point  under  cover — a 
masked  battery — Saturday  night  after  the  fight,  thinking  they  would 
return  to  their  same  position  next  morning.  That  night  we  worked 
300  men  all  night  to  have  two  Columbiads  and  this  battery  of  Walker’s 
in  place,  but  the  enemy  being  so  crippled  did  not  return. 

The  arrangement  Sunday  morning  would  have  sunk  their  ships  in  an 
hour  had  they  resumed  their  position.  We  are  drilling  daily  and  almost 
hourly  and  will  look  to  you  to  give  us  a  chance. 

I  want  one-half  hour’s  talk  with  you,  and  if  you  will  telegraph  Gen¬ 
eral  Holmes  to  send  me  individually  to  Bichmond  for  a  day  I  can  get 
to  go;  otherwise  I  don’t  think  the  Old  Tycoon  (Holmes)  will  let  me,  and 
I  never  disobey  orders.  You  may  be  sure  I  will  not  leave  when  there 
is  a  prospect  of  a  fight.  Everything  is  peaceable  here  now  except  the 
Pawnee,  which  still  coils  about  our  shore  like  a  wounded  viper.  We 
have  vedettes  near  her. 

I  get  information  from  above  and  below  this  point  for  20  miles  every 
day  through  couriers  and  can  know  when  it  is  safe  to  leave  for  Bichmond 
only  a  day. 

Pardon  the  length  of  this  free-and-easy  letter.  I  know  it  is  a  trespass 
on  your  much-engaged  time.  Let  me  hear  from  you.  Send  the  dis¬ 
patch  spoken  of,  or  write  letter,  and  oblige. 

Wm.  B.  Bate. 

Hon.  L.  P.  Walker, 

Secretary  of  War. 

Ik  S. — I  am  expecting  that  field  battery  promised  me  at  Montgomery. 
I  have  a  company  preparing  for  it.

Letter  from  M.  W.  McCluskey,  esq.,  to  tho  Secretary  of  War  of  tho  Confederate  States,  describing 
the  attack  by  United  States  vessels  on  Aquia  Creek  battery,  June  1,  1861. 

Aquia  Creek,  June  1, 1861. 

My  Dear  Sir:  I  bad  the  pleasure  of  witnessing  at  this  point  to-day 
most  ot  the  engagement  between  one  of  our  batteries  and  three  Lin¬ 
coln  men-of-war,  one  of  them  supposed  to  be  the  Pawnee ,  the  other  the 
Anacostia,  and  the  other  unknown.  Our  forces  acted  manfully  and 
suffered  no  injury,  though  some  of  the  enemy’s  shot  were  well  directed, 
and  where  it  seemed  providentially  averted  from  doing  mischief.  The 
tight  was  a  continuation  of  the  one  the  day  before.  Our  battery  fired 
the  first  shot  to-day,  then  all  of  its  garrison  mounted  the  fort  and 
cheered  in  defiance  of  the  enemy.  The  shot  was  promptly  returned 
and  the  enemy  kept  up  a  brisk  canuonading,  firing  before  the  close  592 
shots,  comprised  of  shell  and  balls  of  the  largest  dimensions.  The  only 
damage  to  our  side  was  the  death  of  a  chicken,  though  a  stray  ball  killed 
a  horse  on  the  opposite  side  of  the  creek.  Our  own  battery  fired  but  70 
shots,  three  of  which  are  said  to  have  been  fired  with  effect.  The 
firing  ceased  at  3 : 30  p.  m.,  when  a  barge  from  the  Pawnee  went  to  the 
Maryland  shore  and  returning  the  Anacostia  proceeded  up  the  river, 
supposed  to  be  bound  for  Washington  for  a  fresh  supply  of  ammunition. 

One  of  the  guns  on  our  battery  was  under  the  command  of  one 
of  the  Walker  Legion,  Cadet  Patton  Robertson,  of  Nashville,  who 
fired  the  rifled  cannon  with  remarkable  precision,  and  displayed,  for  a 
youug  man,  not  yet  of  age,  the  most  dauntless  and  cool  bravery.  The 
big  gun  on  the  new  battery,  which  is  garrisoned  by  the  Carolina  Greys, 
of  our  regiment,  under  command  of  Captain  Hunt,  was  placed  in  posi¬ 
tion  about  5  o’clock  this  afternoon  and  will  thunder  in  the  anticipated 
engagement  of  to  morrow.  Another  one  for  the  same  battery  will  be 
planted  to-morrow.  These  guns  are  in  the  most  splendid  locality  to 
command  the  river  that  could  well  be  wished  for. 

To  morrow  Captain  Walker’s  command  of  rifled  cannon  will  be  at  a 
prominent  point  of  laud  at  the  mouth  of  the  creek  on  the  opposite  side, 
which  will  bring  him  within  a  mile  and  a  quarter  of  the  location  of  the 
Lincoln  vessels  in  the  engagement  of  to-day.  Pits  will  also  be  dug 
to-night  at  the  same  place  for  the  use  of  two  of  the  rifle  companies  of 
the  Walker  Legion.  We  are  all  at  the  creek,  though  our  encampment 
is  4  miles  back. 

The  vindictiveness  of  the  enemy  is  shown  by  the  quickness  with 
which  they  throw  their  shells  at  any  body  of  men  who  may  appear  on 
the  height  to  view  the  engagement.  One  of  our  companies  was  fired  at 
with  a  shell  the  moment  they  emerged  from  the  woods  to  obtain  a  more 
satisfactory  view  of  the  fight,  which  exploded  over  them  and  miracu¬ 
lously  scattered  so  as  not  to  hurt  one  of  the  number. 

Colonel  Bate  has  been  assigned  the  command  of  the  brigade  here, 
composed  of  his  own  regiment  and  the  Virginia  troops  present,  and  is 
working  with  a  zeal  consistent  with  the  energy  and  enthusiasm  of  his 
nature.  I  have  written  these  lines  thinking  you  would  be  glad  to 
learn  that  the  regiment  which  has  appropriated  your  name  as  its  des¬ 
ignation  is  coufided  with  the  most  important  posts  of  duty  in  the 
engagement  at  this  point  and  vicinity. 

Your  friend, 


Secretary  L.  P.  Walker. 


M.  W.  McCluskey.

[Enclosure.] 

The  mouth  of  the  Pocomoke  Biver,  in  Maryland,  empties  in  Accomac 
County,  Va.,  and  the  vessels  of  the  Union  men  of  Maryland  are  in 
danger  of  molestation  by  the  secession  parties  of  Virginia.  They  need 
immediate  protection,  and  it  will  require  a  vessel  of  light  draft  of  water 
to  afford  it,  as  at  the  mouth  of  this  river  there  is  a  place  G  miles  long- 
called  the  Mudds,  and  at  low  tides  the  vessels  from  Maryland  stop 
there,  and  would  be  in  greatest  danger  while  thus  aground.  One 
steamer,  the  Wilson  Small ,  from  Baltimore,  has  quit  the  route  in  conse¬ 
quence  of  threats  which  she  considered  well  authenticated.

Letter  from  the  Secretary  of  the  Navy  to  Commander  Ward,  U.  8.  Navy, 
commanding  Potomac  Flotilla,  regarding  movements  of  blockade 
runners. 

Confidential.]  Navy  Department,  June  6, 1861. 

Sir  :  This  Department  has  information  that  vessels  clear  from  Bal¬ 
timore  for  St.  Mary’s  River  laden  with  provisions  and  stores.  Arriving 
at  St.  Mary’s,  they  wait  a  favorable  opportunity ,  cross  the  Potomac,  and 
enter  Coan  River  and  discharge.  Two  vessels  have  been  known  to  have 
discharged  their  cargoes. 

It  is  understood  that  tlie  rebels  have  commenced  throwing  up  earth¬ 
works  between  Aquia  Creek  and  Chopawamsic.  This  is  not  vouched

Report  of  Captain  Palmer ,  TJ.  S.  Army,  of  topographical  reconnoissance 

in  the  Potomac. 

Coast  Survey  Office,  June  8,  1861. 

Dear  Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that  in  conformity  with  your 
instructions  of  the  31st  ultimo  I  have  completed  the  reconnoissance  of 
Lower  Cedar,  Mathias,  and  White  House  points,  on  the  Potomac  River. 
I  was  informed  on  the  3d  at  the  Navy  Department  that  the  small 
steamer  Resolute,  with  sixteen  armed  men,  would  be  placed  at  my  dis¬ 
posal  for  this  duty.  At  7  p.  m.  that  evening  I  left  the  navy  yard  in  that 
vessel  and  the  next  day,  the  4tli,  made  the  necessary  examination  at 
Lower  Cedar  Point,  Md.  On  the  5th  I  carefully  examined  Mathias 
Point,  Va.,  and  the  Maryland  shore  opposite.  On  the  0th  your  instruc¬ 
tions  were  accomplished  at  White  House  Point,  Ya. 

The  three  sketches  herewith  enclosed,  giving  the  width  and  depth  of 
the  river,  the  height  and  topographical  features  of  the  banks,  etc., 
exhibit  the  details  of  the  work  executed  during  my  short  absence. 

I  am  confident  that  at  the  date  of  my  visit  no  batteries  had  been 
erected  at  either  of  these  points,  although  both  are  commanding  posi¬ 
tions  and  thickly  wooded. 


506  OPERATIONS  ON  THE  POTOMAC  AND  RAPPAHANNOCK. 

% 

I  beg  leave  to  state  that  I  am  much  indebted  to  Commander  Bowau, 
U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  the  U.  S.  sloop  of  war  Pawnee ,  whose  ship  I 
found  opposite  the  rebel  batteries  at  Aquia  Creek,  for  the  great  assist¬ 
ance  he  gave  me.  At  Lower  Cedar  Point  he  lent  me  one  of  his  boats 
and  carried  his  ship  to  Mathias  and  White  House  points.  The  proxim¬ 
ity  of  her  guns  may  have  had  a  good  influence  on  the  rebels  there,  as, 
although  I  landed  and  scoured  the  woods  at  these  places  with  an  escort 
of  two  officers  and  twenty  men  only,  I  was  not  disturbed  by  them. 

The  negro  slaves  expressed  a  strong  desire  that  I  should  take  them 
with  me;  this  I  declined  doing. 

Acting  Lieutenant  Blue,  of  the  Paumee,  executed  a  part  of  the  hydrog¬ 
raphy  for  me. 

My  assistants,  Messrs.  Junken  and  Sands,  from  this  office,  were  very 
zealous  and  industrious. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

W.  XL  Palmer, 

Captain ,  Topographical  Engineers , 
Assistant  Coast  Survey,  in  charge  of  office.

Superintendent  U.  S.  Coast  Survey.

Report  of  Commander  Rowan ,  U.  S.  Wavy,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Pawnee ,

schooner  Somerset. 

U.  S.  S.  Pawnee, 

Off  Aquia  Creek,  Va.,  June  10,  1861. 
Sir:  The  blockade  of  the  Potomac  is  conducted  with  as  much  watch¬ 
fulness  as  the  nature  of  the  case  and  the  force  will  admit. 

I  find  it  necessary  to  remain  off  Aquia  Creek  with  this  ship,  particu¬ 
larly  at  night. 

There  is  communication  between  the  Maryland  and  Virginia  shores 
throughout  its  entire  length.  The  people  on  the  Maryland  side  all 
sympathize  with  the  enemy,  so  far  as  I  can  judge. 

On  the  5tli  instant  Lieutenant  Mygatt  captured  a  rowboat  on  the 
Virginia  shore  that  had  crossed  from  the  Maryland  side  at  Budd’s 
Perry,  supposed  to  have  taken  mail  matter  over.  The  crew  took  a 
package  from  the  boat  and  ran  into  the  woods. 

I  gave  Captain  Palmer  the  aid  of  this  ship  to  make  reconnoissance 
and  survey  of  Mathias  I’oint  and  the  White  House.

[Enclosure.] 

U.  S.  S.  Resolute,  June  9 , 1861. 

Sir:  In  obedience  to  your  instructions  I  have  made  an  examination 
of  the  lower  part  of  the  Potomac  River  and  have  the  honor  to  lay 
before  you  the  following  report  of  the  same: 

Leaving  the  anchorage  off  Aquia  Creek  early  on  the  morning  of  the 
6th  instant,  I  proceeded  to  and  landed  at  Blakistone  Island  light  house 
and  learned  from  the  keeper  that  he  had  received  a  letter  a  short  time 
since  threatening  him  with  violence  and  the  building  with  destruction 
if  the  light  was  not  extinguished  at  once.  He  declined  complying  with 
the  order  and  requests  that  arms  and  ammunition  may  be  given  him  to 
defend  himself  and  the  property  intrusted  to  his  charge. 

A  person  named  Blackwell,  living  on  the  Virginia  shore  immediately 
opposite,  and  two  others,  named  Key  and  Harris,  residing  in  Breton’s 
Bay,  Md.,  were,  as  far  as  I  could  ascertain,  the  authors  and  senders  of 
the  letter  above  alluded  to. 

Learning  that  supplies  and  men  were  constantly  passing  from  Breton’s 
Bay  to  Virginia,  I  left  an  officer  and  boat’s  crew  to  keep  a  strict  watch 
on  all  vessels  in  the  vicinity  and  proceeded  to  Piney  Point  light,  the 
keeper  of  which  stated  that  the  supply  of  oil  was  almost  exhausted, 
there  being  only  5  gallons  on  hand  the  day  of  my  visit;  nothing  else 
required  at  this  point. 

After  visiting  St.  Mary’s,  I  returned  to  Breton’s  Bay,  where  I  captured 
the  schooner  Somerset ,  which  vessel  was  there  and  had  been  for  some 
time  engaged  in  carrying  provisions  and  men  from  Maryland  to  Vir¬ 
ginia.  As  I  could  not  spare  men  to  take  care  of  her,  I  towed  her  close 
to  the  Virginia  shore  and  burned  her  on  the  night  of  the  8th. 

From  reliable  information  and  my  observation,  I  am  positive  that 
large  quantities  of  supplies  and  numbers  of  men  are  constantly  passing 
the  Potomac  at  Breton’s  Bay  and  St.  Mary’s.  Vessels  are  loaded  with 
provisions  in  Baltimore  and  dispatched  without  clearances  or  manifests, 
some  for  St.  Mary’s,  others  for  Breton’s  Bay,  and  many  when  boarded 
state  that  their  cargoes  are  for  farmers  along  the  Maryland  shore  of  the 
river.  There  have  been  more  provisions  lauded  in  St.  Mary’s  within 
the  last  month  than  the  inhabitants  of  that  vicinity  would  require  for 
three  years.  One  schooner  after  anchoring  in  the  harbor  crossed  over 
to  Yeocomico  [Va.],  twice  discharged  her  cargo  there,  and  is  now  in 
Baltimore  loading  for  the  third  trip. 


508  OPERATIONS  ON  THE  POTOMAC  AND  RAPPAHANNOCK. 

% 

I  examined  the  Virginia  sliore  closely  down  as  far  as  Hog  Island,  but 
could  not  discover  anything  like  batteries  below  Potomac  Creek.  Hear¬ 
ing  that  there  was  a  battery  at  Ragged  Point  I  went  close  in  there  this 
morning  and  fired  three  or  four  rounds  from  my  bow  gun  without 
receiving  any  reply.  No  works  of  any  kind  were  visible. 

There  are  two  small  vessels  lying  at  Currioman  Bay.  I  could  not  see 
any  others  between  Hog  Island  and  Aquia  Creek.  The  illness  oi  my 
engineer  compelled  me  to  return  without  extending  the  examination  to 
the  mouth  of  the  Rappahannock. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

William  Bitdd, 

Acting  Master ,  Commanding  Resolute. 

Captain  Rowan, 

Commanding  TJ.  8.  8.  Pawnee. 


Additional  report  of  Commander  lioivan,  TJ.  8.  Navy ,  commanding  U.  8.  8. 

Pawnee ,  regarding  reconnoissance  in  the  Potomac  River. 

U.  S.  S.  Pawnee, 
Potomac  River ,  June  12,  1861. 

Sir:  In  my  communication  of  the  10th  instant  I  omitted  to  inform 
the  Department  that  another  schooner  was  burned  on  the  Virginia 
shore  below  Budd’s  Ferry  on  the  morning  of  the  28th  [8th?]  by  the 
Reso  l ute  [  Reliance  ?  ] . 

I  had  dispatched  that  vessel  the  night  previous  with  directions  to 
drop  up  opposite  Budd’s  Ferry  and  watch  that  point.  The  ferry  at 
Thomas’s  Point  [Thom’s  Point?]  is  watched  by  this  ship  in  boats  at 
night.  The  communication  between  the  two  shores  at  these  points  is 
now  very  limited. 

A  colored  man  came  off  this  morning  in  a  small  boat,  stating  that  he 
belonged  to  a  Mr.  Healy,  and  asked  my  protection.  Having  little  faith 
in  the  loyalty  of  the  people  residing  on  the  Maryland  bank  of  this 
river,  I  declined  to  receive  him.  He  left  the  ship  and  continued  down 
the  river. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

S.  C.  Rowan, 

Commander. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy.

Navy  Yard,  Washington,  June  10,  1861 — p.  m. 
Sir:  Acting  Master  Budd,  commanding  the  Resolute,  having  towed 
np  the  disabled  Government  steamer  Young  America,  I  have  directed 
him  to  communicate  verbally  with  the  Department  and  convey  such 
intelligence  gathered  in  the  cruising  service  as  it  may  desire. 

It  will  be  unwise  to  leave  the  Maryland  shore  opposite  Aquia  and 
Potomac  creeks  without  constant  watch,  the  accumulation  of  supplies 
there  being  great,  to  be  run  over  the  moment  obstructions  now  offered 
by  the  Pawnee  cease. 

So  long  as  the  rebels  possess  the  steamer  Page  at  Aquia  only  a  steamer 
is  lit  to  watch  that  place.  I  had  contemplated  an  enterprise  to  burn 
the  Page,  but  she  is  removed  a  considerable  distance  up  the  creek  and 
guarded  by  a  considerable  force.  It  will  be  inexpedient  to  detail  one 
of  my  active  steamers  on  the  service,  nor  is  any  one  of  them  but  the 
Freeborn  of  sufficient  force  to  encounter  the  Page ,  and  even  she,  with 
her  low  sides,  would  fare  badly  if  attacked  by  some  hundreds  of  troops 
in  the  Page. 


The  Bailey,  Cobb,  aud  Dana.

Custom-House,  Baltimore,  June  5, 1861. 

Sir:  We  have  good  reason  to  believe — in  truth  we  have  almost 
undoubted  evidence  of  the  fact — that  there  is  a  large  quantity  of  goods 
now  being  shipped  from  our  city  on  board  the  schooner  Mount  Vernon, 
ostensibly  intended  for  Tall  Pine,  St.  Mary’s  County,  Md.,  but  really  en 
route  for  Yirginia.  If  we  are  correctly  informed,  they  will  be  landed 
at  Tall  Pine  and  from  thence  wagoned  across  the  country  to  the  Poto¬ 
mac,  a  distance  of  12  or  15  miles,  to  the  neighborhood  of  Swan  Point, 
where  a  wagon  road  to  Fredericksburg  intersects.  It  would  be  well  to 
have  a  Government  vessel  in  the  neighborhood  of  said  locality  for  the 
next  two  or  three  nights,  as  no  doubt  such  vigilance  would  detect  the 
parties  in  this  illicit  trade  and  the  seizure  more  than  repay  the  Govern¬ 
ment  expense  and  trouble. 

Yery  respectfully,  etc., 

Wm.  Thos.  Yaliant, 

Deputy  Collector. 

Hon.  S.  P.  Chase, 

Secretary  of  the  Treasury.

Pawnee,  relative  to  an  effective  blockade  of  the  Potomac. 

Flotilla  Steamer  Freeborn, 

Potomac  River,  June  13,  1861. 

Sir  :  You  will  be  pleased  to  remain,  with  the  Pawnee,  under  your 
command,  at  or  not  unnecessarily  far  from  your  present  station  off 
Aquia  Creek  and  effectually  continue  the  blockade  of  that  region 
against  all  egress  of  vessels  or  persons,  and  ingress  of  them,  or  sup¬ 
plies  of  any  sort,  in  any  form,  or  on  any  pretense  whatever. 

No  one  of  the  smaller  vessels  of  my  command  is  fit  to  lie  there,  sub¬ 
ject  to  be  boarded  suddenly  at  night  by  large  numbers  of  troops  put 
on  board  the  rebel  steamer  Page,  known  to  be  in  the  creek,  too  high 
up  for  attack  by  us,  and  too  well  guarded  by  soldiers.  You  will  exer¬ 
cise  every  degree  of  vigilance  against  such  surprise  and  maintain 
yourself  in  all  needed  preparation. 

You  will  permit  no  craft  of  any  description  to  be  underway  at 
night.  The  object  of  this  precaution  is  to  insure  a  discontinuance 
of  all  intercourse  between  the  Maryland  and  Virginia  shores,  which 
object  must  be  carried  out,  and  no  discretion  in  any  case  what¬ 
ever  exercised  to  the  contrary  by  any  one  subject  to  my  command. 
Vessels  sailing  at  night  can  elude  any  amount  of  vigilance  if  permitted 
to  continue  so  and  watch  their  opportunity.  Any  discovered  so  under¬ 
way  are  to  be  ordered  under  the  guns  of  the  Pawnee,  and  if  found  in 
disobedience  after  such  orders,  either  on  the  same  or  a  subsequent 
night,  will  be  made  prize. 

Two  or  three  armed  boats  will  row  guard  or  station  themselves  off 
such  points  on  the  Maryland  shore,  near  Maryland  Point  and  opposite 
Aquia,  or  at  such  other  localities  conveniently  near  as  there  is  reason 
to  apprehend  supplies  may  be  collected  for  transportation  to  Virginia, 
and  exercise  such  vigilance  and  activity  as  will  put  the  effective  execu¬ 
tion  of  the  object  in  view,  as  explained  in  this  communication,  beyond 
a  doubt  or  question  in  the  part  of  the  Potomac  where  you  are  or  may 
be  stationed. 

I  shall  leave  above  Cedar  Point  the  steamer  Reliance  as  an  active, 
movable  force,  subject  to  your  discretion  within  the  limit  of  these 
orders,  directing  the  officer  in  charge  of  her  to  report  to  you  for 
instructions. 

I  shall  further  anchor  one  of  the  flotilla  schooners,  with  a  master’s 
mate  and  six  hands  armed  with  muskets,  off  Port  Tobacco  or  Nanjemoy, 
probably  between  the  two  places,  as  a  permanent  guard,  whom  you  will 
please  see  are  heartily  engaged  in  carrying  out  the  spirit  of  these 
instructions  in  that  quarter,  keeping  the  schooner’s  small  boat  out  at 
night  for  that  purpose,  giving  the  men  rest  during  the  day. 

My  intention  is  that  the  Reliance  shall  as  a  rule  cruise  at  night  under 
low  steam,  giving  the  people  rest  while  at  anchor  during  the  day.  It 
is  at  night  that  the  violation  of  blockade  is  most  apprehended.  Hence 
these  specific  directions. 

I  am  in  expectation  of  another  schooner,  to  be  stationed  as  part  of  a 
cordon  of  observation,  at  or  near  Budd’s  Ferry  (Ohicomuxen  Creek), 
which  place  is  reported  as  a  depot  of  supplies  for  rebel  forces. 

Until  I  get  such  schooner  it  would  be  well  to  put  your  armed  launch 
there  every  night,  to  be  towed  up  by  the  Reliance  and  brought  down  in 
the  morning,  said  launch  being  one  of  the  two  or  three  boats  ordered 
on  guard  at  night.  This  boat  service  can  be  made  easy  for  your  crew 


OPERATIONS  ON  THE  POTOMAC  AND  RAPPAHANNOCK.  513 


by  so  dividing  the  duty  as  to  detail  no  one  upon  it  oftener  than  every 
third  night,  to  which  end  the  boats  need  not,  except  the  launch,  be 
your  heaviest,  nor,  unless  beyond  reach  of  ready  support  from  you,  will 
they  be  fully  manned. 

If  you  have  undoubted  conviction  that  a  depot  of  supplies,  arms, 
ammunition,  or  provisions  exists  in  Maryland  within  your  ready  reach, 
destined  for  Virginia,  awaiting  only  the  opportunity  to  elude  you  and  be 
carried  over,  you  will  seize  such  property  and  hold  it  subject  to  my 
decision.  I  shall  probably  pass  my  time  in  the  lower  Potomac,  but  will 
visit  you  at  short  intervals  and  keep  yon  provided  with  the  necessary 
provisions  and  stores. 

The  schooners  of  this  flotilla,  which  may  be  stationed  above  Cedar 
Point,  you  will  be  pleased  to  look  after  so  far  as  possible  consistently 
with  your  other  duties,  particularly  their  safety.  I  am  aware  of  their 
exposure  to  capture  by  surprise  at  night  and  for  that  reason  have  pre¬ 
ferred  that  they  should  be  armed  only  with  musketry.  They  should 
lie  always  in  a  state  of  preparation  for  scuttling,  the  arms  and  ammu¬ 
nition  ready  to  be  thrown  overboard,  so  that  in  the  event  of  being 
overpowered  by  numbers  the  capture  could  add  neither  trophy  nor 
strength  to  the  rebel  forces. 

The  boats  of  Budd’s  Ferry  must  cease  to  ply,  otherwise  they  must 
be  seized  and  sent  to  Washington,  leaving  the  owners  to  find  a  remedy 
there  against  the  Government.  In  my  absence,  while  perfecting  arrange¬ 
ments  lor  a  more  complete  blockade  on  the  lower  Potomac,  you  will  be 
pleased  to  carry  out  this  order  in  respect  to  Budd’s  Ferry  as  thoroughly 
as  your  means  will  possibly  allow. 

Very  respectfully, 


J.  H.  Ward, 

Commander ,  V.  S.  Navy ,  Senior  Officer  on  the  Potomac , 

Commanding  Blockade. 


Commander  S.  C.  Rowan, 

Commanding  TJ.  S.  S.  Pawnee ,  Potomac  River. 


Report  of  Commander  Rowan ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  commanding  TJ.  S.  S.  Pawnee, 
regarding  George  A.  Bates ,  a  citizen  of  Virginia. 

U.  S.  S.  Pawnee, 
Potomac  River ,  June  14,  1861. 

Sir:  Early  this  morning  a  person  calling  himself  George  A.  Bates 
came  off  to  the  ship  for  permission  to  pass  to  the  Virginia  shore.  He 
informs  me  he  resided  in  Prince  George’s  County,  Md.,  not  far  from 
Annapolis,  until  the  riot  in  Baltimore.  He  then  removed  his  wife  to 
Virginia  and  returned  to  Maryland  to  settle  his  business.  He  is  now 
waiting  for  permission  to  cross  with  some  household  effects  subject  to 
inspection  and  search.  He  declares  himself  a  loyal  citizen  and  willing 
to  take  the  oath  of  allegiance.  Shall  I  permit  him  to  pass  if  he  takes 
the  oath  ? 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

S.  C.  Rowan, 

Commander . 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy,  Washington.

Order  of  the  Secretary  of  the  Navy  to  Commander  Ward ,  TJ.  S.  Navy, 
commanding  Potomac  Flotilla ,  regarding  the  steamer  St.  Nicholas. 

Navy  Department,  June  15,  1861. 

Sir  :  The  Department  has  received  information  from  a  reliable  source 
that  the  steamer  St.  Nicholas,  running  between  Baltimore  and  Wash¬ 
ington,  leaving  the  former  city  on  Friday  afternoons  at  4  o’clock  and 
Washington  every  Tuesday  morniug  at  6  o’clock  (advertised  to  make 
landings  on  the  Maryland  shore  of  the  Potomac),  is  engaged  in  convey¬ 
ing  and  disposing  of  contraband  articles  to  parties  in  Virginia,  par¬ 
ticularly  cloth  for  the  use  of  the  soldiers.  You  will  cause  this  vessel 
to  be  carefully  searched  and  if  the  facts  are  as  supposed  you  will 
seize  her. 

Very  respectfully, 

Gideon  Welles, 

[Secretary  of  the  Navy.) 

Captain  James  H.  Ward. 

Commanding  U.  S.  S.  Thomas  Freeborn. 


[Enclosure.] 

The  steamer  from  Baltimore,  St.  Nicholas ,  arrived  yesterday  (Sun¬ 
day  a.  m.)  and  announces  her  departure  for  to-morrow  a.  m.  The 
captain  reports  being  brought  to  by  a  shotted  gun  on  the  river  and 
compelled  to  lay  by  during  the  night,  and  on  assuring  the  commander 
of  the  war  steamship  of  the  St.  Nicholas  being  a  peaceful  steamer, 
resuming  her  regular  trips  to  and  from  Baltimore  and  Washington,  he 
was  allowed  to  proceed. 

The  plan  of  communication  between  Baltimore  and  Bichmond  is  for 
the  steamer  to  land  at  a  small  port  on  the  Maryland  side  nearly  oppo¬ 
site  Aquia  Creek,  where  a  depot  has  been  established.  Small  boats  are 
ready  to  carry  over  the  passengers,  merchandise,  and  mails  during  the 
night. 

I  would  most  respectfully  suggest  sending  a  person  in  her  to-morrow 
to  observe,  and  then  take  care  of  her  on  the  second  trip,  at  which  time 
the  apparent  success  of  the  first  trip  would  insure  a  good  haul  of 
contraband.

[Enclosure.] 

Port  Ellsworth,  September  26,  1861. 

Sir:  On  the  15th  of  June  I  was  ordered  by  Commander  J.  A.  Dahl- 
gren  to  take  charge  of  the  steamer  Mount  Vernon  and  make  a  recon- 
noissance  of  White  House  Bluff,  to  determine  if  any  rebel  batteries  had 
been  erected  there.  When  off'  the  mouth  of  Pamunkey  Creek  (nearly 
opposite  to  White  House  Bluff)  the  pilot  of  the  Mount  Vernon  pointed 
out  to  me  a  small  sloop  at  anchor  in  the  creek,  which  he  knew  had  been 
engaged  in  carrying  rebel  troops  from  Maryland  across  to  Virginia.  I 
immediately  returned  to  the  navy  yard  to  obtain  the  authority  of  Com¬ 
mander  Dahlgren  to  seize  her;  after  obtaining  this  authority,  I  pro¬ 
ceeded  to  the  creek  and  found  the  sloop  had  got  underway.  I  then  fol¬ 
lowed  the  Maryland  shore  up  the  river  and  found  the  sloop  some  2  or  3 
miles  above  her  original  position.  When  those  on  board  saw  I  was  in 
pursuit  they  ran  the  vessel  on  shore,  after  which  I  seized  and  towed 
her  to  the  navy  yard.  The  name  of  the  vessel  was  the  Alena. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Jas.  M.  Prichett, 

Lieutenant ,  U.  S.  Navy. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy,  Washington,  I).  C. 


Report  of  Commander  Ward,  IJ.  S.  Navy,  commanding  Potomac  Flotilla, 
of  the  burning  of  the  schooner  Christiana  Keen  by  a  party  of  Virgin¬ 
ians  and  transmitting  copy  of  warning  to  vessels  against  sailing  at 
night. 

Flotilla  Steamer  Freeborn, 

Potomac  River,  June  16,  1861. 

Sir  :  Accompanying  this  I  send  a  paper  drawn  up  in  the  form  of  a 
public  notice,  which  contains  information  [that]  it  seems  to  me  should 
be  made  known  to  prevent  an  unnecessary  alarm. 

The  master  of  the  schooner  burned  very  unnecessarily  exposed  him¬ 
self  to  this  disaster  by  sailing  at  night  when  the  navigation  is  very 
intricate  and  keeping  to  windward  on  the  Virginia  shore,  when  the 
channel  lay  on  the  other  shore,  the  wind  being  entirely  fair. 

The  burned  wreck  now  lies  opposite  Cedar  Point,  not  far  from  where 
the  light-boat  was,  where  also  a  buoy  was  until  two  or  three  days  ago. 
The  wreck  is  now  a  good  mark,  one  not  easily  removed. 


OPERATIONS  ON  THE  POTOMAC  AND  RAPPAHANNOCK.  517 


The  party  of  thirty  or  forty  which  made  the  attack  were  uniformed  in 
gray,  with  felt  hats,  so  the  master  of  the  schooner  says,  and  I  judge 
they  were  a  detachment  of  soldiers.  This  fact,  and  their  proximity  to 
Mathias  Point,  together  with  information  gathered  yesterday  at  Coan 
Piver  that  a  company  had  lately  gone  from  there  to  Mathias,  indicates 
the  protection  of  that  point  against  visits  such  as  have  recently  been 
made  in  two  instances  for  reconnoissauces,  once  by  myself  and  since  by 
Captain  Palmer,  of  the  Army.  I  see  yet  no  signs  of  a  battery,  but 
shall  watch  for  any  which  may  be  discoverable. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully, 

-T.  H.  Ward, 

Commander ,  Commanding  Potomac  Flotilla. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy,  Washington ,  I).  C. 


[Enclosure.] 

Flotilla  Steamer  Freeborn, 

Potomac  River ,  June  15,  1861. 

The  schooner  Christiana  Keen,  running  last  night  in  the  Potomac 
near  Lower  Cedar  Point,  grounded  on  the  Virginia  shore  off  Upper 
Machodoc  Creek,  not  far  below  Mathias  Point,  and  was  burned  by  a 
party  of  thirty  Virginians,  Avho  put  out  from  the  creek  in  rowboats  for 
that  purpose. 

The  officer  in  command  on  the  Potomac  does  not,  as  a  rule,  permit 
vessels  to  sail  at  night,  nor  does  he  consider  it  prudent  for  them  to  do 
so  even  when  permitted,  but  counsels  them,  for  mutual  protection 
against  marauders,  to  anchor  at  St.  Mary’s  Kiver,  Blakistone  Island 
light,  Nanjemoy,  or  off  Aquia,  at  each  of  which  points  a  Government 
armed  vessel  will  generally,  if  not  always,  be  found  to  afford  further 
protection. 

By  sailing  two  or  more  in  company,  the  mutual  support  arising  from 
such  an  arrangement,  especially  if  all  vessels  trading  to  this  river  be 
armed  with  musketry  and  observing  the  precautions  indicated,  the 
little  danger  existing  only  in  case  of  calms  and  grounding  will  be 
obviated. 

To  mitigate  alarm,  which  this  accident  will  produce,  it  is  proper  to 
state  that  the  schooner  first  grounded  fast  in  feet,  only  half  a  mile 
from  the  Virginia  shore  on  the  weather  side  of  the  river,  where  it  is2£ 
miles  -wide  and  the  channel  near  the  Maryland  shore. 

The  flotilla  on  that  night  was  distributed  at  Budd’s  Ferry,  Aquia, 
INanjemoy,  Blakistone,  St.  Mary’s,  and  Smith’s  Point,  at  any  of  which 
localities  there  was  protection. 

Since  the  removal  of  buoys,  light-boats,  and  other  marks,  the  navi¬ 
gation  between  Cedar  and  Maryland  points  is  altogether  too  hazardous 
for  the  night.  Some  of  the  buoys,  it  is  true,  remain,  but  one  or  another 
is  from  time  to  time  removed,  so  that  no  dependence  whatever  can  be 
placed  on  them  as  marks.  The  master  of  the  schooner  burned  inferred 
(all  see  now  how  erroneously)  that  because  Piney  Point  and  Blakistone 
Island  lights  are  burning,  all  the  others  on  the  river  were,  including  the 
light-boat  formerly  on  the  flats  where  he  grounded. 

This  fact  is  published  as  a  warning  to  others  against  a  similar  mis¬ 
take.

[Endorsement.] 

[Flotilla  Steamer]  Freeborn,  June  17, 1861. 

The  above  pass  is  not  recognized  because  it  does  not  bear  the  signa¬ 
ture  of  a  commanding  officer,  who  alone  is  authorized  personally  to 
hear  and  decide  cases  of  the  kind  and  to  grant  passes. 

The  present  case  is  one  in  which  the  vessel  had  been  found  by  me  on 
the  Virginia  shore  and  ordered  to  Washington  to  get  a  pass  from 
authority  there  and  not  to  be  found  down  the  Potomac  again  without 
one.  The  master  did  not  go,  but  practiced  this  deception,  for  which  he 
is  a  prize. 

The  Bachelor  has  further  offended  by  being  found  several  miles  below 
Nanjemoy  without  permission,  and  anchored  close  under  the  Maryland 
shore,  opposite  to  and  in  the  nearest  and  most  convenient  position  for 
communicating  with  Mathias  Point,  where  there  are  troops  stationed, 
as  there  is  every  reason  to  believe.  A  small  vessel  like  this  went  to 
Mathias  yesterday  and  escaped  during  the  night.  The  troops  there 
undoubtedly  get  supplies  from  the  Maryland  side  by  means  like  this, 
hence  the  summary  proceedings  in  this  case. 

J.  H.  Ward, 

Commander.

Off  Aquia  Creek,  June  16,  1861. 

The  shallop  H.  Bay,  Henry  Knight  [Neitzey?],  master,  has  permis¬ 
sion  to  pass  to  Nanjemoy  Creek,  to  fish,  and  back.  Not  to  communi¬

[Endorsement.] 

[Flotilla  Steamer]  Freeborn,  June  17,  1861. 

This  and  all  other  passes  given  possess  no  validity,  and  will  not  be 
recognized,  unless  bearing  the  signature,  the  actual  signature,  of  a 
commanding  officer,  who  alone  has  power  to  judge  the  case  and  grant 
the  pass,  and  that  only  after  a  personal  hearing,  which  the  master  of 
the  Bay  says  was  not  had.

P.  S. — The  schooner  Bachelor ,  warned  by  me  three  or  four  days  ago, 
has  been  found  in  disregard  of  it;  has  deceived  Captain  Rowan  by  false 
statements  or  suppression ;  has  violated  Captain  Rowan’s  pass,  and 
been  found  by  me  concealed  on  the  Maryland  side  opposite  Mathias 
Point,  at  the  place  most  convenient  for  crossing.  I  have  therefore 
seized  her  and  send  her  up  by  you  as  at  least  a  more  effectual  warning 
than  was  before  given  her.  Perhaps  some  detention,  while  it  is  just, 
may  be  a  sufficient  penalty  and  deter  the  owner  from  so  exposing  him¬ 
self  again.  It  will  also  put  others  on  their  guard. 

The  sloop  II.  Day ,  belonging  to  the  same  owner,  I  have  detained  for 
use  at  Eanjemoy,  where  just  such  a  vessel  is  needed  to  watch  the  place 
she  was  taken  in.  She  was  taken  in  company  with  the  schooner  and 
under  circumstances  of  equal  suspicion.  What  disposition  is  ultimately 
made  of  her  will  depend,  I  suppose,  in  part  upon  the  necessities  and 
upon  the  justice  of  the  case. 

J.  H.  Ward. 


Report  of  Commander  Rowan ,  U.  S.  Wavy ,  commanding  U.  8.  8.  Pawnee , 
requesting  instructions  regarding  discovery  of  suspicious  stores  at  Mary¬ 
land  Point. 


U.  S.  S.  Pawnee, 

Off  Aquia  Creek ,  June  17,  1861. 

Sir:  Some  two  weeks  since,  we  discovered  a  number  of  hogsheads  of 
bacon,  barrels  of  whisky,  etc.,  in  a  fish  house  near  Maryland  Point. 
Having  suspicions  of  the  loyalty  of  the  owner  of  the  property,  I  caused 
a  strict  watch  to  be  kept  in  boats  at  night,  fearing  that  the  goods  might 
be  intended  for  the  enemy.  To-day  I  sent  Lieutenant  Lowry  on  shore 
to  examine  the  premises  and  ascertain  whether  the  goods  had  been 
removed.  He  reports  that  everything  is  still  there  and  "the  people  about 
the  house  say  that  the  owners  have  not  yet  sent  for  them. 

I  respectfully  request  instructions  in  the  premises.  I  believe  they 
are  intended  for  shipment  to  Virginia,  but  have  no  proof.  I  send  a 
description  of  the  articles  with  the  marks,  etc. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

S.  0.  Rowan, 

Commander. 

Hon.  G.  Welles, 

Secretary  Navy ,  Washington.

Confidential]  Navy  Department,  June  18, 1861. 

Sir  :  Yours  of  the  17th  is  received,  reporting  stores  of  bacon,  whisky, 
and  other  articles  in  a  fish  house  near  Maryland  Point,  which  you  have 
reason  to  believe  are  intended  for  shipment  to  Virginia,  and  requesting 
instructions  in  regard  to  them. 

The  place  of  storage  and  attending  circumstances  are  presumptive 
evidence  that  they  are  intended  for  the  opposite  side  of  the  Potomac; 
and  unless  those  who  have  the  care  and  custody  of  these  stores  can 
satisfy  you  that  such  is  not  their  destination,  but  that  they  belong  in 
good  faith  to  citizens  of  Maryland,  and  are  to  be  retained  and  consumed 
in  that  State,  you  will  be  justified  in  seizing  them. 

Very  respectfully,  etc., 

Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  Navy.

Report  of  Commander  Rowan,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  17.  S.  S.  Pawnee, 
regarding  the  seizure  of  suspicious  stores  at  Maryland  Point. 

IT.  S.  S.  Pawnee, 
Potomac  River,  June  18,  1861. 

Sir:  On  the  3d  instant  I  discovered  stowed  in  a  fish  house  owned 
by  a  Mr.  Carpenter,  residing  at  a  landing  place  opposite  Aquia  Creek, 


522  OPERATIONS  ON  THE  POTOMAC  AND  RAPPAHANNOCK. 


a  number  of  hogsheads  and  some  barrels  and  bags..  'Suspecting  that 
it  might  be  provisions  intended  for  the  enemy,  I  kept  a  close  watch  on 
it  up  to  the  16tli  instant,  when  Lieutenant  Lowry  demanded  the  keys 
and  took  the  marks,  etc.,  which  I  have  already  given  in  my  communi¬ 
cation  of  the  17  th. 

Having  determined  in  my  own  mind  that  this  provision  was  not 
intended  for  consumption  in  Maryland,  partly  from  the  length  of  time 
it  was  allowed  to  remain  in  store,  and  partly  from  a  firm  conviction  that 
Carpenter  holds  intercourse  with  the  enemy  and  has  been  in  Virginia 
the  last  two  weeks,  from  whence  he  returned  the  night  before  last, 
crossing  the  river  in  a  small  boat  near  Yanjemoy  Creek.  The  most  of 
my  information  is  derived  from  colored  people,  who  answer  questions 
without  reserve  when  opportunity  offers.  To-day  I  seized  the  provi¬ 
sions  in  Carpenter’s  fish  house  and  put  them  on  board  a  wood  schooner 
that  happened  to  be  loading  here,  and  directed  Lieutenant  Mygatt,  of 
the  tug  Reliance ,  to  tow  her  to  the  navy  yard  and  deliver  the  provisions 
to  the  commandant  of  the  yard. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

S.  C.  Bowan, 

Commander. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy ,  Washington.

Yaw  Yard,  Washington,  June  18, 1861. 

The  Resolute  is  just  arrived  from  below  with  two  small  prizes.  Reports 
the  Freeborn  coming  out  of  Port  Tobacco  last  evening ;  also  that  Mathias 
Point  is  certainly  occupied  by  a  small  body  of  infantry.  The  Seventy- 
first  left  this  morning  at  3  o’clock  for  Alexandria  by  order  of  General 
Scott. 

About  9  p.  m.  last  evening  a  detachment  of  the  Seventy-first  of  150 
men  proceeded  to  seize  the  arms  said  to  be  collected  near  Port  Tobacco, 
as  directed  yesterday  by  the  Department.  I  expect  them  back  before 
this  evening.  The  Resolute  needs  some  small  repairs  of  engine. 

Jno.  A.  Dahlgren. 

Yaw  Department.

Report  of  commandant  navy  yard,  Washington ,  of  expedition  to  Fort 
Tobacco ,  Md.,  June  17,  and  reconnoissance  to  White  House  Bluff,  Ya., 
June  19. 


Commandant’s  Office,  Navy  Yard, 

Washington ,  June  20,  1861. 

Sir  :  Upon  information  given  by  certain  parties,  a  detachment  of  the 
Seventy-first  Regiment  left  here  at  9  p.  m.  of  the  17th,  in  order  to  seize 
some  arms  said  to  be  collected  near  Port  Tobacco. 

The  movement  was  made  by  night  with  judgment  and  great  celerity, 
the  troops  being  commanded  by  Captain  Ellis,  but  there  is  every  reason 
to  believe  that  it  only  failed  because  the  arms  had  been  removed  to 
Virginia. 

Yesterday  a  reconnoissance  was  made  of  the  White  House  Bluff.  It 
appears  to  have  been  visited  on  Saturday  last  by  an  officer  and  some 
men  of  the  secessionists,  who  were  overheard  to  speak  of  the  probable 
erection  of  a  battery.  On  the  same  day  it  was  also  stated  that  a  small 
village  not  far  from  the  bluff  was  occupied  by  some  companies  of 
secessionists. 

The  steamer  Mount  Vernon  was  subsequently  dispatched  to  seize  a 
small  sloop  Avliich  is  known  to  have  conveyed  armed  men  from  the 
Maryland  to  the  Virginia  shores,  and  in  all  probability  the  arms  secreted 
near  Port  Tobacco. 

This  vessel  is  now  here  subject  to  the  orders  of  the  Navy  Department. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Jno.  A.  Dahlgren, 

Commandant. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy.

Off  Aquia  Creek,  Va.,  June  19,  1861. 
Sill:  One  of  the  boats  rowing  guard  every  night  was  directed  to

[Enclosure.] 


U.  S.  S.  Pawnee, 
Potomac  River ,  June  19,  1861. 

Sir:  In  obedience  to  your  order  of  the  evening  of  the  17tli,  I  took 
the  first  cutter  with  sixteen  men  and,  in  tow  of  the  U.  S.  S.  Reliance , 
proceeded  to  Cockpit  Point,  where  I  landed  and  found  several  boats, 
and  being  satisfied  that  they  were  used  for  bringing  men  and  provisions 
from  the  Maryland  shore,  took  possession  of  them  and  towed  them  to 
the  Reliance,  where  they  were  destroyed.  I  also  skirted  the  beach  for 
several  miles  but  saw  nothing  suspicious.  Prom  this  point  I  proceeded 
to  Evansport,  and  landing  half  a  mile  below,  sent  six  men  in  charge  of 
Master’s  Mate  Bogert  to  reconnoiter,  keeping  the  larger  portion  with 
me.  In  about  ten  minutes  Mr.  Bogert  returned  and  informed  me  that 
they  had  driven  in  a  picket  guard  of  mounted  troopers.  My  not  know¬ 
ing  what  force  the  enemy  may  have  had  stationed  in  the  vicinity,  I 
deemed  it  expedient  to  return  to  my  boat  and  follow  out  your  orders 
farther  down  the  river.  On  arriving  at  Scott’s  Landing  I  landed  and 
found  several  boats  hauled  up  on  shore  under  a  fishing  shed,  and  while 
a  portion  of  my  men  were  getting  these  boats  in  the  water  I  took  the 
rest  up  to  a  dwelling  house  to  examine  the  premises,  and  on  gaining 
the  rear  of  the  house  discovered  three  troopers  who  galloped  off  on 
discovering  who  we  were.  I  then  returned  to  my  boat  and  towed  off 
four  boats  to  the  Reliance,  the  same  I  brought  alongside. 

The  Reliance  then  steamed  up  again  to  Evansport,  where  we  saw  a 
large  number  of  men  running  along  the  shore,  all  of  them  armed,  but 
it  being  early  daylight  we  were  unable  to  tell  how  well. 

We  lay  off  the  place  for  some  time  and  finding  we  could  do  nothing 
further  I  concluded  to  return. 

While  turning  around  some  muskets  were  fired  from  behind  some 
bushes,  which  we  returned  with  canister  from  the  howitzer  on  the 
Reliance.  As  no  other  shots  were  fired  from  the  shore,  and  my  men 
having  been  up  all  night  and  much  fatigued,  we  returned  to  the  ship. 
During  my  absence  from  this  vessel  I  captured  nine  boats,  five  of  which 
were  destroyed. 

I  am,  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

J.  C.  Chaplin, 

Lieutenant ,  U.  8.  Navy 

Commander  S.  C.  Rowan, 

Commanding  U.  8.  S.  Pawnee.
