Letter  from  Mr.  George  D.  Wise,  to  Professor  A.  P.  Bache ,  Superintend¬ 
ent  TJ.  S.  Coast  Survey,  giving  information  regarding  shipment  of 
provisions  to  Virginia. 

Private.]  Baltimore,  June  19, 1861. 

Dear  Sir  :  I  have  reason  to  suspect  that  quite  an  amount  of  aid  and 
comfort  is  being  sent  from  this  city  to  Virginia  by  way  of  the  Rappa¬ 
hannock  River.  Small  crafts  load  here,  ostensibly  for  the  eastern  shore 
of  Maryland,  but  rendezvous  among  the  Tangier  Islands.  Watching 
their  opportunity  they  cross  the  bay  and  sail  up  the  Rappahannock  to 
a  small  town  called  Tappaliannock  and  there  discharge  their  cargo. 
The  principal  articles '  shipped  have  been  provisions,' of  which  I  am 
informed  the  Virginians  are  much  in  want. 

I  write  the  above  in  case  you  should  consider  it  of  sufficient  impor¬ 
tance  to  communicate  to  the  blockading  division. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Geo.  D.  Wise. 

Professor  A.  D.  Bache, 

Superintendent  TJ.  S.  Coast  Survey ,  Washington. 


Report  of  Commander  Ward,  TJ.  S.  Navy ,  commanding  Potomac  Flotilla, 
relating  to  the  capture  of  the  schooner  Buena  Vista  and  other  affairs  on 
the  Potomac  River. 

Flotilla  Steamer  Freeborn, 

St.  Mary's  River,  June  20,  1861. 

Sir:  The  prize  schooner  Buena  Vista  was  sent  by  me  to  Washington 
on  Monday,  the  17tli,  in  charge  of  the  Resolute,  Acting  Master  Budd, 
with  orders  to  report  verbally  the  circumstances  of  the  seizure  and  the 
grounds  on  which  it  was  made. 

Enclosed  is  the  report  *  1  have  required  Acting  Master’s  Mate  [James 
L.]  Gray,  in  charge  of  the  flotilla  schooner  Bailey,  to  make  of  his 
knowledge  and  agency  in  the  case.  By  said  report  it  will  appear  that 
the  Buena  Vista  is  the  first  fruit  of  the  arrangement  by  which  the 
schooners  of  this  flotilla  are  stationed  at  Eanjemoy  aud  Port  Tobacco, 
at  Breton’s  Bay  (Leonardtown),  and  at  St.  Mary’s.  I  had  anchored 
the  Bailey  on  the  evening  of  Friday,  the  14th,  having  that  morning 


Not  found. 


OPERATIONS  ON  THE  POTOMAC  AND  RAPPAHANNOCK.  527 


anchored  the  flotilla  schooner  Cobb  at  Breton’s  Bay  to  cut  off  traffic 
with  Virginia  from  Leonardtown:  at  which  place,  as  well  as  at  Port 
Tobacco,  the  secession  feeling  is  largely  demonstrative. 

The  flotilla  schooner  Dana ,  in  charge  of  Acting  Master’s  Mate 
[Robert  B.]  Ely,  watches  at  Ranjemoy  and  Port  Tobacco,  both  which 
she  is  enabled  to  do  by  means  of  the  small  sloop  H.  Day ,  seized  under 
suspicious  circumstances  a  few  days  ago  and  appropriated  by  me  to 
serve  as  tender  to  the  Dana. 

These  schooners  serve  also  as  depots  for  coal  in  aid  of  the  active  ves¬ 
sels  of  the  flotilla,  the  endeavor  being,  by  taking  coal  from  Government 
or  other  transports  as  they  pass  up  the  river,  to  keep  the  supply  in  each 
schooner  equal  to  40  or  50  tons.  With  the  two  other  schooners  asked 
for  I  shall  be  able  to  stop  the  illicit  trade  with  Virginia  so  far  as  carried 
on  from  the  Potomac  shore  of  Maryland. 

On  Friday  evening,  the  14th,  I  had  sent  the  Resolute  to  Smith’s  Point 
with  orders  to  make  a  thorough  reconnoissance  and  join  me  off  the 
Yeocomico  at  noon  on  Saturday.  On  his  way  up  Saturday  morning 
Acting  Master  Budd  cut  off  from  the  shore  and  captured  two  fisher¬ 
men,  bringing  them  to  me  at  Yeocomico.  On  a  close  examination  of 
the  prisoners  I  extracted  from  them  the  information  that  the  suspected 
schooner  Mount  Vernon  has  not  made  a  successful  trip,  at  least  directly 
to  Coan  River,  but  the  schooner  Bxiena  Vista  had.  I  therefore  issued 
orders  that  said  schooner  should  be  seized  whenever  and  wherever  found 
and  detained  for  my  adjudication.  To  blockade  Coan  River  and  Yeo¬ 
comico  closely  against  entrance  from  Baltimore  direct  I  need  another 
steamer,  one  like  the  Leslie ,  at  the  Washington  yard,  with  a  rifled  how¬ 
itzer,  to  watch  these  points  closely  and  constantly  and  the  whole  breadth 
of  the  Potomac  at  this  point.  To  anchor  a  sailing  vessel  off  either  of 
these  rivers  might  be  hazardous,  both  on  account  of  the  weather  and 
liability  to  attack.  I  think  the  schooners  on  the  Maryland  shore  are 
safe  enough  in  all  respects  with  their  present  force  of  six  men,  visited 
so  often  as  they  are  by  the  steamers.  Whatever  the  force,  unless  very 
large,  it  is  liable  to  possible  capture,  and  if  captured  the  smaller  the 
better.  I  have  an  especial  repugnance  to  the  loss  of  a  cannon,  therefore 
have  not  proposed  one  as  an  armament  for  either  of  the  schooners.  The 
officers  in  charge  have  orders  to  be  in  constant  readiness  to  scuttle  or 
burn  their  vessels,  with  provision  for  the  escape  of  their  men.  They 
express  a  determination  never  to  be  taken  and  I  believe  so  intend. 

In  regard  to  the  reported  rebel  project  of  obstructing  the  channel  of 
the  Potomac,  I  look  upon  it  as  futile;  for  below  White  House  Point  it 
is  not  anywhere  less  than  a  large  three-fourths  of  a  mile  wide,  steep, 
too,  on  both  sides.  The  steamers  or  boats  of  the  flotilla  pass  to  and  fro 
daily,  besides  being  in  constant  communication  with  private  vessels 
trading  up  or  down  or  public  transports,  any  of  whom  would  be  likely 
to  know  and  will  be  instructed  to  report  any  indications  of  the  kind 
which  observation  can  detect.  Above  White  House  Point  I  recommend 
a  reconnoissance  by  boats  from  the  Pocahontas ,  such  as  I  have  directed 
to  be  kept  up  by  the  boats  of  the  Pawnee  between  Aquia  and  Budd’s 
Ferry,  until  I  get  another  schooner  to  anchor  off  that  point. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

J.  H.  Ward, 
Commanding  Flotilla. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy ,  Washington ,  I).  C. 

P.  S. — A  smart  schooner  like  the  Savannah  (privateer)  might  make  a 
good  blockader  off'  Coan  River,  etc.,  in  lieu  of  a  steamer. 

J.  H.  Ward.

Report  of  commandant  navy  yard ,  Washington ,  regarding  measures  for 
the  protection  of  communication  in  the  Potomac. 

Commandant’s  Office,  Navy  Yard, 

Washington,  June  20,  1861. 

Sir:  As  circum stances  may  lead  to  some  attempt  on  the  communica¬ 
tions  of  this  place  by  the  Potomac,  I  beg  leave  to  submit  the  following 
remarks  thereon : 

There  are  only  two  points  where  this  can  be  done  successfully.  The 
lowest  of  these  is  Mathias  Point,  about  50  miles  from  Washington. 

The  channel  is  so  narrowed  here  that  vessels  can  not  keep  farther 
than  1,400  yards  from  the  point  at  one  place,  exposing  them  to  consid¬ 
erable  chance  of  damage  by  daylight. 

The  distance  of  the  opposite  bank  (4,000  yards)  is  so  great  as  to  pre¬ 
clude  the  possibility  of  silencing  batteries  on  Mathias — they  could  only 
be  annoyed. 

If  suffered  to  remain  the  passage  must  be  effected  under  cover  of  the 
night. 

The  best  plan  is  to  seize  and  hold  the  point  at  once,  which,  from  the 
nature  of  the  ground,  would  not  be  difficult  nor  require  a  large  force. 

Its  extreme  margin  presents  firm  ground  of  no  great  extent,  separated 
from  the  remainder  by  a  swamp  which  can  no  doubt  be  made  impassable 
by  some  fieldworks  and  artillery,  supported  by  five  or  six  companies  of 
good  troops,  and  the  guns  of  a  few  vessels  near  the  edge  of  the  channel. 
I  would  recommend  a  reconnoissauce  by  proper  officers  to  this  end,  and 
if  in  their  opinion  advisable,  to  be  carried  out  without  delay. 

White  House  Bluff  is  the  other  position  that  may  be  used  to  hinder 
the  communication  by  the  river. 

This,  like  the  other,  would  be  best  guaranteed  by  occupation,  but  the 
operation  would  require  more  force,  is  not  assisted  by  the  nature  of  the 
ground,  and  is  so  near  to  the  principal  secessionist  force  that  it  could 
hardly  be  made  secure  except  by  a  larger  body  of  men  than  could  be 
spared. 

Resort  must  be  had,  therefore,  to  a  counter  battery  on  the  opposite 
shore,  distant  1,700  to  2,000  yards,  and  some  heavy  pieces  afloat  to 
enfilade  the  principal  front.  Even  with  these  it  would  be  impossible  to 
free  the  bluff'  entirely  from  batteries,  so  that  the  cover  of  the  night 
would  have  to  be  used  m  passing. 

A  railroad  acting  below  this  point  would  obviate  the  difficulty,  but 
might  not  be  made  available  in  the  time  required.  Other  modes  of 
communication  might  also  be  substituted  for  transportation,  which  I 
need  not  enlarge  on  here. 

I  would  advise,  however,  that  some  measures  be  taken  toward  the 
occupation  of  Mathias  Point  and  the  counter  battery  to  the  White 
House  Bluff. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Jno.  A.  Dahlgren, 

Commandant. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy.

Report  of  Commander  Rowan ,  U.  8.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Pawnee , 
transmitting  statement  of  a  deserter  from  the  Confederate  Navy. 

U.  S.  S.  Pawnee, 

Off  .A  quia  Creek,  Va.,  June  21,  1861. 

Sir  :  At  daylight  this  morning  a  man  was  seen  swimming  toward  the 
ship  from  the  Maryland  shore.  A  boat  was  sent  to  his  aid  and  he  wTas 
brought  on  board.  He  states  that  his  name  is  John  Dowling,  of  Great 
Barrington,  Mass.,  is  a  carpenter  by  trade,  and  has  been  residing  in  the 
South  since  April,  1860.  lie  is  last  from  the  batteries  at  Aquia  Creek, 
where  he  arrived  the  day  before  his  desertion.  He  went  down  to  the 
end  of  the  wharf  to  bathe,  and  before  he  was  observed  he  was  half  a 
mile  distant  from  the  batteries,  swimming  for  this  ship.  Several  shots 
from  cannon,  which  he  says  were  rifle,  were  fired  at  him.  ■  We  heard 
the  firing,  but  supposed  it  was  practice. 

This  escape  showed  coolness  and  nerve,  as  well  as  great  physical 
endurance.  The  distance  from  the  battery  to  where  we  landed  on  the 
opposite  shore  is  about  6  miles.  Added  to  this  his  exposure  during  the 
night  on  the  beach  naked,  and  a  walk  of  2  miles  up  the  beach  opposite 
the  ship,  and  another  swim  of  a  mile  to  the  ship,  all  bespeak  character 
and  energy. 

I  enclose  a  detailed  statement  of  all  he  saw  during  his  residence  in 
the  South. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

S.  C.  Rowan, 

Commander. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy ,  Washington ,  D.  C. 


[Enclosure.] 

Statement  of  John  Dowling,  a  deserter  from  the  ( so-called )  Confederate  Navy. 

Aquia  Creek,  June  22,  1861. 

I  reside  in  Great  Barrington,  Mass.  I  left  home  on  the  5th  April, 

1860.  I  am  a  carpenter  by  trade.  I  went  to  Savannah,  Ga.,  and  worked 
there  at  my  trade  till  the  following  November. 

I  left  Savannah  on  the  12th  of  November  for  Montgomery,  Ala, ; 
worked  there  and  in  the  vicinity  five  months.  Having  no  further 
employment,  I  went  to  Columbus,  Ga. 

There  I  joined  the  Confederate  States  Sentinels  on  the  loth  of  May, 

1861,  to  prevent  being  arrested  as  an  abolitionist.  May  18  the  Senti¬ 
nels  were  moved  to  Richmond,  Va.,  where  I  remained  with  the  troops 
six  days  and  deserted.  I  took  the  direction  of  Yorktown  in  hopes  of 
escaping  by  water.  When  within  9  miles  of  Williamsburg  I  was  told 
I  could  not  get  through,  martial  law  being  declared  in  Williamsburg 
and  a  cordon  of  troops  between  the  two  rivers.  I  then  went  off  in  the 
direction  of  York  River  and  crossed  it  at  West  Point,  which  is  the 
terminus  of  the  Richmond  Railroad.  I  there  found  an  earthwork  pre¬ 
pared  for  three  or  four  guns;  the  guns  were  daily  expected  from  Rich- 


OPERATIONS  ON  THE  POTOMAC  AND  RAPPAHANNOCK.  531 

mond.  I  went  to  West  Point  to  enlist  witli  a  hope  that  I  might  have 
an  opportunity  of  deserting,  but  I  was  required  to  take  the  oath  of  alle¬ 
giance,  and  refused  to  do  so.  I  then  took  the  train  for  Richmond,  hav¬ 
ing  seen  in  the  papers  that  carpenters  were  wanted  there.  I  worked 
in  Richmond  six  and  a  half  days.  This  was  in  early  part  of  this  month. 
I  finished  the  work  I  could  get  and  left  Richmond  for  Fredericksburg, 
where  I  was  told  I  could  not  get  to  the  river.  Finding  no  way  of 
escape,  I  shipped  in  the  (so-called)  Confederate  Navy.  Captain  Robert 
Thorburn  shipped  me  for  twelve  months  without  requiring  the  oath  of 
allegiance.  This  was  on  the  19th  instant.  I  came  down  on  the  train 
to  Aquia  Creek  and  reported  to  a  person  by  the  name  of  Cunningham, 
and  he  reported  my  arrival  to  Captain  Lynch.  On  the  evening  of  the 
20th  I  went  to  bathe  and  started  from  the  end  of  the  burned  wharf  for 
the  Pawnee.  After  getting  out  about  a  half  a  mile  I  was  discovered 
and  fired  at  eight  or  ten  times  from  a  rifle  cannon.  I  was  swept  down 
by  the  tide  and  reached  Maryland  shore  near  Maryland  Point.  I  saw 
but  one  company  of  troops  in  Fredericksburg.  There  were  no  defenses 
in  and  around  Richmond  when  I  left  on  the  16th  instant.  I  heard  that 
a  battery  was  being  erected  10  miles  below  Williamsburg,  between  the 
two  rivers.  I  heard  they  were  preparing  or  had  a  battery  near  James¬ 
town.  There  were  some  3,000  troops  between  James  River  and  York- 
town,  mostly  cavalry.  There  were  about  3,000  troops  at  Richmond, 
mostly  from  cotton  States. 

I  was  told  in  Richmond  that  the  principal  crossing  place  for  troops, 
etc.,  from  Maryland  was  at  a  point  about  35  miles  below  Alexandria. 

At  Aquia  Creek  there  are  three  or  four  regiments,  about  3,000  men, 
encamped  behind  the  hills.  Forty-two  men  are  stationed  at  the  depot. 
The  steamboat  Page  is  up  the  creek  and  not  manned  or  armed.  The 
new  battery  on  the  north  hill  lias  three  8-inch  guns;  the  south  battery, 
two  rifled  cannons;  the  lower  battery,  one  rifled  cannon. 

The  earthworks  on  the  point  were  almost  leveled  the  day  of  the  bom¬ 
bardment  and  the  shells  burst  in,  over,  and  around  the  fort,  while  the 
empty  shells  went  through  the  portholes  and  earthworks. 

[Endorsement.] 

II.  S.  S.  Pawnee,  Blockading, 

Aquia  Greek ,  June  22,  [1861.] 

The  above  statement  was  taken  from  the  lips  of  the  person  in  my 
presence. 

S.  C.  R[owanJ.

Pocomoko  from  fear  of  molestation,  but  because  she  could  not,  after  the  blockade  of 
Virginia,  land  freight  and  passengers  in  the  Pungoteague  and  Cliesconessex  rivers 
[creeks?]  in  Virginia,  and  could  get  her  Maryland  freight,  etc.,  at  Annemessex  with¬ 
out  the  time  and  cost  of  going  50  miles  round  to  Newtown  on  the  Pocomoke,  the  end 
of  her  route,  it  being  hut  15  miles  by  land  across  Maryland  territory  from  Annemessex 
to  Newtown. 

Assuming  this  information  to  be  correct,  I  suppose  tbe  Department 
will  not  expect  me  to  abandon  more  important  duties  in  the  river ;  there¬ 
fore  shall  not  at  present  make  the  trip  I  had  contemplated,  to  the  eastern 
shore. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

J.  H.  Ward, 

Commanding  Potomac  Blochade. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy ,  Washington ,  P.  C.

Letter  from  J.  B.  Mannar,  esq.,  to  Lieutenant-General  Scott ,  TJ.  S.  Army, 
giving  information  of  regular  communication  between  Margland  and 
Virginia. 

No.  137  Aisqitith  Street, 

Baltimore,  June  24,  1861. 

Dear  Sir  :  You  may  not  be  aware  that  there  is  a  regular  communi¬ 
cation  between  Salisbury,  eastern  shore  of  Maryland,  and  some  point 
in  Virginia.  It  is  a  fact  known  to  the  writer  of  this  n'ote;  a  channel 
through  which  passes  men  and  munition  of  war.  The  travel  to  that 
point  is  by  the  Delaware  Railroad  and  by  the  Chesapeake  Bay.  The 
name  of  the  principal  agent  at  that  point  is  Andrew  Scoot.  Letters 
reach  Virginia  with  as  much  facility  through  this  route  as  through  the 
regular  mail  when  it  was  in  operation. 

Yours,  respectfully, 


Lieutenant-General  Winfield  Scott. 
P.  S. — The  above  is  confidential. 


J.  B.  Mannar.

Report  of  Commander  Ward ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  commanding  Potomac  Flotilla , 
requesting  200  troops  to  assist  in  clearing  Mathias  Point. 

Flotilla  Steamer  Freeborn, 
Potomac  River ,  Cedar  Point ,  June  24,  1861. 

Sir:  I  sent  yesterday  informally  to  Captain  Dahlgren  asking  the 
aid  of  200  troops  with  materials,  for  the  purpose  of  denuding  Mathias 
Point  of  the  jungle  and  thicket  of  young  growth  which  now  conceal 
from  view  soldiery  and  their  works.  They  have  fired  several  volleys 
of  rifle  bullets  into  the  Freeborn,  as  I  understand  also  into  other  vessels. 
The  distance  they  fire  is  about  500  or  000  yards.  It  is  the  alarm  more 
than  the  material  damage  produced  by  this  firing  which  is  injurious 
and  ought  to  be  abated.  Hence  the  enterprise  I  propose.  It  is  possi¬ 
ble  I  could  effect  it  without  troops;  nevertheless  it  is  best  to  be  sure 
and  have  them  if  convenient. 

Vessels  in  the  river,  bound  up,  report  to  me  that  they  have  been 
advised  at  Cape  Henry  to  await  convoy  in  Hampton  Boacls  for  Wash¬ 
ington.  This  is  decidedly  unnecessary  and  wrong.  Will  the  Depart¬ 
ment  please  apply  the  correction?  No  convoy  is  necessary  except  that 
which  three  or  four  vessels  together  will  afford  one  another,  and  for 
this  purpose  they  should  assemble  at  Blakistone  Island  light  house, 
where  there  is  a  man-of-war  schooner  for  protection. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

J.  H.  Ward, 
Commanding  Blockade. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy,  Washington,  1>.  C. 


Descent  on  Mathias  Point,  Va.,  June  25,  1861. 

Report  of  Acting  Master  Budd,  IT.  S.  Navy,  commanding  IJ.  S.  S.  Resolute,  relative  to  his 

burning  of  a  depot  for  contraband  goods. 

U.  S.  S.  Kesolute,  June  25,  1861. 

Sir  :  I  made  a  descent  on  the  Virginia  shore  yesterday  and  broke  up 
a  depot  that  was  there  for  harboring  and  forwarding  men  and  supplies 
to  the  enemy.  Dr.  Hooe,  the  proprietor  and  owner,  has  been  very  active 
in  his  efforts  against  the  Government.  He  sent  for  the  marauders  and 
requested  them  to  burn  the  Christiana  Keen  (that  New  Jersey  schooner 
that  was  burned  a  short  time  since). 

She  got  ashore  before  daylight  within  one-quarter  of  a  mile  of  his 
place,  and,  as  I  said,  he  caused  her  destruction.  He  has  had  a  number 
of  mounted  troopers  quartered  in  and  lying  about  his  premises,  who 
were  there  for  the  purpose  of  protecting  boats  which  got  across  from 
Maryland  with  men,  etc. 

My  boats  and  the  boats  of  the  flotilla  have  been  fired  upon  from  his 
place  when  not  interfering  with  his  property. 

Major  Watson,  on  the  Maryland  shore  opposite,  receives  the  contra¬ 
band  supplies  and  forwards  them  to  Hooe.  His  boats  and  his  negroes 
have  been  actively  engaged  in  this  business,  and  his  house  is  the  ren¬ 
dezvous. 

Hooe’s  place  was  a  barracks;  he  had  accommodations  put  up  in  his 
schoolhouse  and  outhouses  for  twenty-five  men. 


534  OPERATIONS  ON  THE  POTOMAC  AND  RAPPAHANNOCK. 

At  the  time  of  my  attack  there  were  few  troopers  at  the  house.  I 
dispersed  them  with  a  few  rounds  from  my  bow  gun,  and  before  they 
could  return  in  force  I  landed  and  fired  the  premises,  which  were  com¬ 
pletely  destroyed.  I  got  some  information  also. 

I  took  a  secession  dragoon  uniform  (officer’s)  that  I  found  there,  and 
destroyed  everything  else. 

I  enclose  a  description  of  an  agent  of  the  rebels,  who  is  a  spy  and 
is  now  in  Baltimore  procuring  arms  to  run  across  the  river.  He  has 
made  two  trips  already. 

I  send  you  this,  as  Captain  Ward  is  not  here. 

Very  respectfully, 

William  Budd, 

Actinq  Master ,  Commanding  Resolute.

Report  of  Brigadier-General  Holmes,  C.  S.  Army,  relative  to  the  burning  of  the  house  of  Dr. 

Hooe. 

Headquarters,  Brooke’s  Station,  Ya.,  June  27 ,  1861. 

Sir:  I  have  to  report  that  a  small  party  of  the  enemy  landed  at 
Mathias  Point  on  the  25th  and  burned  the  house  of  Dr.  Howe  [Hooej. 
The  landing  was  effected  under  the  guns  of  the  enemy,  and  doubtless 
was  with  a  view  to  discover  whether  we  were  erecting  a  battery  there. 
If  it  be  the  wish  of  the  commanding  general  that  a  battery  should  be 
erected  to  prevent  the  free  navigation  of  the  river,  I  respectfully 
recommend  that  the  neighborhood  of  Fvansport  should  be  preferred 
to  Mathias  Point.  There  is  very  little  difference  in  the  distance  of  the 
channel  from  the  shore,  and  large  guns  will  command  either.  From 
Fvansport  there  is  a  good  road  to  Fredericksburg,  which  would  turn 
this  position,  and  a  good  road  to  Manassas,  turning  that  position; 
whereas  from  Mathias  Point  it  would  require  a  long  land  travel  to  any 
vulnerable  point.  If  you  can  send  me  two  32-pounders  (rifled),  or  two 
8-inch  Columbiads,  I  believe  I  could  stop  the  navigation  of  the  river, 
if  the  general  commanding  thinks  it  a  matter  of  sufficient  importance 
to  justify  the  expense.  I  could  use  the  rifled  6-pounders  that  I  now 
have  in  Walker’s  battery  to  annoy  the  enemy’s  commerce,  but  we  have 
not  the  ammunition  to  spare. 

I  am,  colonel,  very  respectfully, 

T.  H.  Holmes, 

Brigadier-  General ,  Commanding. 

Colonel  George  Deas, 

Assistant  Adjutant- General,  C.  8.  Army.

Report  of  Commander  Rowan ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  commanding  U.  8.  8.  Pawnee , 
of  a  reconnoissance  of  Mathias  Point. 

IT.  S.  S.  Pawnee, 
Potomac  River ,  June  25 ,  1861. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  inform  the  Department  that  I  left  Aquia 
Creek  this  morning  at  half  past  2  o’clock  and  proceeded  to  Mathias  Point, 
accompanied  by  the  steamboat  James  Guy,  having  on  board  Captain 
Woodbury,  Engineer  Corps,  and  Captain  Palmer,  Topographical  Engi¬ 
neer  Corps,  U.  S.  Army,  for  the  purpose  of  making  a  reconnoissance 
of  the  point  and  to  ascertain  whether  the  enemy  was  erecting  batteries 
or  not.  At  5  o’clock  a.  m.,  I  sent  an  escort  on  shore,  in  two  boats,  of 
forty  sailors  and  marines,  in  charge  of  Lieutenant  Chaplin  and  Master 
Blue,  and  placed  them  under  the  command  of  Captain  Woodbury. 

As  we  approached,  the  enemy  appeared  in  numbers  equal  to  one  or 
more  companies.  A  few  shell  from  the  Pawnee  soon  made  them  scam¬ 
per  over  the  hills,  and  an  occasional  shell  kept  them  in  check  while  the 
officers  completed  their  work.  Our  sailors  captured  two  horses,  sad¬ 
dled  and  bridled,  and  compelled  the  riders  to  seek  shelter  in  flight. 
One  of  the  men  received  a  slight  graze  from  a  revolver  ball  on  the 
wrist.  The  horses  were  brought  off  to  the  ship  and  hoisted  into  the 
James  Guy  and  sent  to  the  navy  yard,  Washington,  as  prizes. 

During  the  reconnoissance  I  threw  some  thirty  shell,  which  kept  the 
enemy  in  check,  notwithstanding  their  reported  force  is  600  men,  of 
whom  100  or  more  are  mounted.  On  the  return  of  the  party  to  the 
ship  I  was  informed  that  they  saw  the  enemy’s  camp  from  Grimes’s 
house  on  the  hill,  and  having  pointed  out  its  direction,  I  hauled  the 
ship  inside  the  shoal  and  with  15-second  shells  dispersed  the  camp  and 
set  fire  to  something  behind  the  hills.  A  negro  man,  who  was  stand¬ 
ing  by  a  boat  on  the  beach  that  I  sent  Lieutenant  Chaplin  to  bring  off 
or  destroy,  came  off  and  gave  us  information  that  200  troops  are  kept 
on  the  beach  constantly,  and  the  remainder  in  camps  aforesaid.  I 
regret  that  the  negro  was  brought  off,  but  being  on  board  I  don’t  know 
what  to  do  with  him.  I  send  him  in  the  Guy  to  the  navy  yard  to  be 
disposed  of  as  you  may  direct. 

Yery  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

S.  C.  Bo  WAN, 

Commander. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy.

[Enclosure.] 


U.  S.  S.  Pawnee, 
Potomac  River ,  June  27,  1S61. 

Sir  :  About  sundown  the  evening  of  the  20th  instant,  while  at  anchor 
off  Aquia  Creek,  I  received  an  order  from  Commander  Ward,  a  copy  of 
which  is  herewith  enclosed,  to  send  him  two  boats,  armed  and  equipped, 
in  command  of  Lieutenant  Chaplin.  This  order  was  immediately  com¬ 
plied  with  in  all  its  details  and  the  party  left  the  ship  in  tow  of  the 
Resolute  at  9  o’clock  p.  m.  To  day  about  noon  the  Resolute  returned 
with  a  request  from  Captain  Ward  that  I  should  send  her  back  if  I 
had  no  more  important  service  for  her.  I  immediately  dispatched  the 
Reliance  to  Captain  Ward,  knowing  the  danger  to  which  our  people 
would  be  exposed  if  he  contemplated  a  landing  at  Mathias  Point,  as  I 
feared  was  his  intention,  judging  from  the  nature  of  the  order  he  gave 
me  to  furnish  him  with  such  equipments  as  were  necessary  to  cut  down 
the  trees  on  the  point  and  burn  them.  At  9  o’clock  this  evening  the 
Freeborn  and  Reliance  came  up,  having  been  repulsed  by  the  rebels  at 
Mathias  Point,  in  which  Lieutenant  Chaplin  and  his  command  escaped 
utter  destruction  by  a  miracle. 

It  becomes  my  painful  duty  to  announce  to  the  Department  the  death 
of  Commander  J.  II.  Ward,  of  the  Freeborn.  Lie  was  shot  in  the  abdo¬ 
men  while  in  the  act  of  sighting  his  bow  gun. 

I  beg  leave  to  call  the  attention  of  the  Department  to  the  gallantry, 
coolness,  and  presence  of  mind  of  Lieutenant  Chaplin,  of  the  Pawnee , 
commanding  the  party  on  shore.  He  remained  steady  and  cool  amongst 
a  perfect  hail  of  musketry  from  hundreds  of  men,  while  he  collected  his 
own  people  and  made  good  his  retreat  without  leaving  the  enemy  a  trophy 
beyond  a  few  sand  bags  and  some  axes  and,  so  far  as  I  can  ascertain,  the 
muskets  of  the  wounded  men.  The  last  man  left  the  shore  with  him,  and 
not  being  able  to  swim  to  the  boat  with  his  musket,  Lieutenant  Chaplin 
took  him  on  his  shoulders,  musket  and  all,  and  safely  reached  the  boat 
without  a  scratch,  save  a  musket  hole  through  the  top  of  his  cap. 

In  consequence  of  the  want  of  ordinary  comforts  in  the  Freeborn  for 
wounded  men,  I  brought  the  two  wounded  men  belonging  to  that  ves¬ 
sel,  with  those  two  of  this  ship,  with  the  remains  of  the  late  commander 
J.  H.  Ward,  to  the  navy  yard,  Washington,  where  I  now  await  orders. 

I  must  also  call  attention  of  the  Department  to  the  bravery  of  John 
Williams,  captain  of  the  maintop  of  the  Pawnee,  who  told  his  men  while 
lying  off  in  the  boat  that  every  man  must  die  on  his  thwart  sooner  than 
leave  a  man  behind,  and  when  the  flagstaff  of  his  boat  was  shot  away 
and  the  ensign  fell,  he,  although  suffering  from  a  gunshot  wound  of 
the  thigh,  seized  it  in  his  hand  and  bravely  waved  it  over  his  head. 

A  copy  of  the  surgeon’s  report  of  casualties  is  herewith  enclosed. 
The  wounded  have  been  removed  to  the  hospital.  I  also  enclose  copies 
of  orders  addressed  to  Lieutenant  Lowry. 

Lieutenant  Chaplin’s  report  of  the  affair  is  not  yet  ready.  When  it  is 
presented,  I  shall  forward  a  copy  for  the  information  of  the  Department. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

S.  C.  Bo  wan, 

Commander,  and  Senior  Officer  of  the  Potomac. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  Navy,  Washington.

Flotilla  Steamer  Freeborn, 

Lower  Potomac ,  June  26,  1861. 

Sir  :  On  receipt  of  this  order  you  will  be  pleased  to  send  your  second 
launch,  by  which  I  mean  your  second-sized  boat;  also  your  smallest 
boat,  not  estimating  your  gig,  which  need  not  be  sent,  with  their  crews 
armed  with  muskets  having  bayonets,  or,  if  without  bayonets,  their  cut¬ 
lass  with  each  musket,  and  a  suitable  amount  of  ammunition;  also  pro¬ 
visions  for  three  or  four  days,  in  charge  of  Lieutenant  Chaplin,  down 
to  Ranjemoy,  alongside  the  schooner  Dana  there,  and  await  my  arrival 
in  the  Freeborn ,  when  Lieutenant  Chaplin  will  report  to  me  with  the 
boats  so  armed  and  provisioned. 

You  will  further  be  pleased  to  send  in  the  boats  all  the  tar  you  have 
on  board  the  Pawnee ,  a  gallon  of  spirits  of  turpentine  in  a  can,  all  the 
shovels  and  all  the  coal  bags  you  have,  except  twelve  retained  to  handle 
coal  with ;  all  the  oakum  you  have,  not  exceeding  one  bale  in  quantity; 
a  quantity  of  old  canvas,  all  you  can  possibly  spare,  and  your  gunner’s 
dark  lantern.  Send  also  every  ax  and  hatchet  you  have,  except  the 
cook’s.  The  launch  and  boat  you  will  see  are  provided  with  their 
hedges  and  all  other  expeditionary  outfits,  as  prescribed  in  the  ord¬ 
nance  regulations,  including  howitzer  for  the  large  boat,  if  you  have 
two  and  one  is  fitted  to  sailboat. 

You  will,  while  your  boat  expedition  ordered  down  to  Ranjemoy  is 
serving  as  I  intended  at  Matthias  Point,  let  the  Reliance  visit  me  at 
least  once  every  day,  and  twice  or  ofteuer  if  convenient  with  other 
duties  you  may  need  her  for. 

I  am,  sir,  respectfully, 

J.  Ef.  Ward,

U.  S.  Steam  Sloop  Pawnee, 

Washington,  D.  C.,  June  28,  1861. 

Sir:  In  obedience  to  your  orders  of  the  26th  instant,  I  took  charge 
of  the  first  and  third  cutters,  with  twenty-three  men,  and  went  to  the 
Reliance  to  be  towed  to  Nanjemoy  to  report  to  Captain  Ward,  of  the 
Freeborn.  Not  finding  her  that  night,  anchored  at  Nanjemoy,  and  yes- 


540  OPERATIONS  ON  THE  POTOMAC  AND  RAPPAHANNOCK. 


terday  morning  proceeded  to  Mathias  Point  and  discovered  tlie  Free¬ 
born  some  4  or  5  miles  below.  I  immediately  went  to  her  and  reported 
to  Commander  Ward  for  service. 

The  Freeborn  then  stood  up  for  Mathias  Point,  and  on  arriving  there 
threw  shot,  shell,  and  grape  into  the  woods  near  where  we  were  to  land. 
About  10  [a.  m.]  the  landing  was  effected,  my  party  under  the  charge 
of  Commander  Ward,  who  landed  with  me.  I  threw  my  men  out  as 
skirmishers,  and  on  getting  about  300  yards  from  the  boats  discovered 
the  enemy’s  pickets,  who  tired  and  retreated.  My  men  followed  them 
for  a  short  distance  and  tired  on  them.  I  then  discovered  the  enemy 
coming  toward  me  over  the  brow  of  a  hill  and  judged  there  were  some 
four  or  five  hundred  men.  I  went  back  to  Commander  Ward  and 
reported,  when  he  ordered  me  to  take  to  the  boats  and  lie  off  while  he 
went  on  board  of  his  vessel  and  tired  into  the  bush  again.  After  some 
fifteen  minutes’  firing  I  was  ordered  to  land  again  and  throw  up  a  breast¬ 
work  of  sand  bags.  I  sent  out  four  men  as  pickets  and  commenced  the 
work,  and  at  5  [p.  m.]  had  nearly  completed  it,  when  the  signal  was  made 
for  me  to  return.  I  sent  everything  to  the  boats  and  with  seven  or  eight 
men  covered  the  bags  with  limbs,  that  the  enemy  might  not  distinguish 
it  from  the  dense  thicket  near,  and  was  about  leaving  when  the  enemy 
opened  onus  with  muskets  at  a  distance  of  250  yards,  and  for  some  rea¬ 
son  the  Freeborn  did  not  open  on  the  place  with  her  heavy  guns  to  cover 
my  retreat.  I  sent  all  my  men  in  the  boats  and  stayed  on  the  beach  till 
1  had  counted  and  found  they  were  all  safe. 

By  this  time  the  boats  had  drifted  some  distance  out,  and  rather 
than  bring  the  men  any  nearer,  swam  to  the  third  cutter  and  pulled  off 
to  the  Freeborn. 

My  boat  was  riddled  with  shot,  the  flagstaff  shotaway,  and  nineteen 
holes  through  the  flag. 

I  am  sorry  to  report  that  two  of  my  men  were  seriously  injured: 
John  Williams,  captain  maintop,  musket  ball  in  thigh;  William  J.  Best, 
ordinary  seaman,  wounded  in  four  places,  the  hand,  the  arm,  the  leg, 
and  body. 

I  can  not  speak  in  too  high  terms  of  the  gallantry  of  my  men,  and 
particularly  of  John  Williams.  Though  wounded  he  retained  charge  of 
his  boat,  and  Avlien  the  staff  was  shot  away  held  the  stump  in  his  liaud 
with  the  flag  till  we  got  alongside  the  Freeborn ,  when  I  learned  of  the 
injury  to  Commander  Ward  and  also  to  several  of  his  men.  Com¬ 
mander  Ward  not  being  able  to  give  any  orders,  and  with  the  advice  of 
the  surgeon,  started  for  the  Pawnee  for  medical  aid,  where  I  arrived  at 
9  last  evening. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

J.  C.  Chaplin, 
Lieutenant ,  U.  S.  Navy. 

Commander  S.  C.  Rowan,  U.  S.  Navy.

Report  of  Acting  Assistant  Surgeon  Moore,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  TJ.  S.  S.  Thomas  Freeborn,  regarding 
the  death  of  Commander  Ward,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  late  commanding  Potomac  Flotilla. 

Washington,  June  28,  1861. 

Sir:  I  liereby  certify  that  J.  H.  Ward,  who  was  a  commander  in  the 
U.  S.  Navy,  while  attached  to  the  steamer  Freeborn  and  holding  rank 
above  mentioned,  departed  this  life -on  the  27th  day  of  June,  1861,  and 
that  he  died  of  a  gunshot  wound  of  the  abdomen  received  while  acting 
in  the  line  of  his  duty,  as  held  forth  in  the  record  of  his  case  of  which 
the  following  is  a  copy : 

Commander  Ward  had  been  on  shore  with  a  party  consisting  of  34 
seamen  besides  Lieutenant  Chaplin,  of  the  Pawnee,  and  Master’s  Mate 
[John]  Kellogg,  of  the  Freeborn.  He  returned,  however,  soon  after  and 
remained  on  board  until  his  death,  which  took  place  off  Mathias  Point 
about  6  p.  m.  He  was  struck  by  a  musket  ball  from  the  enemy  while 
sighting  his  forward  gun.  The  ball  entered  at  a  point  just  above  and 
a  little  to  the  right  of  the  umbilicus  and  passed  directly  through  the 
abdomen,  escaping  at  a  point  opposite,  about  2  inches  to  the  right  of 
the  spinal  column.  He  died  from  internal  hemorrhage  about  an  hour 
after  being  shot. 

Yerv  respectfully,  vour  obedient  servant, 

J.  W.  Moore, 

[Acting]  Assistant  Surgeon ,  Steamer  [ Thomas ]  Freeborn. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles,

gies  of  an  affair  at  Mathias  Point.  There  are  now  there  fifteen  com¬ 
panies  of  volunteers,  and  I  have  ordered  a  section  of  Walker’s  battery

Headquarters, 

Camp  Ruggles,  Ya.,  June  27,  1861 — 9:30  p.  m. 

Sir  :  I  have  the  honor  to  state  for  the  information  of  the  general  com¬ 
manding  that  in  conformity  to  his  orders  received  last  evening  at  7 
o’clock  I  ordered  Major  Mayo  with  his  battalion,  composed  as  indicated, 
to  proceed  without  delay  to  Brooke’s  Station,  for  which  ample  prepara¬ 
tion  has  been  made,  to  commence  the  movement  to-morrow  morning. 

I  have  also  the  honor  to  state  that  at  an  early  hour  this  morning  a 
steamer,  supposed  to  be  the  Freeborn,  and  two  "tugs,  having  in  tow  a 
large  open  boat  or  raft,  with  several  small  boats  suitable  for  landing 
men,  took  position  nearly  in  front  of  this  camp,  and  was  represented  to 
have  effected  that  purpose.  The  employment  of  the  principal  part  of 
command  for  some  hours  was  thus  rendered  necessary  to  ascertain  the 
fact,  with  a  view  of  repelling  the  enemy,  which  fortunately  proved 


OPERATIONS  ON  THE  POTOMAC  AND  RAPPAHANNOCK.  543 

groundless.  At  about  1  p.  m.  our  pickets  reported  that  the  eueiuy7 
whose  steamers  liad  returned  to  the  immediate  vicinity  of  Mathias 
Point,  had  already  effected  a  landing  of  a  strong  detachment  of  men  at 
the  point,  from  which  the  pickets  w ere  mainly  driven  by  the  raking  fire 
of  shell  and  shot  from  the  enemy’s  steamers.  The  condition  of  things 
rendered  vigorous  measures  on  our  part  indispensable,  and  which  has 
resulted,  I  am  happy  to  inform  you,  in  complete  success.  The  enemy, 
who  had  landed,  as  before  reported,  with  a  detachment  of  at  least  fifty 
men,  was  driven  after  a  short  conflict  on  board  of  his  steamers  in  a 
state  of  undoubted  discomfiture,  and  immediately  withdrew  from  our 
shores.  Night  having  closed  in  about  the  time  this  success  was  obtained, 
full  particulars  as  to  any  loss  of  the  enemy  have  not  yet  been  obtained. 
1  shall  embrace  an  early  moment  to  forward  detailed  reports  of  subor¬ 
dinate  commanders. 

I  deem  it  of  the  utmost  importance  for  your  information  that  we  dis¬ 
covered,  immediately  after  the  enemy  was  driven  off,  the  foundation  of 
a  regular  sand-bag  battery,  in  the  erection  of  which  considerable  prog¬ 
ress  had  been  made  during  the  brief  period  the  enemy  had  occupied  the 
position,  which  would  have  completely  commanded  Mathias  Point, 
where  it  has  been  in  contemplation  that  a  permanent  battery  may  be 
established  commanding  the  Potomac  Eiver  channel.  In  addition  to 
the  sand  bags  we  captured  a  considerable  number  of  axes  and  spades, 
a  very  large  coil  of  heavy  rope  (evidently  to  draw  heavy  guns  on  shore), 
left  by  the  enemy  in  his  precipitate  flight.  I  have  been  thus  particular 
in  stating  the  arduous  service  in  which  this  entire  command  has  been 
engaged  to-day,  and  from  which  we  have  this  moment  returned,  at  9 : 30 
p.  in.,  to  apprise  you  as  to  how  completely  paralyzed  we  are  for  the 
want  of  a  battery  of  heavy  guns  to  command  the  channel  and  one  field 
battery  of  effective  rifled  guns  to  enable  us  to  drive  the  enemy’s  steam¬ 
ers  from  almost  every  portion  of  the  extended  range  of  coast  constantly 
threatened  by  them.  During  the  entire  period  of  our  operations  this 
afternoon  one  or  more  of  the  enemy’s  steamers  has  thrown  shot  and 
shell  in  rapid  succession ,  sweeping  almost  the  whole  space  in  which  the 
successive  positions  of  our  troops  were  taken,  and  at  times  greatly 
endangering  them.  Under  the  circumstances  I  am  constrained  to 
request  that  you  will  send  me  Captain  Walker’s  light  battery  of  rifled 
guns,  or,  in  the  event  that  it  can  not  be  spared,  Captain  Braxton’s  field 
battery,  for  a  brief  period  of  service  which  I  consider  of  vital  impor¬ 
tance  to  the  interests  of  the  State.  I  am  also  constrained  to  delay  the 
movement  of  Major  Mayo’s  command,  owing  to  the  very  critical  condi¬ 
tion  of  affairs  in  this  district,  rendering  it  necessary  to  employ  strong 
pickets  to-night  and  to  commence  the  erection  of  breastworks  at 
Mathias  Point  and  near  Grimes’s  house  without  a  moment’s  delay,  and 
for  which  purpose  detachments  are  now  moving  to  the  ground,  until  1 
may  be  enabled  to  receive  further  orders  of  the  general  in  the  case.  I 
have  reason  to  apprehend  that  the  enemy  may  return  strongly  reen¬ 
forced  before  morning.  I  have  the  gratification  of  being  able  to  bear 
testimony  as  to  the  excellent  tone  which  has  been  exhibited  by  this 
command  to  day  and  the  zeal  with  which  officers  and  men  have  partici¬ 
pated  in  the  stirring  scenes  through  which  we  have  passed. 

In  conclusion  I  feel  constrained  to  express  the  opinion,  in  which  all 
the  field  officers  concur,  that  without  artillery  this  command  can  not 
hold  this  important  position  and  prevent  the  enemy  from  effecting  a 
substantial  lodgment  and  strike  an  irretrievable  blow  against  the  inter¬ 
est  and  material  defenses  of  the  State.

Report  of  Major  Mayo,  C.  S.  Army. 

Matiiias  Point,  Va.,  June  2S:  1801. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  of  communicating  to  you  the  action  of  my 
command  yesterday.  About  3  o’clock  I  received  a  communication 
from  Colonel  Brockenbrough  that  the  enemy  were  landing  at  the  point 
and  that  he  wished  my  cooperation.  The  distance  from  my  camp  to 
the  point  is  about  3  miles.  I  immediately  put  my  command,  consisting 
of  one  cavalry  and  three  infantry  companies,  in  motion.  On  arriving 
near  the  point  1  found  Colonel  Claybrook  with  several  companies  in 
reserve.  Being  confident  that  1  was  better  acquainted  with  the  topog¬ 
raphy  of  this  point  than  almost  any  officer  in  this  district,  I  determined, 
without  waiting  further  orders,  to  take  my  command  through  the  woods 
in  an  entirely  different  direction  from  that  followed  by  Colonel  Brock¬ 
enbrough  and  yourself.  Having  heard  from  Colonel  Brockenbrough’s 
pickets  that  they  thought  the  enemy  were  erecting  a  battery  in  the 
pines  on  the  end  of  the  point,  I  took  ten  men  from  Captain  Gouldin’s 
company,  and,  halting  the  rest  of  my  forces,  went  into  the  bushes 
with  them  to  ascertain  the  correctness  of  the  report.  Having  pro¬ 
gressed  some  distance  into  the  pines,  and  on  the  immediate  brink  of 
the  river,  where  we  could  see  a  steamer  and  a  sail  vessel  about  300  or 
400  yards  from  the  shore,  I  found  that  my  skirmishing  party  was  too 
small  to  examine  properly  the  ravines  and  bushes,  and  returning  to  my 
command  deployed  Captain  Gouldin’s  company  and  Lee’s  Legion  (under 
command  of  Lieutenant  Beale,  Captain  Garnett  being  sick  and  absent) 
dismounted  as  skirmishers,  leaving  the  rest  of  my  command  in  reserve. 
We  swept  entirely  through  the  bushes  on  the  point  and  did  not  get  in 
view  of  the  enemy  until  rve  reached  a  marsh  that  sejiarated  us  from 
them,  and  was  entirely  commanded  by  the  steamer  and  the  vessel.  On 
arriving  in  this  position  we  discovered  the  enemy  getting  into  their 
boats  about  250  or  300  yards  distant,  and  we  immediately  commenced 
a  tire  both  upon  the  boats  and  the  steamer.  The  boats  returned  our 
fire  two  or  three  times,  and  then  all  of  their  men,  except  two  or  three 
who  had  fallen  overboard,  lay  down  in  their  boats  and  it  was  some 
time  before  they  could  get  their  oarsmen  to  pull  the  boats  from  the 
shore. 

We  feel  confident,  from  the  number  of  men  who  never  rose  from  the 
bottom  of  the  boats  and  the  blood  upon  the  shore,  that  there  were 
eight  or  ten  killed  and  several  more  wounded. 

After  we  had  fired  five  or  six  rounds  the  steamer  opened  fire  upon  us 
with  shot  and  shell,  but  by  making  my  men  lie  down  nobody  was  hurt. 
After  firing  several  times  went  high  up  the  river  in  order  to  meet  then- 
boats,  which  could  not  come  to  them,  as  they  would  have  to  approach 
nearer  to  our  skirmishers.  Having  accomplished  my  purpose  I  would 


OPERATIONS  ON  THE  POTOMAC  AND  RAPPAHANNOCK.  545 


not  allow  my  men  to  cross  the  marsh,  as  it  would  have  exposed  them  to 
a  raking  lire  from  the  steamer,  but  returned  in  the  same  direction  we 
had  come. 

I  have  never  realized  until  yesterday  how  absolutely  necessary 
artillery  is  at  this  point.  With  a  single  smooth-bore  12-pounder  I 
could  have  sunk  the  steamer  and  vessel  without  exposing  my  men  more 
than  they  were.  I  am  happy  to  say  that  my  men  acted  very  gallantly 
throughout  the  action. 

Yery  respectfully  submitted. 

Eo.  M.  Mato, 

Major ,  Commanding. 

Colonel  It.  Euggles.

Report  of  Lieutenant  Lowry,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Thomas 
Freeborn,  of  the  condition  of  that  vessel  upon  his  assuming  command. 

U.  S.  S.  Freeborn, 

Off  Aquia  Creek,  June  28,  1861. 

Sir:  In  obedience  to  your  order*  of  yesterday  I  assumed  command 
of  this  vessel. 


N  W  R — VOL  4 


Seo  p.  539. 


546  OPERATIONS  ON  THE  POTOMAC  AND  RAPPAHANNOCK. 


Upon  examination  I  have  to  report  that  the  condition  of  said  vessel 
is  far  from  serviceable.  The  frequent  firings  from  her  heavy  32-pound¬ 
ers  and  stern  gun  have  very  much  shattered  the  upper  works  and 
weakened  the  frame,  at  no  time  a  strong  one.  The  crew  are  very  muck 
worn  out  by  exposure,  bad  quarters,  want  of  fresh  provisions,  and 
constant,  severe  duty.  The  ship’s  account  of  stores,  men,  and  ammu¬ 
nition  seems  to  be  in  utter  confusion,  as  the  crew’s  stores,  etc.,  of  all 
the  flotilla  come  under  one  head.  The  sudden  death  of  Commander 
Ward  has  deprived  me  of  all  clue  to  readily  taking  it  in  hand.  The 
accounts  are  still  at  the  navy  yard,  New  York. 

On  an  examination  of  the  magazine  I  found  only  67  charges  of  pow¬ 
der,  32  shell,  100  round  shot,  no  grape.  The  32-pounder  gun  is  worn, 
honeycombed,  and  past  effective  service. 

The  provisions  of  the  flotilla  are  very  much  reduced,  as  per  report 
from  Acting  Paymaster  [Edward]  Foster  enclosed.  The  propellers  [  sic] 
order  from  this  ship.  1  enclose  engineer’s  report  on  condition  of  engines 
and  boilers,  which  speaks  for  itself.  The  vessel  leaks  badly.  On  yes¬ 
terday  eleven  Sharps  rifles  were  lost  by  the  men  of  this  ship,  leaving 
only  ten  on  board,  insufficient  to  arm  her  men  for  proper  defense. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  respectfully,  etc., 

R.  B.  Lowry, 

Lieutenant ,  Commanding  Freeborn. 

Commander  S.  C.  Rowan, 

Senior  Officer  Blockading  Potomac. 

[Enclosure.] 

Potomac  River,  June  27,  1861. 

Sir:  The  following  damage  has  been  done  to  the  machinery  of  the 
U.  S.  S.  Freeborn  and  will  need  repairing. 

The  engine  is  very  much  out  of  line;  the  expansion  joint  on  the 
exhaust  pipe  is  cracked,  and  the  joint  on  the  condenser  and  steam 
chest  is  blowui  out,  all  caused  by  the  cannonading  the  vessel  has  been 
subjected  to. 

A  great  amount  of  sand  has  accummulated  in  the  boilers,  on  account 
of  our  having  been  run  ashore  so  often,  and  require  cleaning.  Steam 
has  been  kept  on  the  boilers  constantly  since  the  12th  June. 

The  vessel  is  leaking  very  freely,  caused  by  having  been  hard  aground 
several  times. 

There  are  about  fifteen  tons  of  coal  aboard.  The  state  of  the 
machinery  is  such  that,  in  my  opinion,  the  repairs  should  be  made 
without  delay. 

C.  B.  Spencer, 

Chief  Engineer. 

Lieutenant  R.  B.  Lowry,  U.  S.  Navy, 

Commanding  U.  S.  S.  Thomas  Freeborn.

Report  of  Lieutenant  Lowry,  U.  S.  Navy ,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Thomas 
Freeborn ,  of  condition  of  affairs  on  his  line  of  blockade. 

U.  S.  S.  Freeborn, 

Off  Aquia  Creek,  June  29,  1861. 

Sir  :  I  liave  to  report  all  quiet  on  my  line  of  blockade.  Yesterday 
the  enemy  at  this  place  exposed  five  large  fishing-  boats  filled  with 
armed  men,  which  he  was  exercising-  up  and  down  the  beach,  in  embark¬ 
ing-  and  disembarking  and  other  drills  belonging  to  boat  expeditions. 
At  sunset  the  five  boats  were  left  off  the  beach  at  different  points, 
extending  from  the  outer  point  with  the  White  House  as  far  as  the 
gorge  below  the  railroad  curve.  I  am  convinced  that  he  is  preparing 
his  men  for  boat  service  of  some  sort.  Not  feeling  able  to  defend  this 
vessel,  with  her  guards  and  bulwarks,  against  a  strong  boarding  party, 
I  deemed  it  prudent  to  move  my  position  till  daylight. 

The  Reliance  reconnoitered  off  Mathias  Point  all  of  yesterday. 
Lieutenant  Mygatt  reports  seeing  a  large  body  of  men  and  a  camp 
near  Grimes’s  house.  The  master’s  mate  in  charge  of  schooner  Dana 
reported  seeing  men  at  work  near  where  the  Pawnee’s  party  had  been. 
Three  armed  steamers  from  Boston,  with  the  Ninth  Massachusetts  Reg¬ 
iment,  passed  this  morning  at  9  a.  m.  They  reported  having  tried  their 
guns  on  the  point  with  shell. 

Two  of  those  steamers  seemed  admirably  adapted  for  service  in  this 
river,  one  being  armed  with  four  heavy  broadside  guns,  the  other  with 
a  bow  and  stern  chaser,  evidently  rifie ;  names  Cambridge  and  Pembroke. 
On  going  to  quarters  last  night  at  11,  owing  to  tho  suspicious  move¬ 
ments  of  a  steamer,  which  proved  to  be  the  0".  S.  S.  Mount  Vernon ,  I 
found  great  difficulty  in  working  the  gun  carriages  of  this  vessel.  In 
shifting  the  guns  from  the  turntable  to  the  slide,  great  nicety  must  be 
observed,  as  the  slightest  deviation  from  a  straight  line  destroys  the 
continuous  line  of  rails  and  prevents  the  running  out  to  fighting  posi¬ 
tion.  A  connecting  block  in  front  of  the  gun  is  also  difficult  of  adjust¬ 
ment;  this,  at  night  when  the  men  must  go  by  feeling,  is  a  serious 
objection.

There  is  not  in  this  vessel  one  cartridge  belt  or  box,  not  one  belt  for 
captain  of  gun;  never  lias  been. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

R.  P>.  Lowry, 

Lieutenant ,  Commanding  Freeborn. 

Commander  S.  C.  Rowan, 

Senior  Officer  of  Flot  illa.

U.  S.  S.  Reliance,  June  30,  1861. 


Sir  :  After  leaving  the  steamer  Mount  Vernon  I  made  the  best  of  my 
way  down  the  Potomac  River. 

On  my  way  down  a  boat  was  seen  that  was  trying  to  escape  to  the 
Virginia  shore.  In  it  were  two  men.  They  state  that  the  St.  Nicholas 
was  captured  by  a  party  of  men  off  Point  Lookout,  W'ho  went  on  board 
in  women’s  clothes  at  the  point  and  took  possession  of  her  after  leaving 
the  wharf.  She  was  afterwards  taken  into  Coan  River  and  then  taken 
down  the  bay,  the  man  says,  into  the  Rappahannock. 

He  accounts  for  his  being  in  the  river  by  saying  that  he  had  taken 
some  men  over  who  were  on  their  way  to  Baltimore,  and  that  they  gave 
him  $5  in  paper  money.  On  examining  I  found  $13  in  Virginia  paper 
money  and  70  cents  in  silver.  Under  the  circumstances  I  think  it  best 
to  send  the  men  to  you. 

Respectfully,  etc., 


J.  P.  K.  Mygatt, 

Acting  Lieutenant.

Report  of  commandant  navy  yard,  Washington. 

Navy  Yard  [Washington,  D.  C.],  July  1,  1861. 

Sir:  The  Resolute  has  just  (2  p.  m.)  arrived  from  below,  bringing 
information  of  the  seizure  of  the  St.  Nicholas  at  Point  Lookout  by  a 
party  of  men  just  after  midnight  on  Saturday  morning.  ,  They  carried 
the  steamboat  over  to  Coan  River,  and  after  a  short  stay  left,  supposed 
for  the  Rappahannock. 

The  Freeborn  is  off  Aquia,  and  reports  that  the  Page  has  had  steam 
up;  also  the  presence  of  three  large  launches  at  Aquia  wharf  with  men, 
who  are  being  exercised. 

The  Reliance  reports  the  continued  passage  of  men  from  Maryland  in 
the  lower  Potomac.  Passed  Mathias  Point  early  this  morning  and  saw 
only  the  usual  pickets. 

I  regret  to  say  that  the  Pocahontas  has  not  yet  left  Alexandria. 
Captain  Dove  came  up  to  the  yard  not  long  since,  and  I  urged  him  to 
return  to  his  vessel  and  proceed  at  once  down  the  river. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully, 

John  A.  Dahlgren, 

Commandant. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy. 


Letter  from  Charles  Worthington  esq.,  to  the  Secretary  of  the  Navy,  reporting  the  capture  by 
a  party  of  Confederates  of  the  steamer  St.  Nicholas. 

Washington,  July  1,  1861. 

Dear  Sir:  The  steamer  St.  Nicholas  left  Baltimore  on  Friday  last  at 
4  p.  m.,  laden  with  freight  for  the  consumption  of  the  citizens  of  St. 
Mary’s  and  Charles  counties,  Md.,  and  with  other  cargo  for  Washing¬ 
ton,  Alexandria,  and  Georgetown.'  She  also  had  on  board  a  number  of 
passengers  who  were  to  be  landed  at  her  regular  landings  on  the 
Maryland  shore  of  the  Potomac  River. 

It  is  reported  by  the  officers  of  the  steamer  Diamond  State ,  which 
arrived  here  on  Saturday,  that  they  saw  her  about  1  o’clock  that  morn¬ 
ing  leaving  Point  Lookout  and  heading  under  great  speed  for  the  Vir¬ 
ginia  shore,  presumed  to  be  destined  to  Kinsale.  There  is  no  doubt 
but  that  she  was  taken  forcible  possession  of  either  by  parties  who 
came  passengers  on  her  from  Baltimore  or  by  a  force  from  Virginia. 


OPERATIONS  ON  THE  POTOMAC  AND  RAPPAHANNOCK.  551 


It  is  not  known  that  she  had  on  board  any  suspicions  persons  when  she 
left  Baltimore,  but  such  may  have  been  the  case  unknown  to  her  officers. 
Nothing  has  been  heard  of  her  since. 

I  will  add  that  after  an  interview  with  yourself  and  your  chief  clerk 
a  week  since,  I  took  passage  on  her  on  Tuesday  last  for  Baltimore  for  the 
purpose  of  consulting  with  Captain  Ward  as  to  the  most  effectual  mode 
of  preventing  the  landing  on  the  Maryland  shore  of  any  articles 
intended  for  transportation  across  the  river  into  Virginia  and  at  the 
same  time  avoiding  any  unnecessary  detention  to  her.  The  arrange¬ 
ment  we  made  was  mutually  satisfactory,  and  he  promised  to  meet  her 
on  every  Saturday  morning  at  the  mouth  of  the  river  and  give  her  a  pass 
to  proceed  on  her  trip.  But  alas!  he  is  no  more.  Doubtless  ill-disposed 
persons  took  advantage  of  the  absence  of  a  Government  vessel  and 
made  the  seizure.  As  the  lives  and  property  of  loyal  citizens  of  Mary¬ 
land  and  the  District  of  Columbia  are  hazarded  by  her  detention,  may 
I  ask  that  measures  may  at  once  [be]  taken  for  her  recapture. 

Yours,  respectfully, 

Chas.  Worthington. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  Navy. 


Letter  from  Samuel  Hints,  esq.,  to  the  Secretary  of  the  Navy,  regarding  steamer  St.  Nicholas. 

Baltimore,  July  2, 1861. 

Dear  Sir:  I  heard  to-day  that  the  steamboat  St.  Nicholas  affair  was 
a  trap  set  to  catch  the  Pawnee.  There  may  be  other  enterprises  of  the 
same  character  on  foot  and  it  would  be  well  to  be  on  the  lookout  for 
them. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Samuel  Hinks. 

Hon.  G.  Welles, 

Secretary  of  Na  vy.

Report  of  Brigadier-General  Holmes,  C.  S.  Army. 


Headquarters, 
Brooke's  Station ,  June  27,  1S61. 

Sir:  In  answer  to  yours  relative  to  cooperating  with  Commander 
Lewis,  Confederate  Navy,  I  have  respectfully  to  say  that  I  did  not  feel 
justified  in  ordering  volunteer  troops  on  an  expedition  so  fraught  with 
ruinous  consequences  if  it  failed,  and  the  success  of  which  required 
that  so  many  contingencies  should  be  effectually  accomplished.  I 
referred  the  matter  to  the  colonels  of  regiments  and  they  declined  to 
volunteer  their  men. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 


Hon.  L.  P.  Walker, 

Secretary  of  War. 


Tn.  II.  Holmes, 
Brigadier- General,  Commanding. 


Report  of  Brigadier-General  Holmes,  C.  S.  Army. 

Headquarters, 
Brooke's  Station,  June  28,  1861. 

Sir:  Pursuant  to  your  instructions  received  last  night  I  dispatched 
Colonel  Bate,  with  the  effective  force  of  his  regiment  present,  to  sup¬ 
port  Commander  Lewis,  C.  S.  Navy.  I  consider  the  command  (about 
400)  unnecessarily  strong,  as  Colonel  Bate  is  positively  ordered  to  take 


OPERATIONS  ON  THE  POTOMAC  AND  RAPPAHANNOCK.  553 

no  part  iii  the  expedition  on  the  water.  I  sincerely  hope  your  excel¬ 
lency  will  not  consider  me  extra  cautious  in  this  matter,  for  when  we 
consider  that  an  indispensable  requisite  to  success  would  be  the  abso¬ 
lute  concealment  of  300  or  TOO  men  on  a  comparatively  small  steamer, 
and  those  men  untrained  volunteers,  and  that  this  is  only  one  of  several 
other  contingencies  equally  difficult  to  be  reconciled,  it  seems  to  me 
that  success  would  be  miraculous. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Tie  IT.  Holmes, 
Brigadier- General ,  Commanding. 

Hon.  L.  P.  Walker, 

Secretary  of  War. 


Extracts  from  notes  by  Commander  George  N.  Hollins,  C.  S.  Navy. 

At  0  o’clock  a.  m.,  June  18,  1861,  I  left  Baltimore  on  the  Mary  Wash¬ 
ington,  a  steamboat  running  to  the  Patuxent.  On  landing  at  one  of 
the  landings  on  the  river  I  went  to  the  plantation  of  Mr.  S.,  where  1 
suggested  the  idea  (which  originated  entirely  with  myself),  of  seizing 
the  St.  Nicholas ,  a  boat  running  between  Baltimore  and  W ashington,  and 
manning  her  with  volunteers,  and  then  to  take  the  Pawnee ,  a  United 
States  steamer  commanded  by  Yankee  Ward,  and  which  was  a  great 
annoyance  to  the  boats  on  the  Potomac.  I  was  told  that  the  plan  could 
not  be  carried  out,  as  there  were  so  many  Union  men  about;  that  it  must 
be  certainly  discovered  before  it  could  be  executed.  Finding  I  could  not 
act  there,  1  crossed  the  Potomac  in  an  open  boat  pulled  by  lour  negroes. 
On  reaching  the  Virginia  side  I  went  to  the  residence  of  Dr.  Howe 
[Ilooe],  about  20  miles  from  Fredericksburg.  This  place  I  reached  at 
1  a.  in.  This  gentleman  was  a  perfect  stranger  to  me,  but  he  received 
me  kindly,  entertained  me  handsomely,  he  and  his  charming  family  so 
soon  to  be  rendered  houseless  and  homeless  by  the  incendiary  act  of  the 
vandal  Captain  Budd,  of  the  United  States  gunboat,  a  name  ever  to  be 
remembered,  desecrated  as  the  insulter  of  unprotected  females,  firing 
into  barns  and  houses,  and  everything  but  what  might  have  been 
expected  of  an  officer  or  a  gentleman. 

The  same  day  Dr.  Howe  [Hooe]  chartered  a  buggy  and  drove  me  to 
Fredericksbiug,  where  I  arrived  at  6  o’clock  in  the  afternoon.  On 
registering  my  name  at  the  hotel,  a  gentlemen,  Mr.  Chew,  introduced 
himself  to  me  and  insisted  most  kindly  on  taking  mo  to  his  house, 
where  he  entertained  me  most  handsomely  and  hospitably.  Next  morn¬ 
ing  I  went  to  Bichmond  on  the  cars.  I  immediately  proceeded  to  the 
Navy  Department  and  reported  myself  to  the  Secretary,  and  at  once 
received  my  commission  as  captain  in  the  Confederate  States  Navy. 
After  getting  my  position  and  commission  I  went  into  the  Bureau  of 
Details,  where  I  met  many  of  my  old  friends,  who  had  also  resigned — 
Barron,  Maury,  Lewis,  Spotswood,  and  many  others.  In  conversation 
in  that  office  I  suggested  my  plan  of  seizing  the  St.  Nicholas  and  carry¬ 
ing  out  the  scheme  that  had  suggested  itself  to  me  at  Colonel  S’s.  I 
was  told  that  the  Secretary,  Mr.  Mallory,  would  not  agree  to  the  plan, 
but  that  the  governor  (Letcher)  would.  I  then  remarked  that  I  would 
obtain  Mr.  Mallory’s  permission  to  apply  to  the  governor.  1  walked 
into  Mr.  Mallory’s  room  and  asked  his  permission.  He  granted  it,  and 
I  at  once  went  straight  to  the  governor’s.  When  I  made  my  proposi¬ 
tion,  Governor  Letcher,  without  a  moment’s  hesitation,  acceded  to  the 


554  OPERATIONS  ON  THE  POTOMAC  AND  RAPPAHANNOCK. 

$ 

proposal  and  gave  me  a  draft  for  $1,000  to  send  North,  for  arms  and 
men,  etc.  He  then  and  there  introduced  me  to  Colonel  Thomas,  of 
Maryland,  alias  Zarvona,  as  a  person  who  could  be  trusted  to  go  North 
and  purchase  arms  or  transact  other  business.  That  same  afternoon  I 
started  oft'  for  Point  Lookout  via  Fredericksburg.  After  leaving  Fred¬ 
ericksburg  I  met  my  two  sons,  who  were  on  their  way  to  Bichmond; 
they  joined  me,  of  course.  That  next  evening  we  recrossed  the  Poto¬ 
mac  to  the  Maryland  side,  St.  Mary’s  County,  where  I  went  to  the 
house  of  a  friend  and  remained  untii  sundown,  when  I,  my  two  sons, 
and  five  men  started  in  a  wagon  in  a  pouring  rain,  a  nasty,  dirty  night, 
for  Point  Lookout,  where  the  St.  Nicholas  had  to  stop  on  her  way  to 
Washington.  About  an  hour  after  our  arrival  at  Point  Lookout  the  St. 
Nicholas  came  to  the  wharf.  After  reaching  the  Maryland  side  I  signed 
the  draft  and  Colonel  Thomas  took  the  Patuxent  boat  and  went  on  to  Bal¬ 
timore  and  Philadelphia  to  purchase  the  arms,  etc.  I  directed  him  to  get 
the  arms  and  return  down  the  bay  in  the  St.  Nicholas,  and  get  as  many 
men  to  join  him  as  he  could.  I  also  stated  to  him  that  I  should  join  him 
at  Point  Lookout.  At  12  p.  m.  midnight  I  went  on  board  with  my  party ; 
I  saw  Colonel  Thomas  dressed  as  a  woman,  to  avoid  suspicion,  as  he  had 
high,  large,  trunks  such  as  milliners  use ;  they  contained  arms  and  ammu¬ 
nition.  I  told  Colonel  T.  to  hold  himself  in  readiness;  as  soon  as  we 
cleared  the  wharf  we  would  take  the  steamer.  In  a  few  minutes  we 
left  the  wharf  and  I  soon  made  the  appointed  signal.  The  trunks  were 
then  opened,  the  men  seized  the  arms;  I  took  a  musket,  or  rather  a 
Sharps  rifle,  and  a  pair  of  pistols,  ran  up  to  the  wheelhouse,  put  my 
hand  on  the  captain’s  shoulder  and  told  him  I  had  captured  his  boat,  and 
ordered  him  to  take  the  boat  over  to  Coan  Biver,  but  he  declined,  say¬ 
ing  he  was  no  pilot.  I  told  him  I  knew  he  was  a  pilot  and  that  if  lie 
did  not  pilot  me  over  1  would  set  fire  to  the  St.  Nicholas  and  land  all 
my  men  in  his  boats,  as  I  was  determined  she  should  not  fall  into  the 
hands  of  the  enemy.  I  learned  since  that  the  captain  became  so 
uneasy  that  another  man  piloted  her  over.  About  an  hour  after  my 
arrival  at  Coan  Eiver  Landing  a  body  of  Confederate  soldiers  and 
sailors  came  down  to  assist  me,  the  soldiers  commanded  by  Captain 
Lewis.  I  then  read  the  Baltimore  morning  papers  and  ascertained  that 
Captain  Ward  had  been  killed  while  making  an  attack  on  Mathias 
Point  and  all  the  gunboats  had  left  the  river  and  gone  up  the  river  to 
Washington  to  the  funeral. 

There  were  several  passengers  on  board,  but  I  landed  them  and  gave 
permission  to  all  who  wished  to  return  to  Baltimore  to  do  so.  Few 
returned,  as  nearly  all  were  on  their  way  South,  and  although  it  was 
Sunday  the  ladies  amused  themselves  by  making  Confederate  flags  out 
of  the  Yankee  flags  I  had  captured. 

Finding  there  was  no  chance  of  capturing  the  Pawnee ,  and  deeming 
it  unsafe  to  remain  where  I  was  in  a  steamer  without  guns,  I  resolved 
to  go  up  to  Fredericksburg,  and  immediately  ran  out  into  the  Chesa¬ 
peake  Bay.  I  saw  a  fine  brig;  ran  alongside  of  her;  she  proved  to  be 
the  brig  Monticello ,  from  Eio,  loaded  with  coffee  and  bound  for  Balti¬ 
more.  I  merely  captured  her,  taking  the  crew  on  board  the  St.  Nicholas 
and  leaving  the  captain  and  his  wife  on  board,  as  I  did  not  wish  to  ter¬ 
rify  the  lady  or  render  her  uncomfortable.  I  put  Lieutenant  Eobert 
[!).]  Minor  on  board  with  orders  to  take  the  brig  to  Fredericksburg. 
The  coffee,  a  full  cargo,  was  a  great  treat  to  our  “  boys  in  gray,”  who 
were  already  beginning  to  endure  some  of  the  many  privations  that 
made  them  in  later  days  “  truly  an  army  of  martyrs.”  In  an  hour  or 
less  I  captured  a  schooner  from  Boston  loaded  with  ice  and  bound  for 


OPERATIONS  ON  THE  POTOMAC  AND  RAPPAHANNOCK.  555 


Washington.  I  placed  an  officer  and  prize  crew  on  board  and  dis¬ 
patched  her  to  Fredericksburg.  The  ice  just  got  there  in  time,  for  the 
wounded  and  sick  in  the  hospitals  were  suffering  for  the  want  of  it;  and 
the  Yankee  captain  of  the  schooner  attended  the  sale,  and  seeing  the 
fine  prices  paid  for  the  ice  he  came  to  me  and  proposed  that  he  should 
go  to  Boston,  get  another  vessel  loaded  with  ice,  bring  her  down  and 
let  me  know  precisely  when  to  meet  him  that  I  might  capture  him,  take 
the  vessel  to  Fredericksburg,  sell  the  ice  and  divide  the  proceeds. 
Would  anyone  but  a  Yankee  have  been  guilty  of  such  rascality  ?  He 
had  a  splendid  flag  of  a  74,  an  ensign  that  he  had  borrowed  from  the 
navy  yard,  Boston,  to  hoist  on  the  occasion  of  Douglas’s  death,  but  of 
that  same  ensign  a  goodly  number  of  secession  flags  were  made.  I 
next  captured  another  vessel  from  Baltimore,  loaded  with  coal,  bound 
to  Boston — a  most  fortunate  prize,  as  I  was  on  my  last  bucket  of  coal 
in  the  St.  Nicholas.  I  filled  up  as  I  went  along,  as  I  began  to  feel  a 
little  fearful  that  some  of  the  gunboats  might  be  after  me,  so  we  went 
up  to  Fredericksburg,  I  towing  my  prize.  We  reached  there  safely. 
The  Government  bought  the  St.  Nicholas  for  about  $45,000  and  turned 
her  into  a  gunboat.  The  coffee  sold  well,  but  as  she  was  a  Baltimore 
vessel  and  owned  by  gentlemen  of  that  city,  Government  ascertained 
the  price  of  the  coffee  in  Baltimore  and  paid  Messrs.  Spence  and  Beid 
12  cents  a  pound,  and  sold  it  at  25  or  30  cents  in  Kichmond.  The  ves¬ 
sel  was  returned  to  the  owners.  I  then  went  to  Richmond  and  was 
ordered  to  the  command  of  fortifications  on  the  James  River.  After 
having  been  there  for  some  time,  and  knowing  I  was  not  competent  to 
build  longshore  fortifications,  whatever  other  navy  officers  might  have 
been,  1  applied  for  other  duty  more  in  the  line  of  my  profession,  and 
was  ordered  to  take  command  of  the  station  at  Few  Orleans,  with  the 
rank  of  commodore.

U.  S.  S.  Reliance,  June  30,  1861. 

Sir:  This  morning  on  my  way  down  the  river  I  fell  in  with  a  sloop 
capsized.  A  moment  after  we  saw  a  man  floating  in  the  water,  evi¬ 
dently  trying  to  conceal  himself  by  floating  behind  the  centerboard, 
which  he  was  using  to  make  the  best  of  his  way  to  Virginia.  Enclosed 
I  send  you  some  papers  that  were  found  on  him  which  are  apparently 
trivial,  but  may  give  some  information. 

She  was  the  sloop  Passenger,  of  Baltimore.  The  man’s  name  is  Kerr. 
He  says  that  he  crossed  to  Virginia  on  Thursday  last.  I  have  destroyed 
the  sloop.  I  have  not  met  the  Resolute.  Excuse  my  writing  in  pencil, 
as  I  am  in  a  great  hurry. 

Respectfully,  etc., 


J.  P.  Iv.  Myg-att, 

Lieutenant.

Letter  f  rom  the  Secretary  of  the  Navy  to  the  Secretary  of  War,  representing 
the  need  of  troops  at  prominent  points  on  the  Potomac. 

Navy  Department,  July  l,  1861. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  inform  you  that  this  Department  is  entirely 
satisfied  from  reports  ot  its  officers  that  the  Potomac  River  will  soon 
be  closed  by  the  batteries  of  the  rebels  unless  one  or  more  prominent 
points  are  occupied  by  the  Federal  troops. 

I  am,  with  high  respect,  your  obedient  servant, 

Gideon  Welles. 

Hon.  Simon  Cameron, 

Secretary  of  War,  Washington.

Report  of  Commander  Rowan ,  U.  S.  Navy,  senior  officer  present,  Potomac 
River,  regarding  movements  of  vessels  in  those  waters. 

U.  S.  S.  Pawnee, 

Off  Mathias  Point,  July  3,  1861. 

Sir  :  On  my  way  to  St.  Mary’s  and  Leonardtown  I  fell  in  with  the 
tug  Reliance  on  her  return  from  Hampton  Roads  and  the  Rappahan¬ 
nock.  Lieutenant  Mygatt  reported  to  Flag-Officer  Stringham  that  the 
steamboat  St.  Nicholas  had  been  captured  and  taken  into  the  Rappa¬ 
hannock.  The  Penguin,  Commander  Livingston,  was  ordered  immedi¬ 
ately  to  the  mouth  of  the  river  and  subsequently  relieved  by  the  Mount 
Vernon.  The  tug  Reliance  returned  to  the  Potomac,  touching  at  St. 
Mary’s  and  Breton’s  Bay. 

It  is  reported  that  the  steamers  Patuxent,  Planter ,  and  Mary  Wash¬ 
ington  are  in  the  habit  of  carrying  numbers  of  men  from  Baltimore  and 
landing  them  at  some  point  on  the  Patuxent  from  whence  they  cross  to 
the  Potomac  and  so  into  Virginia. 

I  passed  Mathias  Point  to  day  without  seeing  anyone.  The  point  is 
apparently  deserted.  I  saw  no  signs  of  entrenchments.  The  Poca¬ 
hontas  is  anchored  off  the  point,  keeping  a  close  watch  on  the  rebels’ 
movements. 

Lieutenant  Mygatt,  commanding  Reliance,  reports  serious  defects  in 
the  engine,  which  makes  it  necessary  to  send  him  to  Washington  for 
repairs.  The  engineer’s  report  of  defects  is  L  erewith  enclosed. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  j  our  obedient  servant, 

S.  C.  Rowan, 

Commander,  and  Senior  Officer  in  Potomac. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  Navy,  Washington.

Report  of  Commander  Dove,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Pocahontas , 
regarding  the  erection  of  batteries  on  the  Potomac. 

U.  S.  S.  Pocahontas, 

Mathias  Point ,  July  4,  1861. 

Sir  :  I  have  to  report  that  yesterday  I  left  here  early  in  the  morning 
for  Aquia  Creek  to  look  after  the  smaller  steamers  and  examine  the 
river,  and  had  the  pleasure  of  seeing  also  the  Pawnee  and  James  Guy 
there.  After  communicating  with  Captain  Rowan  and  sending  letters 
by  the  Guy,  I  returned  herein  the  afternoon. 

The  steamers  Ben  Deford  and  Pembroke  came  down  past  the  point  in 
company  with  me. 

On  passing  Nanjemoy  Reach  the  officer  in  charge  of  the  tender  Dana 
reported  that  during  my  absence  a  large  party  of  men  came  down  on 
the  point  and  tore  down  two  fish  sheds  and  carried  off  the  boards  for 
the  purpose,  he  supposed,  of  erecting  batteries. 

The  large  lighter  or  longboat  used  by  Captain  Ward  having  dragged 
her  anchor  from  the  Maryland  to  the  Virginia  shore,  I  towed  her  back 
again.  I  cautioned  the  two  steamers  about  passing  too  near  the  point 
and  to  keep  outside  of  me,  as  the  report  of  batteries  might  be  true, 
the  absence  of  the  fishing  sheds  confirming  it  partly. 

N  W  R — VOL  4 - 36 


562  OPERATIONS  ON  THE  POTOMAC  AND  RAPPAHANNOCK. 

% 

They  mistook  a  wood  pile  for  one  and  opened  fire  as  they  went  by. 
Their  shells  were  well  thrown,  but  it  was  a  useless  expenditure.  I 
anchored  near  the  same  position  I  had  before  and  could  discover  noth' 
ing.  One  part  of  the  point  is  a  dense  pine  thicket;  the  other  and  the 
highest,  where  Captain  Ward  attempted  to  make  a  lodgment,  is  partly 
cleared,  but  nothing  is  yet  visible. 

Professor  Lowe  and  his  military  balloon  are  the  only  means  of  ascer¬ 
taining  the  fact  of  erecting  fortifications.  The  commanding  officer  of 
the  Dana  also  reports  that  a  schooner  in  passing  was  fired  at  with  rifles. 

Both  the  Freeborn  and  Reliance  are  in  bad  condition  and  it  is  a  diffi¬ 
cult  matter  to  decide  which  can  be  best  spared.  Captain  Rowan  passed 
by  yesterday,  bound  down,  to  be  absent  two  or  three  days.  He  sent 
me  a  short  note,  leaving  the  matter  to  me,  but  I  can  only  decide  on 
consultation  with  Lieutenants  Lowry  and  Mygatt,  whom  I  will  see  this 
afternoon,  as  I  will  go  up  to  Aquia  for  that  purpose. 

You  will  oblige  me  very  much  if  you  will  send  me  down  100  bags  of 
coal.  The  tops  of  the  cylinders  are  quite  exposed  and  a  single  well- 
directed  rifle  cannon  shot  may  disable  the  steamer.  I  wish  the  bags 
for  a  barricade  on  the  spar  deck,  around  them,  and  to  fill  up  the  pas¬ 
sages.  The  sooner  I  receive  these  bags  the  better,  as  there  is  no  telling 
the  emergency  requiring  them. 

I  have  also  to  report  the  erection  of  an  earthwork  on  the  south  side 
of  Potomac  Creek  at  the  entrance.  Three  embrasures  look  toward  the 
river  and  one  to  the  northward  across  I  he  creek. 

Respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Benj.  M.  Dove, 

Commander. 

Captain  Daiilgren, 

Commanding  Navy  Yard,  Washington. 

P.  S. — The  chief  engineer  informs  me  that  there  [were]  250  gunny- 
bags  left  at  the  navy  yard  by  this  ship  in  charge  of  your  master  laborer.

Off  Nang  emoy  Reach ,  July  5,  1861. 

Sir  :  Enclosed  are  the  license  of  the  sloop  Teaser ,  of  Washington? 
and  the  report  of  Mr.  Ely,  of  the  schooner  Dana,  who  brought  her  to, 
this  afternoon.  On  examining  the  case  I  find  that  her  owner  was  for 
merly  keeper  of  the  Long  Bridge  and  gave  up  that  office  to  join  the 


OPERATIONS  ON  THE  POTOMAC  AND  RAPPAHANNOCK.  563 


Confederates.  The  sloop  lias  nominally  been  employed  in  fishing,  but 
there  seems  little  doubt  that  she  has  long  been  made  use  of  for  the  pur¬ 
poses  mentioned  in  the  report. 

A  thorough  search  was  made  of  her,  but  nothing  like  letters  or 
papers  could  be  found.  She  has  two  women  as  passengers  and  a  load 
of  crabs  from  St.  Clement’s  Bay. 

I  have  ordered  the  Mount  Vernon  to  tow  her  up  to  Washington  navy 
yard  and  to  give  the  women  more  comfortable  quarters  on  the  way,  sub¬ 
ject  to  your  approval.

[Enclosure.] 

TJ.  S.  Schooner  Dana, 

Nanjemoy  Creek ,  July  5,  1861. 

Sir  :  I  have  the  honor  to  report  to  you  the  capture  of  the  sloop  Teaser , 
answering  to  the  following  description,  viz :  Painted  black,  with  a  yellow 
bead  and  white  topmast,  clean  built,  and  a  fast  sailer.  This  sloop  was 
reported  to  me  nearly  three  weeks  ago  by  the  captain  of  a  small  fishing 
vessel  as  being  engaged  in  carrying  letters,  arms,  and  other  contraband 
goods  from  the  Maryland  to  the  Virginia  shore.  My  informant  was 
unwilling  to  give  iue  his  name,  fearing  (as  he  said)  that  in  the  event  of 
the  capture  of  the  Teaser  the  owner  of  her  might  by  some  means  find 
out  who  gave  me  the  information  and  do  him  some  personal  injury. 
Since  then  I  have  heard  the  same  reports  concerning  the  Teaser  from 
other  vessels  trading  up  and  down  the  river.  Their  testimony  concern¬ 
ing  her  corresponded  exactly  with  what  I  had  heard  at  first.  I  have 
consequently  been  on  the  alert  for  her  and  this  afternoon  succeeded  in 
capturing  her. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

R.  B.  Ely,

Statement  of  Dr.  John  B.  Blake  to  commandant  navy  yard,  Washington,  regarding  the 
character  of  the  owner  of  the  sloop  Teaser. 

July  8, 1861. 

Dear  Sir:  The  bearer,  Mrs.  Huselman,  informs  me  that  while  on 
her  way  to  this  city  in  her  son’s  sloop,  the  Teaser ,  the  sloop  was  seized 
by  a  United  States  vessel  and  ordered  to  report  to  you  at  the  navy 
yard.  I  know  the  old  lady  and  her  son  Charles  well.  They  formerly 
lived  in  this  city,  but  are  now  residents  of  Charles  County,  Md.  They 
are  honest,  truthful,  and  in  all  respects  well-meaning  people,  and  I 
do  not  think  would  do  anything  wrong  knowingly.  Charley  mainly 
depends  upon  ducking  and  fishing  for  the  support  of  his  old  mother 
and  his  wife  and  four  children. 

Very  truly,  yours, 

Jno.  B.  Blake. 

Captain  John  A.  Dahlgren, 

Commanding  Washington  Navy  Yard.
