Report  of  Commander  Rowan ,  TJ.  S.  Navy ,  commanding  JJ.  S.  S.  Pawnee , 

transmitting  report  of  Lieutenant  Lowry ,  U.  8.  Navy ,  commanding 

TJ.  8.  8.  Thomas  Freeborn ,  regarding  the  rescue  of  schooner  J.  11. 

Maitland. 

IT.  S.  S.  Pawnee, 

Off  Aquia  Creek ,  Ya.,  July  6,  1861. 

Sir:  I  enclose  herewith  a  report  made  by  Lieutenant  Lowry,  com¬ 
manding  the  Freeborn ,  of  the  manner  he  rescued  the  schooner  Mait¬ 
land,  laden  with  Government  property,  from  a  most  perilous  situation, 
and  of  the  conduct  of  the  officer  in  charge  of  the  steamer  Yankee. 

I  would  call  to  the  recollection  of  the  Department  the  fact  that  a 
schooner  had  been  burned  a  few  days  since  at  this  point,  and  had  it 
not  been  for  the  presence  of  the  Freeborn  and  the  exertion  made  by 
Lieutenant  Lowry  this  schooner  would  have  shared  the  same  fate.  The 
conduct  of  the  Yankee  was  doubly  reprehensible  in  not  offering  assist¬ 
ance  to  the  schooner  and  in  treating  with  contempt  the  order  of  Lieu¬ 
tenant  Lowry.  I  refer  the  matter  for  the  consideration  aud  action  of 
the  Department. 

These  men  should  be  taught  common  civility  at  least,  and  if  they 
persist  in  refusing  to  answer  hails,  as  some  of  them  do,  they  may  get 
shot.  In  these  times  we  can’t  tell  at  night  who  are  friends  unless  we 
get  prompt  evidence. 

Lieutenant  Lowry  would  have  been  justified  in  sending  a  shot  after 
the  Yankee  and  compelling  him  at  all  hazards  to  answer  him  and 
explain  the  reason  for  his  hurry. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

S.  G.  Eowan, 

Commander. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy,  Washington. 


[Enclosure.] 


U.  S.  S.  Pawnee,  July  6, 1861. 

Sir  :  While  proceeding  down  the  Potomac  last  night,  about  11 : 30 
p.  m.,  I  observed  several  suspicious  lights  on  board  of  some  vessels. 
On  giving  chase  I  found  that  the  Government  steamer  Mount  Vernon 


OPERATIONS  ON  THE  POTOMAC  AND  RAPPAHANNOCK.  565 


had  been  on  shore  off  Yates  Shoal,  and  that  she  had  left  the  Govern¬ 
ment  steamer  Yankee  hard  aground  on  the  same  shoal.  I  steamed  to 
within  hailing  distance  and  anchored.  I  then  found  the  schooner  J.  W. 
Maitland ,  from  Philadelphia  (with  280  tons  of  Government  coal  on 
board),  hard  aground  on  Lower  Cedar  Point  shoals,  and  within  three 
cables’  length  of  the  Yankee.  As  this  was  the  place,  the  most  danger¬ 
ous  on  the  river,  where  the  Virginia  rebels  had  burned  a  vessel  under 
the  same  circumstances,  I  decided  to  remain  by  them  till  daylight.  At 
about  3:30  a.  m.  the  Yankee  floated  aud  steamed  within  20  yards  of  me. 
I  hailed  him  and  received  for  a  reply,  “  Halloo.”  I  said,  “This  is  the 
Freeborn ;  that  schooner  is  loaded  with  Government  property.  I  want 
you  to  lie  by  me  till  I  get  her  off,  when  I  want  you  to  convoy  her  to 
Mathias  Point.”  To  my  utter  surprise,  the  Yankee  took  no  further 
notice,  but  steamed  directly  up  the  river  without  taking  the  slightest 
notice. 

I  have  no  knowledge  who  the  commander  of  the  Yankee  is,  but  as  she 
is  in  the  employ  of  the  United  States,  I  suppose  he  is  subject  to  some 
of  the  rules  of  the  naval  service.  If  he  is  my  senior  in  the  service  he 
exhibited  an  amount  of  discourtesy  and  indifference  to  the  public 
service  not  usual;  if  my  junior,  a  positive  disrespect  to  me,  which 
sanctions  me  in  asking  for  the  action  of  the  Department.  My  con¬ 
sideration  for  him  and  the  public  service  prompted  me  to  stay  by  him 
all  night  when  I  had  other  important  duty  to  perform. 

Finding  the  schooner  J.  W.  Maitland  in  a  precarious  situation,  I 
remained  by  her,  using  every  exertion  to  get  her  afloat.  To  that  end 
I  transferred  from  her  to  this  ship  about  25  tons  of  coal  for  the  use  of 
the  Freeborn.  Having  parted  all  the  hawsers  and  lines  belonging  to 
this  vessel  and  the  schooner,  I  proceeded  to  Yanjemoy  and  obtained  a 
new  4J-inch  manila  hawser;  with  this  I  was  fortunate  enough  to  get 
the  Maitland  afloat  at  3  p.  m.,  having  worked  at  her  incessantly  for 
nearly  twelve  hours.  The  crew  and  engineer  department  are  very 
much  exhausted,  while  the  engineer  reports  his  engine  needing  repairs 
very  badly. 

1  have  towed  the  Maitland  to  this  anchorage. 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  etc.,  your  obedient  servant, 

R.  B.  Lowry, 

Lieutenant ,  Commanding  Freeborn. 

Commander  S.  0.  Rowan, 

Senior  and  Commanding  Officer ,  Potomac  Blockade. 


Report  of  Commander  Dove ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  commanding  TJ.  S.  S.  Pocahontas, 
of  demonstration  by  that  vessel  on  the  steamer  George  Page ,  July  7 , 
1861. 

U.  S.  S.  Pocahontas, 

Aquia  Creek ,  July  9 ,  1861. 

Sir:  I  have  to  report  that  on  the  suggestion  of  Commander  Rowan 
I  made  a  demonstration  on  the  George  Page ,  steamer,  last  Sunday 
morning. 

I  got  underway  and  steamed  up  the  river  a  short  distance  to  enable 
me  to  get  ready  for  action,  lowered  down  the  launch  and  starboard 
quarter  boat  and  towed  them  astern;  shifted  the  port  quarter-deck  gun 
to  the  starboard  gangway,  making  four  in  battery.  When  all  ready  I 


566  OPERATIONS  ON  THE  POTOMAC  AND  RAPPAHANNOCK. 

ran  down  the  Virginia  shore  to  about  500  yards  of  Brent’s  Point.  The 
Page’s  smoke  pipe  was  the  target  and  I  estimated  the  distance  to  her 
across  the  point  about  500  more.  Heel  of  the  steamer  by  the  spirit 
level  of  the  pivot  gun  was  1  degree.  A  quartermaster  was  stationed 
in  the  fore-topmast  crosstrees  with  a  spyglass  to  observe  the  effect. 

The  first  shell  from  the  10-inch  was  directed  admirably  by  Lieutenant 
Semmes,  and  broke,  after  grazing  the  top  of  the  hill  on  or  immediately 
over  her.  Four  shots  were  then  fired  from  the  batteries  on  the  hills 
south  of  the  creek,  but  we  were  not  within  their  range  and  they  discon¬ 
tinued.  After  our  first  shot  a  large  gang  of  men  was  immediately  set 
to  work  on  the  Page ,  but  for  what  purpose  the  lookout  could  not  deter¬ 
mine.  Some  of  the  32-pounder  shells  broke  well,  but  the  most  of  them 
were  too  high.  Three  round  shot  from  them  ricochetted  in  the  creek 
and  went  into  the  cornfield  on  the  other  side.  The  third  and  last  shell 
from  the  10-inch  I  think  set  the  Page  on  fire.  There  was  smoke  of  a 
different  color  from  that  of  the  charge,  which  lasted  about  ten  minutes, 
the  men  at  work  on  her  all  the  time. 

We  laid  off  about  an  hour,  during  which  we  were  able  to  throw  about 
fourteen  shells.  The  steamer  grounded  in  backing  up  nearer  the  shore, 
but  she  did  not  stick  long. 

The  Page  was  moved  higher  up  the  creek,  out  of  range,  and  I  returned 
to  the  anchorage  at  7  a.  m.  on  the  Maryland  side.  She  was  afterwards 
again  moved  down  to  a  place  from  which  her  smoke  pipe  could  not  be 
seen. 

I  ought  to  add  that  the  gangway  gun  was  manned  by  our  marine 
guard,  and  they  made  the  second  best  shot  of  the  32-pounders. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Benj.  M.  Dove, 

Commander. 

Captain  John  A.  Dahloren, 

Commanding  Navy  Yard ,  Washington,  D.  C.

TJ.  S.  S.  Pawnee, 

Off  Aquia  Creelc ,  Va.,  July  9  [7],  1861. 

Sir:  This  afternoon  two  large  casks  were  seen  floating  down  the 
river,  passing  within  some  200  yards  of  this  ship.  The  Resolute  being- 
in  the  act  of  getting  underway  to  proceed  down  the  river  on  special 
service,  went  to  the  casks  and  brought  them  alongside  of  her  with  one 
of  her  boats.  Mr.  Budd  towed  them  under  the  stern  of  this  ship,  when 
I  directed  him  to  be  careful,  that  they  might  be  explosive  machines  act¬ 
ing  upon  concussion  or  friction,  and  to  tow  them  to  Xanjemoy  to  the 
schooner,  and  there  land  them  on  shore  and  examine  them  and  report 
to  me  the  result.  In  doing  so  one  of  the  casks  sprung  a  leak  and  sunk. 
I  enclose  a  diagram  of  the  machine,  drawn  by  Mr.  Budd,  which  I  find 
upon  personal  examination  to  be  correct  of  the  one  saved,  and  the  other 
was  of  course  of  the  same  character.  The  evident  intention  of  the 
design  of  the  machine  was  to  drop  it  down  with  the  tide,  and  at  a  suit- 


OPERATIONS  ON  THE  POTOMAC  AND  RAPPAHANNOCK.  567 

able  distance  to  set  fire  to  matches,  and  when  it  had  swung  across  the 
cable  with  one  of  the  machines  close  under  each,  bow,  to  explode  in  due 
time  and  so  destroy  the  ship. 

The  idea  was  a  wicked  one,  but  the  execution  clumsy.  I  send  the 
machine  by  the  Freeborn  to  Captain  Dahlgren  to  receive  that  close  and 
thorough  examination  on  shore  which  would  not  be  safe  to  make  on 
board  ship. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

S.  C.  Rowan, 

Commander.

Secretary  of  the  Navy ,  Washington.

U.  S.  S.  Resolute,  July  8, 1861. 

Sir  :  On  proceeding  down  the  river  to  destroy  the  infernal  machine 
I  picked  up  yesterday  morning  I  discovered  that  there  was  some  heavy 
substance  attached  to  the  casks  underneath  the  surface  of  the  water. 
On  attempting  to  raise  one  of  the  casks,  which  had  partially  filled,  the 
iron  straps  parted  and  it  immediately  sank.  I  secured  the  other,  with 
its  attendant  torpedo,  and  hoisted  the  whole  affair  on  board  this  vessel 
complete. 

The  apparatus  in  its  perfect  state  consisted  of  two  large  oil  casks 
connected  by  25  fathoms  of  3^-iuch  manila  line,  the  line  being  kept  on 
top  of  the  water  by  corks  secured  to  it  at  intervals  of  2  feet.  Under¬ 
neath  each  cask,  at  a  distance  of  G  feet,  was  slung  an  iron  cylinder, 
4  feet  6  inches  in  length  and  18  inches  in  diameter  at  one  end  and  17 
inches  at  the  other.  The  faze  for  igniting  the  combustible  material 
contained  in  the  cylinder  was  placed  in  the  cask  in  the  following  man¬ 
ner:  The  upper  end  of  the  fuze  was  secured  on  the  top  and  near  the 
outer  end  of  the  cask,  being  protected  from  moisture  by  a  square  box 
and  gutta-percha  pipe  following  it  through  the  aperture  it  was  placed 
in.  It  was  carefully  coiled  on  a  platform  secured  on  the  inside  of  the 
cask  for  the  purpose  of  protecting  it  from  any  water  that  might  lodge 
in  the  bottom.  From  the  platform  it  entered  a  copper  pipe  that  con¬ 
nected  with  a  gutta  percha  hose,  the  lower  end  of  which  was  secured 
to  the  iron  cylinder  below.  In  each  cask  were  two  fuzes,  each  about 
40  feet  in  length.  All  four  had  been  on  fire.  Whether  they  were  on 
fire  or  not  when  I  first  reached  them  I  can  not  say,  as  ray  first  act  was 
to  throw  -water  down  the  air  holes  that  were  bored  in  the  upper  stave 
of  each  cask.  I  enclose  a  rough  sketch  with  the  distances  marked 
according  to  measurements  made  by  me  at  the  time  I  secured  the 


apparatus. 

The  sunken  torpedo  I  think  I  can  obtain,  as  I  took  ranges  to  deter¬ 
mine  its  position  before  leaving  the  locality  it  went  down  in. 

Very  respectfully, 

William  Budd, 

Acting  Master ,  Commanding  Resolute. 


Commander  S.  C.  Rowan,

[Enclosure.] 

Memorandum. — A  man  of  notoriously  bad  character  named  James  C. 
Hurry,  a  resident  of  Baltimore,  has  formed  a  plan  for  the  capture, 
during  the  present  week,  of  one  of  the  steamboats  plying  between 
Baltimore  and  the  Patuxent  River,  either  by  putting  his  men  on  board 
the  boat  at  Baltimore,  or  at  Millstone  Landing,  on  that  river. 

This  Millstone  Landing,  or  Point,  is  a  position  whence  more  smug¬ 
gling  of  men  and  provisions  is  carried  on  than  any  other  place  in  the 
Chesapeake  waters.  Small  vessels  are  constantly  plying  between  that 
position  and  the  Rappahannock  and  Coan  rivers,  chiefly  to  the  latter, 
where  a  Tennessee  regiment  is  posted. 

These  vessels  are  run  outside  of  Captain  Budd’s  lines.

U.  S.  S.  Pocahontas,  July  9, 1861. 
Sir:  In  obedience  to  your  order  I  proceeded  down  the  river  and  car¬ 
ried  out  the  programme  except  as  to  communicating  with  the  tender  at 
Breton’s  Bay,  which  I  did  not  find. 


570  OPERATIONS  ON  THE  POTOMAC  AND  RAPPAHANNOCK. 


Nothing  required  my  particular  attention  until  I  reached  Point  Look¬ 
out,  when  I  learned  that  a  pungy  had  come  over  from  Ooan  River  and 
landed  the  crews  of  the  three  vessels  captured  by  the  St.  Nicholas. 
The  crews  proceeded  by  land  to  Millstone  Landing,  on  the  Patuxent, 
and  the  pungy  went  on  a  cruise  up  the  Chesapeake  Bay.  She  was 
manned  by  well-armed  men,  variously  estimated  from  eighteen  to  thirty. 
I  then  debated  whether  I  should  send  a  force  on  board  the  tender  sta¬ 
tioned  in  the  neighborhood  with  the  howitzer,  or  whether  1  would  go 
up  to  the  mouth  of  the  Patuxent  myself  in  the  steamer,  and  decided 
upon  the  latter  cruise. 

Upon  arriving  there  yesterday  afternoon  about  7,  I  communicated 
with  a  Bremen  bark,  at  anchor,  and  learned  that  the  men  overland 
arrived  safely  and  had  taken  passage  in  the  steamer  Mary  Washington 
for  Baltimore,  but  that  the  piratical  pungy  had  not  been  seen. 

The  notorious  Thomas  went  up  in  disguise,  and  the  idea  of  him  and 
the  armed  party  in  the  pungy  is  to  capture  the  next  steamer  from  Bal¬ 
timore,  which  will  be  the  George  Weems.  I  have  therefore  to  request 
that  I  maybe  allowed  to  return  immediately  and  try  to  prevent  it.  The 
pungy  is  too  powerful  for  any  of  the  tenders  and  the  presence  of  one 
of  the  larger  steamers  is  very  necessary  between  Point  Lookout  and 
the  Patuxent. 

All  the  inhabitants  on  the  Maryland  shore  are  put  to  great  inconven¬ 
ience  from  not  having  a  regular  steam  communication  as  formerly  by  the 
line  from  Baltimore  to  Washington.  It  is  of  such  importance  to  them 
as  to  require  notice  given  to  the  Department  to  which  it  belongs. 

Respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Benjamin  M.  Dove, 

Commander. 

Commander  S.  C.  Rowan,

ing  as  soon  as  was  indicated  in  your  order  of  the  7th.

U.  S.  S.  Thomas  Freeborn,  of  warning  given  to  steamer  George  Weems. 

U.  S.  S.  Pawnee, 

Off  Point  Lookout,  July  10,  1861. 

Sir:  I  informed  the  Department  under  date  of  the  7tli  [9th]  instant 
that  I  should  move  down  the  river  with  this  ship,  Freeborn,  and  tug 
Resolute  for  the  purpose  of  intercepting  the  steamer  Weems  and  frus¬ 
trating  the  designs  of  the  party  that  crossed  to  seize  her.  The  Free¬ 
born  and  tug  were  sent  in  advance  to  the  Patuxent,  while  this  ship 
followed  shortly  after  and  took  a  position  for  the  night  to  cut  the 
rebels  off  from  Coan  River. 

Not  being  certain  that  the  blockade  of  the  Rappahannock  was  kept 
up,  I  left  the  Potomac  as  soon  as  the  weather  was  clear  enough  to  run 
and  shaped  a  course  for  the  Rappahannock.  Arriving  within  10  or  12 
miles  of  that  river,  I  saw  a  Government  steamer  at  anchor,  and  being 
satisfied  that  all  was  safe,  hauled  toward  the  Virginia  shore  to  examine 
a  wreck,  which  I  found  to  be  a  ship  or  bark  that  had  been  grounded 
on  the  flats,  laden  with  corn.  While  making  this  examination  the 
Mount  Vernon ,  Commander  Glisson,  came  up  from  the  mouth  of  the 
Rappahannock  and  informed  me  that  he  held  the  mouth  of  that  river. 
I  returned  to  the  mouth  of  the  Potomac,  where  I  found  the  Freeborn 
and  Yankee. 

Lieutenant  Lowry’s  report  of  his  visit  to  the  Patuxent  is  enclosed. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

S.  C.  Rowan, 

Commander. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy.

U.  S.  S.  Freeborn, 
Potomac  River ,  July  10,  1S61. 

Sir:  In  obedience  to  your  order  I  proceeded  down  the  river  last 
night  as  far  as  St.  Mary’s,  for  the  double  purpose  of  securing  an 
anchorage  for  the  night — the  night  being  dark  and  squally — and  for 
supplying  provisions  to  the  schooner  Bailey ,  which  vessel  I  did  not  find 
at  her  anchorage.  At  3: 30  I  got  underway  and  stood  by  Point  Look¬ 
out  and  thence  to  the  Patuxent  Eiver.  There  I  found  at  anchor  the 
U.  S.  steam  gunboat  Penguin.  Communicated  with  Commander  Liv¬ 
ingston,  who  informed  me  that  he  had  been  in  search  of  a  schooner 
named  the  Georgiana ,  said  to  be  armed  and  full  of  men. 

A  plan  was  supposed  to  be  laid  to  seize  any  steamer  which  might  run 
to  the  Patuxent.  At  8  a.  m.  the  Penguin  left.  I  remained  till  the 
George  Weems  came  down  the  river:  boarded  her;  found  a  large  num¬ 
ber  of  passengers,  twenty-five  men  and  about  twelve  women.  Warned 
the  captain  about  the  attempt  to  take  him.  He  vouched  for  all  his  pas¬ 
sengers,  that  they  were  planters  and  farmers  and  that  he  knew  every 
one  of  them.  I  beg  leave  here  to  suggest  that  all  steamers  running 
from  Baltimore  should  have  a  guard  of  United  States  soldiers  on  board. 
I  observed  sufficient  from  the  manner  and  bearing  of  the  passengers  to 
satisfy  me  that  all  were  enemies  of  our  flag  and  the  Union. 

The  women  did  not  hesitate  to  insult  us  by  sneering  remarks  and 
cries  of  three  cheers  for  Jeff.  Davis.  The  object  of  [my]  visit  to  the 
Patuxent  being  accomplished,  viz,  to  look  after  the  safety  of  the  Weems , 
I  have  returned  to  await  further  orders. 

Respectfully,  etc.,  your  obedient  servant, 

E.  B.  Lowry, 

Lieutenant ,  Commanding  Freeborn. 

Commander  S.  C.  Rowan, 

U.  8.  8.  Pawnee. 


Report  of  Lieutenant  Lowry ,  U.  8.  Navy,  commanding  77.  8.  8.  Thomas 
Freeborn,  of  the  impaired  condition  of  that  vessel. 

U.  S.  S.  Freeborn, 
Potomac  River,  Va.,  July  10,  1861. 

Sir  :  I  have  to  report  that  the  condition  of  the  Freeborn  is  such  that 
repairs  are  positively  needed  to  make  her  efficient.  The  battery  requires 
changing,  as  the  bow  gun,  a  32-pounder  of  1819,  is  vent- worn,  cracked, 
and  unsafe.  The  gun  carriages  are  very  much  broken  by  incessant  use. 
The  engines  are  very  much  out  of  line  and  various  parts  require  repair¬ 
ing,  an  engineer’s  report  of  which  I  forwarded  through  Commander 
Rowan  some  weeks  since.  The  crew  is  much  reduced  by  detailing  men 
for  the  schooners  and  by  men  going  to  Few  York  with  the  body  of  Com¬ 
mander  Ward  who  have  not  and  who  may  not  return.  The  arms  and 
stores  of  the  vessel  are  very  much  reduced  in  consequence  of  the  affair 
at  Mathias  Point,  when  at  least  eleven  Sharps  rifles  were  lost.  The 
effectiveness  of  the  vessel  has  been  kept  up  by  a  detachment  of  men 
from  the  Pawnee  who  must  be  returned  to-night.  The  ammunition 
has  been  reduced  to  about  70  charges  of  all  calibers,  26  shell,  70  round 
shot,  20  canister.  The  ship  leaks  badly,  but  that  can  be  remedied

only  by  docking,  which  I  do  not  propose.  The  engine  pumps  can  keep 
her  free. 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  sir,  your  obedient  servant, 

R.  B.  Lowry, 

Lieutenant ,  Commanding  Freeborn. 

Commander  Th.  T.  Craven,

[Telegram.] 

Navy  Yard  [Washington,  D.  C.],  July  11,  1861. 

The  captain  of  police  at  the  Capitol  calls  with  a  written  request  from 
General  Mansfield  to  go  by  steam  to  Port  Tobacco  to  arrest  a  person 
who  is  in  possession  of  papers  of  great  importance  and  who  is  to  cross 
the  river  this  evening.  There  is  not  time  to  wait  an  order  from  the 
Department,  as  every  moment  is  stated  to  be  important.  I  have  there¬ 
fore  sent  the  Guy  to  take  the  captain  of  police  down  the  river,  hoping 
the  Department  would  approve  the  action. 

Jno.  A.  Dahlgren. 

Hon.  Secretary  of  Navy.

Approved. 

G.  W.

Report  of  Commander  Dove,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  TJ.  S.  S.  Pocahontas, 
regarding  the  pursuit  and  capture  of  one  Taliaferro. 

H.  S.  S.  Pocahontas, 

Aquia  Creek,  July  12,  1861. 

Sir  :  I  have  to  report  that  yesterday  at  8 : 30  p.  m.  the  steamer  James 
Guy  came  down  from  the  navy  yard,  having  on  board  the  U.  S.  mar¬ 
shal,  in  pursuit  of  one  Taliaferro,  who  left  Washington  in  the  morning 
by  stage  for  Port  Tobacco,  in  whose  trunk  was  correspondence  for  vari¬ 
ous  parties  in  Virginia,  which  he  intended  to  carry  over  and  deliver. 

The  steamer  having  left  the  navy  yard  in  great  haste,  and  the  mar¬ 
shal  being  of  opinion  that  she  had  not  sufficient  force  on  board  in  case 
of  resistance,  her  commanding  officer  applied  to  me;  whereupon  I  sent 
the  launch  with  her  howitzer  and  crew  armed  with  Sharps  rifles  and 
our  marine  guard,  sergeant,  and  eleven  men. 

She  was  taken  in  tow  by  the  steamer  to  Port  Tobacco  Greek  [River] 
and  this  morning  at  8  returned,  having  been  entirely  successful  in  the 
object  of  the  expedition. 

The  marshal  expressed  himself  much  pleased  with  the  assistance  ren¬ 
dered  and  with  the  activity  and  zeal  with  which  his  orders  were  carried 
out  by  the  party  furnished  to  him. 

The  Guy,  after  returning  the  launch  and  men,  proceeded  up  to  Wash¬ 
ington  in  all  haste  with  the  prisoner  and  his  correspondence. 

Respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Benjamin  M.  Dove, 

Commander. 

Commander  T.  T.  Craven, 

Commanding  Potomac  Flotilla ,  U.  S.  S.  Yankee,  Aquia  Creek.

Report  of  Commander  Craven,  TJ.  S.  Xavy,  commanding  Potomac  Flotilla , 

transmitting  report  of  Commander  Rowan,  TJ.  S.  Xavy,  commanding 

U.  S.  S.  Pawnee,  regarding  the  examination  and  detention  of  Mr.  and 

Mrs.  Travers. 

U.  S.  S.  Yankee, 

Off  Piney  Point,  July  13,  1861. 

Sir  :  Herewith  I  have  the  honor  to  enclose  a  report  from  Commander 
S.  C.  Eowan.  Upon  questioning  Mr.  Travers  and  liis  wife  as  to  their 
motives  in  crossing  the  Potomac  Eiver  they  informed  me  that  they  had 
left  their  residence  in  Washington  on  Monday  last  for  the  sole  purpose 
of  receiving  some  valuable  property  which  they  had  near  the  mouth  of 
Coan  Eiver. 

Mr.  Travers  was  by  my  order  thoroughly  searched  for  papers,  etc., 
and  there  being  nothing  found  upon  his  person  I  ordered  Acting  Mas¬ 
ter  Bndd,  in  command  of  the  Resolute ,  to  take  him  to  his  place  of  des¬ 
tination  and  aid  him  in  saving  his  property  and  while  doing  so  not  to 
allow  him  to  communicate  with  any  person  on  shore.  Mr.  Bndd  per¬ 
formed  the  duty  assigned  him,  removing  to  the  Resolute  a  quantity  of 
household  furniture  from  the  shore,  and  returned  to  this  anchorage  at 
about  10:30  p.  m.  of  yesterday. 

The  fact  of  Mr.  Travers  having  so  much  luggage  with  him  when  cap¬ 
tured  excites  in  my  mind  the  suspicion  that  he  must  have  had  some 
further  object  in  view  than  that  of  landing  for  tlie  purposes  assigned, 
and  I  have  thought  proper  to  order  Commander  Bowan,  who  necessa¬ 
rily  goes  up  the  river  for  the  purpose  of  filling  up  his  water,  to  take 
them  in  charge  and  send  them,  under  a  proper  officer,  to  Washington 
navy  yard,  there  to  await  your  further  orders. 

Since  joining  this  flotilla  the  vessels  composing  it  have  been  con¬ 
stantly  and  actively  employed  in  cruising. 

On  my  visit  to  the  mouth  of  the  Patuxent  Eiver  on  the  afternoon  of 
the  11th  instant  I  learned  that  since  the  capture  of  the  St.  Xicholas 
there  had  been  no  communication  by  the  usual  steamers  between  that 
place  and  Baltimore  and  I  have  since  heard  it  reported  that  the  owners 
had  withdrawn  their  steamers  from  that  line. 

On  my  way  down  the  Potomac  on  the  10th  instant  I  steamed  suffi¬ 
ciently  close  in  toward  Aquia  Creek  to  satisfy  myself  that  there  were 
one  or  two  small  batteries  there,  but  not  so  well  manned  [or]  armed  as 
I  had  been  previously  led  to  believe;  and  passing  within  000  yards  of 
Mathias  Point  I  could  discover  no  indications  of  the  rebels  or  of  their 
having  made  attempts  to  fortify  it. 

Yery  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Thos.  T.  Craven, 

Commander,  U.  S.  Xavy. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Xavy,  Washington,  D.  C.

ing  toward  the  shore;  stood  for  her  and  found  it  to  contain  two  persons, 
a  lady  and  gentleman  named  Travers,  man  and  wife.  I  took  them  on 
board  this  ship  with  some  baggage — a  trunk,  carpetbag,  and  bonnet 
box — and  brought  them  to  Piney  Point,  when  I  reported  the  circum¬ 
stance  to  you.  I  shall  put  Mr.  and  Mrs.  Travers  on  board  the  Mount 
Vernon ,  as  you  directed,  to  be  landed  at  the  navy  yard,  Washington.

retaining  the  empty  bags  on  board.  On  Sunday,  the  14th,  while  cruis¬ 
ing  in  the  river,  spoke  the  propeller  Sophia,  bound  to  Washington,  and 
received  information  from  an  officer  on  board  of  her  that  he  saw  a 
schooner  close  inshore  near  Coan  Biver.  Immediately  made  sail  and

ran  over  to  Virginia  and  examined  it  from  Jackson’s  Creek  to  Coan 
River,  but  could  not  discover  anything.  At  4: 30  p.  m.  came  to  anchor 
oft  Point  Lookout.  Ou  Tuesday,  16th,  went  up  the  St.  Mary’s  River 
for  water,  and  while  on  shore  had  conversation  with  several  of  the

Report  of  Commander  Craven ,  TJ.  S.  Wavy,  commanding  Potomac  Flotilla , 
of  the  seizure  of  the  schooners  Brunette  and  Ring  Dove  and  other  serv¬ 
ices  performed  by  the  vessels  under  his  command. 

U.  S.  S.  Yankee, 

Off  Aquia  Creek,  July  19,  1861. 

Sir  :  On  the  morning  of  the  16th  instant,  while  off  the  mouth  of  the 
Patuxent  River,  I  was  informed  by  an  oysterman  that  there  were  two 
suspicious  schooners  anchored  in  the  Nanticoke,  on  the  eastern  shore 
of  Maryland.  I  immediately  stood  across  the  bay,  and  on  our  arrival 
at  a  point  about  5  miles  above  Vienna,  discovered  the  schooners  Bru¬ 
nette,  of  Vienna,  and  Ring  Dove ,  of  Georgetown,  D.  C.  The  Brunette 
was  found  to  be  partially  laden  with  about  10  tons  of  pig  iron,  500  kegs 
of  nails,  and  a  quantity  of  camp  kettles;  the  Ring  Dove  with  about  80 
tons  of  pig  iron  and  two  carboys  of  vitriol.  Upon  examining  one 
George  H.  Stewart,  who  was  on  board  the  Brunette,  he  said  the  Ring 
Dove  was  loaded  at  Philadelphia  and  her  cargo  was  consigned  to  some 
one  in  Richmond.  The  Brunette  was  loaded  at  Baltimore  and  was 
destined  to  Norfolk  and  Petersburg. 

As  there  was  no  doubt  that  these  two  vessels  were  in  the  employment 
of  the  rebels,  I  have  seized  them  and  placed  them  in  charge  of  Lieuten¬ 
ant  Commanding  R.  H.  Wyman,  who  is  directed  to  take  them  to  the 
navy  yard  at  Washington  and  to  await  your  further  orders. 

On  Sunday  last,  as  I  was  proceeding  down  the  Potomac,  off  Mathias 
Point,  spoke  the  steamer  Sophia,  bound  to  Washington.  The  officer  in 
charge  of  her  informed  me  that  he  [had]  just  been  tired  into  from  the 
point.  The  Yankee  was  then  steamed  in  close  under  the  land,  and 
throwing  three  shells  in  among  the  trees  I  was  unable  to  discover  any 
signs  of  an  enemy. 

On  Monday,  with  the  Resolute  and  three  boats  from  the  Paumee  in 
company,  I  made  a  thorough  reconnoissance  of  the  Yeocomico  and  its 
branches.  We  found  several  small  schooners  there,  but  all  except  one 
had  their  sails  unbent  and  had  apparently  been  laid  up  for  some  time. 
The  one  with  her  sails  bent,  the  Favorite,  was  evidently  preparing  for 
a  trip  outside.  We  took  her  in  tow  and  anchored  her  off  Piney  Point, 
when,  on  my  return  yesterday,  I  found  she  had  been  sunk,  either  by 
n  w  r — vol  4 - 37 


578  OPERATIONS  ON  THE  POTOMAC  AND  RAPPAHANNOCK. 

being  carelessly  run  into  by  another  vessel  or  frotn  the  neglect  on  my 
part  to  leave  men  on  board  to  watch  and  keep  her  pumped  out. 

Yesterday  morning  Master  Budd,  commanding  the  Resolute ,  towed 
into  Piney  Point  a  tine  little  pungy,  the  Ocean  Wave ,  of  Great  Wicomico, 
which  he  had  captured  after  a  long  chase  off  the  mouth  of  the  Great 
Wicomico.  Her  officers  and  crew  made  their  escape  by  taking  to  their 
boat,  taking  with  them  everything  from  the  vessel.  She  is  now  being 
employed  under  the  direction  of  Commander  Rowan,  whom  I  have 
detailed  to  watch  by  night  the  coast  from  Smith’s  Point  down  toward 
the  Rappahannock  River,  where  I  am  satisfied  from  information  obtained 
while  in  the  Nanticoke,  the  greater  part  of  the  supplies  furnished  the 
rebels  is  conveyed  from  the  eastern  shore  or  Tangier  Sound. 

Those  points — Tangier  and  Pocomoke  sounds — require  a  thorough 
examination,  and  as  I  can  spare  the  vessels,  a  search  will  be  made. 
The  Resolute  left  yesterday  for  Wicomico  River,  where  I  am  informed 
is  a  schooner  laden  with  supplies  of  ammunition  for  the  rebels. 

Commander  Dove,  with  the  Pocahontas ,  Release ,  and  Reliance ,  is 
stationed  off  Aquia,  where  he  is  directed  to  watch  the  movements  of 
the  rebel  steamer  Page ,  and  to  offer  protection  to  vessels  passing  up 
and  down  the  river.  The  tenders  Bailey ,  Dana ,  and  Cobb  are  engaged 
constantly  in  affording  convoy  by  day  and  in  watching  the  movements 
of  all  boats  by  night.  They  are  so  stationed  as  to  be  within  easy  access 
of  some  one  of  the  steamers  of  the  flotilla. 

Judging  from  appearances  and  from  what  Commander  Dove  has 
mentioned  to  me,  I  am  satisfied  that  the  rebels  have  been  moving  the 
greater  part  of  their  forces  from  the.  heights  back  of  Aquia  Creek. 
Their  camp,  wlrich  was  quite  conspicuous  a  few  days  ago,  is  now 
broken  up. 

Yery  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Thos.  T.  Craven, 

Commander ,  TJ.  8.  Navy. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy ,  Washington ,  D.  C.

[Enclosure.] 

Marine  Barracks,  Headquarters, 

Washington ,  July  24,  1861. 

Colonel  :  I  have  the  honor  to  report  the  movements  and  operations 
of  the  battalion  of  marines  under  my  command,  detailed  to  cooperate 
with  the  Army. 

The  battalion  left  the  barracks  at  headquarters  in  time  to  reach  the 
Virginia  end  of  the  Potomac  Long  Bridge  at  3  p.  m.  July  16,  and 
proceeded  up  the  Columbia  turnpike  until  an  officer  purporting  to  be 
the  assistant  adjutant- general  of  Colonel  [Andrew]  Porter’s  brigade 
came  up  and  assigned  ns  position  in  the  line  of  march,  which  placed  us 
immediately  in  the  rear  of  Captain  [Charles]  Griffin’s  battery  of  flying 
artillery.  This  assignment  was  continued  up  to  the  period  of  the  bat¬ 
tle  of  Bull  Run.  On  reaching  the  field,  and  for  some  hours  previously, 
the  battery’s  accelerated  march  was  such  as  to  keep  my  command  more 
or  less  in  double-quick  time;  consequently  the  men  became  fatigued  or 
exhausted  in  strength.  Being  obliged  at  this  period  to  halt,  in  order 
to  afford  those  in  the  rear  an  opportunity  of  closing  up  and  taking 
their  proper  place  in  line,  the  battery  was  lost  to  protection  from  the 
force  under  my  command. 

This  I  stated  to  Colonel  Porter,  who  was  ever  present  watching  the 
events  of  the  day.  The  position  of  the  battery  was  pointed  out  and  1 
was  directed  to  afford  the  necessary  support.  In  taking  this  position 
the  battalion  was  exposed  to  a  galling  fire.  While  holding  it,  General 
McDowell  ordered  the  battalion  to  cover  or  support  the  Fourteenth 
Hew  York  Regiment,  which  was  about  to  be  engaged.  The  battalion 
in  consequence  took  the  position  indicated  by  the  general,  but  was 
unable  to  hold  it,  owing  to  the  heavy  fire  which  was  opened  upon  them. 
They  broke  three  several  times,  but  as  frequently  formed,  and  urged 
back  to  their  position,  when  finally  a  general  rout  took  place  in  which 
the  marines  participated.  Ho  effort  on  the  part  of  their  officers  could 
induce  them  to  rally.  I  am  constrained  to  call  your  attention  to  the 
fact  that,  when  taking  into  consideration  the  command  was  composed 
entirely  of  recruits,  not  one  being  in  service  over  three  weeks,  and  many 
had  hardly  learned  their  facings,  the  officers  likewise  being  but  a  short 
time  in  the  service,  their  conduct  was  such  as  to  elicit  the  highest  com¬ 
mendation.  Of  the  350  officers  and  enlisted  men  under  my  command, 
there  were  but  2  staff  officers,  2  captains,  1  first  lieutenant,  and  9 
noncommissioned  officers,  and  2  musicians  who  were  experienced  from 
length  of  service.  The  remainder  were  of  course  raw  recruits,  which 
being  considered,  I  am  happy  to  report  the  good  conduct  of  officers  and 
men.  The  officers,  although  but  little  experienced,  were  zealous  in  their 
efforts  to  carry  out  my  orders.  In  the  death  of  Lieutenant  Hitchcock 
the  corps  has  been  deprived  of  a  valuable  acquisition.  On  the  field  he 
was  ever  present  and  zealous.  He  sought  and  won  the  approbation  of 
his  commanding  and  brother  officers.  Enclosed  please  find  a  return  of 
the  battalion,  showing  its  present  strength  with  casualties,  etc.  The 
abrupt  and  hasty  retreat  from  the  field  of  battle  presents  a  deplorable 
deficiency  in  both  arms  and  equipments.  The  rout  being  of  such  a 
general  character  the  men  of  all  arms  commingled,  the  only  alternative 


OPERATIONS  ON  THE  POTOMAC  AND  RAPPAHANNOCK.  581 


left  was  to  hasten  to  the  ground  occupied  by  the  brigade  to  which  we 
were  attached  on  the  morning  of  the  day  of  the  battle.  On  my  way 
thither  I  had  the  good  fortune  to  fall  in  with  General  Meigs,  whose 
consternation  at  the  disastrous  retreat  was  pictured  upon  his  counte¬ 
nance.  He  was  of  the  opinion  the  army  should  hasten  to  Arlington, 
fearing  otherwise  the  enemy  would  follow  up  their  successes  and  cut 
us  off  on  the  road.  My  men  being  weary  and  much  exhausted,  without 
blankets  and  other  necessaries,  I  determined  to  strengthen  such  as 
should  pass  the  wagons  by  hot  coffee,  and  move  on  to  headquarters  at 
Washinton  City,  where  their  wants  could  be  supplied.  But  few  came 
up,  others  continued  on  to  the  Long  Bridge,  where,  on  my  arrival,  I 
found  some  seventy  or  more,  who,  at  my  urgent  solicitation  were  per¬ 
mitted  to  accompany  me  to  the  barracks.  In  assuming  the  responsi¬ 
bility  of  the  return  to  headquarters,  I  trust  my  course  will  meet  the 
approbation  of  authority. 

Blankets  were  thrown  aside  by  my  order  on  entering  the  field,  which, 
from  force  of  circumstances,  we  were  afterwards  unable  to  recover. 

All  of  which  is  respectfully  submitted. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Jno.  Geo.  Reynolds, 

Major ,  Commanding  Battalion. 

Colonel  John  Harris, 

Commandant  Marine  Corps ,  Headquarters.

Report  of  Commander  Rove ,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  8.  8.  Pocahontas , 
stating  the  cause  of  his  presence  off  Alexandria,  Va. 

U.  S.  S.  Pocahontas, 

Off  Alexandria,  July  22,  1S61. 

Sir  :  Having  waited  some  hours  after  Lieutenant  Parker  (with  orders 
for  the  flotilla)  passed  down  this  morning  for  Captain  Craven  and  the 
other  steamers,  and  they  not  making  their  appearance,  I  considered 
the  emergency  to  require  the  presence  of  this  steamer  up  here  and  have 
accordingly  arrived  to  render  such  service  as  may  be  in  my  power.  I 
left  the  Ice  Boat  to  guard  Aquia  Creek. 

Yery  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Benj.  M.  Dove, 

Commander. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy,  Washington,  _Z>.  C.

Instructions  from  the  Secretary  of  the  Navy  to  Commander  Rowan ,  U.  S. 

Navy ,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Pawnee ,  regarding  refugees. 

Ravy  Department,  July  26,  1861. 

Sir:  I  have  received  your  communication  of  the  23d  instant  con¬ 
cerning  certain  free  negroes  and  slaves  belonging  to  Virginia  who  are 
now  on  board  the  Pawnee. 

It  has  not  been  the  policy  of  the  Government  to  encourage  the  emi¬ 
gration  of  this  class  of  persons,  whether  bond  or  free;  but  where  you 
have  them,  as  in  this  case,  on  board,  you  can,  as  I  understand  verbally 
you  do,  employ  the  slaves,  and  those  who  are  free  need  not  be  returned. 
I  am,  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Gideon  Welles. 

Commander  S.  C.  Rowan, 

Commanding  TJ.  S.  S.  Pawnee ,  Potomac  River. 


Report  of  Lieutenant  Parrott ,  TJ.  S.  Navy ,  commanding  TJ.  S.  brig  Perry , 
transmitting  communication  from  Major  Haskin ,  U.  S.  Army ,  com¬ 
manding  Fort  Washington ,  Md.,  regarding  steamer  Cipsy. 

U.  S.  Brig  Perry, 

Off  Alexandria,  July  24,  1861. 

Sir:  On  the 22d  instant  the  commander  at  Fort  Washington  sent  to 
me  the  steamer  Cipsy  with  a  guard  on  board  with  a  letter,  a  copy  of 
which  I  enclose.  I  have  since  kept  her  alongside,  under  the  advice 
of  the  commanders  of  the  Pawnee  and  Pocahontas.  Our  pilot  and  the 
captain  of  the  Cipsy  both  say  she  has  not  power  enough  to  tow  the 
Perry  against  the  tide,  but  I  have  thought  she  might  be  of  service  in 
towing  under  some  circumstances,  and  have  kept  her  alongside  rather 
than  send  her  to  the  yard.  The  commandant  at  Fort  Washington  sent 
a  verbal  message  that  her  owner  was  a  secessionist,  and  that  a  rifle 
secession  company  had  lately  been  raised  at  Piscataway. 

I  await  your  orders  in  regard  to  the  steamer  Cipsy. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

E.  G.  Parrott, 
Lieutenant ,  Commanding. 

Commander  J.  A.  Daiilgren, 

Commandant  Navy  Yard,  Washington,  I).  C.

[Enclosure.] 

Fort  Washington,  Md.,  July  22,  1861. 

The  steamer  Gipsy ,  belonging  in  Piscataway,  Md.,  having  returned 
here  before  her  regular  hour,  and  believing  this  steamer  may  be  of  serv¬ 
ice  to  the  Government,  I  send  her  back  to  report  to  you.  Piscataway 
is  a  strong  disunion  place,  and  for  the  present  I  do  not  think  it  prudent 
that  she  should  go  there  if  the  reports  which  she  brought  here  are  true. 
I  send  a  guard  with  her  and  one  of  the  boats  belonging  here.  They 
can  return  in  the  boat  if  you  detain  the  Gipsy. 

In  haste,  yours,  etc., 

J.  A.  Haskin, 

Brevet  Major,  and  Captain,  U.  S.  Army,  Commanding  Post. 

Commander  of  U.  S.  Navy, 

At  Alexandria ,  Va. 


Report  of  commandant  navy  yard,  Washington,  regarding  the  furnishing 
of  reenforcements  for  the  forts  of  the  Potomac. 

Commandant’s  Office,  Navy  Yard, 

Washington ,  July  24,  1861. 

Sir:  On  the  22d  instant  I  received  a  request  from  Major  [G.  D.] 
Ramsay  to  furnish  some  seacoast  howitzers  or  ammunition  to  assist  the 
forts  on  the  south  side  of  the  Potomac. 

Last  night  I  also  received  your  order  to  send  some  officers  and  men 
to  assist  in  working  the  guns  of  Fort  Ellsworth;  also  to  have  landed 
from  the  Pawnee  and  Perry  some  officers  and  men  for  the  same  purpose. 

With  a  view  to  meet  both  of  these  contingencies  contemplated  by 
your  order  and  the  request  of  Major  Ramsay,  I  have  forwarded  some 
IX-inch  cannon  and  eight  howitzers  with  70  seamen  from  the  yard,  20 
from  the  Pawnee,  and  20  from  the  Perry,  with  a  request  to  the  com¬ 
manding  general  to  assign  a  position  where  the  detachment  can  be 
kept  together  under  its  own  officers. 

This  amount  of  ordnance  will  be  well  supplied  with  ammunition,  and 
I  have  also  made  arrangements  for  the  subsistence  of  fhe  detachment. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Jno.  A.  Dahlgren, 

Commandant, 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Wavy.

Report  of  Acting  Master  Budd ,  U.  8.  Navy ,  commanding  U.  8.  8.  Resolute , 
of  a  reconnoissance  in  Wicomico  and  Pocomoke  rivers. 

IT.  S.  S.  Resolute,  July  25,  1861. 

Sir  :  By  direction  of  Commander  Craven  I  have  the  honor  to  lay  before 
you  the  following  information  obtained  by  me  in  a  recent  reconnoissance 
of  the  Wicomico  and  Pocomoke  rivers  and  of  Tangier  and  Pocomoke 
sounds: 

Large  numbers  of  men  and  quantities  of  supplies  are  constantly  [car¬ 
ried]  into  Accomac  County,  Ya.,  and  from  there  tranferred  to  the  York 
and  Rappahannock  rivers,  leaving  the  eastern  Yirginia  shore  by 
Pungoteague,  Onancock,  and  Cherrystone  inlets,  the  means  of  trans¬ 
portation  across  the  bay  being  small  schooners  and  large  rowboats; 
the  trips  are  made  principally  at  night.  A  person  named  Wilson,  pro¬ 
prietor  of  the  Washington  House  at  Princess  Anne,  Md.,  receives  and 
harbors  supplies  and  recruits.  He  forwards  them  by  hacks  and  wagons 
to  Newtown,  Md.  At  the  latter  place  H.  Dryden,  of  the  Union  Hotel, 
forwards  them  to  Yirginia.  Yirginia  hacks  and  wagons  come  and  go 
to  and  from  Newtown;  the  men  and  arms  pass  through  daily.  There  is 
a  large  number  of  Union  men  iu  Newtown,  but  they  are  helpless  and 
unarmed.  I  would  particularly  call  your  attention  to  the  steamer 
Wilson  Small ,  running  between  Baltimore  and  Princess  Anne,  making 
an  intermediate  weekly  trip  to  Annemessex.  She  has  violated  the 
blockade  twice  by  going  twice  into  Yirginia  during  her  absence  from 
Baltimore  during  the  past  twenty  days.  She  carries  large  quantities  of 
goods  to  Annemessex  marked  P.  Cary  &  H.  Dryden.  These  goods  all 
find  their  way  to  Accomac  and  from  thence  to  west  Yirginia.  The 
captain  of  the  Wilson  Small  owns  a  store  in  Pungoteague,  Ya. 

In  the  river  Wicomico,  at  Salisbury,  a  person  named  Parker  is 
engaged  in  forwarding  supplies  obtained  from  Baltimore  to  Yirginia. 

The  United  States  collector  at  Deal’s  Island,  W.  Price,  has  issued 
licenses  to  vessels  owned  in  Yirginia,  permitting  them  to  hail  from 
Deal’s  Island  under  sub  rosa  owners.  These  vessels  are  engaged  in 
furnishing  supplies  to  the  rebels,  regularly  clearing  from  Baltimore.  I 
obtained  the  name  of  only  one,  the  Dispatch.  I  had  information  that 
the  collector  at  Snow  Hill  had  also  issued  licenses  in  the  same  way. 
Supplies  are  sent  also  from  the  North  to  Chincoteague,  on  the  Atlantic 
coast,  from  thence  across  country  and  ultimately  to  west  Yirginia.  A 
person  named  Clark,  a  pretended  Union  man  in  Newtown,  furnishes 
large  quantities  of  supplies  to  rebels  in  east  Yirginia.  There  is  a  camp 
of  insurgents  near  Eastville,  one  at  Horntown,  one  at  Drummond 
Town,  also  at  Pungoteague  and  Onancock  inlets;  they  are,  as  far  as  I 
could  ascertain,  well  supplied  with  arms.  The  inhabitants  of  Tangier 
and  Watt’s  islands  are  constantly  threatened  with  attacks  from  maraud- 


OPERATIONS  ON  THE  POTOMAC  AND  RAPPAHANNOCK.  587 


ing  parties  from  east  Virginia.  They  are  able  to  give  plenty  of  inform¬ 
ation,  and  would  hail  with  delight  the  appearance  of  a  couple  of  our 
small  steamers,  who,  by  cruising  in  Tangier  and  Pocomoke  sounds,  would 
effectually  stop  the  passage  of  supplies  and  protect  them  at  the  same 
time.  I  captured  three  small  schooners  who  have  been  and  are  engaged 
in  carrying  supplies  to  the  rebels,  namely,  the  Artist ,  the  Chesapeake, 
and  the  Jno.  McCabe.  I  would  respectfully  again  call  your  attention  to 
the  steamer  Wilson  Small.  She  will  be  seized  at  Annemessex,  as  the 
St.  Nicholas  was  in  the  Potomac,  if  measures  are  not  instantly  taken  to 
stop  her  nefarious  traffic. 

While  in  the  Pocomoke  River  an  attempt  was  made  by  the  Virginians 
to  intercept  and  capture  my  vessel  on  my  return  down  the  river.  Six 
hundred  riflemen  were  sent  up  with  two  fieldpieces  from  Horntown. 
Happily,  I  got  a  hint  of  what  was  going  on  and  dropped  quietly  down 
at  night  below  the  point  of  danger.  The  insurgents  came,  but  too  late. 

I  remain,  respectfully, 

William  Budd, 

Acting  Master ,  U.  S.  Navy,  Commanding  JJ.  S.  S.  Resolute. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy.

Report  of  Commander  Craven ,  U.  S.  Wavy,  commanding  Potomac  Flotilla, 
requesting  assistance  in  the  seizure  of  secreted,  arms. 

IT.  S.  S.  Yankee, 

Off  Piney  Point,  July  26,  1861 — 11  p.  m. 

Sir  :  I  have  received  reliable  information  that  there  are  now  secreted 
at  Leonardtown,  Md.,  two  pieces  of  cannon  and  about  forty  stand  of 
arms.  The  cannon  have  arrived  there  but  recently  and  are  en  route 
for  the  rebels.  The  small  arms  are  supposed  to  belong  to  the  State  and 
should  have  been  turned  in,  in  obedience  to  a  proclamation  issued  some 
time  since  by  the  governor. 

Could  I  be  assisted  by  the  marshal  or  one  of  his  deputies  with  the 
necessary  search  warrant,  I  have  no  doubt  that  these  arms  can  be 
found  and  seized. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Thos.  T.  Craven, 

Commander ,  Commanding  Potomac  Flotilla. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Wavy,  Washington.

Report  of  commandant  navy  yard ,  Washington ,  regarding  further  reen¬ 
forcement  for  Fort  Ellsworth. 

Commandant’s  Office,  Navy  Yard, 

Washington ,  July  27,  1861. 

Sir  :  In  pursuance  of  your  telegraphic  order*  of  the  22d  I  sent  a 
detachment  of  officers  and  men  from  this  yard  to  assist  in  the  defense 
of  Fort  Ellsworth,  and  having  some  pieces  of  heavy  and  light  ordnance 
also  at  hand,  which  would  be  very  useful  and  to  which  the  seamen  are 
better  accustomed  than  to  army  ordnance,  I  sent  them  also. 

A  suitable  position  having  been  designated  by  the  proper  military 
authority  the  guns  have  been  placed  there  and  I  have  now  the  satis¬ 
faction  to  inform  you  that  last  night,  when  a  general  beat  to  quarters 
occurred,  our  naval  battery  of  three  IX-inch  guns  and  five  howitzers 
was  manned  and  ready  to  take  its  part  in  defending  the  lines. 

The  site  of  the  battery  is  a  spur  of  the  plateau  where  stands  Fort 
Ellsworth,  but  to  which  the  work  can  not  be  conveniently  extended. 
It  is  therefore  of  importance  and  is  perhaps  the  most  accessible  to 
attack  from  the  character  of  the  ground. 

The  total  force  is  110  seamen  and  40  marines. 

Lieutenant  Parker,  to  whom  I  have  assigned  this  charge,  has  asked 
of  me  some  reenforcement  of  seamen  and  marines,  which  I  am  unable 
to  give  without  lessening  the  force  in  the  yard  too  much. 

I  would  like  to  do  so,  however,  if  the  Department  thinks  proper  and 
would  allow  me  a  reenforcement  of  about  100  seamen  for  the  yard. 

It  is  due  to  our  men  to  say  that  they  have  laid  the  platforms  and 
done  all  the  work  necessary  to  the  operation  of  the  guns. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Jno.  A.  Daiilgren, 

Commandant. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy.

Report  of  Commander  Craven ,  IT.  8.  Wavy ,  commanding  Potomac  Flotilla , 
regarding  exchange  of  shots  with  the  battery  on  Marlborough  Point. 

U.  S.  S.  Yankee, 

Off  Aquia  Creek,  July  29,  1861 — 11:30  a.  m. 

Sir  :  At  about  10  o’clock,  as  I  was  passing  the  mouth  of  Potomac 
Creek,  I  discovered  an  encampment  of  the  rebels  upon  Marlborough 
Point,  and  at  the  same  time  a  battery  of  about  five  heavy  guns  on  the 
southern  bank  of  the  creek. 

With  a  view  of  ascertaining  if  the  rebels  were  there  in  force,  accom¬ 
panied  by  the  steamer  Reliance,  I  opened  fire  upon  the  encampment. 
Our  fire  was  promptly  returned  by  a  concealed  battery  on  Marlborough 
Point,  the  first  shot  from  a  rifled  cannon  taking  effect  upon  our  port 
wheelhouse,  but  without  doing  any  material  damage.  The  little  Reli¬ 
ance  gallantly  tried  her  best  to  reach  the.  rebels.  Having  accomplished 
the  object  of  my  examination,  and  finding  our  guns  had  not  sufficient 
range  to  be  effective,  I  proceeded  on  my  course. 

At  Marlborough  Point  there  is  encamped  at  least  one  regiment  of 
men.  They  have  mounted  at  least  five  rifled  cannon,  besides  the  five 
just  mentioned  on  the  south  side  of  the  creek. 

When  passing  Mathias  Point  it  was  supposed  by  several  of  the  officers 
on  board  of  the  Reliance  and  this  vessel  that  they  observed  signs  of 
the  rebels  having  been  at  work  throwing  up  batteries  of  earthworks. 
Respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Thos.  T.  Craven, 

Commander,  U.  8.  Wavy. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Wavy,  Washington,  I).  C. 


Order  of  the  Secretary  of  the  Wavy  to  Commander  Craven ,  U.  S.  Wavy, 
commanding  Potomac  Flotilla,  enjoining  a  critical  examination  of 
cargoes  of  vessels  to  prevent  smuggling. 


Navy  Department,  July  29,  1861. 

Sir  :  The  Department  would  impress  upon  you  the  importance  of 
examining  very  critically  the  cargoes  of  vessels  that  are  engaged  in 
commerce  with  the  Maryland  shore  for  the  purpose  of  ascertaining  that 
they  are  such  as  described  in  their  manifests.  As  an  instance  of  the 
means  resorted  to  for  smuggling  arms  and  contraband  goods  into  the 
insurrectionary  States,  the  case  of  the  schooner  Buena  Vista  I  would 
refer  to.  She  cleared  from  Baltimore  for  St.  Mary’s  with  an  assorted 
cargo  and  was  seized  by  the  late  Commander  Ward  as  a  suspicious 
vessel  and  brought  to  the  navy  yard  here.  Her  cargo  was  sold,  and  it 
has  since  come  to  light  that  5  barrels  purporting  to  contain  whisky 
were  filled  with  pistols. 

I  am,  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 


Commander  T.  T.  Craven, 

Commanding  U.  8.  Flotilla,  Potomac  River. 


Gideon  Welles. 


P.  S.— The  articles  as  per  manifest  were  shipped  from  Baltimore  bv 
G.  R.  H.  Leffler.

[Enclosure.] 

[IT.  S.  S.]  Freeborn, 

Potomac  River,  July  29,  1861. 

Sir  :  In  obedience  to  your  order  I  have  been  cruising  in  this  vessel 
between  Fort  Washington  and  Budd’s  Ferry.  The  prize  schooner 
Ocean  Wave  is  in  progress  [of]  refitting.  Major  Haskin,  commandant 
at  Fort  Washington,  having  no  regular  means  of  communicating  with 
Alexandria,  I  have  placed  the  schooner  at  his  disposal  when  he  needs 
her.  As  my  crew  is  small  I  proposed  to  place  an  officer  and  a  few  men 
on  board  at  night  to  cruise  near  the  White  House  to  intercept  parties. 
This  morning  I  discovered  two  boats  pulling  for  the  Virginia  shore 
opposite  Indian  Head.  They  succeeded  in  landing,  but  my  boat  was 
so  close  in  pursuit  that  she  succeeded  in  picking  up  three  carpetbags 
which  the  fugitives  threw  away. 

They  contain  some  clothing  of  no  value  and  the  enclosed  letter.  I 
have  information  that  a  great  deal  of  communication  is  carried  on  near 
Marbury’s  Landing  and  near  White  House.  I  have  just  begun  to  be 
familiar  with  the  ground  and  think  that  if  I  continue  on  this  ground  I 
can  succeed  in  effectually  destroying  [communication].  I  cruised  all 
last  night  off  Budd’s  Ferry,  but  could  discover  no  indications  of  com¬ 
munication. 

On  the  Virginia  shore  I  found  a  large  bateau,  evidently  lately  used, 
which  I  have  seized;  another,  too  large  to  launch,  I  destroyed. 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  etc., 

R.  B.  Lowry, 

II.  8.  Navy,  Commanding  Freeborn. 

Commander  Thomas  T.  Craven, 

Commanding  Potomac  Squadron.

Report  of  Lieutenant  Lowry ,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Freeborn , 
regarding  permit  in  the  case  of  William  Clare. 

U.  S.  S.  Freeborn, 

Potomac  River ,  July  29,  1861. 

I  have  investigated  the  case  of  William  Clare,  a  resident  of  Accotink, 
Ya.,  who  has  a  family  at  that  place  and  also  much  property.  He  pro¬ 
fesses  to  be  a  Union  man  and  has  been  ordered  to  leave  Virginia.  In 
the  execution  of  my  duty  I  have  stopped  him  from  passing  this  point 
in  the  longboat  Crystal  Palace,  which  vessel  has  a  pass  from  the  honor¬ 
able  Secretary  of  the  Navy.  I  think  his  case  one  of  great  hardship 
and  meriting  the  indulgence  of  the  Government;  but  not  feeling  justi¬ 
fied  in  passing  him,  am  obliged  to  send  him  back  to  Alexandria  for  a 
proper  permit. 

R.  B.  Lowry,

Letter  from  the  Secretary  of  the  Navy  to  the  TJ.  S.  collector  of  customs  at 
Baltimore,  regarding  the  cargo  of  the  captured  schooner  Buena  Vista. 


Navy  Department,  July  29,  1861. 

The  Department  deems  it  proper  to  communicate  the  following  facts 
to  you : 

The  schooner  Buena  Vista,  William  Fallon,  master,  which  cleared 
from  Baltimore  about  the  11th  ultimo  for  St.  Mary’s  River  with  an 
assorted  cargo,  was  seized  as  a  suspicious  vessel  by  the  Potomac  Flotilla 
and  brought  to  Washington.  Her  cargo  was  sold  and  it  has  just  come

Report  of  Commander  Craven ,  TJ.  S.  Navy ,  commanding  Potomac  Flotilla , 
regarding  the  search  for  secreted  arms  at  Leonardtown ,  Md. 


U.  S.  S.  Yankee, 

Off  Aquia,  August  1 ,  1861. 

Sir  :  Acting  under  your  authority,*  I  yesterday  proceeded  to  Leon¬ 
ardtown  with  the  Freeborn ,  Reliance ,  and  Yanlcee  and  lauded  a  party 
from  each  of  these  vessels  under  the  command  of  Lieutenant  Command¬ 
ing  Wyman,  who  had  my  instructions  to  visit  the  town  and  state  to  the 
chief  magistrate  that  he  was  there  for  the  purpose  of  searching  for  ord¬ 
nance,  small  arms,  etc.,  which  I  had  been  informed  were  secreted  in  the 
place.  After  a  careful  search  without  finding  any  of  the  articles  in 
question,  and  being  informed  by  some  of  the  most  prominent  gentlemen 
of  the  town  that  there  was  nothing  of  the  kind  there,  Lieutenant  Com¬ 
manding  Wyman  returned  on  board. 

I  can  not  help  feeling  a  distrust  in  the  statements  of  these  people, 
and  have  stationed  the  tenders  Dana  and  Cobb  off  the  mouth  of  Breton’s 
Bay,  with  orders  to  cruise  night  and  day,  for  the  purpose  of  intercept¬ 
ing  any  vessels  or  boats  which  may  have  contraband  articles  on  board. 
Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Thomas  T.  Craven, 

Commander ,  U.  S.  Navy. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy,  Washington ,  D.  C.

Navy  Department,  August  1,  1861. 
Str:  On  the  22d  June  the  Department  gave  permission  to  the 
schooner  Robert  R.  Scott,  John  Johnson,  master,  to  follow  fishing  from 
Washington  to  Point  Lookout  on  the  Potomac.  The  master  and  one 
of  tbe  crew  of  the  schooner  have  made  affidavit  that  the  vessel  was 
detaiued  at  Piney  Point  by  James  L.  Gray,  U.  S.  schooner  Bailey,  by 
which  detention  they  sustained  damages  in  the  way  of  the  loss  of  fish,

It  also  appears  from  an  endorsement  in  pencil  on  the  permit  made 
by  James  L.  Gray  that  the  schooner  Robert  K.  Scott  was  detained  from 
the  22d  to  the  25th  of  July  by  your  order.  You  will  please  inform  the

Report  of  Commander  Craven ,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  commanding  Potomac  Flotilla, 
stating  the  cause  of  the  detention  of  the  schooner  Robert  K.  Scott. 

U.  S.  S.  Yankee, 
Potomac  River,  August  3,  1861. 

Sir  :  I  have  the  honor  to  acknowledge  the  receipt  of  yours  of  the  1st 
instant  calling  my  attention  to  the  detention  of  the  schooner  Robert  K. 
Scott,  and  asking  me  why  she  was  detained. 

On  the  morning  of  the  22d  ultimo  I  received  verbal  orders  from  the 
Department,  through  Lieutenant  F.  A.  Parker,  to  take  what  measures 
I  thought  proper  to  prevent  the  rebels  from  following  our  army  across 
the  Potomac. 

In  accordance  thereto,  as  there  were  a  great  many  of  such  craft  sail¬ 
ing  upon  the  river,  and  which  of  all  others  would  be  made  available  for 
the  transportation  of  troops,  I  ordered  the  commanders  of  the  different 
vessels  composing  the  flotilla  to  intercept  and  detain  until  further 
orders  all  fishing  smacks,  flatboats,  scows,  etc.,  in  fact  everything  sailing 
up  the  river,  excepting  such  as  were  laden  or  freighted  by  the  Govern¬ 
ment,  until  further  orders  from  me.  It  was  not  until  about  the  24th 
ultimo  that  I  thought  it  prudent  to  revoke  this  order. 

Yery  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Thos.  T.  Craven, 

Commander,  TJ.  S.  Navy. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy,  Washington.

Order  of  the  Secretary  of  the  Navy  to  Commander  Craven,  commanding 
Potomac  Flotilla,  for  the  suppression  of  all  communication  between 
Maryland  and  Virginia. 

Navy  Department,  August  2, 1861. 
Sir  :  This  Department  has  granted  some  passes  to  small  vessels  to 
run  wood  from  Virginia  shore  to  Washington.  As  it  is  very  important 
that  no  communication  should  exist  you  will  cancel  these  passes  as 
soon  as  found.  Those  now  granted  are  with  the  express  understanding 
that  any  visit  or  communication  Avith  the  Virginia  shore  renders  their 
vessel  liable  to  immediate  destruction.  You  are  hereby  directed  to 
destroy  all  vessels  violating  sucb  passes,  also  all  craft  found  on  the 
Virginia  shore  or  up  its  creeks;  and  you  will  search,  without  further 
warrant,  upon  the  Maryland  shore  for  arms,  ammunition,  or  supplies,

where  there  are  reasonable  grounds  for  believing  they  are  intended  for

Report  of  Commander  Dove ,  II.  S.  Navy ,  commanding  JJ.  S.  S.  Pocahon¬ 
tas ,  regarding  information  received  from  two  refugees. 

TJ.  S.  S.  Pocahontas, 

Off  Aquia  Creel',  August  3 ,  1861. 

Sir  :  By  direction  of  Captain  Craven  I  send  up  herewith  two  colored 
men  whom  I  picked  up  off  Maryland  Point  while  cruising  yesterday 
morning.  The  account  they  gave  of  themselves  seemed  of  so  much 
importance,  if  their  statement  can  be  relied  upon,  that  I  sent  them  first 
down  to  him  off  Point  Lookout  by  the  Reliance ,  as  he  could  more 
readily  from  them  ascertain  the  truth,  and  they  were  brought  back 
to-day  with  the  orders  above  mentioned. 

They  say  that  they  belong  to  Mr.  Duingerfield  Lewis,  of  Marmion, 
about  3  miles  back  from  the  Virginia  shore;  that  the  governor  sent  an 
order  to  their  master  for  his  people  to  go  to  the  mouth  of  the  Rappa¬ 
hannock  to  assist  in  building  a  fort  there;  that  Mr.  Lincoln’s  steam¬ 
boat  (meaning,  I  suppose,  the  St.  Nicholas ),  a  brig,  and  a  large  scow, 
loaded  with  men,  cannon,  and  tools  for  that,  purpose  [were  there] ;  that 
their  master  did  not  like  it,  and  told  them  to  get  off  if  they  could,  and 
that  they  followed  his  advice  and  escaped. 

The  boat  was  very  old  and  leaky,  calked  with  strips  of  guano  bags, 
one  of  the  men  bailing  her  constantly,  the  other  rowing.  It  contained 
besides  two  bags  of  clothes  a  bag  of  corn  meal,  and  one  of  peaches. 
There  was  a  heavy  fog  on  the  river  all  the  morning,  to  which  they 
owed  their  safety,  as  the  shores  seem  to  be  well  guarded. 

Yery  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Benj.  M.  Dove, 

Commander. 

Captain  John  A.  Daiiloren, 

Commanding  Navy  Yard,  Washington,  D.  C. 


Report  of  Acting  Master  Bogert,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  of  the  capture  of  the  schooner 
Pocahontas  and  sloop  Mary  Grey. 


U.  S.  S.  Freeborn,  August  4,  1861. 

Sir:  In  obedience  to  your  orders  to  bring  out  the  vessel  seen  from 
the  steamer  in  Pohick  Creek,  I  took  the  first  cutter  and  a  crew  of  seven 
men  to  obey.  On  getting  alongside  I  found  her  to  be  the  schooner 
Pocahontas,  loaded  with  wood. 

Saw  several  persons  on  the  hills  at  some  distance  from  us,  but  could 
not  get  them  within  speaking  distance.  1  then  took  possession  and  got 
her  underway. 

There  were  several  other  vessels- farther  up  the  creek,  but  being  short 
of  men  was  only  able  to  bring  off  one  more,  the  sloop  Mary  Grey,  said 
to  belong  to  Mr.  Jonathan  Roberts. 


OPERATIONS  ON  THE  POTOMAC  AND  RAPPAHANNOCK.  599 


Iii  getting  out  of  tlie  creek  I  was  considerably  troubled  by  head 
winds  and  tide,  but  at  last  got  them  out  by  towing  first  one  a  short 
distance  and  then  the  other. 

I  saw  a  couple  of  armed  men  come  down  on  a  point  it  was  necessary 
to  weather,  and  sit  down  behind  some  driftwood.  Thinking  it  more 
than  probable  they  were  going  to  fire  into  me  on  my  rounding  the 
point,  and  being  alone  in  the  sloop,  I  took  the  first  shot  myself,  upon 
receiving  which  they  left  over  the  hill.  I  then  got  the  vessels  out  to 
the  steamer  and  delivered  them  to  you. 

Very  respectfully,  etc., 

J.  W.  Bogert, 

Acting  Master. 

Lieutenant  T.  H.  Eastman, 

Commanding  U.  S.  S.  Freeborn.

Letter  from  the  Secretary  of  the  Navy  to  Commander  Craven ,  77.  S.  Navy , 

commanding  Potomac  Flotilla ,  regarding  ferrying  across  the  Potomac. 

Navy  Department,  August  5, 1861. 

Sir  :  The  following  information  has  been  communicated  to  the  Depart- 
men  t  from  a  reliable  source,  and  the  matters  referred  to  should  receive 
attention : 

The  sloop  James  Skidmore  and  other  boats  ferry  across  the  Potomac 
between  Pamunkey  Creek  and  Mattawoman.  They  go  to  Evansport 
and  into  Occoquan  Creek.  A  family  of  Johnsons,  from  Alexandria, 
located  at  Stump  Neck,  are  engaged  in  ferrying  boats  from-  Stump 
Neck  to  Cockpit  Point.  It  is  said  that  the  James  Skidmore  has  moved 
down  to  Sandy  Point  recently,  between  Chicomuxen  and  Maryland 
Point.  A  strict  watch  should  be  kept  over  Herring  Creek. 

The  ferrying  is  carried  on  both  night  and  day  in  the  interim  between 
the  passage  of  the  steamers  up  and  down  the  river. 

I  am,  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Gideon  Welles. 

Commander  T.  T.  Craven, 

Commanding  Potomac  Flotilla.

Report  of  Commander  Craven ,  77.  8.  Navy ,  commanding  U.  8.  8.  Pawnee, 
regarding  prisoner  on  that  vessel. 

IT.  S.  S.  Yankee,  August  9 ,  1861. 

Sir:  This  morning,  as  I  was  off  Sandy  Point,  there  came  alongside 
in  a  small  skiff  a  man  calling  himself  William  McCue,  who  said  he  had 
yesterday  escaped  from  the  Virginia  shore  and  wanted  my  permission 
to  go  down  the  river  as  far  as  Thom’s  Gut  (opposite  to  Aquia)  to  see 
his  mother. 

He  stated  that  about  a  month  ago  he  left  Alexandria  in  a  small  row¬ 
boat  for.  the  purpose  of  visiting  his  parents,  who  live  between  Thom’s 
Gut  and  Smith’s  Point,  and  being  driven  over  toward  the  Virginia  shore 
by  a  strong  gale  he  was  captured  at  Cockpit  Point  by  a  party  of  seven 
armed  men.  Since  his  capture  he  has  been  kept  under  strict  guard  for 
about  three  Aveeks  at  Aquia  Creek.  He  was  then  taken  to  Chopawam- 
sic  Creek,  where  he  was  also  kept  carefully  watched  and  not  allowed 
to  see  or  hear  anything  of  their  movements. 

At  Quantico  Creek  lie  says  there  is  an  encampment  of  about  2,000 
men  from  Tennessee,  commanded  by  one  Colonel  [W.  B.]  Bate.  At 
Chopawamsic  there  is  a  troop  of  cavalry  numbering  some  300  men, 
commanded  by  Captain  [Samuel  A.]  Swann,  and  at  Aquia,  or  in  its 
immediate  neighborhood,  a  regiment  of  men  is  always  kept  somewhere 
back  of  the  hills. 

As  my  pilots,  who  say  they  know  the  man  by  sight,  have  hinted  that 
the  man’s  reputation  is  bad,  and  as  I  have  my  doubts  as  to  the  cause  of 
his  being  in  Virginia,  I  have  sent  him  on  board  of  the  Pawnee ,  there  to 
await  your  further  orders. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Thomas  T.  Craven, 

Commander ,  TJ.  8.  Navy. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy.

Letter  from  Major-General,  McClellan ,  U.  S.  Army ,  to  the  Secretary  of  the 
Navy ,  recommending  the  destruction  of  all  small  boats  on  the  Potomac 
River ,  in  order  to  prevent  the  enemy  from  crossing  into  Maryland. 

Headquarters  Division  of  the  Potomac, 

Washington  City,  P.  C.,  August  10,  1861. 
Sir:  The  major-general  commanding  this  division  directs  me  to  say 
to  you  that  he  has  been  of  late  frequently  informed  from  sources  of 
indisputable  authority  that  a  flotilla  is  being  gathered  together  at  or 
near  Aquia  Creek  by  the  rebels,  consisting  of  several  small  steamers, 
scows,  and  flatboats.  This,  he  has  no  doubt,  indicates  their  intention 
to  make  some  demonstration  toward  Maryland  and  perhaps  by  that 
means  to  reach  Washington.  The  general  respectfully  suggests  that 
measures  be  immediately  taken  to  frustrate  this  design  by  destroying 
any  craft  that  may  be  assembled,  and  thinks  the  most  effectual  method 
of  doing  so  would  be  the  employment  of  as  many  more  steamers  as 
can  be  made  available  by  the  Navy  Department. 

I  am,  sir,  with  great  respect,  your  obedient  servant, 

Lawrence  Williams, 

Captain  and  Aid-de-Camp. 

Hon.  Secretary  of  the  Navy, 

Washington  City ,  D.  C.

Confidential.]  Bureau  of  Detail, 

Navy  Department ,  August  10,  1861. 

My  Dear  Craven:  The  Secretary  has  requested  me  to  say  to  you 
that  a  confidential  communication  has  been  received  from  headquarters 
to  the  effect  that  a  column  of  the  enemy,  14,000  strong,  is  about  to 
move  across  the  river  somewhere  below  Alexandria,  and  that  in  fur¬ 
therance  of  this  movement  there  is  a  more  than  usually  active  inter¬ 
course  between  the  two  banks,  advantage  being  taken  of  the  night  and 
of  the  unavoidable  absence  of  the  vessels  of  the  flotilla  from  points 
most  favorable  for  this  intercourse.

U.  S.  S.  Yankee, 

Off  Piney  Point ,  August  11,  1861. 

Sir:  Herewith  I  send  you  a  letter  from  Acting  Master  Budd,  which 
speaks  for  itself.  I  received  it  last  night  from  on  board  the  Dana 
while  on  my  way  down  the  river. 


OPERATIONS  ON  THE  POTOMAC  AND  RAPPAHANNOCK.  603 


As  the  vessels  of  tlie  flotilla  are  getting  sliort  of  provisions,  I  liave 
ordered  Mr.  Budd  to  proceed  with  the  Resolute  to  tRe  navy  yard  to 
obtain  a  full  supply  for  sis  weeks;  also  to  report  to  you  in  person  tRe 
circumstances  attending  tRe  capture  of  tRe  ten  negroes,  wRo  Rave  been 
returned  to  liis  vessel  to  await  your  further  orders. 

Four  other  negroes  taken  by  Lieutenant  Mygatt  are  also  sent  up;  Ris 
report  concerning  them  is  herewith  enclosed. 

This  evening  at  sunset  a  negro  came  on  board  and  intimated  to  my 
steward  that  Re  could  give  me  some  important  information.  Upon 
questioning  Rim  Re  stated  that  there  was  at  Herring  Creek  one  Mad¬ 
dox,  an  Irishman,  who  has  been  quite  active  in  procuring  supplies  of 
men,  munitions  of  war,  clothing,  etc.,  for  the  rebels,  and  that  Re  Rad 
sent  many  boat  loads  of  them  over  to  Virginia;  that  on  Tuesday  last 
Re  sent  eight  wagons  and  sixteen  horses  to  Maryland  Point  (one  wagon 
was  loaded  with  uniforms),  and  on  the  same  day  eight  men,  who  came 
from  Baltimore,  were  sent  across  tlie  river.  Cooperating  with  Maddox 
is  one  Dr.  Combe,  [Coombs?]  who  has  appropriated  an  old  outhouse 
as  a  barrack  for  the  reception  of  volunteers  for  the  rebel  Army.  Yes¬ 
terday  week  there  were  ten  men  lodged  in  this  barrack  and  two  men 
and  a  woman  in  Ris  Rouse.  The  man  Maddox  and  Dr.  Combe  employ 
their  negroes,  horses,  and  wagons  in  transporting  recruits  to  the  vari¬ 
ous  landings,  at  night,  watching  their  opportunity  when  our  cruisers 
are  out  of  sight. 

One  Ben.  Hughes  furnishes  the  recruits  with  shoes.  His  brother  ran 
the  Pocahontas  with  freight  to  and  from  Baltimore  and  has  brought 
provisions  for  the  rebels.  Maddox  has  been  absent  for  a  few  days  in 
Baltimore;  was  expected  back  to-day  (he  was  seen  this  afternoon  by 
Mr.  Budd).  Two  boats  are  now  in  Herring  Creek.  They  came  from 
Virginia,  containing  three  men,  one  woman  and  child,  and  the  owner  of 
the  boat,  who  is  now  at  the  house  of  one  Johnson.  Johnson’s  house  is 
also  a  depot  for  recruits.  At  his  house  there  is  a  minister  who  came 
from  Virginia  and  acts  as  a  spy,  and  is  in  constant  communication  with 
one  Bell.  Bell  came  over  from  Virginia  on  Wednesday  night;  does  not 
stay  at  any  particular  place  for  fear  of  being  taken. 

This  statement,  sir,  although  made  by  a  negro,  has  every  appearance 
of  being  truthful,  and  from  hints  which  have  come  to  me  from  the  pro¬ 
prietor  of  the  hotel  here,  I  am  convinced  that  all  these  persons  are 
active  participators  in  the  rebellion  and  are  constantly  engaged  in 
traitorous  acts. 

At  11  p.  m.  (it  is  now  1  a.  m.  of  the  12th)  I  started  a  party  of  eight 
men,  under  charge  of  Acting  Master’s  Mate  Street  and  my  clerk,  Mr. 
Swift,  to  seize  the  boats.  1  shall  use  my  utmost  efforts  to  obtain  other 
and  legal  evidence  against  these  people,  and,  if  good  and  sufficient,  shall 
adopt  such  means  as  will  insure  their  capture. 

From  all  I  can  see  and  learn  of  the  people  of  Maryland  I  am  con¬ 
vinced  that  along  the  shores  of  the  Potomac  there  is  not  one  in  twenty 
who  is  true  to  the  Union,  and  I  sometimes  think  there  are  many  hun¬ 
dreds  of  them  thoroughly  organized  into  companies,  perhaps  regiments, 
and  prepared  to  act  against  the  Government  at  any  moment. 

5  a.  on.,  12th.— The  boat  under  charge  of  Acting  Master’s  Mate  Street 
has  just  returned  with  three  fine  boats  as  prizes. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Thos.  T.  Craven, 

Commander. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy.

U.  S.  S.  Resolute,  August  10,  1861. 

Sir:  I  broke  up  tlie  depot  for  receiving  recruits  aud  supplies  from 
Herring  Creek  this  morning,  said  depot  being  near  the  mouth  of  the 
Machodoc  Creek,  Virginia.  On  going  into  the  creek  I  was  tired  at  with 
musketry.  I  landed,  destroyed  the  premises,  and  captured  a  large  boat 
that  arrived  from  Maryland  the  night  before.  When  I  landed  there 
was  a  party  of  secessionists  from  Maryland  in  the  house;  they  made 
their  escape  into  the  woods.  I  chased  them  for  a  mile,  but  they  got  off. 
I  took  ten  contrabands  who  belonged  to  the  person  (Colonel  Brown) 
owning  the  premises.  Colonel  Brown  has  been  the  receiver  and  for¬ 
warder  of  supplies  and  recruits,  and  of  course  his  property  used  for 
that  purpose  is  confiscated.  As  the  schooner  Dana  is  entirely  out  of 
provisions,  and  I  have  none  to  supply  her,  I  send  her  up  with  the  con¬ 
trabands.  The  foreman  of  the  contrabands,  who  is  a  remarkably  intel¬ 
ligent  negro,  informs  me  that  an  expedition  is  organized  in  Machodoc 
to  capture  any  of  the  schooners  that  are  anchored  or  becalmed  in  that 
vicinity.  I  am  getting  out  of  provisions  and  it  will  be  necessary  to 
supply  me  soon. 

V ery  respectfully, 

William  Budd, 
Commanding  Resolute. 

Captain  Craven, 

Commanding  Flotilla.

to  use  them  for  military  purposes,  or,  to  use  their  own  word,  “because 
he  wanted  to  send  them  to  the  wars.”  I  detained  them  subject  to  vour 
action.  • 

In  obedience  to  your  order  they  have  been  sent  to  the  Resolute  for 
transportation  to  Washington.

Letter  from  the  Assistant  Secretary  of  the  Navy  to  Captain  Craven,  U.  8. 
Navy  commanding  Potomac  Flotilla,  regarding  a  rumor  of  the  intention 
of  the  Confederates  to  throw  a  force  across  the  river  from  Aquia  Creek. 


Unofficial.] 


Washington,  D.  C.,  August  12,  1861. 


My  Dear  Sir:  I  had  a  talk  last  eve  with  General  McClellan,  who 
feels  somewhat  anxious  about  a  small  force  being  thrown  across  the 
river  from  Aquia  in  combination  with  other  movements. 

I  suggested  that  you  better  come  up  and  have  a  talk  with  him,  which 
he  wished  very  much.  Will  you  come  in  the  next  three  days? 

The  boat  that  takes  this  note  is  bound  to  Hampton  Eoads  for  four 
launches,  each  having  a  12-pound  rided  gun  and  equipments  complete. 
You  can  have  these  boats  delivered  to  you  as  they  return,  or  they  can 
be  landed  at  the  navy  yard  and  ammunition  provided,  etc.  I  am  more 
afraid  of  the  capture  of  the  Ice  Boat  than  anything  else. 

We  have  several  prizes  here.  If  they  could  be  sunk  in  the  Aquia 
Creek  channel  they  are  at  your  service.  Your  force  will  be  much 
increased  very  soon,  as  we  have  purchased  several  very  nice  tugs  and 
are  dttiug  them  with  iron  bulwarks  to  resist  rided  shot  from  muskets. 

Uery  truly, 

G.  V.  Fox. 

Captain  T.  T.  Craven.

[Enclosure.] 

Headquarters  Division  of  the  Potomac, 

Washington,  August  12,  1861. 

Sir  :  I  have  to-day  received  additional  information  which  convinces 
me  that  it  is  more  than  probable  that  the  enemy  will,  within  a  very  short 
time,  attempt  to  throw  a  respectable  force  from  the  mouth  of  Aquia 
Creek  into  Maryland.  This  attempt  will  probably  be  preceded  by  the 
erection  of  batteries  at  Mathias  and  White  House  points.  Such  a  move¬ 
ment  on  the  part  of  the  enemy,  in  connection  with  others  probably 
designed,  would  place  Washington  in  great  jeopardy.  I  most  earnestly 
urge  that  the  strongest  possible  naval  force  be  at  once  concentrated 
near  the  mouth  of  Aquia  Creek,  and  that  the  most  vigilant  watch  be 
maintained  day  and  night,  so  as  to  render  such  passage  of  the  river 
absolutely  impossible.  I  recommend  that  the  Minnesota  and  any  other 
vessels  available  from  Hampton  Roads  be  at  once  ordered  up  there,  and 
that  a  quantity  of  coal  be  sent  to  that  vicinity  sufficient  for  several 
weeks’  supply.  At  least  one  strong  war  vessel  should  be  kept  at  Alex¬ 
andria,  and  I  again  urge  the  concentration  of  a  strong  naval  force  in 
the  Potomac  without  delay.  If  the  naval  department  will  render  it 
absolutely  impossible  for  the  enemy  to  cross  the  river  below  Washing¬ 
ton,  the  security  of  the  capital  will  be  greatly  increased.  I  can  not  too 
earnestly  urge  an  immediate  compliance  with  these  requests. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Geo.  B.  McClellan, 

Major-  General,  Gommanding. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary,  If.  S.  Navy.
