Report  of  Commander  Craven ,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  Potomac  Flotilla, 
suggesting  for  the  Army  measures  of  cooperation  in  preventing  the  move¬ 
ment  of  the  enemy  across  the  Potomac. 


U.  S.  S.  Yankee, 

Off  Aquia  Creek,  August  13,  1861 — 10  p.  m. 

Sir  :  I  have  tlie  lionor  to  acknowledge  the  receipt  of  your  communi¬ 
cation  of  this  date  and  its  accompanying  copy  of  a  letter  from  General 
McClellan. 

I  have  at  present  lying  off  Aquia  Creek  the  Pocahontas,  Ice  Boat, 
Reliance,  and  Yankee.  Have  sent  by  the  Mount  Vernon  for  the  Freeborn, 
which  is  somewhere  between  (his  and  Fort  Washington.  She  will 
probably  arrive  here  before  daylight. 

The  Resolute  is  now  at  the  navy  yard  and  will  be  down  here  early  in 
the  morning.  I  was  on  my  way  to  Washington,  in  compliance  with  a 
request  received  this  morning  from  Assistant  Secretary  Fox,  and  for  the 
purpose  of  having  my  rudder  repaired,  when  I  received  your  letter. 

I  have  been  apprehensive  for  some  time  past  that  points  this  side  of 
Washington  would  be  chosen  by  the  rebels  in  case  they  should  attempt 
the  passage  of  the  Potomac,  and  in  view  of  strong  secession  feeling 
which  prevails  all  along  the  Maryland  shore  and  the  possibility  that 
they  have  already  organized  bands  to  assist  the  rebels,  I  would  respect¬ 
fully  suggest  through  you  to  General  McClellan  whether,  as  a  matter  of 
precaution,  batteries  should  be  erected  and  occupied  by  two  or  three 
regiments,  so  as  to  command  the  crossings  at  or  near  Marshall’s  Point, 
Indian  Head,  Stump  Neck,  Budd’s  Ferry,  Smith’s,  Lower  Thom’s,  and 
Upper  Cedar  points,  and  at  the  mouth  of  Port  Tobacco  River.  Such 
occupancy  on  the  part  of  our  military  forces,  with  the  small  force  under 
my  command,  would  in  my  opinion  render  it  absolutely  impossible  for 
the  enemy  to  cross  the  river. 

Be  assured,  sir,  that  no  effort  on  my  part  shall  be  spared  to  render 
the  Potomac  Flotilla  worthy  of  the  confidence  reposed  in  it. 

Yery  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Thos.  T.  Craven, 

Commander,  U.  8.  Navy,  Commanding  Potomac  Flotilla. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy,  W ashington.

[Enclosure.] 

IT.  S.  S.  Resolute,  August  16  [15],  1861. 

In  obedience  to  your  orders  I  proceeded  down  the  river  to  make  an 
examination  of  Mathias  Point  and  the  immediate  vicinity.  Nothing 
indicating  a  hostile  movement  could  be  discovered  at  or  about  the 


N  w  R — vol  4 - 39 


610  OPERATIONS  ON  THE  POTOMAC  AND  RAPPAHANNOCK. 


point.  Hearing  that  a  schooner  was  ashore  at  Lower  Cedar  Point  I 
thought  it  advisable  to  go  down  to  her  and  get  her  off  if  possible.  A 
boat  was  seen  on  the  Virginia  shore  a  short  distance  this  side  of  Per¬ 
simmon  Point,  and  I  dispatched  an  officer  and  five  men  in  a  boat  for 
the  purpose  of  capturing  her.  They  had  just  readied  her  and  were  in 
the  act  of  making  fast  when  a  volley  of  musketry  was  fired  from  the 
adjoining  bushes,  not  more  than  5  or  6  yards  distant,  instantly  killing 
three  of  the  boat’s  crew  and  wounding  another.  I  immediately  opened 
fire,  throwing  shell  into  the  cover  that  sheltered  the  enemy.  After  four 
or  five  rounds  they  were  driven  out,  running  in  parties  of  three  and 
four  in  different  directions,  some  of  them  running  into  some  dwelling 
houses  on  the  right.  The  survivors  of  the  boat’s  crew  succeeded  in 
getting  her  off  from  shore  while  I  was  firing.  The  Reliance  coming  up 
at  this  moment  commenced  throwing  shell  at  the  flying  enemy,  and  also 
sent  a  boat  to  assist  in  getting  my  boat  off".  Nothing  was  left  behind. 

My  boat  is  completely  riddled,  particularly  in  the  after  part.  The 
attacking  party  numbered  about  thirty.  Lieutenant  Mygatt  remained 
with  his  vessel  in  the  vicinity  until  I  could  report  to  you.  The  follow¬ 
ing  persons  were  killed  and  wounded: 

Killed. — John  T.  Fuller,  master’s  mate;  George  Seymour,  seaman; 
Thomas  Tally,  seaman. 

Wounded. — Ernest  Walter,  seaman. 

The  men  that  escaped  state  that  the  boat  on  the  shore  had  two  cracks 
in  her.  We  were  unable  to  secure  her. 

Very  respectfully, 


Captain  Craven, 

Commanding  Potomac  Flotilla. 


William  Budd, 

Commanding  Resolute.

OPERATIONS  ON  THE  POTOMAC  AND  RAPPAHANNOCK.  611 


Letter  from  Acting  Master  Budd ,  U.  8.  Navy,  commanding  TJ.  8.  8.  Reso¬ 
lute,  to  General  McClellan,  U.  8.  Army,  regarding  the  activity  of  the 
enemy  and  laxity  of  the  Federal  Government. 


U.  S.  S.  Resolute, 

Off  Aquia,  August  15, 1861. 

Sir:  The  whole  naval  force  in  the  Potomac,  with  the  exception  of 
the  brig  Ferry,  at  Alexandria,  is  now  at  anchor  at  this  point.  The 
squadron  consists  of  the  Pawnee,  Pocahontas,  Ice  Boat,  Yankee,  Free- 
horn,  Resolute,  and  Reliance. 

There  is  not  a  single  Federal  gun  between  Aquia  Creek  and  Fort 
Washington,  nor  from  Aquia  to  the  mouth  of  the  Rappahannock. 

I  would  call  your  attention  to  the  fact  that  close  to  the  mouth  of  the 
Potomac,  in  Virginia,  are  two  rivers  (Coan  and  Yeocomico),  both  capa¬ 
ble  of  admitting  vessels  drawing  12  feet  of  water. 

Also,  between  the  Potomac  and  Rappahannock,  there  is  an  estuary 
(Great  Wicomico  Bay  [River]),  also  haviug  a  depth  of  14  feet.  These 
inlets  possess  admirable  facilities  for  concealing  vessels  and  boats, 
and  are  all  unguarded.  You  will  see  by  consulting  any  map  of  the 
county  that  there  is  an  abundance  of  land  and  water  communication 
from  these  places  to  the  Rappahannock. 

The  enemy  has  within  a  short  time  cut  down  all  the  woods  and  large 
trees  on  Brent’s  Point  (which  forms  one  side  of  Aquia  Creek),  so  as  to 
enable  him  to  sweep  the  point  with  guns,  which  have  lately  been  placed 
in  position  on  the  opposite  side  of  the  creek,  and  are  as  yet  masked, 
his  object  being  to  guard  himself  from  any  attempt  to  land  above  and 
out  of  the  range  of  his  main  works.  Last  night  he  threw  up  an  earth¬ 
work  connecting  two  of  his  hill  batteries,  about  1,200  yards  distant  from 
each  other.  While  I  write  this  he  is  fortifying  a  ravine  between  Poto¬ 
mac  and  Aquia  creeks.  The  Pawnee  is  within  good  shelling  distance 
looking  at  the  performance.  His  rifle  guns  will  hunt  her  out  of  that 
when  he  gets  them  in  position.  The  enemy  is  evidently  strengthening 
his  position  by  every  possible  means.  We  do  nothing. 

1  suppose  if  anything  takes  place  here  we  are  all  to  fight  on  our  own 
hook,  as  we  have  no  plan  of  signals,  organization,  or  attack. 

The  promised  increase  of  force  has  not  yet  arrived,  and  the  enemy 
has  the  river  to  himself  above  and  below  us. 

2  p.  m.  I  have  just  returned  from  an  examination  of  Mathias  Point. 
Nothing  indicating  a  new  or  hostile  movement  is  visible,  but  the  woods 
and  undergrowth  are  so  dense  that  it  is  impossible  to  find  out. 

Pushing  my  reconnoissance  a  little  farther  down,  and  endeavoring 
to  cut  out  a  boat  with  supplies  for  the  insurgents,  I  fell  on  a  party  of 
about  thirty  Confederates.  We  had  a  brush.  I  lost  three  killed  and 
one  wounded,  but  can  not  tell  the  loss  on  the  other  side.  I  hunted  them 
out  of  their  cover  with  shell  and  shrapnel,  but  only  one  of  their  number 
was  actually  seen  by  me  to  be  killed.  I  was  not  in  force  to  penetrate 
the  cover  after  they  abandoned  it. 

Will  you  not  change  the  policy  of  the  naval  force  and  Department, 
and  compel  them  to  drop  Micawber’s  role  and  do  something? 

Very  respectfully, 

William  Budd, 

Commanding  Resolute ,  Potomac  Flotilla. 

Major-General  G.  B.  McClellan, 

Commanding  Potomac  Division.

Instructions  from  the  Secretary  of  the  Navy  to  Commander  Craven ,  U.  S.

Navy  Department,  August  15 ,  1861. 
Sir:  In  forwarding  the  enclosed  memorandum,  received  from  the 
Assistant  Secretary  of  War,  the  Department  desires  to  place  you  fully 
on  your  guard,  and  to  require  of  you  to  destroy  every  vessel  or  boat

have  been  given  to  trade  on  the  Potomac.  These  may  be  canceled  by

Gideon  Welles.

August  13  [1861], 

President  Davis  has  written  within  two  days : 

Have  no  street  fights ;  keep  Baltimore  quiet  for  the  present ;  in  ten  days  I  shall 
command  the  Potomac  and  cross  between  Mathias  Point  and  Aquia  Creek  into 
Charles  and  St.  Mary’s  counties  (they  are  all  friends  there)  and  march  upon  Annapo¬ 
lis.  Then,  having  two  of  the  approaches  to  Washington  in  possession,  let  Baltimore 
rise  and  burn  the  bridges.  The  movements  in  the  upper  Potomac  are  only  feints. 

Source  unquestionable.  The  same  party  informs  me  that  a  regular 
communication  exists  by  means  of  the  St.  Mary’s  steamboat  line  from 
Baltimore  up  the  Patuxent  and  then  in  an  open  boat  from  Port  Tobacco 
to  the  Virginia  shore  after  the  police  boat  has  passed.  This  was  inter¬ 
rupted  bv  [General]  Banks  for  a  time,  to  the  great  confusion  of  the 
enemy.

[Enclosure — Newspaper  clipping.] 

Philadelphia  Ice  Boat  at  Aquia  Creek. — Bad  treatment  of  the  crew. 

U.  S.  S.  Ice  Boat, 

Aquia  Creek,  August  10,  1861. 

Dear  Sir:  The  object  of  this  letter  is  to  give  yourself  and  our 
friends  at  honqe  a  sketch  of  the  manner  in  which  we  have  been  used 
since  leaving  Philadelphia.  At  that  time  we  had  no  less  than  four 
captains,  one  lieutenant,  purser,  gunner,  and  purser’s  clerk.  Since 
that  time  we  have  changed  commanders  no  less  than  eight  times,  so 
that  by  the  time  one  commander  has  about  become  acquainted  with  the 
boat  and  her  crew  he  is  ordered  away  and  another  takes  his  place,  and 
he,  finding  out  his  own  position  and  about  [how]  long  he  will  probably 
remain,  cares  not  how  the  men  are  cared  for  and  leaves  everyone  to 
shift  for  himself.  By  that  means  you  will  see  there  are  no  regulations 
of  any  kind  and  no  one  to  take  an  interest  in  the  men.  By  that  means 
we  are  left  to  suit  our  own  taste  about  the  arrangement  of  matters 
aboard  the  vessel.  Four  weeks  after  we  had  left  Philadelphia  we  had 
no  whisky,  coffee,  or  stove  in  which  to  cook  what  provisions  we  had 
on  board,  the  pay  for  which  we  will  never  get.  At  one  time,  some¬ 
where  in  the  neighborhood  of  two  weeks,  while  outside  cruising  in  the 
bay,  we  lived  entirely  on  raw  meat  and  biscuit.  At  another  time  we 
were  for  seven  weeks  without  fresh  provisions  of  any  kind,  although 
we  were  in  port  every  few  days.  There  are  now  some  forty  blue  jackets 
on  board,  and  we  can  sling  but  fourteen  hammocks,  and  I  have  seen 
the  time,  when  it  rained  very  heavy,  that  no  one  on  the  vessel  closed 
his  eyes  for  twenty-four  hours  at  a  time,  there  not  being  even  a  dry 
place  to  stow  our  bags  in,  our  clothes  being  always  in  a  damp  and 
dirty  condition.  Before  we  came  around  here  to  Washington  some  of 
the  men  had  gone  barefooted  for  two  weeks,  the  officers  telling  us  that 
we  were  likely  to  be  out  of  commission  soon  and  such  things  would  not 
be  needed  until  we  got  aboard  our  regular  seagoing  ship. 

Now,  sir,  we  all  know  it  is  not  the  right  thing  for  any  man,  especially 
in  times  like  these,  to  complain  of  their  officers,  and  we  have  not  done 
so  until  forbearance  has  ceased  to  be  a  virtue,  and  we  are  now  com¬ 
pelled  to  speak  for  ourselves.  At  the  time  we  shipped  we  did  so  with 
our  minds  made  up  to  go  through,  without  complaint,  any  task  or 
hardship  that  might  tall  to  our  lot;  but,  sir,  for  all  that,  we  do  still  con¬ 
sider  ourselves  men,  and  think  that  we  should  be  treated  as  such,  and 
not  like  dumb  brutes.  At  the  present  time  our  battery  consists  of  one 
9-inch  shell  gun,  one  6-incli  rilled  gun,  two  32-pounders,  one  12-pounder 
howitzer,  beside  Minie  muskets,  carbines,  boarding  pistols,  cutlasses, 
boarding  pikes,  and  battle-axes,  with  revolvers  for  the  picked  men. 
And  now  we  are  stationed  here  without  even  the  common  necessaries 
of  life,  to  lead  the  van  in  every  affair  where  there  is  likely  to  be  plenty 
of  hard  work  and  no  thanks  for  the  same;  and  at  this  present  time  1 
can  safely  say  there  is  not  a  man  on  the  vessel  who  will  not  dare  as 
much  to  serve  his  country  as  any  man  in  the  United  States  Navy,  but 
at  the  same  time,  as  we  have  said  before  and  now  repeat,  we  wish  to  be 
treated  as  men.  There  is  not  a  week  goes  by  but  we  are  short  in  our 
allowance  in  some  way  or  another.  At  present  we  are  living  on  ten 
days’  allowance  of  old,  moldy  bread  that  they  would  not  or  could  not 
use  themselves,  and  also  drinking  our  coffee  without  sugar,  although 
we  arc  only  55  miles  from  the  capital.  Now,  sir,  we  expect  nothing  but 
what  is  allowed  us,  and  want  nothing  unreasonable,  but,  sir,  as  a  mat¬ 
ter  of  justice,  we  demand  our  rights,  or,  whatever  may  be  the  conse- 


614  OPERATIONS  ON  THE  POTOMAC  AND  RAPPAHANNOCK. 

I 

quence,  the  muster  roll  aboard  this  vessel  will  be  found  short  before 
many  days  pass  by,  and  to  let  you  know  that  these  are  not  the  senti¬ 
ments  of  one  man,  but  of  the  whole  ship’s  crew,  every  man  on  the 
vessel  signs  this  letter  of  his  own  free  will ;  and,  sir,  if  you  will  be  kind 
enough  to  have  this  inserted  in  your  paper  you  will  receive  the  thanks 
of  the  whole  ship’s  crew. 

With  much  respect,  sir,  we  sign  ourselves  unanimously,

Report  of  Commander  Craven ,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  commanding  Potomac  Flotilla, 
recommending  the  erection  of  batteries  on  the  Maryland  shore  opposite 
A  quia  Creel. 

TJ.  S.  S.  Yankee, 

Off  Aquia,  August  15,  1861 — 10  p.  m. 
Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  acknowledge  the  receipt  of  your  two  com¬ 
munications  of  this  date,  one  accompanied  by  information  relative  to 
the  movements  ot  the  enemy,  the  other  without  its  intended  accom¬ 
panying  enclosure. 

Since  our  arrival  off  this  station  the  rebels  have  been  constantly  at 
work  in  throwing  up  heavy  earthworks  in  every  available  position  com- 


OPERATIONS  ON  THE  POTOMAC  AND  RAPPAHANNOCK.  615 


mantling  tlie  mouth  off  Aquia  Creek  and  are  beyond  doubt  making 
extensive  preparations  for  some  great  move.  Unless  the  landings  on 
the  Maryland  side  are  immediately  occupied  by  our  troops  and  made 
secure  by  extended  batteries  I  shall  be  placed  between  two  tires,  and  it 
will  be  hardly  possible  with  the  small  force  under  my  command  to  pro¬ 
tect  the  passages  across  the  river. 

As  I  informed  you  in  my  letter  of  yesterday,  the  rudder  of  the  Yankee 
is  badly  injured,  and  in  case  of  having  any  extroardinary  work  to  do  it 
will  be  very  difficult  to  maneuver  her.  I  hope,  sir,  in  view  of  the  pres¬ 
ent  aspect  of  affairs  the  Department  will  see  the  necessity  of  largely 
increasing  my  forces  immediately. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Thos.  T.  Craven, 

Commander ,  Commanding  Potomac  Flotilla. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy,  Washington ,  I).  C.

Petition  of  John  Lawrence,  esq.,  captain  of  sloop  Jane  Wright,  for  damages  in  the  case 
of  the  destruction  of  that  vessel  by  U.  S.  S.  Yankee. 

Washington,  D.  C.,  September  12,  1861. 

Sir:  Tour  petitioner,  Captain  Jolm  Lawrence,  of  St.  Mary’s  County, 
Md.,  captain  and  owner  of  the  sloop  Jane  Wright ,  on  the  15tli  day  of 
August,  A.  D.  1861,  obtained  from  the  Navy  Department,  a  written 
permission  to  go  with  his  said  sloop  from  the  city  of  Washington  to  his 
home  in  St.  Mary’s  County,  and  on  that  day,  accompanied  by  Mr.  John 
F.  Russell,  his  hand  on  said  sloop,  your  petitioner  left  Washington  at 
about  3  p.  m.  and  proceeded  on  his  way  down  the  river,  and  on  the 
morning  following  (to  wit,  the  16tli  of  August),  about  one  hour  after 
sunrise,  when  near  Smith’s  Point,  your  petitioner  was  hailed  by  the  Gov¬ 
ernment  war  vessels  and  ordered  to  come  to,  when  your  petitioner 
immediately  obeyed  and  ran  his  said  sloop,  as  ordered,  alongside  of 
the  war  steamer  Yankee,  and  the  papers  of  said  sloop  were  demanded 
and  delivered  over  to  one  of  the  officers  or  men,  and  your  petitioner 
was  informed  that  his  said  sloop  would  be  sunk  and  destroyed. 

Your  petitioner  immediately  protested  against  such  an  act,  and 
claimed  that  he  had  the  right  to  go  home,  and  that  the  permission  was 
endorsed  on  one  of  the  papers  delivered  up,  and  your  petitioner  requested 
the  commandant  of  the  Yankee  to  inform  him  the  reason  why  his  sloop  was 
thus  seized,  but  no  reason  was  given  for  the  act,  and  your  petitioner 
was  told  that  he  might  go  on  shore  in  his  small  boat,  but  that  his  sloop 
would  be  sunk  and  destroyed,  which  has  since  been  done. 

Your  petitioner  further  states  that  he  is  acquainted  with  Mr.  William 
H.  Bailey,  the  engineer  of  the  Yankee ,  to  whom  he  refers  the  Depart¬ 
ment  for  the  evidence  of  the  facts  herein  stated  in  reference  to  the 
seizure  of  his  said  sloop. 

Your  petitioner,  who  is  a  poor  man,  is,  in  consequence  of  the  loss  of 
his  said  sloop,  greatly  distressed,  having  been  heretofore  engaged  in 
carrying  oysters  and  fruit,  etc.,  to  the  Washington  market  for  a  support. 

Your  petitioner  further  says  that  he  should  not  have  started  down 
the  river  with  his  sloop  had  he  not  first  received  the  aforementioned 
written  permission,  which  he  was  advised  would  insure  him  protection 
and  a  safe  conduct  home;  and  inasmuch  as  your  petitioner  has  lost  his 
sloop  under  such  circumstances,  according  to  justice  and  equity,  your 
petitioner  should  be  paid  the  amount  of  damages  sustained  thereby; 
and  your  petitioner  prays  the  Government  to  pay  him  the  amount  of 
damages  he  has  sustained  in  consequence  of  the  loss  of  his  said  sloop, 
which  is  about  $450. 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

John  (his  x  mark)  Lawrence. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy.

Report  of  Captain  Craven,  IJ.  S.  Navy,  commanding  Potomac  Flotilla,  regarding  the  destruction 

of  sloops  Jane  Wright  and  T.  W.  Riley. 

U.  S.  S.  Yankee,  September  14,  1861. 

Sir  :  I  have  the  honor  to  acknowledge  the  receipt  of  your  letter  of 
the  13tli  instant  asking  for  information  relative  to  the  destruction  of  the 
sloop  Jane  Wright,  near  Smith’s  Island  [Point?],  on  the  morning  of  the 
16th  August. 

On  that  morning  I  received  a  special  dispatch  from  the  Department, 
with  an  enclosure  of  a  memorandum  from  the  Assistant  Secretary  of 
War,  relative  to  the  intended  invasion  of  Maryland  by  the  rebels. 

In  that  dispatch  I  was  authorized  under  certain  contingencies  to 
destroy  every  vessel  or  boat  within  my  reach.  Under  that  order  the 
sloops  T.  IV".  Riley  and  Jane  Wright  were  scuttled  and  sunk. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Thos.  T.  Craven, 
Commanding  Potomac  Flotilla. 

Hon.  G.  V.  Fox, 

Acting  Secretary  of  the  Navy,  Washington,  I).  C. 


Letter  from  the  governor  of  Maryland  to  the  Secretary  of  War,  relative  to 
increasing  the  force  on  the  Potomac  in  vieiv  of  a  descent  upon  Maryland 
by  the  Confederates. 

State  of  Maryland,  Executive  Chamber, 

Annapolis,  August  16,  1861. 

Dear  Sir:  I  am  advised  in  a  way,  and  it  comes  from  a  source  that 
leaves  no  ground  for  doubt,  that  the  Confederate  forces  south  of  the 
Potomac  and  the  disloyal  men  of  Maryland  are  acting  in  vigilant  con¬ 
cert,  with  a  design  to  make  a  descent  upon  Maryland  at  some  point, 
most  likely,  I  think,  to  be  from  St.  Mary’s  or  Charles  counties.  Will  it 
not  be  well,  I  respectfully  suggest,  to  increase  the  Government  forces 
with  efficient  vessels  to  ply  between  Washington  and  the  mouth  of  the 
Potomac  River  to  cut  off  their  forces  if  they  attempt  to  cross;  also 
allow  me  to  advise  an  increased  force  of  men  and  vessels  to  watch  the 
two  eastern  shore  counties  of  Virginia  in  General  Butler’s  division. 
The  20tli  instant  is  the  time  designated  by  them  for  assault.  Do  not 
think  me  scared;  I  only  wish  to  head  off'  the  rebels. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Thomas  H.  Hicks. 

Hon.  S.  Cameron, 

Secretary  War.

Report  of  Lieutenant  Parker,  U.  S.  Wavy,  commanding  U.  8.  8.  -Release 
{Ice  Boat),  relative  to  the  condition  of  that  vessel. 

CL  S.  S.  Release  [Ice  Boat], 

Off  Aquia  Creek ,  August  17,  1861. 

Sir  :  It  becomes  my  duty  for  the  good  of  the  service  to  make  known 
to  you  that  on  the  loth  instant  when  I  took  charge  of  this  vessel  she 
was  in  a  disorganized  and  almost  defenseless  condition. 

The  crew  were  not  properly  stationed  at  quarters  or  armed.  There 
were  no  boarding  nettings  or  defenses  against  boarders  rendered  imper¬ 
atively  necessary  in  a  vessel  without  bulwarks  whose  guards  are  not 
above  3  feet  from  the  water. 

The  shot  and  ammunition  for  the  bow  guns  were  aft  and  the  shot  for 
the  after  guns  forward,  while  the  long  engine  room  would  have  pre¬ 
vented  these  articles  being  moved  rapidly  in  time  of  action. 

In  the  after  magazine,  with  open  barrels  of  powder,  were  stowed  iron 
shovels  and  other  articles  belonging  to  the  engineer’s  department  and 
a  number  of  percussion  shells  for  the  rifled  gun  (whether  idled  or  not 
I  have  been  unable  to  ascertain)  were  exposed  in  the  engine  room. 

The  crew  are  now  stationed  and  armed,  the  arms  and  ammunition 
properly  distributed  and  stowed,  and  boarding  nettings  are  being  made. 
To  man  all  the  guns,  however,  twenty  more  men  are  requisite. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  your  obedient  servant, 

Foxhall  A.  Parker, 

Lieutenant,  Commanding. 

Captain  Thomas  Craven, 

Commanding  Potomac  Flotilla.

Report  of  Commander  Craven ,  U.  8.  Navy,  commanding  Potomac  Flo¬ 
tilla,  transmitting  report  of  Acting  Master’s  Mate  Fly ,  II.  8.  Navy , 
commanding  U.  8.  schooner  Dana,  of  reconnoissance  on  8t.  George’s 
Island,  Md. 

TJ.  S.  S.  Yankee, 

Off  Aquia,  August  19,  1861. 

Sir:  The  accompanying  report  and  letters  were  received  by  me  last 
night,  and  I  take  the  earliest  opportunity,  by  the  Robert  Leslie ,  to  for¬ 
ward  them. 

Mr.  Ely’s  opinion  of  the  organization  of  military  bodies  of  men,  is 
without  the  slightest  doubt  correct,  and  I  am  more  than  ever  convinced 
that  the  people  on  the  Maryland  shore  are  secretly  lying  [in]  wait  for  a 
move  on  the  part  of  the  rebels  to  uncover  and  fly  to  their  assistance. 

As  yet,  sir,  I  see  no  signs  of  a  reenforcement  of  this  flotilla.  I  hope 
you  [will]  pardon  me  for  the  solicitude  I  feel  for  seeing  not  only  a  large 
increase  of  the  forces  afloat,  but  an  immediate  occupation  of  some  of 
the  prominent  landings  hereabouts  by  our  military  forces. 

Yery  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Thos.  T.  Craven, 

Commander,  TJ.  8.  Navy ,  Commanding  Potomac  Flotilla. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy,  Washington,  D.  C. 


[Enclosure.] 

II.  S.  Schooner  Dana,  August  18,  1861. 

Sir  :  I  have  the  honor  to  report  to  you  the  proceedings  of  Mr.  Gray 
and  myself  as  follows,  viz: 

On  the  night  of  the  14th  instant,  a  Mr.  Smith,  who  keeps  a  store  on 
St.  George’s  Island,  came  alongside  of  my  vessel  and  made  complaint  to 
me  that  he  had  been  threatened  with  personal  injury  by  several  parties 
residing  on  the  Maryland  shore,  in  particular  by  Captain  Code  [Coad'f], 
on  account  of  his  Union  sentiments,  and  requested  of  me  that  I  would 
solicit  protection  for  himself  and  the  other  inhabitants  of  the  island, 
who  are  all  Union  men,  from  the  commander  of  the  flotilla.  At  the 
suggestion  of  myself  and  Mr.  Gray  they  drew  up  a  memorial,  which  I 
enclose  to  you,  signed  by  the  two  most  prominent  men  on  the  island. 
After  some  further  conversation  with  Smith  I  found  that  the  aforesaid 
Code  [Goad?]  and  his  father  (Colonel  Code  [Coad?]),  who  resides  in  the 
neighborhood,  have  been  in  the  habit  of  sending  provisions  to  Virginia, 
and  that  Captain  Samuel  Trader,  of  St.  George’s  Island,  was  the  man 
whom  they  had  endeavored  to  persuade  to  engage  in  this  contraband 
trade,  and  that  he  had  at  present  in  his  possession  certain  goods  bound 
to  the  sacred  soil. 

Acting  upon  this  information,  Mr.  Gray  and  myself  got  our  vessels 
underway  and  went  to  St.  George’s  Island,  where  we  landed  in  two 


OPERATIONS  ON  THE  POTOMAC  AND  RAPPAHANNOCK.  62 1 

boats  and  called  on  Captain  Trader.  Having  called  him  aside  I  told 
him  that  I  had  sufficient  evidence  of  his  contraband  predilections  to 
warrant  me  in  searching  his  premises.  He  immediately  delivered  to 
me  one- half  barrel  of  coffee,  one-half  barrel  of  sugar,  and  some  salt, 
which  lie  said  had  been  given  to  him  by  Colonel  Dix  to  take  to  Virginia 
on  the  4th  of  July  last;  that  he  had  had  them  ever  since,  and  had  been 
using  them  in  his  family  and  never  intended  to  take  them  to  their  places 
of  destination.  I,  however,  took  them  and  have  them  now  on  board 
awaiting  your  orders  as  to  what  disposition  I  shall  make  of  them.  I 
would  respectfully  suggest  that  they  may  be  useful  as  a  bribe  to  him 
for  further  information.  The  idea  struck  me  that  he  might  have  some 
letters,  and  I  asked  him  for  any  letters  he  might  have  in  his  possession; 
he  at  once  gave  me  the  enclosed  letters,  which  implicate  several  other 
parties;  one  of  them,  Mr.  Dix,  who  sent  the  captured  articles  and  the 
letters,  I  found  upon  enquiry  had  a  large  six-oared  boat  which  had 
taken  several  loads  of  men  to  Virginia.  I,  therefore,  went  that  night 
and  took  her,  and  being  without  a  boat,  I  have  appropriated  her  to  the 
use  of  my  vessel.  On  returning  to  our  vessels  we  met  a  Mr.  Boswell, 
whose  father  is  the  principal  owner  of  St.  George’s  Island.  He  thought 
it  more  than  probable  that  we  might  find  a  quantity  of  contraband 
goods  in  possession  of  Captain  Code  ICoad1?].  A  difficulty  now  arose 
in  my  mind  as  to  what  might  be  the  best  mode  of  procedure.  Mr.  Gray 
thought  we  were  not  allowed  to  search  private  property  in  Maryland 
without  an  order  from  yourself  or  the  Secretary  of  the  Navy.  Force, 
therefore,  being  out  of  the  question,  we  determined  to  try  a  stratagem. 
After  some  deliberation  we  decided  on  the  following  plan,  in  the  execu¬ 
tion  of  which  Mr.  Roswell  kindly  offered  his  assistance,  as  he  was  well 
acquainted  with  Captain  Code  [Coad?].  It  made  the  execution  of  the 
following  plan  comparatively  easy: 

The  night  being  very  dark,  1  got  the  Dana  underway,  and  with  Mr. 
Gray  and  six  of  his  men  on  board,  and  Mr.  Roswell  and  Captain  Trader 
as  pilots,  we  steered  our  course  up  St.  George’s  Creek  and  anchored 
within  musket  shot  of  Code’s  [Coad?]  house.  I  then  disguised  myself 
and  two  of  my  men  and  in  company  with  Mr.  Roswell  went  on  shore  to 
pay  our  compliments  to  the  captain.  Mr.  Gray  had  his  boat  filled  with 
armed  men  and  ready  to  give  any  necessary  assistance  should  our  dis¬ 
guise  be  discovered. 

The  darkness  and  rain,  together  with  the  dilapidated  condition  of  the 
boat  in  which  I  landed,  made  recognition  next  to  impossible. 

Mr.  Roswell  introduced  me  as  Captain  Williams,  of  the  schooner 
John  Grant,  a  good  secessionist,  and  bound  to  Coan  River  with  bacon 
and  salt  from  Port  Tobacco.  Captain  Code  [Coad?]  asked  me  howl 
had  escaped  the  steamers.  I  told  him  that  was  easily  done;  that  I  had 
been  carrying  coal  for  the  Government;  that  almost  all  the  steamers 
had  taken  coal  out  of  my  vesselj  consequently,  being  well  acquainted 
with  me  and  believing  me  to  be  a  good  Union  man,  they  never  took  the 
trouble  to  search  me.  He  then  asked  me  if  I  was  not  afraid  of  being 
seen  by  the  cutters.  I  said  no;  that  the  night  was  very  dark  and  that 
one  of  the  cutters  was  up  the  river  and  the  other  two  had  gone  out  into 
the  bay.  He  complimented  me  on  my  sagacity  and  said  it  rejoiced  him 
to  meet  a  man  of  my  stamp  and  wished  me  all  possible  success.  The 
conversation  then  became  general.  He  freely  expressed  his  sentiments 
to  me,  offered  us  wine  and  cigars,  and  gave  me  much  valuable  informa¬ 
tion  as  to  the  state  of  feeling  in  his  neighborhood;  told  me  that  several 


622  OPERATIONS  ON  THE  POTOMAC  AND  RAPPAHANNOCK. 

parties  liad  crossed  from  his  immediate  vicinity  and  expressed  his  sym¬ 
pathy  for  them,  and  from  the  tenor  of  his  conversation  I  was  led  to 
believe  that  there  were  organized  companies  of  armed  men  ready  to 
cooperate  with  any  forces  which  might  laud  from  Virginia  in  an  attack 
upon  the  Government,  which  event,  he  said,  the  Unionists  had  more 
cause  to  fear  than  armed  men  going  from  Maryland  to  Virginia.  As 
Colonel  Code  [Coad?]  is  an  influential  man  and  a  politician,  I  report  his 
conversation  thus  minutely. 

It  now  showed  signs  of  clearing  away,  and  daylight  coming  on  I  sig¬ 
nified  my  intention  of  leaving  while  the  darkness  favored  me.  I  called 
him  to  one  side  and  offered  to  carry  any  goods  or  letters  he  might  wish 
to  send  over  to  Virginia. 

He  said  he  was  sorry  he  had  nothing  at  present,  but  that  he  thought 
if  I  had  the  time  I  might  get  quite  a  quantity  up  the  St.  Mary’s  River, 
near  the  factories;  but,  said  I,  “I  may  speak  to  a  Union  man  and  get 
myself  into  trouble.”  Said  he:  “You  can  not  find  a  Union  man  from 
Breton’s  Bay  to  Point  Lookout,  except  Dr.  Jones  and  the  inhabitants  of 
St.  George’s  Island.”  I  then  left  him,  having  promised  to  call  and  see 
him  again  and  let  him  know  how  I  succeeded  in  my  enterprise. 

We  had  intended  to  go  up  to  the  factories,  but  when  we  got  into  the 
St.  Mary’s  River  it  was  broad  daylight.  We  therefore  gave  it  up  and 
returned  to  our  anchorage  with  my  prize  and  information. 

I  have  since  thought  it  was  better  to  keep  things  dark  and  content 
ourselves  with  keeping  a  strict  watch  until  we  got  advice  and  further 
orders  from  yourself  as  to  our  future  movements. 

I  forgot  to  mention  that  Mr.  Gray  took  a  runaway  negro,  claimed  by 
Colonel  Code  [Coad?]  and  also  by  his  son-in  law,  Dr.  Coombs.  The 
negro  says  that  his  master  threatened  to  shoot  him  for  reporting  cer¬ 
tain  boats  to  you  as  having  been  engaged  in  contraband  trade  and  that 
he  ran  for  his  life. 

He  says  he  is  the  person  who  was  on  board  your  vessel  last  Sunday 
night  and  gave  you  the  information  for  which  he  is  now  a  fugitive. 
Colonel  Code  [Coad?]  and  Dr.  Coombs  both  came  to  Piney  Point  yes¬ 
terday  and  demanded  him  from  Mr.  Gray,  but  he  refused  to  give  him 
up  without  orders  from  you. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Robert  B.  Ely, 

Acting  Master’s  Mate ,  Commanding  U.  S.  Schooner  Dana. 

Commander  Craven, 

Commanding  Chesapeake  Flotilla.

St.  George’s  Island,  August  15, 1861. 

Sir:  We,  the  undersigned,  do  hereby  certify  and  are  willing  to  take 
oath  to  the  same,  that  we,  the  inhabitants  of  this  island  (St.  George’s), 
have  been  threatened  by  Captain  Edward  Code  [Coad?J,  captain  of  a 
cavalry  company  in  Maryland,  and  residing  on  St.  George’s  Creek,  and 
having  in  his  possession  the  arms  for  a  cavalry  company,  and  never 
having  taken  the  oath  of  allegiance  to  the  United  States,  as  follows, 
viz: 

First.  On  August  6  at  9  o’clock  a.  m.  Captain  Code  [Coad?]  said  in 
conversation  that  should  the  Southern  Confederacy  by  any  means  gain 
so  much  the  advantage  of  the  North  as  to  enable  Maryland  to  secede 
or  to  be  able  to  declare  her  sentiments,  that  we,  the  inhabitants  of  this

island  (St.  George’s)  will  be  compelled  to  leave  oor  homes  at  the

to  expel  us  if  necessary. 

Richard  J.  Benedick. 

Z.  R.  Smith.

[Enclosure.] 

New  York,  August  12, 1861. 

Sir  :  The  rebels  are  at  work  now  planting  two  8-inch  Columbiads  on 
Mathias  Point.  At  present  only  the  two  guns  and  the  round  shot  are 
there.  The  carriages  are  now  about  ready  to  be  conveyed.  They  are 
being  constructed  a  few  miles  back.  Sappers  and  miners  are  throwing 
up  earthworks  to  enclose  about  100  by  100  feet  round  the  guns  and  an 
outer  work  20  or  30  yards  distant.  No  soldiers  are  there  now,  but 
there  are  plenty  near  by.  Do  not  move  to  suppress  it  with  less  than 
5,000  men  that  can  be  depended  on.  No  water  attack  with  guns  would 
avail  after  it  is  planted,  but  it  could  now  be  taken  from  the  water  side. 
A  secret  night  expedition  might  easily  bring  away  the  two  guns  with 
a  small  force,  but  that  would  be  of  no  use,  as  they  have  plenty  more 
guns.  If  attacked  it  should  be  held,  and  it  is  a  good  spot  for  us  to 
have.  And  a  dock  should  be  built  there  for  open  communication. 

Respectfully,  yours, 


The  President. 


J.  B.  Benson.

[Enclosure.] 

Washing-ton,  August  14,  1861. 

Sir:  I  thought  that  I  would  just  drop  you  a  few  lines  to  give  you 
some  sort  of  a  notion  about  the  laud  side  of  the  Potomac  from  Aquia 
Creek  up  as  far  as  Mrs.  Nelly  Moncure’s  farm — about  8  miles.  Aquia 
Creek  or  Bay  is  about  2  miles  long  and  one-fourth  to  one-half  mile  wide. 
Our  boats  could  not  get  up  there  unless  the  rebels  would  let  them  go, 
and  they  would  not  tire  a  gun  until  you  got  in  there,  and  then  you 
would  never  get  out  again.  Just  across  from  the  creek  landing  on  that 
point  it  is  called  Smith’s  Point.  It  is  a  level  country  all  around  there 
for  about  2  miles,  and  I  have  no  doubt  but  they  have  a  heavy  battery 
on  that  point,  and  7  miles  up  this  way  also,  to  prevent  us  from  going 
up  and  down  the  river.  The  river  is  only  miles  wide  all  along  there, 
and  at  low  tide  a  man  can  wade  out  about  one-half  a  mile  all  along  that 
shore.  In  that  case  they  could  land  10,000  men  over  on  the  Maryland 
side  in  twenty- four  hours.  Look  out  for  Smith’s  Point.  And  8  miles 
this  side  of  the  creek,  there  is  a  creek — I  think  it  is  called  Quantico — 
where  there  is  a  small  bay  that  would  hold  100  fishing  boats,  and  you 
could  not  see  them  going  up  and  down  the  river.  There  is  a  small 
ivsland  called  Fox  Island  that  hides  that  little  ducking  river.  We 
might  make  a  halt  there  about  daybreak  some  morning ;  but  look  out  for 
masked  batteries.  There  is  a  large  brick  house  a  little  below  it  as  you 
go  down  the  river.  It  is  between  two  high  hills.  But  the  mischief  is 
how  to  get  ashore  unless  you  have  small  boats.  The  channel  is  on  the 
Maryland  side  of  the  river. 

Up  the  Aquia  Creek,  I  have  no  doubt,  at  the  place  called  the  Land¬ 
ing,  there  are  several  schooners  in  the  wood  and  rock  business.  With 
a  fair  wind  they  could  soon  run  out  of  that  place. 

I.  C.  C.

[Enclosure _ Telegram.  ] 

New  York,  August  19,  1S61. 

The  following  reports  come  to  us: 

The  rebels  are  preparing  to  attack  General  Banks  with  50,000 men;  part  are  now 
at  Leesburg;  threatened  attack  on  Washington  only  a  blind.  At  Mathias  Point 
two  Columbiads,  8-inch;  two  32-pounders,  rifled;  garrison,  700  riflemen  and  two 
12-pounders:  5,000  men  encamped  5  miles;  5,000,  10  miles  distant,  with  telegraph 
lines  between.  Below  the  point,  7  miles,  on  Maryland  side,  extensive  preparations 
for  formidable  battery ;  1,000  men  at  work  to  plant  twenty  10-inch  Columbiads  to 
come  at  night  from  Norfolk;  each  gun  on  flotilla  covered  with  railroad  iron.  A 
force  will  move  from  Leesburg  Tuesday  night,  though  not  entirely  certain,  I  hope 
the  information  will  do  no  harm. 

Lieutenant-General  Scott.

Letter  from  the  Secretary  of  the  Wavy  to  the  Secretary  of  War,  urging 
the  necessity  of  fortifying  Mathias  Point. 

Navy  Department,  August  20, 1861. 

Sir:  The  importance  of  keeping  open  the  navigation  of  the  Potomac 
is  so  obvious  that  no  argument  is  necessary  on  the  subject. 

So  far  as  is  possible  this  Department  has  and  will  continue  to  discharge 
its  duty  in  this  matter  by  an  armed  flotilla;  but  there  are  one  or  two 
points  where  shore  batteries  can  bemade  tointerceptcommunication,  and 
in  view  of  that  danger  and  recent  investigations  I  would  most  urgently 
request  that  immediate  measures  be  taken  by  the  War  Department  to 
fortify  and  intrench  Mathias  Point.  A  single  regiment  aided  by  two  of 
our  steamers  could  heretofore,  and  perhaps  may  still,  take  possession 
and  secure  it;  but  if  more  than  a  regiment  is  required  it  appears  to  me 
indispensable  that  the  requisite  number  should  be  furnished. 

Attention,  on  separate  occasions,  has  been  called  to  the  particular 
necessity  of  holding  that  place  as  absolutely  essential  to  the  unob¬ 
structed  navigation  of  the  Potomac.  The  Navy  will  at  any  moment 
contribute  its  efforts  toward  seizing  and  holding  that  place,  and  I 
apprehend  there  should  not  be  any  delay.  Can  not  a  sufficient  force  be 
sent  down  forthwith  to  seize  and,  in  connection  with  such  armed  ves¬ 
sels  as  we  can  order  for  that  purpose,  hold  Mathias  Point  and  thus  keep 
open  tlie  navigation  of  the  Potomac? 

I  understand  that  troops  will  be  sent  to  the  lower  Maryland  counties 
to  keep  the  peace  and  prevent  batteries  from  being  erected  on  the  left 
bank.  This  is  a  timely  and  wise  precaution,  but  it  is  equally  neces¬ 
sary  that  we  should  take  possession  of  Mathias  Point.  Should  the 
insurgents  get  possession  of  that  point  it  will  require  a  very  large 
force  to  dispossess  them. 

•  I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully, 

Gideon  Welles 

Hon.  Simon  Cameron, 

Secretary  of  War.  •

Engagement  of  TJ.  S.  steamers  Jacob  Bell  and  Ice  Boat  (Release)  with 

Confederate  batteries  at  mouth  of  Potomac  Creek ,  August  23,  1861. 

Report  of  Lieutenant  McCrea,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  IJ.  S.  S.  Jacob  Bell. 

U.  S.  S.  Jacob  Bell, 

Off  Aquia  Creek,  August  24,  1861. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  make  the  following  report: 

Having  heard  that  there  was  an  encampment  of  the  enemy  conspicu¬ 
ous  on  Potomac  Creek,  I  ottered  to  go  in  and  examine  closely  the  possible 
strength,  by  permission  of  Commander  Dove,  to  report  to  Commander 
Goldsborough,  of  the  Union.  I  got  underway  with  the  Resolute  and 
Reliance  and  proceeded  off  the  creek.  After  communicating  with  Com¬ 
mander  Goldsborough  I  stood  in  with  the  Resolute ,  but  she  drawing  too 
much  water  I  stood  in  alone.  Getting  close  to  the  encampment,  in  9 
feet  water,  I  threw  two  shells  over  their  tents,  which  caused  them  to 
rally  around  the  colors.  At  that  moment  a  battery  on  their  left  and  on 
the  beach  opened  upon  me.  I  threw  several  shells  at  it,  when  it  ceased 
firing  and  two  batteries  of  rifled  guns  opened  from  the  point  of  the 
creek.  They  tired  rapidly  and  all  the  shots  and  shells  came  close,  and 
several  passed  over,  but  none  struck  the  vessel.  Fiuding  my  guns 
would  not  reach,  I  came  out  of  range  of  the  enemy’s  batteries,  when 
they  then  engaged  the  Ice  Boat,  which  had  just  arrived  in  position  for 
her  rifled  gun.  No  damage  sustained  by  her.  At  6:30  I  returned  to 
my  anchorage  here. 

Yery  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Edward  P.  McCrea, 

Lieutenant ,  Commanding. 

Captain  T.  T.  Craven, 

Commanding  Potomac  Flotilla. 


Report  of  Lieutenant  Pattison,  IJ.  S.  Navy,  commanding  steamer  Ice  Boat. 

U.  S.  S.  Ice  Boat, 

Off  Potomac  Creek,  August  23,  1861. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that  in  obedience  to  orders  I  got 
underway  at  half  past!  p.  m.  and  stood  over  to  the  Virginia  shore  and 
engaged  two  of  the  enemy’s  batteries  of  rifled  guns,  placed  on  opposite 
sides  of  the  Potomac  Creek.  One  battery  consisted  of  four  heavy 
guns,  the  other  of  two  long-ranged  rifled  guns.  At  4:45  I  opened 
upon  the  enemy  with  my  heavy  rifled  gun,  and  soon  after  brought 
my  9-inch  Dahlgren  gun  to  bear  upon  the  batteries.  At  half  past 


OPERATIONS  ON  THE  POTOMAC  AND  RAPPAHANNOCK.  633 


5  the  battery  on  the  south  side  of  the  creek  ceased  firing-,  conse¬ 
quently  I  devoted  my  attention  to  the  rifled-gun  battery  on  the  north 
side  of  the  creek,  which  was  playing  upon  me  with  vigor.  Two  shells 
passed  over  my  hurricane  deck  and  six  or  eight  burst  under  the  bows, 
doing-  no  injury  to  the  vessel  or  crew.  At  0  p.  in.  I  withdrew  from  the 
batteries,  in  obedience  to  a  signal  from  my  commanding  officer. 

Captain  Mygatt,  of  the  Reliance ,  came  on  board  just  as  I  was  getting 
underway,  and  was  of  the  greatest  service  to  me.  Being  thoroughly 
acquainted  with  the  river,  he  piloted  me  into  safe  water,  and  then  at  my 
request  took  command  of  our  enormous  rifled  gun  and  fought  it  during 
the  action  with  skill  and  judgment  that  entitles  him  to  all  praise. 

The  conduct  of  the  officers  and  men  meet  my  warmest  approbation. 

Respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

T.  Pattison, 

Lieutenant ,  Commanding  Ice  Boat. 

Captain  T.  T.  Craven, 

Commanding  Potomac  Flotilla ,  off  Aquia  Creek. 


Report  of  Acting  Lieutenant  Mygatt,  TT.  S.  Navy. 

U.  S.  S.  Penguin,  August  24,  1861. 

Sir:  In  obedience  to  your  order  I  submit  the  following  statement: 

When  down  the  river  yesterday  an  encampment  was  seen  on  the 
bluff  to  the  southward  of  Potomac  Creek.  Commander  Dove  was 
informed  of  the  matter  and  he  gave  the  commanding  officers  of  the 
Jacob  Bell  and  Resolute  and  myself  permission  to  go  in  and  see  what 
they  were  doing.  The  Jacob  Bell  and  Resolute  went  close  in  and  tired 
a  shot,  wffien  they  immediately  tired  from  three  different  points.  I 
went  in  on  the  lee  Boat ,  Lieutenant  Commanding  Pattison.  Several 
shots  were  fired  from  her  rifled  gun,  but  the  effect  could  not  be  seen. 
The  encampment  is  a  very  large  one. 

I  think  that  I  discovered  another  large  encampment  on  the  hills 
nearly  opposite  Sandy  Point,  but  could  not  see  distinctly  as  the  light 
was  too  glaring. 

Very  respectfully,  etc., 

J.  P.  K.  Mygatt, 

Acting  Lieritenant. 

Commander  J.  W.  Livingston, 

Commanding  TJ.  S.  8.  Penguin,  Potomac  River. 


Report  of  Colonel  Cary,  C.  S.  Army,  commanding  Thirtieth  Virginia  Infantry. 

Headquarters  Marlborough  Point,  August  23,  1861. 

Colonel:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that  this  afternoon  at  about 
4:30  o’clock  the  enemy’s  steamer  Yankee  [Jacob  Bell]  and  a  tug  were 
seen  standing  in  the  mouth  of  Potomac  Creek.  I  ordered  down  on  to 
the  point  the  siege  rifled  gun  (Betty  Holmes)  and  a  section  (rifle)  of 
Walker’s  battery. 

The  enemy  fired  the  first  shot,  not  aimed  at  this  point,  however. 
Smith’s  battery  replied.  As  soon  as  our  fieldpieces  opened,  the  II.  S.  S. 
Release  [Ice  Boat ]  stood  in  and  engaged  us. 

The  officers  in  charge  of  the  pieces  and  the  men  behaved  with  proper 
coolness  and  deliberation.  They  were  Lieutenants  Hagerty,  Pegram, 
and  Dabney. 


634  OPERATIONS  ON  THE  POTOMAC  AND  RAPPAHANNOCK. 


The  enemy’s  fire  was  very  accurate,  frequently  bursting  his  shell  in 
close  proximity  to  our  pieces.  It  is  believed  that  both  the  Yankee  and 
the  Release  were  hit,  the  former  more  than  once.  No  one  was  hurt  on 
our  side. 

The  action  lasted  about  forty  minutes,  during  which  we  fired  some 
twenty-five  shot  and  shell,  the  enemy  as  many  more.  Captain  E.  L. 
Walker  was  present,  in  immediate  command  of  all  the  pieces. 

I  am,  colonel,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

E.  M.  Cary, 

Thirtieth  Virginia  Infantry ,  Commanding. 

D.  H.  Maury, 

Asst.  Adjt.  Gen.,  Department  of  Fredericksburg ,  Brooke's. 


Report  of  Lieutenant- Colonel  Moses ,  commanding  Third  Regiment,  Excel¬ 
sior  Brigade,  of  active  aid  furnished  to  the  Confederates. 

Camp  Caldwell, 
Washington ,  D.  C.,  August  19,  1861. 

Major  :  I  have  to  report  on  the  authority  of  two  negroes  who  pre¬ 
sented  themselves  in  camp  last  night,  that  about  20  or  25  miles  below 
camp,  at  the  crossing  of  the  Potomac  where  there  is  a  schoolhouse, 
armed  men  are  said  to  have  taken  possession  and  parties  are  crossing 
the  river  from  the  Virginia  side.  Also  that  there  are  a  number  of  arms 
in  the  vicinity  and  a  general  appearance  of  complicity  and  active  aid 
being  afforded  to  the  rebels. 

Very  respectfully, 

I.  Moses, 

Lieutenant- Colonel,  Third  Regiment ,  Excelsior  Brigade.

Report  of  commandant  navy  yard ,  Washington ,  of  the  seizure  of  twenty- 

eight  boats. 

Commandant’s  Office,  Navy  Yard, 

Washington,  August  25,  1861. 

Sir:  The  four  steamers  sent  last  evening  in  command  of  Captain 
Wainwright  to  secure  all  boats  along  the  shore  by  verbal  direction  of 
the  Assistant  Secretary  of  the  Navy  returned  last  night  at  3  o’clock, 
having  taken  twenty-eight  boats,  most  of  them  small.  They  are  now 
in  the  yard  awaiting  the  disposition  of  the  Department. 

Learning  this  morning  that  there  might  be  a  number  remaining  in 
the  Tiber,  which  were  not  visible  in  the  night,  1  dispatched  an  officer 
with  a  small  steamer  to  complete  the  order. 

I  telegraphed  this  morning  to  ask  the  pleasure  of  the  Department  in 
case  a  request  was  made  by  Mr.  Bussell,  of  the  London  Times,  to  pass 
down  the  river  in  one  of  our  boats,  which  he  has  in  view,  I  believe. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Jno.  A.  Dahlgren, 

Commandant. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy.

Report  of  Commander  Rove,  U.  8.  Navy,  commanding  U.  8.  8.  Pocahon¬ 
tas,  of  occurrences  during  absence  of  Commander  Craven,  XJ.  8.  Navy, 
commanding  Potomac  Flotilla. 

U.  S.  S.  Pocahontas,  August  27, 1861. 
Sir:  Nothing  very  particular  has  occurred  during  your  absence. 

The  Jacob  Bell  and  Release  [Ice  Boat ]  made  a  reconnoissance  of  Poto¬ 
mac  Creek  and  its  vicinity  last  Friday  [Thursday].  A  few  shots  were 
exchanged  without  damage  to  either  side.  The  encampment  near  was 
found  much  increased,  indicating  large  reenforcements. 

The  wreck  of  the  sloop  which  you  sunk  has  been  drifting  about  the 
river  and  I  have  made  several  attempts  to  get  her  on  shore  without 
success. 

While  two  of  the  launches  were  employed  about  here  yesterday 
afternoon  they  drifted  toward  Aquia  Creek  and  the  upper  battery  fired 
a  blank  charge,  I  suppose  by  way  of  warning,  and  I  made  the  signal  of 
recall. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Benj.  M.  Dove, 

Commander. 

[Captain  T.  T.  Craven, 

Commanding  Potomac  Flotilla .]

transmitting  report  of  Lieutenant  Prichett ,  U.  S.  Wavy ,  commanding 

U.  8.  S.  Underwriter,  regarding  the  condition  of  that  vessel. 

U.  S.  S.  Yankee,  August  28,  1861. 

Sir:  Herewith  I  have  the  honor  to  enclose  a  report  from  Lieutenant 
Prichett,  relative  to  the  condition  of  the  steamer  Underwriter.  I  have 
ordered  Lieutenant  Prichett  to  proceed  immediately  to  the  navy  yard 
for  the  purpose  of  having'  the  Underwriter  put  in  proper  serviceable 
order.  Her  decks  particularly  require  strengthening. 

There  is  great  want  of  efficient  officers  in  all  of  the  vessels  recently 
sent  to  join  the  flotilla,  and  for  the  proper  discipline  of  their  crews  I 
most  earnestly  request  that  at  least  six  or  eight  competent  drill  officers 
may  be  ordered  to  report  to  me  immediately. 

Y ery  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Thos.  T.  Craven,

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Wavy,  Washington: 

[Enclosure.] 

TJ.  S.  S.  Underwriter,  August  27,  1861. 

Sir  :  I  am  compelled  to  report  to  you  the  condition  of  this  vessel,  as 
I  consider  her  unfit  for  service. 

The  armament  of  the  vessel  consists  of  one  8-inch  shell  gun,  of  63 
hundredweight,  and  one  6-inch  rifled  gun,  of  about  the  same  weight, 
and  there  are  only  twenty-one  men  to  work  these  guns  and  pass  powder 
and  shells. 

The  cooking  arrangements  are  very  incomplete,  there  being  but  a 
small  stove  for  this  purpose,  thus  making  it  necessary  to  cook  the 
rations  in  small  portions. 

Neither  officers  nor  men  have  sufficient  quarters;  the  latter  are  com¬ 
pelled  to  sleep  about  the  deck,  and  even  then  it  is  difficult  to  find  suffi¬ 
cient  room  to  protect  them  from  the  weather. 

The  apartment  in  which  the  ammunition  is  stowed  is  very  incomplete, 
as  the  projectiles  and  powder  are  stowed  together. 

There  are  neither  day  nor  night  signals  on  board.  But  one  small  boat 
belongs  to  the  vessel,  and  there  are  n©  boat  davits. 

No  small  arms  of  any  description  whatever  or  spyglass  have  been 
allotted  to  the  vessel. 

The  bdiler  is  leaking  so  much  that  it  is  necessary  to  get  underway 
every  eight  or  ten  hours  to  pump  it  up.  The  vessel  itself  is  leaking  so 
much  that  it  requires  from  three  to  four  hours  pumping  to  keep  her  clear. 
Yery  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant,  . 

Jas.  M.  Prichett, 

JAeutenant,  Commanding. 

J.  W.  Livingston, 

Commanding  U.  8.  8.  Penguin,  and  Senior  Officer,  Potomac  Flotilla. 


Report  of  Commander  Craven,  U.  S.  Wavy,  commanding  Potomac  Flotilla, 
of  the  overhauling,  by  U.  8.  8.  Yankee ,  of  schooner  Remittance,  of 
Baltimore. 


U.  S.  S.  Yankee, 

Off  A  quia,  August  30,  1861. 

Sir:  On  the  28th  instant,  off  Lower  Cedar  Point,  we  overhauled  the 
schooner  Remittance,  of  Baltimore,  from  Port  Tobacco,  bound  to  Balti- 


640  OPERATIONS  ON  THE  POTOMAC  AND  RAPPAHANNOCK. 


* 


more,  commanded  and  owned  by  one  James  H.  M.  Burroughs.  Upon 
examining  this  vessel,  which  is  laden  with  tobacco  and  grain,  we  found 
five  passengers,  three  of  whom,  viz,  Alexander  Johnson,  Edward  San¬ 
ders,  and  Charles  A.  Yates,  say  they  are  farmers,  living  in  the  neigh¬ 
borhood  of  Port  Tobacco,  are  owners  of  part  of  the  cargo  of  tobacco, 
and  are  going  to  Baltimore  for  the  purpose  of  selling  it.  One,  a  Mr. 
Lancaster,  is  going  to  St.  Mary’s  for  the  purpose  of  collecting  debts. 
The  fifth,  calling  himself  John  P.  Richards,  is  a  person  who  came  down 
in  the  schooner  on  her  last  trip  from  Baltimore.  He  asserts  that  his 
trunk,  which  is  a  large  one,  was  thoroughly  searched  by  the  boarding 
officers  at  Baltimore  and  “ passed”  by  them;  that  it  contained  nothing 
more  than  it  has  in  it  at  the  present  moment,  which  consists  of  very 
few  articles  of  old  and  dirty  clothing  and  could  readily  be  made  up  into 
a  very  small  bundle.  One  of  the  crew  of  this  schooner,  William  Posey 
(colored),  who  has  sailed  in  her  for  several  years,  states  most  positively 
that  the  trunk  was  not  examined  at  Baltimore,  and  moreover  that  it 
was  tightly  packed  with  some  heavy  articles  which  he  believes  to  have 
been  contraband  and  that  they  have  been  conveyed  over  into  Virginia. 

In  the  left-hand  end  of  the  trunk  are  evidences  of  there  having  been 
false  lining,  which  was  stuck  to  the  true  lining  by  wafers,  affording  a 
space  between  the  two  where  letters,  etc.,  could  have  been  concealed. 
As  this  person,  John  P.  Richards,  could  not  give  a  satisfactory  account 
of  himself,  and  his  whole  manner  and  appearance  are  suspicious,  I  have 
thought  proper  to  send  him  to  Washington  for  further  examination. 

The  man,  William  Posey,  states  that  the  master,  James  H.  M.  Bur¬ 
roughs,  is  a  rank  secessionist;  that  his  vessel  has  been  used  for  carry¬ 
ing  contraband  goods  from  Baltimore,  and  that  his  boats  have  been 
frequently  used  for  conveying  goods,  men,  horses,  and  other  contraband 
articles  across  the  river  to  Virginia,  and  that  Thomas  F.  Burroughs, 
brother  of  the  master  and  mate  of  the  vessel,  has  been  in  the  habit  of 
going  over,  and  that  lie,  William  Posey,  has  been  made  to  help  pull  the 
boat  on  these  “excursions,”  and  he  states  further  that  the  Remittance., 
with  the  same  master,  mate,  and  crew  who  are  now  on  board  of  her, 
was  one  of  the  vessels  which  went  alongside  the  light-boat  off  Cedar 
Point  and  set  fire  to  her  in  March  or  April  last.  Edward  Ellis,  who 
was  one  of  the  light-boat  keepers  and  now  a  resident  of  Allen’s  Fresh, 
Charles  County,  Md.,  may  be  able  to  identify  these  brothers,  Burroughs, 
as  a  part  of  the  party  concerned  in  the  destruction  of  the  light-boat. 

I  send,  under  charge  of  Lieutenant  Mygatt,  James  H.  M.  and  Thomas 
F.  Burroughs  and  John  P.  Richards,  with  the  witness,  William  Posey, 
to  the  navy  yard  at  Washington,  with  orders  to  deliver  them  in  charge 
of  Commander  Dahlgren,  there  to  await  further  instructions  from  the 
Department. 

The  Remittance  is  now  at  anchor  at  Piney  Point  under  the  safe-keep¬ 
ing  of  Acting  Master’s  Mates  [James  L.]  Gray  and  [A.  J.]  Frank,  whom 
I  have  ordered  to  detain  her  until  next  Wednesday,  when,  if  they 
should  receive  no  further  order  from  yourself,  to  allow  her  to  sail  for 
Baltimore. 

Very  respectfully,  etc., 


Thos.  T.  Craven, 
Commanding  Potomac  Flotilla. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy ,  Washington.

[Telegram.] 

Navy  Yard  [Washington,  D.  C.],  August  28,  1861. 

The  400  men  left  for  Fort  Ellsworth  at  3:  40.  I  had  to  ask  Captain 
Morris  to  loan  a  lieutenant,  which  he  did — Lieutenant  Roe.  The  men 
have  their  hammocks  and  bags,  but  nothing  else.  Please  ask  General 
McClellan  to  order  tents,  rations,  etc.,  for  these  men.  The  night  will 
be  inclement,  and  if  not  under  cover  there  will  be  many  sick.  A  guard 
of  fifty  marines  should  also  be  detailed  by  Colonel  Harris. 

Jno.  A.  Dahlgren. 

Navy  Department. 


[Telegram.] 

Navy  Yard  [Washington,  D.  C.],  August  [58],  1861. 

The  400  seamen  left  here  as  directed  for  Fort  Ellsworth.  Lieutenant 
Roe  reports  that  on  arriving  at  Alexandria  he  went  out  to  the  fort  and 
found  it  occupied  by  other  troops.  He  could  not  find  the  commanding 
general  of  brigade.  No  provision  being  made  for  our  men,  either  as 
regards  food  or  shelter,  he  writes  me  that  he  remains  at  the  wharf  under 
shelter  with  the  men  until  further  orders.  I  shall  immediately  cause  a 
steamboat  to  return  with  the  men’s  rations.  Captain  Wainwright  has 
been  sent  for  and  will,  I  hope,  report  in  season  to  go  down  in  the  steam¬ 
boat.  Should  there  be  an  alarm  in  the  night  the  seamen  will  speedily 
be  at  the  fort.  It  would  be  well,  however,  that  General  McClellan 
should  know  the  circumstances  above  stated. 

J.  A.  Dahlgren. 

Hon.  G.  Y.  Fox, 

Assistan  t  Secretary  of  Navy.

Report  of  Commander  Craven,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  Potomac  Flotilla , 
of  information  received  from  refugees. 

TJ.  S.  S.  Yankee, 

Off  Aquia ,  August  30,  1861. 

Sir  :  This  morning  as  we  were  passing  Upper  Cedar  Point  there  came 
on  board  four  colored  men ;  one,  named  James  Scott,  states  that  he 
belongs  to  a  Mr.  Benjamin  Weaver,  of  King  George  Court-House,  Va., 
and  that  he  (Scott)  and  Henry  Young  have  been  employed  helping  to 
build  batteries  at  Mathias  Point.  There  are  two  batteries  now  at  the 
point  ready  for  their  guns,  which  are  now  on  their  way  from  Bichmond 
and  are  daily  expected.  Henry  Young  says  he  belongs  to  one  Dr. 
Young,  who  lives  at  Lemon  [Orange?]  Court-House,  Ya. ;  he  states  also 
that  he  has  worked  at  a  battery  which  is  being  built  at  Mathias  Point, 
and  that  there  are  three  heavy  guns  to  be  mounted  there  sometime 
during  the  present  week. 

The  other  two  slaves,  William  Henderson,  belonging  to  one  John  E. 
Wilson,  of  Wakefield,  Ya.,  and  Grandison  Piper,  belonging  to  one  Dr. 
Frederick  Wheelwright,  of  Westmoreland,  Ya.  These  four  men  left 
Virginia  in  a  small  skiff  last  night.  I  sent  them  to  the  navy  yard  for 
your  final  disposition. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Thos.  T.  Craven, 
Commanding  Potomac  Flotilla. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy,  Washington. 


Report  of  Commander  Craven ,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  Potomac  Flotilla, 
urging  immediate  action  for  the  protection  of  navigation  in  the  Potomac. 

U.  S.  S.  Yankee, 

Off  Aquia,  August  30,  1861. 

Sir:  The  more  I  witness  the  operations  of  the  rebels,  the  more  I  am 
satisfied  that  if  some  prompt  and  efficient  step  is  not  taken  to  prevent 
it,  the  navigation  of  the  Potomac  River  will  be  entirely  cut  off. 

U nless  there  are  batteries  immediately  erected  opposite  Mathias  Point 
and  the  White  House,  and  the  Maryland  shore  occupied  by  a  strong 
military  force,  the  vessels  of  this  flotilla,  instead  of  being  able  to  enforce 
the  blockade,  are  momentarily  threatened  with  some  serious  disaster. 
Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Thos.  T.  Craven, 
Commanding  Potomac  Flotilla. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy,  Washington.

Letter  from  the  Secretary  of  the  Navy  to  the  Secretary  of  War ,  urging 
cooperation  for  the  protection  of  navigation  in  the  Potomac. 

Navy  Department,  August  31, 1861. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  enclose  copies  of  dispatches  received 
from  Captain  Craven,  in  command  of  the  Potomac  Flotilla,  and  beg  to 
call  your  attention  to  his  suggestions  of  the  necessity  of  prompt  and 
efficient  measures  for  keeping  open  the  navigation  of  the  Potomac. 

I  have  heretofore,  on  repeated  occasions,  called  the  attention  of  the 
War  Department  to  this  subject,  which  is  of  immense  importance  to 
this  city  and  the  operations  of  the  Army  as  well  as  of  the  Navy. 

It  appears  to  me  there  should  be  no  delay  in  taking  the  precautionary 
steps  recommended  by  Captain  Craven,  and  this  Department,  with  the 
naval  force  on  the  Potomac,  is  ready  at  all  times  to  aid  in  this  measure. 
I  remain,  very  respectfully,  etc., 

Gideon  Welles. 

Hon.  Simon  Cameron, 

Secretary  of  War.

August  26, 1861. 

There  have  been  forwarded  to  the  eastern  shore  of  Virginia,  across 
the  bay  from  Richmond,  Va.,  six  brass  cannon  for  the  troops  in  Accomae 
County,  Va.,  and  from  a  good  source  I  learn  that  they  are  in  camp 
drilling,  etc.,  3,000  strong  and  well  suppled  with  ammunition  of  ail 
kinds,  and  also  are  receiving  and  forwarding  the  same  to  the  western 
shore  to  the  enemy.  The  way  the  cannon  were  sent  over  to  eastern 
Virginia  from  Richmond  was  down  the  Rappahannock  River  to  a  point 
inside  the  said  river  10  miles  and  then  sent  to  a  place  called  the  Divid¬ 
ing  Creek,  running  up  into  the  laud  above  the  mouth  of  the  Rappahan¬ 
nock  River  some  12  miles.  You  can  carry  12  feet  water  up  this  creek 
some  5  miles  out  of  sight  of  the  Chesapeake  Bay.  It  is  at  this  point 
where  powder  is  being  received  and  sent  to  the  enemy  in  various  parts

of  western  Virginia.  It  is  sent  into  Chincoteague  Inlet,  on  the  coast,  in 
vessels  on  the  southerly  side  of  Cape  Charles  and  taken  across  the 
county  [of  |  Accomac  to  Cherrystone,  and  from  there  sent  across  the  bay 
to  this  Dividing  Creek,  above  the  Rappahannock  River,  inland,  and  then 
sent  to  the  various  rebel  armies.  The  supplies  sent  are  large,  as  the 
vessels  discharge  the  powder  on  the  sea  side  of  Accomac  County  and 
have  been  doing  so  for  some  time.  The  powder  isfrorn  New  York  and 
Philadelphia.  I  believe  that  the  larger  portion  of  their  powder  lias

[Enclosure.] 

U.  S.  S.  Resolute,  August  31,  1861. 
Sir  :  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that  at  5  o’clock  p.  m.  of  this  day  I 
discovered  four  boats  on  the  Virginia  shore,  at  a  place  called  Ferry 
Landing,  which  I  deemed  necessary  to  destroy.  I  first  endeavored  to 
shove  the  boats  out  and  tow  them,  but  failing  in  this  I  proceeded  to 
burn  them.  Learning  that  rebel  pickets  were  in  the  habit  of  frequent¬ 
ing  the  place,  I  fired  two  shots  in  the  nearest  thicket  to  drive  away 
anyone  who  might  be  concealed  there.  I  then,  with  a  boat’s  crew  of 
five  men,  went  on  shore  and  set  fire  to  the  boats  and  boathouse,  having 
my  gun  ready  to  cover  my  crew  in  case  of  an  attack.  The  flames  from 
the  boats  communicated  to  the  small  dwelling,  which  was  also  destroyed. 

Respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Amos  P.  Foster, 

Acting  Master’s  Mate ,  Commanding  U.  8.  8.  Resolute. 
Commodore  T.  T.  Craven, 

Commanding  Potomac  Flotilla ,  TJ.  8.  8.  Yankee ,  Potomac  River.

Report  of  Captain  Craven,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  Potomac  Flotilla , 
regarding  the  capture  of  the  schooner  Eagle. 

U.  S.  S.  Yankee,  September  1,  1861. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  acknowledge  the  receipt  of  yours  of  the 
31st  ultimo. 

The  schooner  Eagle,  Captain  Laycock,  was  detained  by  Acting  Mas¬ 
ter  Budd,  of  the  Resolute,  on  or  about  the  21st  ultimo,  lie  had  spoken 
her  during  the  night  and  ordered  her  to  go  up  the  river  and  anchor  near 
the  Penguin ,  and  apparently  the  Eagle  started  to  go  in  that  direction, 
but  some  time  afterwards,  when  on  his  tour  of  night  scouting,  he  dis¬ 
covered  the  Eagle  running  down  the  river,  evidently  intending  to  dis¬ 
obey  the  order. 

Under  these  circumstances,  and  the  then  apprehended  attempt  of  the 
rebels  to  cross  the  river,  Mr.  Budd  took  charge  of  the  schoouer,  and 
upon  his  report  of  the  circumstances  I  ordered  her  to  be  taken  to  the 
Washington  navy  yard,  there  to  await  further  instructions  from  yourself. 
Yery  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Thos.  T.  Craven, 
Commanding  Potomac  Flotilla. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy,  W ashington.

Seizure  of  schooner  T.  J.  Evans,  September  1,  1861. 

Report  of  Captain  Craven,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  commanding  Potomac  Plofilla,  transmitting  report  of 
Acting  Master’s  Mate  Ely,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  schooner  Dana. 

U.  S.  S.  Yankee, 

September  2,  1861. 

Sir  :  I  have  the  honor  herewith  to  enclose  the  report  of  Acting  Mas¬ 
ter's  Mate  Ely,  relative  to  the  capture  of  the  sloop  T.  J.  Evans. 

I  had  received  information  of  the  Evans  being  at  anchor  off  Holland 
Island,  on  the  eastern  shore  of  Maryland,  on  the  29th  ultimo,  and  that 
she  was  suspected  of  being  engaged  in  illicit  trade,  and  dispatched  the 
Dana  with  orders  to  seize  her. 

Mr,  Ely’s  account  of  the  escape  of  the  owner  of  the  cargo,  George 
Henry,  is  not  satisfactory  to  me,  and  I  regret  that  from  the  representa¬ 
tions  made  to  me  by  one  of  the  Dands  crew,  there  appears  to  be  strong 
ground  for  suspecting  Mr.  Ely  of  having  been  bribed  by  the  rebel  to 
allow  him  to  escape.  I  respectfully  request  that  his  conduct  may  bo 
thoroughly  investigated. 

By  Acting  Master  Foster,  temporarily  in  charge  of  the  Resolute,  I 
send  the  prize  T.  J.  Evans,  with  her  master,  calling  himself  Thomas 
Stewart,  and  cargo,  consisting  of  9  bales  of  waterproof  blankets,  6 
cases  of  surgical  instruments,  4  boxes  of  percussion  caps  and  friction 
primers,  and  4  Colts  navy  revolvers,  to  be  delivered  to  the  care  of  Com¬ 
mander  Dahlgren  at  the  navy  yard,  Washington,  there  to  await  further 
orders  from  the  Department. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Thos.  T.  Craven, 
Commanding  Potomac  Flotilla. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy,  Washington. 

P.  S. — My  informant  of  the  suspicious  sloop  T.  J.  Evans  was  one 
Thomas  J.  Potts,  master  of  the  schooner  North  Star,  of  Deal’s  Island, 
Somerset  County,  Md. 

Respectfully, 

Thos.  T.  Craven, 
Captain,  U.  S.  Navy. 

P.  S. — One  of  my  pilots,  Bailey,  informs  me  that  Thomas  Stewart  is 
a  fictitious  name;  that  his  true  name  is  Daniel  Bird,  of  Accomac  County, 
Ya. 

Yery  respectfully, 

Thos.  T.  Craven.

In  accordance  with  your  orders  I  started  in  pursuit  of  her  from  Piney 
Point  on  the  29th  day  of  August.  By  your  instructions  I  went  to  Hoi-

laud  Island,  where  the  vessel  was  reported  to  be,  but  on  arriving  there 
I  found  that  the  vessel  and  one  of  the  men  had  left.  I  immediately 
took  charge  of  the  other  man,  whom  I  found  there  and  whom  I  now 
deliver  to  you,  and  obtained  the  following  information  in  regard  to  the 
vessel,  viz: 

That  the  owner  of  the  cargo  had  pushed  the  vessel  off  from  the  beach 
in  spite  of  the  efforts  of  several  of  the  inhabitants  to  detain  him.  He 
threatened  to  shoot  the  first  man  who  put  a  foot  upon  his  vessel.  Not 
understanding  the  mode  of  working  a  small  vessel  he  got  her  aground 
near  Clay  Island,  where  he  was  captured  by  stratagem  by  some  of  the 
islanders,  who  had  followed  him  in  their  canoes,  and  taken  to  the  mag¬ 
istrate’s  house  on  Clay  Island.  I  then  took  six  men  in  my  boat  and 
pulled  to  Clay  Island,  where,  after  walking  5  miles,  I  found  the  man 
and  the  sloop,  and  at  once  took  them  in  charge  and  returned  to  the 
vessel.  I  then  got  underway  and  came  to  Piney  Point,  where  I  found 
the  steamer  George  [ E .  II.]  Herbert ,  which  towed  me  up  the  river  to 
your  vessel  this  morning. 

While  lying  at  Piney  Point  Mr.  George  Henry,  one  of  the  prisoners 
and  the  owner  of  the  cargo,  who  was  very  sick,  asked  permission  of  me 
to  go  on  shore  and  get  his  supper,  as  he  could  not  eat  the  salt  provis¬ 
ions  which  I  had  on  board  of  my  vessel.  I  granted  his  request  and 
went  on  shore  with  him,- where  we  took  supper  at  the  hotel.  After  tea 
he  asked  me  to  permit  him  to  go  out  to  fulfill  the  call  of  nature.  I 
permitted  him  to  go,  but  fearing  that  he  might  attempt  to  escape,  I 
followed  immediately  after  him,  but  favored  by  the  darkness  and  the 
thick  growth  of  trees,  I  am  sorry  to  say  that  he  succeeded  in  making 
good  liis  escape.  The  other  man,  Thomas  Stewart,  the  vessel  and 
cargo,  I  now  deliver  to  you. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

B.  B.  Ely,

Statement  of  officers  of  U.  S.  schooner  Dana  regarding  conduct  of  commanding  officer  of  that 
vessel  in  permitting  the  escape  of  owner  of  cargo  of  schooner  T.  J.  Evans. 

U.  S.  Schooner  Dana,  September  5 , 1861. 

Sir:  As  instructed  I  have  questioned  the  undersigned  men  and  they 
give  this  as  their  statement  in  regard  to  Mr.  Ely  and  the  escape  of  his 
prisoner.  After  taking  the  prize,  with  two  prisoners,  he  returned  to 
Piney  Point,  being  absent  two  days.  Mr.  Ely  immediately  after  arriv¬ 
ing  took  the  cargo  out  of  the  prize  and  loaded  her  with  hawsers,  etc., 
to  take  them  on  shore,  taking  the  starboard  watch  with  him  (four  men). 
Leaving  them  on  shore,  he  then,  with  Mr.  Marshall’s  boy,  went  back 
to  the  schooner  and  asked  the  prisoners  to  go  on  shore  with  him,  which 
they  did.  The  captain  of  the  prize  took  several  articles  out  of  his  car¬ 
petbag  and  tokl  one  of  the  men  that  if  he  did  not  return  the  man  might 
have  it.  They  then  went  on  shore,  Mr.  Ely  returning  again  to  the 
schooner  for  the  balance  of  his  crew  to  help  draw  the  wagon  on  which 
the  four  men  had  placed  the  rigging,  leaving  one  man  without  arms  to 
take  charge  of  the  prisoners.  When  the  crew  got  on  shore  the  captain 
of  the  prize  gave  one  of  the  men  $1  to  treat  themselves  with.  After  they 


OPERATIONS  ON  THE  POTOMAC  AND  RAPPAHANNOCK.  651 


drank  Mr.  Ely  treated  them  again.  The  crew  then  hauled  the  rigging 
up  and  put  it  away,  alter  which  they  went  on  board  to  get  their  supper, 
leaving  Mr.  Ely  and  the  prisoners  at  the  hotel  to  get  their  suppers. 

The  crew,  after  getting  their  suppers,  went  again  on ’shore  and  saw 
Mr.  Ely  and  the  two  men  going  out  of  the  dining  room  into  the  bar¬ 
room,  shutting  the  door  when  they  saw  the  crew  coming  on  the  porch. 
They  remained  in  the  room  about  fifteen  minutes,  when  Mr.  Ely  came 
out.  He  had  Mr.  Marshall  and  one  of  the  prisoners  with  him,  leaving 
the  captain  of  the  prize  in  the  room,  Mr.  Ely  then  ordered  the  crew  to 
the  boat  and  went  on  board  the  Bailey.  While  there  he  wrote  a  letter, 
intending  it  for  you.  When  finished  he  asked  Captain  Gray  how  it 
would  do.  Mr.  Ely  went  on  shore  with  the  prisoners  at  4:  30  p.  m.  and 
did  not  return  until  10  o’clock. 

These  men  say  they  felt  satisfied  the  prisoner  would  not  come  back 
when  he  left  the  vessel,  an  d  further  that  Mr.  Ely  was  very  familiar  with 
him,  telling  him  of  all  proceedings  of  the  flotilla  on  the  river. 

This  being  all  I  have  been  able  to  learn,  I  remain,  very  respectfully, 
your  obedient  servant, 

Wm.  T.  Street, 

Master's  Mate. 

Signed : 

Joseph  E.  Eoss.  *

Letter  from  Thomas  R.  Stewart,  esq.,  to  the  Assistant  Secretary  of  the  Navy,  requesting  an 

early  investigation  of  his  case. 

U.  S.  S.  Anacostia,  Sunday ,  September  8 ,  1861. 

Dear  Sir  :  I  would  like  very  much  for  you  to  have  my  case  brought 
up  for  trial  or  whatever  process  of  law  I  have  to  go  through.  I  am  an 
innocent  man  and  would  like  to  be  released.  I  will  state  the  circum¬ 
stance  under  which  I  was  arrested  or  taken: 

I  was  not  arrested;  I  gave  myself  up  to  the  captain  of  the  U.  S. 
schooner  Dana]  his  name  is  Elbe  [ElyJ.  I  was  hired  in  Baltimore  by 
a  man  by  the  name  of  George  Henry  as  a  sailor  or  pilot  in  his  boat,  to 
go  as  far  as  Annemessex  Kiver,  Maryland.  We  stopped  to  get  a  rudder 
on  Holland  Island.  There  was  an  officer" came  down  and  requested  the 
captain  to  show  him  what  those  things  were,  or  what  kind  of  goods  he 
had  on  board,  which  he  refused  to  do.  I,  thinking  something  was 
wrong,  left  the  boat.  He  ordered  me  to  get  on  board,  which  I  refused 
to  do.  He  then  started  away,  and.  was  arrested  .some  15.  miles  from 
where  I  was  by  the  officer  of  Dorchester  County,  aud  kept  until  the 
cutter  came  over  and  took  charge  of  the  boat  and  Captain  Henry  and 
myself.  He  acknowledged  to  the  captain  of  the  cutter  that  I  knew 
nothing  about  what  kind  fif  goods  he  had  on  board;  that  he  was  the 
owner  of  the  goods,  and  I  was  hired  by  him  as  a  sailor  or  to  pilot  him 
to  Annemessex  River.  I  asked  him  what  those  things  were  and  he  told 
me  they  were  dry  goods  and  ready  made  clothing.  The  captain  and 
myself  were  allowed  to  go  on  shore  at  Piney  Point  with  Captain  Elbe

Ely]  to  get  supper,  and  after  supper  Captain  Henry  ran  off  and  made 
ins  escape.  Then  I  was  sent  here.  By  your  having  my  case  investi¬ 
gated  would  oblige  me  very  much. 

Yours,  respectfully, 

Thos.  li.  Stewart.

O'.  S.  S.  Penguin, 
Potomac  Flotilla ,  September  2, 1861. 

Sir:  I  send  you  this  morning,  by  the  steam  tug  Tigress ,  a  white 
boy  of  20  years  of  age,  who  was  captured  this  morning  on  the  river, 
making  his  escape  from  the  Virginia  shore.  He  seems  deplorably  poor 
and  destitute ;  says  his  father  told  him  to  escape  and  seek  some  employ¬ 
ment  on  the  Maryland  shore. 

He  seems  disposed  to  give  information  of  what  is  going  on  there, 
and  if  true  is  valuable.  He  says  they  are  preparing  a  fort  at  some 
position  on  Shipping  Point,  Quantico  Creek,  and  that  they  have  laid 
straw  on  the  road  to  bring  the  guns  over,  and  that  soldiers  are  assem¬ 
bling  at  Dumfries,  the  village  near,  and  more  which  you  will  obtain 
from  him  yourself. 

Respectfully,  etc., 

J.  W.  Livingston, 
Commanding  TJ.  S.  S.  Penguin.

Letter  from  the  Secretary  of  the  Navy  to  Captain  Craven ,  TJ.  S.  Navy,

Department. 

Navy  Department,  September  2,  1861. 
Sir  :  The  following  information  has  been  given  the  Department : 

Mouth  of  Smith’s  Cheek,  St.  Mary’s  County,  Md. 
There  is  a  great  deal  of  passing  to  and  from  Virginia  at  this  place — men  and  con¬ 
trabands.  This  has  been  going  on  some  time,  and  not  being  molested,  they  pass  in 
open  day.  They  have  gone,  a  great  many,  from  my  neighborhood,  I  think  as  high 
as  forty  of  a  night.  I  think  it  would  be  sufficient  to  put  a  tug  at  that  place,  and  I 
think  it  would  soon  put  a  stop  to  the  passing.  The  passing  is  principally  from  the 
mouth  of  Smith’s  Creek. 


Very  respectfully,  etc., 

Captain  T.  T.  Craven, 

Commanding  Potomac  Flotilla. 


Gideon  Welles.
