Letter  from  the  commandant  navy  yard ,  Washington ,  to  Captain  Craven , 
U.  S.  Navy ,  commanding  Potomac  Flotilla ,  regarding  vessels  under 
repair. 


Navy  Yard,  September  3 ,  1861. 

Dear  Sir:  I  believe  the  bags  and  hammocks  have  all  been  sent; 
also  5,000  rounds  for  Sharps  rifles  and  50  pistols  with  ammunition. 

It  is  not  possible  to  man  the  cutters  and  the  steamers  now  fitting. 

The  Ceres  is  being  pushed  forward  and  will  soon  be  ready.  She 
has  been  calked  and  coppered,  etc. 

The  Underwriter  is  now  on  the  rail  [ways]  and  will  be  thoroughly 
repaired — calked,  coppered,  etc. 

Then  comes  the  Island  Belle  (like  the  Ceres),  and  then  the  Anacostia ; 
so  you  see  there  is  plenty  to  do. 

The  Ceres  has  the  lightest  gun  above  a  boat  howitzer;  hope  it  will 
not  be  too  heavy. 

We  have  possession  of  Fort  Ellsworth,  and  yesterday  the  Chief 
Engineer  of  the  Army  asked  if  I  had  cannon  that  would  reach  Mun¬ 
son’s  Hill,  3  miles  oft'.  So  I  offered  to  put  a  number  of  rifled  80-pound¬ 
ers  there  on  the  condition  that  I  should  conduct  the  operation;  not 
accepted  yet. 

The  Savannah  has  been  fired  at  and  I  sent  her  a  rifled  80-pounder 
last  night. 

Very  truly,  yours, 


Jno.  A.  Dahlgren. 


[Captain  Thomas  T.  Craven,  IT.  S.  Navy, 

Commanding  Potomac  Flotilla.]

Camp  Federal  Hill, 

Baltimore,  August  24,  1861. 

Sir:  On  the  morning  of  the  21st,  in  compliance  with  special  order 
No.  138,  I  embarked  with  thirty-four,  rank  and  file,  of  my  company,  on 
board  the  steamer  Hugh  Jenkins ,  and  accompanied  her  as  a  guard  on 
her  trip  to  Point  Lookout,  St.  Mary’s  County,  Md.,  arriving  there  on 
the  evening  of  the  same  day  at  8: 15. 

We  discharged  our  passengers  and  anchored  in  the  stream  till  Fri¬ 
day  morning  at  8  o’clock  on  the  23d,  at  which  time  we  again  touched  at 
the  dock,  took  on  our  passengers,  and  left  for  this  citjr,  arriving  at 
5:45  p.  m.  same  day. 

The  sentiment  of  the  people  at  Point  Lookout  is  intensely  Southern, 
and  I  was  informed  by  slaves  who  came  on  board  to  sell  fruit  that  their 
masters  offered  every  facility  to  the  rebels  in  the  way  of  information 
and  passing  to  and  from  the  loyal  States.  Our  anchorage  was  in  the 
Potomac  River,  opposite  Coan  River.  Vessels  were  passing  in  and  out

Report  of  Captain  Craven,  JJ.  S.  Navy ,  commanding  Potomac  Flotilla, 

denying  the  charge  of  negligence  on  the  part  of  the  officers  of  his  com- 

mand. 

U.  S.  S.  Yankee,  September  5,  1861. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  acknowledge  the  receipt  of  your  letter 
of  the  3d  instant,  with  its  accompanying  copy  of  a  report  of  an  expe¬ 
dition  sent  by  Major-General  Dix  to  the  mouth  of  the  Potomac.  As 
the  report  of  Captain  H.  Duryea,  Yew  York  State  Volunteers,  seems 
to  imply  that  the  officers  of  this  flotilla  are  negligent  in  the  perform¬ 
ance  of  their  duties,  and  it  has  apparently  been  endorsed  by  no  less  a 
person  than  General  McClellan,  I  beg  leave  to  submit  the  following 
statement.  Captain  Duryea  in  his  report  of  the  24th  August  says: 

Our  anchorage  was  in  the  Potomac  River  opposite Coan  River.  Yessels  were  pass¬ 
ing  in  and  out  close  under  the  Virginia  shore  at  all  times  with  perfect  freedom,  there 
being  no  blockading  vessel  at  the  mouth  of  the  Potomac,  and  I  saw  none  while  we 
wero  at  Point  Lookout  or  during  our  trip. 

When  I  was  called  by  your  order  of  the  13th  August  to  concentrate  my 
forces  before  Aquia  Creek,  knowing  that  the  schooners  Dana ,  Bailey, 
and  Cobb  could  be  of  no  earthly  assistance  to  me,  1  left  them  near  the 
mouth  of  the  river,  with  orders  to  watch  closely  the  movements  of 
rebel  sympathizers,  whom  I  knew  to  be  located  about  Herring  Creek, 
St.  Mary’s  River,  and  Point  Lookout.  On  my  first  visit  to  Piney  Point, 
after  an  absence  from  there  of  about  ten  days,  Acting  Master’s  Mates 
Ely  and  Gray  both  informed  me  of  the  visit  made  to  Point  Lookout 
by  the  steamer  Hugh  Jenkins  on  the  evening  of  the  21st  August.  They 
were  both  in  the  vicinity  of  that  point  when  she  first  made  her  appear¬ 
ance  and  there  during  her  stay,  watching,  not  only  her  movements,  but 
as  usual  that  of  all  other  vessels  passing  up  or  down  the  river,  and 
to-day  upon  questioning  those  gentlemen  as  to  the  passing  of  vessels 
“close  under  the  Virginia  shore  at  all  times,”  they  state  such  was  not 
the  fact.  1  can  only  attribute  this  misstatement  of  Captain  Duryea’s 
to  his  ignorance  of  nautical  affairs,  and,  therefore,  incapacity  to  dis¬ 
tinguish  a  national  cruiser  from  a  wood  barge.  Vessels  passing  4  or 
5  miles  from  Point  Lookout  might  to  the  inexperienced  eye  appear  to 
be  close  to  the  Virginia  shore,  when  in  reality  they  would  be  at  least 
3  or  4  miles  distant  from  it.  Notwithstanding  the  foregoing  statement, 
sir,  I  must  confess  from  what  I  can  learn  that  for  the  past  two  weeks 
there  has  been  an  unusual  amount  of  intercourse  between  the  rebels  of 
either  shore  of  the  Potomac,  particularly  from  Mathias  Point  down  as 
far  as  Herring  Creek;  but  situated  as  I  have  been,  with  so  few  vessels 
at  my  command,  and  these  few  but  half  equipped  and  manned,  it  has 
been  impossible  to  prevent  it.  Yesterday  and  to-day  I  received  an 
accession  to  my  forces  of  two  small  steam  tugs  and  three  cutters.  The 
steam  tugs  have  each  a  small  rifle  cannon,  and  a  crew  of  but  six  or 
seven  men;  they  are  totally  unprovided  with  muskets,  pistols,  pikes, 


OPERATIONS  ON  THE  POTOMAC  AND  RAPPAHANNOCK.  659 


or  sabers.  Tlie  cutters,  instead  of  being  manned  by  thirteen  or  fifteen 
men,  which  is  the  least  number  sufficient  to  manage  them,  have  come 
down  with  but  six  and  seven  men.  As  poorly  provided  as  they  are,  I 
have  been  busy  all  day  in  stationing  them  at  the  most  important  points 
from  Pope’s  Creek  to  the  mouth  of  the  river:  At  Pope’s  Creek,  a 
steam  tug;  at  Lower  Cedar  Point,  a  cutter;  at  Cobb’s  Point,  a  steam 
tug;  Blakistoue’s  Island,  a  schooner,  and  so  on  down;  four  steam  tugs, 
three  schooners,  and  three  cutters.  With  two  additional  steamers  and 
four  more  cutters,  properly  armed  and  manned,  this  part  of  the  river 
would  be  perfectly  secure  against  crossings,  and  a  large  amount  of  aid 
and  comfort  which  has  but  recently  accumulated  on  the  Maryland 
shore  would  have  to  seek  some  other  outlet  in  order  to  reach  its  desti¬ 
nation. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Tnos.  T.  Craven, 
Commanding  Potomac  Flotilla. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Wavy,  Washington.

Letter  from  commandant  navy  yard,  Washington,  to  Captain  Craven, 
U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  Potomac  Flotilla ,  regarding  progress  of 
repairs  to  vessels. 

Navy  Yard,  September  4,  1861. 

Dear  Sir  :  I  regret  that  you  feel  troubled  by  the  unavoidable  dimi¬ 
nution  of  your  force.  Whatever  can  be  done  here  shall  be  done.  The 
Reliance,  Herbert,  and  Pusey  I  hurry  down  to  join  you  to-night,  and 
two  cutters,  perhaps  three,  the  difficulty  being  to  man  them.  The 
Navy  now  furnishes  400  men  at  Fort  Ellsworth,  100  to  the  naval  bat¬ 
tery  near  it,  and  detachments  to  the  bridge  and  magazine.  The  instruc¬ 
tion  department  has  much  less  than  100  in  it  and  to  draw  them  off  too 
soon  is  not  good  policy. 

A  reenforcement  of  men  is  on  the  way. 

The  boiler  of  the  Ceres  is  not  finished ;  when  it  is  the  vessel  will  join 
you.  The  Underwriter  can  not  be  ready  in  less  than  two  weeks,  but 
the  Island  Belle  will  be,  which  will  add  materially  to  your  number.

Letter  from  Lieutenant  Parker,  U.  S.  Navy,  to  Captain  Craven ,  77.  S. 

Navy,  commanding  Potomac  Flotilla,  regarding  concealed  arms. 

[Navy  Yard,  Washington,]  September  4,  1861. 

The  negro,  Henry  Young,  who  was  sent  to  this  yard  from  the  Poto¬ 
mac  Flotilla  on  the  30th  day  of  August,  reports  that  in  a  barn  on  the 
plantation  of  Captain  Cox,  3  miles  from  Chapel  Point  [Md.],  are  secreted 
a  keg  of  powder  and  a  sack  of  musket  balls.  Young  further  says  that 
Captain  Cox’s  colored  overseer  told  him  he  could  show  him  a  place 
where  many  arms  were  concealed. 

Foxhall  A.  Parker. 

Captain  T.  T.  Craven.

Report  of  Captain  Cra  ven,  U.  S.Navy,  commanding  Potomac  Flotilla,  of 
reconnoissances  at  Leonardtown  and  Port  Tobacco. 

U.  S.  S.  Yankee, 

Off  Piney  Point,  September  5,  1861. 

Sir  :  I  have  the  honor  to  acknowledge  the  receipt  of  your  two  com¬ 
munications  of  the  4tli  instant,  one  asking  for  a  report  of  the  result  of 
the  examinations  made  at  Leonardtown,  Port  Tobacco,  etc.,  as  called 
for  by  you  in  your  letter  of  the  24th  August,  the  other  accompanying 
information  from  the  provost-marshal  relative  to  crossings  made  nightly 
from  Breton’s  Bay,  St.  Mary’s  River,  etc. 

In  reply  to  the  first,  I  would  respectfully  state  that  but  two  days 
previous  to  its  receipt  there  was  an  examination  made  under  the  charge 
of  Major  Reynolds,  of  the  Marine  Corps,  who  proceeded  to  these  two 
places  and  to  Pope’s  Creek  with  200  marines  in  the  Mount  Vernon. 
He  was  accompanied  by  Lieutenant  Commanding  Harrell,  in  the  Free¬ 
born.  Major  Reynolds  reported  to  me  verbally  that  he  could  discover 
nothing  at  either  of  these  places.  The  positions  named  in  your  letter 
of  the  24tli  August  were  thoroughly  searched,  and  so  was  every  place 
likely  to  contain  concealed  arms  or  supplies  for  the  rebels,  but  without 
being  able  to  discover  anything. 

On  the  31st  of  July  I  had  myself  been  at  Leonardtown  in  search  of 
these  two  pieces  of  cannon,  and  reported  the  result  to  the  Department 
on  the  1st  of  August.  A  few  days  since  that  time,  and  only  a  few  days 
after  the  search  made  by  Major  Reynolds,  I  was  informed  by  three  or 


OPERATIONS  ON  THE  POTOMAC  AND  RAPPAHANNOCK.  663 


four  different  parties  that  the  guns  in  question  had  been  at  Leonard- 
town,  hiit  about  the  middle  of  July  they  were  removed  back  toward 
the  Patuxent  River. 

I  am  aware,  sir,  that  I  should  have  made  a  full  statement  of  these 
facts  to  you  at  the  time  of  their  occurrence,  but  I  was  then  so  absorbed 
in  the  task  assigned  me  by  an  order  from  the  Department  of  the  13th 
August,  requiring  the  concentration  of  all  my  forces  before  Aquia 
Creek  for  the  purpose  of  preventing  the  enemy’s  crossing  the  river, 
that  I  overlooked,  perhaps,  many  things  of  minor  importance. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Tuos.  T.  Craven, 
Commanding  Potomac  Flotilla. 

G.  Y.  Fox, 

Assistant  Secretary  of  the  Navy ,  Washington.

Navy  Department,  September  6,  1861. 
Sir:  The  following  is  sent  for  your  information: 


Washington,  D.  C.,  September  6, 1861. 

I  liave  the  honor  to  report  that  I  have,  while  on  guard,  received  reliable  informa¬ 
tion  that  numbers  of  persons  are  crossing  the  Potomac  from  Maryland  to  Virginia 
nightly  at  Pope’s  Creek.  They  use  punts  or  low  ducking  boats,  by  which  a  person 
is  enabled  to  pass  within  a  short  distance  of  a  sentinel  without  being  observed. 

Very  respectfully, 


Wm.  Fletcher, 

Sergeant  of  Guard,  Alexandria  Steamboat. 


The  Commanding  Officer,  Battalion,  Eighth  Infantry.

Report  of  Lieutenant  McCrea ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  commanding  IT.  S.  S.  Jacob 
Bell ,  of  the  result  of  an  inspection  of  the  Virginia  coast. 

U.  S.  S.  Jacob  Bell,  September  6,  1861. 

Sir  :  In  obedience  to  your  order  of  this  date,  I  made  a  thorough 
inspection  of  the  coast  of  Virginia  from  opposite  the  anchorage  as 
far  as  Indian  Head.  I  saw  no  batteries,  mounted  or  dismounted  guns, 
and  no  changes  on  the  said  coast.  I  saw  six  men  near  a  house  on  the 
beach  opposite  Sandy  Point.  I  communicated  with  the  Penguin ,  but 
received  no  intelligence  of  any  moment. 

Yery  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

E.  P.  McCrea, 
Lieutenant ,  Commanding. 

Commander  Benjamin  M.  Dove, 

Commanding  Second  Division ,  Potomac  Flotilla.

[Telegram.] 

Alexandria,  September  6 ,  1861. 

General  Montgomery,  commanding  Alexandria,  understands  the  ferry 
line  has  been  closed  by  order  of  the  honorable  Secretary  of  the  Navy. 

Citizens  here  are  anxious  to  have  it  reestablished  for  market  purposes  ; 
indeed,  public  interest  would  be  promoted  thereby.  Will  the  Secretary 
authorize  its  reestablishment  between  here  and  Maryland? 

W.  E.  Montgomery, 
Brigadier- General ,  Commanding . 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  Navy.

Quartermaster- General’s  Office, 

Washington  City ,  September  3,  1861. 

I  have  ordered  the  purchase  of  the  Balloon  and  Hugh  Jenkins ,  two  of 
the  three  Baltimore  steamboats,  the  purchase  of  which  you  lately  rec¬ 
ommended.  They  need  some  slight  repairs  and  will  be  ordered  here  as 
soon  as  ready.  Mr.  Tucker,  of  Philadelphia,  who  has  conducted  the 
negotiation  for  them,  advises  that  one  of  them  be  armed  and  put  into 
the  creek  at  Port  Tobacco,  from  which  place  he  says  he  knows  that  a 
large  trade  is  carried  on  with  Virginia. 

He  knows  of  overtures  being  made  to  persons  in  Philadelphia  to 
embark  in  this  trade  as  profitable  and  safe;  dark  nights  and  foggy 
days  cover  it. 

Would  it  not  be  well  to  put  a  small  vessel  there  before  these  are  made 
ready?  I  presume  that,  though  bought  by  the  quartermaster,  these 
vessels  will  be  armed  by  the  Navy  and  at  this  navy  yard.  *  *  # 

Respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

M.  0.  Meigs, 
Quartermaster-  General.

tug  E.  PL.  Herbert,  of  shelling  a  light  on  the  Virginia  shore. 

Steam  Tug  Herbert, 
Sunday  Morning ,  September  8 ,  1861. 
Sir  :  My  coal  will  not  last  more  than  two  days  longer.  None  on  the 
way  from  Philadelphia  for  Government  as  I  learn. 

I  put  out  a  revolving  light  very  suddenly  on  Friday  morning,  3  a.  m., 
on  the  Virginia  shore.  I  watched  it  for  two  hours ;  it  worked  beautifully. 
Two  Union  shells  made  it  disappear  very  suddenly.  I  want  coal. 

Charles  Bentrick, 

Master’s  Mate ,  in  Charge.

Report  of  Lieutenant  Wyman,  U.  8.  Navy,  commanding  IT.  8.  8.  Poca¬ 
hontas ,  regarding  the  blockade  of  the  Potomac. 

U.  S.  S.  Pocahontas, 

September  11,  1861. 

Sir  :  When  the  moon  went  down  last  night  I  sent  our  launch  in 
toward  High  Point  with  orders  to  keep  a  lookout  that  no  boats  passed 
close  inshore.  This  morning  the  coxswain  in  charge  reports  that  near 
midnight  he  discovered  a  large  boat  coming  from  the  direction  of  the 
Occoquan  River  toward  High  Point.  He  pulled  in  and  the  boats  crew 
seeing  our  launch  pulled  back.  She  pulled  very  fast,  and  though  he 
tried  to  get  his  gun  to  bear,  she  was  out  of  sight  inside  the  point  before 
he  succeeded.  As  you  remarked  a  day  or  two  since,  should  they  attempt 
a  crossing  they  would  be  likely  to  pull  up  close  under  the  land  to  Hal¬ 
lowing  Point  [Va.],  and  then  cross  to  the  creek  which  makes  up  at 
Chapman’s  Point  [Md.],  within  a  very  short  distance  of  the  road  lead¬ 
ing  to  Piscataway.  The  head  of  the  creek  is  also  but  a  short  distance 
from  the  head  of  Mattawoman  Creek. 

When  a  boat  goes  down  to  Aquia  Creek,  can  I  be  permitted  to  send 
down  the  launch  now  here  and  take  the  launch  originally  belonging  to 
this  vessel,  which  is  now  at  the  Freeborn ,  and  in  which  are  some  articles 
belonging  to  the  crew  of  this  launch? 

Should  there  be  a  smoothbore  12-pounder  howitzer  available,  it  would 
add  to  this  vessel’s  efficiency  to  mount  it  on  the  field  carriage  which  we 
have  on  the  poop  deck,  our  12  [pounder]  being  mounted  on  the  boat  car¬ 
riage  on  the  topgallant  forecastle. 

The  crew  of  the  vessel  are  short  three  ordinary  seamen  and  two  or 
three  messenger  boys,  which  can  be  had  from  the  Freeborn,  they  wishing 
to  transfer  them.  Even  could  we  have  three  howitzers  on  field  car¬ 
riages  they  could  be  mounted  astern  with  advantage. 

1  find  that  some  time  ago  Mr.  Budd  took  Mr.  Page  over  to  Dr.  Stew¬ 
art’s  (once  if  not  often er)  to  see  one  of  Dr.  Stewart’s  daughters,  to  whom 
he  is  engaged;  that  Dr.  Stewart  told  Commander  Dove,  who  went  in

$ 

under  a  flag  of  truce,  that  lie  wished  Mr.  Budd  to  discontinue  coining 
there,  as  he  feared  that  some  of  the  neighbors  might  kill  him,  and  he 
would  not  wish  that  to  happen  on  his  property.  I  return  enclosed  the 
order  marked  confidential.  Commander  Dove  appeared  to  be  wholly

Report  of  Captain  Craven ,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  Potomac  Flotilla , 
forwarding  information  regarding  battery  under  construction  by  the 
Confederates  on  Mathias  Point. 

U.  S.  S.  Yankee,  September  11, 1861. 
Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  inform  you  of  the  arrival  last  evening  on 
board  the  Yankee  of  four  contrabands  from  Virginia,  three  of  whom, 
viz., 'James  Minor,  George  Washington,  and  Samuel  Bunn,  belong  to 
Phelan  [Fielding]  Lewis,  who  resides  on  the  Rappahannock  River. 
The  fourth,  James  Lawson,  a  house  servant,  belonging  to  John  Tayloe, 
of  King  George  County,  Va.,  a  colonel  in  the  rebel  Army,  is  quite  an 
intelligent  man,  states  that  the  rebels  are  building  a  battery  at  Mathias 
Point,  for  which  there  are  now  in  Fredericksburg  seven  guns,  three  of 
9-inch  bore,  and  the  rest  are  from  8  to  7^-inch  bore.  They  intend  to 
convey  these  guns  to  Hop  Yard  Wharf,  which  is  2  miles  above  Cherry 
Point,  on  the  Rappahannock,  and  from  thence  across  to  Mathias  Point, 
so  that  they  will  have  them  the  day  the  battery  is  prepared,  and  they 
will  clear  the  trees  off  in  front  of  the  battery  as  soon  as  it  is  fully 
equipped.  The  statement  of  this  man  is  similar  to  that  I  have  received 
from  other  sources.  He  also  says  they  have  700  militia  encamped  5 
miles  back  from  Mathias  Point,  on  Machodoc  Creek,  and  2,000  men  on 
Potomac  Creek.  I  will  send  them  by  the  first  opportunity  to  the  navy 
yard,  there  to  await  the  disposition  of  the  Department. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Tiios.  T.  Craven, 
Commanding  Potomac  Flotilla. 

G.  V.  Fox, 

Acting  Secretary  of  the  Navy,  Washington.

On  Tuesday,  September  10, 1  saw  a  small  sloop  under  cover  of  night 
run  into  a  creek  near  my  anchorage  and  maimed  the  boat  and  pursued 
him.  He  appeared  well  acquainted  with  the  ships  of  the  flotilla,  and,  in 
answer  to  some  questions,  stated  that  there  is  in  Pope’s  Creek  a  boat  that 
did  belong  to  the  light-ship  that  was  burned  some  time  since.  Said  boat 
is  used  by  an  individual  at  the  creek  in  transporting  sundry  articles 
across  to  the  Virginia  shore.  A  few  days  since  a  wagonload  of  boots 
and  shoes  and  mail  matter  were  sent  across.  This  information,  if  deemed 
of  any  importance  from  such  a  source,  is  respectfully  submitted. 

Chas.  Bentrick, 

Steam  Tug  F.  H.  Herbert. 


Report  of  Lieutenant  Wyman,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  commanding .  TJ.  S.  S.  Poca¬ 
hontas,  regarding  boats  concealed  in  creeks. 

U.  S.  S.  Pocahontas, 

September  12,  1861. 

Sir  :  In  a  creek  which  makes  up  just  below  Freestone  Point  I  have 
seen  this  afternoon,  for  the  first  time,  the  three  masts  of  a  longboat  and 
the  single  mast  of  another  boat. 

This  creek  has  its  entrance  below  Freestone  Point,  but  makes  up  (as 
the  pilot  says)  to  the  northward,  the  boats  being  seen  over  the  low  laud 
above  Freestone  Point.  I  am  inclined  to  believe  that  there  is  a  creek 
making  in  just  to  the  northward  of  the  point. 

The  masts  of  these  boats  have  again  been  taken  down,  so  it  may  be  that 
there  are  many  more  in  this  creek  that  are  concealed  by  the  land.  It  has 
occurred  to  me  that  the  u  varmints”  might  try  and  spring  a  fire  ship  on  us 
out  of  some  of  these  creeks,  but  I  will  look  out  for  these  two  entrances 
with  the  tug  and  launch.  Sending  aloft,  three  boats  can  be  seen  in  this 
creek,  two  large  and  one  small.  Above  and  over  the  sandy  beach  which

makes  inside  of  High  Point  toward  Occoquan  Biver,  a  longboat  is  vis¬ 
ible,  hauled  up,  and  some  six  to  eight  men  appear  to  be  working  on  her. 

Bespectfully, 

B.  H.  Wyman, 
Lieutenant ,  Commanding.

[Enclosure.] 

Clerk’s  Office, 
Hagerstown,  August  31,  1861. 

Dear  Sir:  I  dislike  very  muck  to  be  obtruding  so  frequently  upon 
your  attention,  but  a  matter  lias  come  to  my  knowledge  recently  that 
were  I  not  to  disclose  it  I  should  feel  that  I  was  derelict  in  my  duty  as 
a  good  citizen. 

I  learn  from  a  gentleman  just  returned  from  Richmond,  Va.,  that  the 
Baltimore  papers  are  received  there  almost  as  regularly  and  promptly 
as  they  are  here  in  Hagerstown,  and  that  they  cross  at  Mathias  Point. 

The  gentleman  from  whom  I  derived  this  information  has  been  to 
Richmond,  by  permission  of  our  Government,  on  a  mission  of  mercy, 
to  obtain  the  release  of  a  prisoner  who  had  fallen  into  the  hands  of  the 
rebels  while  General  Patterson’s  division  was  at  Charlestown;  and  my 
informant  was  only  defeated  in  his  errand  by  the  appearance  in  Rich¬ 
mond  one  morning  of  the  Baltimore  American  and  Sun,  containing  a 
notice  of  its  [his]  visit  and  its  object. 

I  do  not  know,  of  course,  that  your  Department  is  aware  of  this  point 
of  transit  for  the  newspapers  of  Baltimore,  and  therefore  make  this 
communication  for  what  i-t  is  worth.  A  much  closer  watch  than  that 
heretofore  observed  must  be  inaugurated  so  as  to  prevent  all  intercom¬ 
munication  between  us  and  the  rebels,  or  our  plans  will  be  constantly 
liable  to  be  frustrated. 

With  great  regard,  your  most  obedient  servant, 

Isaac  Nesbitt. 

Hon.  M.  Blair,

Report  of  Acting  Lieutenant  Rudd,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  commanding  V.  S.  S. 
Penguin,  relative  to  movements  of  vessels  on  the  Potomac  River. 

U.  S.  S.  Penguin, 
Potomac  Flotilla,  September  13,  1861. 

Sir:  I  have  to  report  that  a  short  time  before  midnight  a  howitzer 
was  fired  down  the  river  and  two  blows  from  a  steam  whistle  heard.  I 


672  OPERATIONS  ON  THE  POTOMAC  AND  RAPPAHANNOCK. 


at  once  unshackled  chain  and  prepared  to  go  to  her  assistance,  suppos¬ 
ing  it  to  be  the  Herbert.  Soon  after  a  tug  hove  in  sight  with  a  launch 
in  tow,  and  although  hailed  frequently  by  me  and  a  musket  fired  no 
reply  was  given  except  two  blows  from  her  whistle.  I  thought  I  rec¬ 
ognized  her  to  be  the  Resolute.  Please  instruct  me  whether  I  am  to 
allow  these  vessels  to  pass  under  like  circumstances  or  whether  I  am 
to  enforce  an  answer  to  my  hail. 

About  1  o’clock  a.  m.  it  was  reported  to  me  that  exhaust  steam  was 
heard  toward  the  Virginia  shore  and  a  dim  light  seen.  I  watched  very 
closely  the  position  designated,  but  saw  nor  heard  nothing,  else  1  should 
have  reconnoitered.  This  morning,  however,  the  tug  James  Murray 
was  seen  at  daylight  anchored  between  us  and  Cockpit  Point.  Her 
officer  stated  that  he  had  been  instructed  to  watch  for  two  boats  that 
had  been  seen  under  Freestone  Point.  He  had  therefore  evidently  mis¬ 
taken  his  position. 

Respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Thos.  A.  Budd, 

Acting  Lieutenant ,  Commanding  U.  S.  S.  Penguin . 

Captain  T.  T.  Craven,  U.  S.  Navy, 

Commanding  Potomac  Flotilla. 

My  instructions  to  the  captain  of  the  Herbert  are  to  allow  no  vessels 
to  pass  up  at  night  unless  in  the  Government  service.  Is  this  correct1?

[Enclosure.] 

The  Richmond  Examiner  of  the  9th  says,  before  many  hours  the 
Potomac  will  be  effectually  closed  by  powerful  batteries.  The  chief  of 
ordnance  in  Virginia  is  responding  to  the  call  for  all  the  field  artillery. 
The  Examiner  also  says  that  ten  batteries  are  now  ready  for  immediate 
duty,  and  that  eight  or  ten  more  could  soon  be  got  ready. 

The  Examiner  further  remarks  that  President  Davis  has  so  far  recov¬ 
ered  from  his  recent  severe  illness  as  to  take  an  airing  in  a  carriage  on 
Saturday. 

It  it  stated  in  the  papers  that  Captain  Buchanan,  late  II.  S.  Navy,  is 
engaged  in  erecting  a  battery  near  the  White  House. 


Report  of  Captain  Craven,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  Potomac  Flotilla, 
urging  prompt  action  to  prevent  the  closing  of  the  Potomac  River. 

U.  S.  S.  Yankee, 

Off  Indian  Head,  September  14,  1861. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  acknowledge  the  receipt  of  your  commu¬ 
nication  of  yesterday,  with  its  enclosed  extract  from  the  Richmond 
Examiner. 

The  information  contained  in  this  paper  coincides  with  all  I  have 
been  able  to  pick  up  since  joining  this  flotilla,  and  I  am  fully  satisfied 
that  there  is  much  truth  in  it. 

Unless  something  is  speedily  done  to  protect  the  channels  at  Mathias 
and  Whitestone  points  [House]  the  Potomac  River  may  be  sooner  and 
more  effectually  closed  than  seems  to  be  apprehended  by  authorities  in 
Washington. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Thomas  T.  Craven, 
Commanding  Potomac  Flotilla. 

Hon.  G.  V.  Fox, 

Acting  Secretary  of  the  Navy,  Washington,  I).  C.

Report  of  Acting  Master's  Mate  Frank ,  TJ.  S.  Navy ,  commanding  TJ.  8. 
schooner  Howell  Cobh,  of  the  operations  of  his  vessel  from  September 


9-14,  1861. 


U.  S.  Schooner  Howell  Cobb, 

Potomac  River,  September  14,  1861. 

Sir  :  This  is  a  part  of  my  work  that  I  have  performed  since  9th  of 
this  present  month. 

September  10. — I  went  on  shore  at  Ledowes  Ferry,  Mr.  Henry  Fergu¬ 
son’s,  and  learned  that  there  was  a  boat  there,  [in]  which  he  had  been 
conveying  men  across  the  river  to  Virginia;  so  I  took  her  in  charge  and 
kept  her  until  Friday,  10th  [13th],  and  she  proved  to  leak  very  badly; 
so  I  had  her  cut  up. 

September  13. — I  took  three  men  on  board  from  Lower  Cedar  Point, 
who  were  fugitives  from  Richmond,  taken  at  the  battle  of  Manassas, 
from  their  statement,  viz:  First,  Quartermaster  Charles  J.  Murphy,  of 
the  Thirty-eighth  Regiment  Few  York  Volunteers;  Second,  Captain 
J.  R.  Hurd,  Second  Regiment  Kentucky  Volunteers,  Scott  Life  Guards; 
Third,  Lieutenant  W.  H.  Raynor,  First  Ohio  Regiment. 

13th. — I  took  a  reconnoissance  and  found  one  of  the  best  boats  that 
has  been  captured  for  the  use  of  the  secesh  [to]  cross  to  Mathias  Point.  It 
was  belonging  to  Mr.  George  Dent.  The  boat  was  used  on  the  12th  at 
night.  She  carried  over  four  men,  from  what  I  can  learn.  There  was 
some  wheat  to  go  on  the  same  night,  but  I  have  not  learned  whether 
the  wheat  went  or  not. 

Captain  Craven,  sir,  as  far  as  I  have  learned,  and  my  judgment  serves 
me,  I  think  it  would  be  advisable  to  have  three  or  four  of  these  gentle¬ 
men  arrested,  viz,  Mr.  Jones,  Mr.  Watson,  Mr.  Deut,  Mr.  Ferguson. 

I  boarded  twenty-one  vessels  on  the  14th,  bound  up  the  river,  laden 
with  assorted  articles — coal,  wood,  wheat,  hay,  oats,  lumber,  etc. 

Respectfully,  yours, 


Captain  Craven, 


A.  J.  Frank, 

Acting  Master's  Mate. 


U.  S.  S.  Yankee.

Report  of  Acting  Lieutenant  JBudd,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  commanding  TJ.  S.  S. 
Penguin,  regarding  movements  of  a  suspicious  vessel. 

U.  S.  S.  Penguin, 
Potomac  River,  September  15,  1861. 
Sir:  I  was  informed  last  evening  by  Captain  Cottrell,  of  schooner 
J.  R.  Griffiths,  employed  in  transporting  lumber  for  the  quartermaster’s 


OPERATIONS  ON  THE  POTOMAC  AND  RAPPAHANNOCK.  675 

department,  that  on  Thursday  afternoon  last,  when  between  Barn  [Bar¬ 
ren"?]  Island  and  Hooper  Strait  [Maryland],  he  saw  a  pungy  off  his  port 
bow,  and  when  near  Point  Lookout  he  distinctly  saw  from  thirty-five 
to  forty  men  on  her  deck.  She  stood  over  between  Goan  Greek  [River] 
and  Smith’s  Point.  I  desired  him  to  communicate  these  facts  to  you. 

I  have  further  to  report  that  in  accordance  with  your  permission  I 
allowed  Mr.  Posey  to  enter  the  creek  below  me  with  his  guano,  but 
hearing  subsequently  a  rumor  that  he  had  been  engaged  with  others 
previously  to  the  present  rigid  blockade  of  the  river  in  swimming 
horses  across  from  the  Maryland  side  to  the  Virginia  shore,  I  deemed 
it  my  duty  to  have  his  vessel  thoroughly  searched  and  shall  further 
attend  to  her.  He  had  quite  a  large  flatboat  in  tow. 

I  have  been  informed  by  Lieutenant  Commanding  McCrea  that  an 
order  existed  prohibiting  any  communication  between  the  officers  of  the 
flotilla  and  the  residents  on  the  Maryland  shore.  I  respectfully  ask 
whether  these  instructions  apply  to  supplies  of  vegetables  furnished  by 
the  negroes. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Thos.  A.  Btjdd, 

Acting  Lieutenant ,  Commanding  U.  S.  8.  Penguin. 

Captain  Thos.  T.  Craven, 

Commanding  Potomac  Flotilla. 


Order  of  the  Secretary  of  the  Navy  to  Captain  Craven ,  TJ.  8.  Navy , 
commanding  Potomac  Flotilla  regarding  supplies ,  in  view  of  the  pos¬ 
sible  closing  of  the  river. 

Kavy  Department,  September  15 ,  1861. 
Sir  :  The  Department  and  the  major-general  are  fully  apprised  of  the 
probability  of  closing  the  river  by  the  enemy  at  certain  points. 

In  such  an  event  supplies  must  be  conveyed  to  you  by  land,  and  the 
Department  will  thank  you  for  any  suggestions  as  to  the  point  where 
they  should  be  delivered,  as  well  as  any  other  considerations  connected 
with  such  a  movement  by  the  enemy.  You  will  notify  the  Department 
at  once  of  any  important  act  of  the  enemy  and  act  upon  your  own  good 
judgment  until  the  major-general  shall  feel  himself  called  upon  to  act. 
You  should  get  as  much  coal  and  provisions  as  possible  to  retain  your 
position  in  case  of  being  cut  off  above  and  below. 

I  am,  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Gideon  Welees. 

Captain  T.  T.  Craven, 

Commanding  Potomac  Flotilla. 


Report  of  Captain  Craven ,  TJ.  8.  Navy ,  commanding  Potomac  Flotilla , 
urging  immediate  occupation  of  Mathias  Point  by  United  States  troops. 

U.  S.  S.  Yankee, 

Off  Indian  Head ,  September  16,  1861. 
Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  acknowledge  the  receipt  of  your  communi¬ 
cation  of  the  15th,  in  reference  to  the  probability  of  the  closing  of  the 
river  by  the  enemy.  To  prevent  such  an  event  I  would  respectfully 


676  OPERATIONS  ON  THE  POTOMAC  AND  RAPPAHANNOCK. 

suggest  that  Mathias  Point  bo  immediately  taken  possession  of  and 
occupied  by  a  strong  body  of  our  troops.  Batteries  from  Chapman’s 
to  Marshall’s  points  would  command  the  opposite  positions  on  Hallow¬ 
ing  and  Whitestone  points.  To  prevent  the  possibility  of  the  enemy’s 
crossing  the  river,  either  I  must  have  a  much  more  powerful  and  efficient 
force  than  I  have  at  present,  or  I  should  be  backed  by  batteries  to  the 
positions  whence  the  enemy  would  be  most  likely  to  make  a  demonstra¬ 
tion.  Those  places,  in  my  opinion,  are  Occoquan  and  Neabsco  rivers, 
Powell’s,  Quantico,  Chopawamsic,  Aquia,  and  Potomac  creeks.  Should 
such  an  attempt  as  the  closing  of  the  river  by  the  enemy  be  successful, 
supplies  could  reach  me  at  or  near  the  mouth  of  the  Matta woman  Creek. 
While  employed  here  with  the  whole  of  my  force  to  guard  against  a 
possible  attempt  to  cross  the  river,  I  frequently  hear  rumors  and 
occasional  reports  of  the  intercourse  kept  up  from  the  Maryland  shore 
to  Mathias  Point.  Within  the  past  three  weeks  I  have  had  seized  from 
Pope’s  Creek  no  less  than  three  line  boats,  which  are  said  to  belong  to 
one  Mr.  Dent,  who  is  largely  engaged  in  the  transportation  to  Yirginia 
of  mails,  passengers,  and  munitions  of  war. 

Again,  sir,  I  beg  leave  to  remind  the  Department  of  the  very  inefficient 
condition  of  the  vessels  comprising  this  flotilla.  With  the  exception  of 
the  Pocahontas ,  Seminole,  Penguin,  and  Union ,  there  is  not  [one]  of  the 
steamers  that  is  not  liable,  in  consequence  of  the  exposed  condition  of 
their  engine,  to  utter  disability  by  even  a  musket  ball ;  and  besides  all 
this  there  are  almost  daily  complaints  from  some  one  of  them  of  repairs 
needed  to  engines,  strengthening  of  decks,  etc. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Thos.  T.  Craven, 
Commanding  Potomac  Flotilla. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy ,  Washington.

Dear  Sir  :  On  the  15th  I  sent  you  a  dispatch  by  the  steamer  Bal¬ 
timore,  but  not  hearing  from  you  I  avail  myself  of  this  opportunity  to 
report  to  you  these  few  facts. 


OPERATIONS  ON  THE  POTOMAC  ANI)  RAPPAHANNOCK.  679 


Sir,  last  Saturday  niglit  was  set  apart  by  Messrs.  Ferguson,  Watson, 
Jones,  and  Dent,  with  a  posse  of  1G  men  and  5  boats,  which  they  have 
in  Virginia,  from  what  I  can  learn,  to  capture  me  and  vessel.  I  was  at 
Lower  Cedar  Point  last  Saturday  night.  The  schooner  John  Wilson , 
of  Baltimore,  Captain  Benjamin  Hardy,  and  the  schooner  Catharine 
Jane ,  of  Baltimore,  Captain  Rosenbrock.  These  rebels  took  the  schoon¬ 
ers’  boats  and  took  two  loads  apiece,  and  sent  the  boats  back  and  said 
to  the  men  they  would  want  them  when  they  commenced  their  batteries 
in  Maryland. 

I  took  a  boat  from  Mr.  Ferguson  and  cut  her  up,  and  since  then  I 
took  Mr.  Dent’s  boat,  which  has  been  their  main  boat,  so  these  men  are 
hot  foot  after  me  and  threaten  to  capture  me  the  first  opportunity. 

Captain  Craven,  sir,  I  call  on  you  -for  more  arms  and  ammunition. 
If  you  please,  let  me  have  a  howitzer,  for  I  can  assure  you  it  is  for  the 
safety  of  the  vessel  and  crew.  If  you  should  send  me  any  help  I  think 
the  steamer  Rescue ,  Captain  Haines,  seems  to  be  well  acquainted,  and 
the  steamer  makes  less  noise  than  any  I  have  seen. 

If  you  conclude  to  send  the  arms,  I  should  like  four  men  more,  and  I 
think  that  we  can  take  care  of  ourselves  then  with  the  assistance  of  a 
steamer.  My  ammunition  is  getting  short  and  had  to  get  some  from 
Captain  Haines. 

We  are  well  at  present  but  the  cook,  who  has  something  of  a  bilious 
attack. 


I  hope,  captain,  this  will  meet  your  approbation. 
Respectfully,  yours. 


A.  J.  Frank. 


Captain  Craven.

U.  S.  S.  Rescue, 
Potomac  River,  September  20,  1861. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that  in  obedience  to  your  order  I 
proceeded  with  this  vessel,  on  the  18th  instant,  to  make  an  examination 
of  Mathias  Point  and  Pope’s  Creek.  On  arrival  at  the  latter  place  dis- 


680  OPERATIONS  ON  THE  POTOMAC  AND  RAPPAHANNOCK. 


covered  tlie  schooner  Harford ,  loaded  with  3,800  bushels  of  wheat  and 
160  hogsheads  of  tobacco.  She  being  without  papers  of  any  description 
I  seized  her,  and,  leaving  her  in  charge  of  Master’s  Mate  Frank,  com¬ 
manding  U.  S.  schooner  Dana,  I  returned  to  this  anchorage,  having 
discovered  nothing  suspicious  except  the  schooner  above  mentioned. 

Yesterday,  in  obedience  to  your  order,  I  proceeded  to  Pope’s  Creek 
for  the  purpose  of  towing  up  the  schooner  Harford ,  and  when  opposite 
the  house  of  Mr.  Grimes  was  fired  upon  with  musketry  by  a  force  of  at 
least  200  cavalry.  I  returned  the  fire  with  four  shell,  which  put  them 
to  flight.  While  at  Pope’s  Creek  I  received  on  board  two  negroes,  the 
property  of  Henry  Ferguson,  a  resident  of  Maryland,  living  on  the 
Maryland  shore  above  Cedar  Point.  The  negroes  inform  me  that  their 
owner,  Mr.  Ferguson,  has  been  engaged  in  carrying  mails  and  passen¬ 
gers  from  Maryland  to  Virginia  and  that  when  I  received  them  on 
board  they  were  returning  from  having  landed  Mr.  Ferguson  in  Virginia. 

My  master’s  mate  and  myself  know  that  the  schooner  Harford  had 
painted  on  her  stern  as  late  as  August  1,  u  Tappahannock,  Va.,” 
although  she  now  hails  from  Baltimore.  This  is  confirmed  by  one  of 
the  crew  now  on  board. 

From  Mr.  Burrows,  residing  at  Lower  Cedar  Point,  I  received  infor¬ 
mation  that  Mr.  George  Dent,  residing  on  the  high  bluff"  opposite 
Mathias  Point,  which  bluff  has  a  commanding  view  up  and  down  the 
river,  signalizes  to  the  rebels  at  Mathias  Point  all  the  movements  of 
the  flotilla. 

From  one  of  the  crew  of  the  schooner  Harford  I  have  the  following 
information:  George  Brent,  lawyer,  at  Port  Tobacco;  J.  H.  Neil,  two 
farms  above  Dent’s,  and  John  Ware,  first  farm  above  Dent’s,  have 
aided  in  conveying  men  and  provisions  to  Virginia. 

Walter  and  Heb  Mitchell,  residing  near  Port  Tobacco,  left  three  days 
since  to  join  the  rebels  in  Virginia.  John  Johnson,  William  Campbell, 
Alexander  Campbell,  Frank  Clements,  and  Alfred  Naley,  are  the  names 
of  the  parties  who  burned  the  light-boat.  All  of  them  are  now  in  Vir¬ 
ginia  except  the  latter,  who  resides  at  Chapel  Point,  Port  Tobacco 
Creek  [Biver]. 

Francis  Dilehay,  with  several  others,  took  up  arms,  joined  rebel  com¬ 
pany  organizing  at  Port  Tobacco.  He  is  still  in  Maryland  and  resides 
at  Chapel  Point. 

With  the  schooner  Harford  in  tow,  her  officers  and  crew  in  custody, 
and  the  negroes  received  on  board  at  Pope’s  Creek,  I  returned  to  this 
anchorage  at  1  a.  m.  this  morning. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Edward  L.  Haines, 

Commanding  Steamer  Rescue. 

Commodore  Thomas  T.  Craven,  U.  S.  Navy, 

Commanding  Potomac  Flotilla.

Report  of  Lieutenant  Wyman ,  II.  8.  Wavy,  commanding  U.  8.  8.  Poca¬ 
hontas,  of  reconnoissance  of  Whitestone  Point. 

U.  S.  S.  Pocahontas,  September  19, 1861. 

Dear  Sir  :  From  the  reconnoissance  made  last  night  of  Whitestone 
Point  there  are  no  troops,  breastworks,  or  anything  of  the  kind  there; 
neither  have  there  been  any  troops  there.  About  2  miles  up  the  creek 
(Pohick)  there  is  a  body  of  troops,  but  how  many  could  not  be  ascer¬ 
tained.  We  have  been  lying  here  now  two  days  and  no  court  yet.  Our 
coal  is  in,  dues  and  boilers  cleaned,  and  we  are  ready  to  go.  I  suppose 
that  the  court  will  meet  to-day.  There  is  nothing  new  here.  The 
Underwriter  looks  as  if  she  might  be  ready  in  a  week,  and  the  Forbes  is 
on  the  ways.  I  have  not  seen  Captain  Dove,  but  intend  calling  there 
this  forenoon. 

^Respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

E.  H.  Wyman, 
[Lieutenant,  Commanding. \ 

Captain  Craven.

constant  intercourse  between  Maryland  and  Virginia. 

U.  S.  S.  Yankee,  September  30,  1861. 

Sir  :  From  all  I  can  hear  there  is  a  considerable  traffic  being  carried 
on  between  the  eastern  shore  of  Maryland  and  the  mouth  of  the  Rap¬ 
pahannock  River,  and  below  Mathias  Point  there  is  almost  constant 
intercourse  between  the  rebels  and  the  Maryland  shore. 

If  there  is  no  further  apprehension  of  the  enemy’s  attempting  a  pas¬ 
sage  across  this  river,  1  would  like  to  make  a  reconnoissance  about  the 
places  above  indicated. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Thos.  T.  Craven, 
Commanding  Potomac  Flotilla.

Letter  from  Acting  Master's  Mate  Bentrich ,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S. 
tug  E.  H.  Herbert,  to  Captain  Craven,  commanding  Potomac  Flotilla, 
requesting  instructions  in  regard  to  the  destruction  of  boats  on  the  river. 

Steam  Tug  E.  H.  Herbert,  September  31, 1861.  . 
Sir:  The  steam  tug  Resolute  hailed  me  at  midnight  September  19, 
and  stated  that  the  captain  of  the  Lee  Boat  gave  him  orders  to  bring 
away  or  destroy  a  certain  fishing  boat  in  Chicomuxen  Creek,  and  he 
requested  that  I  might  attend  to  the  matter.  On  Friday  afternoon  I 
took  my  yawl  boat,  lead,  and  line  and  proceeded  up  the  creek.  I  saw 
several  boats,  some  on  the  shore  and  two  housed.  The  person  I  met  on 
shore  (Mr.  Posey)  claimed  longboat  General  Worth,  an  old  affair  sunk 
since  December,  I860. 

Mr.  Posey  owns  two  good  boats,  housed,  20  and  21  feet  keel,  used  for 
gilling  and  occasionally  going  to  mill  in  Virginia;  one  small  scow;  also 
Rising  Sun ,  licensed,  and  a  scow  tender  and  bateau  for  Rising  Sun. 


684  OPERATIONS  ON  THE  POTOMAC  AND  RAPPAHANNOCK. 


I  was  informed  that  one  good  boat  on  the  shore  belonged  to  a  Mr. 
Joseph  K.  Spransey,  formerly  of  Marcus  Hook,  Pa.,  now  working  in  the 
navy  yard,  Washington,  as  a  ship  carpenter.  J.  L.  Speake  owns  a  boat; 
also  Captain  Wheeler  one  boat.  A  large  seine  boat  lies  sunk  at  the 
head  of  the  creek.  I  saw  two  wherries  at  the  upper  point  at  the  entrance 
of  the  creek.  Not  having  official  notice  for  the  taking  or  destroying 
any  boats,  I  conferred  with  Captain  Budd,  of  the  steamer  Penguin ,  who 
deemed  it  advisable  to  bring  the  matter  before  you  for  such  instructions 
as  you  may  be  pleased  to  give  in  the  case. 

I  would  respectfully  ask  if  it  is  right  to  ask  questions  of  a  citizen  of 
Maryland,  as  in  the  above  case,  when  information  for  the  U.  S.  Gov¬ 
ernment  may  be  obtained  without  committing  myself  in  questioning 


parties. 

Bespectfully,  yours,

Report  of  Midshipman  Walker ,  U.  8.  Wavy,  regarding  sloop  Maryland 
and  signals  between  the  Maryland  and  Virginia  shores. 

IJ.  S.  Steam  Sloop  Seminole, 

Potomac  Flotilla ,  September  22 ,  1861. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  make  the  following  report: 

Last  night,  while  cruising  between  Indian  Head  and  Chapman’s  Point, 
rapid  signals  were  discovered  between  the  Virginia  and  Maryland 
shores.  Pulling  in  toward  the  latter  side,  I  discovered  and  boarded  a 
small  sloop,  the  Maryland ,  but  found  no  persons  on  board.  Her  sails 
were  loosed  and  the  cabin  hatch  left  open,  although  the  weather  was 
very  inclement  and  rainy.  On  boarding  her  a  signal  was  made  from 
the  Maryland  shore,  and  I  was  hailed  with  “What  boat  is  that!” 
Keturning  no  answer,  all  lights  were  at  once  extinguished. 

Judging  from  circumstances  and  contents  of  vessel  (a  list  of  which 
is  herein  enclosed),  I  sent  her  to  the  Seminole.  Continuing  the  cruise, 
the  signals  still  being  exchanged  between  the  two  shores,  I  ran  close  in 
to  the  Maryland  side  and  remained  for  about  an  hour,  when  all  signals 
ceased. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Edward  A.  Walker, 

Midshipman.  U.  S.  Navy. 

Captain  T.  T.  Craven,  U.  S.  Navy, 

Commanding  Potomac  Flotilla.

[Enclosure.] 

Oepice  Superintendent  Metropolitan  Police, 

New  Yorlc,  September  24,  1861. 

Sir  :  A  day  or  two  since  I  received  intimations  that  parties  in  Phila¬ 
delphia  were  forwarding  pistols,  fuses,  caps,  etc.,  in  vessels  sailing 
from  that  port  up  the  Potomac,  with  hay,  etc.,  which  were  landed  on 
the  Virginia  side  of  the  river. 

1  was  also  informed  that  it  made  but  little  difference  whether  the 
vessels  were  in  the  employ  of  the  Government  or  not,  as  the  price  paid 
for  carrying  such  articles  was  liberal. 

To-day  I  am  further  informed  that  the  principal  operator  in  that  way 
was  William  Gilchrist,  who  was  arrested  at  Philadelphia  a  day  or  two 
since  and  sent  to  [Fort]  Lafayette. 

I  telegraphed  to  you  to-day  to  search  vessels  having  hay  on  board 
coming  up  the  Potomac.  I  would  now  add,  that  it  now  appears  proper 
that  the  search  should  be  thoroughly  made.  There  is  little  doubt  that 
vessels  both  from  Philadelphia  and  Baltimore  have  been  so  employed 
as  well  as  from  other  places. 

Very  truly,  yours, 


Hon.  W.  H.  Seward, 

Secretary  of  State. 


John  A.  Kennedy, 

Superintendent.

Report  of  Lieutenant  McCrea ,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  TJ.  8.  8.  Jacob 
Bell,  of  information  obtained  regarding  batteries  at  Evansport ,  Va. 


IT.  S.  S.  [Jacob]  Bell,  Potomac  Flotilla, 

Off  Indian  Head,  September  24,  1861. 

Sir:  Considering  the  following  intelligence  and  report  of  great  and 
immediate  value  I  send  it  directly  to  the  Department,  the  commander 
in  chief  being  absent  down  the  river  some  ten  hours  distant,  leaving 
me  senior  officer  present  at  this  point  commanding  the  division.  The 
following  is  a  copy  of  my  dispatch  to  the  commodore,  which  I  sent 
immediately  to  him  by  a  tng: 

I  proceeded  to  Indian  Head  this  day  at  meridian.  I  took  that  anchorage  to  facili¬ 
tate  overhauling  vessels,  as  all  vessels  were  sent  to  me  for  examination.  As  soon  as 
anchored  a  person  came  down  to  the  beach  in  front  of  Smoot’s  house.  I  sent  a  boat 
and  brought  him  off.  He  proved  to  be  Lieutenant  [E.  A.]  Sherburne,  of  the  Arkan¬ 
sas  regiment,  in  the  service  of  the  Confederates.  I  have  examined  him  and  gleaned 
the  following :  He  was  a  two  years’  resident  of  Arkansas,  formerly  of  Wisconsin ;  his 
regiment  is  encamped  a  short  distance  hack  of  Evansport;  he  left  the  lines  yester¬ 
day  at  3  p.  in.,  and  left  the  Virginia  shore  at  dark,  having  constructed  a  raft  of 
wood  logs  to  get  across  the  river.  He  landed  near  Budd’s  Ferry  and  came  up  on 
foot  till  opposite  to  my  anchorage.  He  reports  erecting  heavy  batteries  at  Evans¬ 
port  and  along  the  connecting  shore  1|  miles;  four  rifled  guns  and  one  64-pounder 
at  Evansport.  Lieutenant  Simms,  formerly  U.  S.  Navy,  conducts  operations;  their 
object,  says  Lieutenant  Simms,  is  to  get  all  ready  with  their  batteries,  leaving  the 
woods  up  in  front  of  their  works  till  then,  when  at  night  “let  fall”  and  open  on  the 
vessels.  He  says  there  are  10,000  troops  within  one  and  a  half  hours  from  Evans¬ 
port,  General  Holmes,  brigadier-general  commanding;  and  that  the  St.  Nicholas, 
steamer,  is  fitting  out  at  Fredericksburg.  He  speaks  of  the  men  of  the  Confede¬ 
rates  as  indifferently  supplied  with  blankets  and  shoes. 

I  made  a  reconnoissance  of  all  the  shore  near  where  he  mentions  the 
batteries  and  found  his  information  correct  as  far  as  points  go,  but 
could  not  see  any  guns,  though  evidently  a  change  since  my  last  scout 
of  the  Virginia  shore  some  four  days  ago.  At  Freestone  Point  I 
observed  persons  on  the  hill  evidently  laying  out  positions  for  batteries, 
and  I  am  informed  by  some  contrabands  that  200  men  are  employed 
digging  at  night,  and  that  there  are  now  two  guns  mounted.  The 
thick  chaparral  makes  it  impossible  to  see  anything  beyond  the  front, 
though  I  go  as  close  as  the  draft  of  my  vessel  will  permit  (about  6  feet 
is  the  draft).  I  would  inform  the.  Department  that  I  am  in  no  condi¬ 
tion  for  attacking  batteries,  having  carried  the  deck  away  forward, 
which  supports  my  8-inch  shell  gun,  a  month  ago  while  engaged  with 
the  batteries  at  Potomac  Creek.  I  have  only  15  working  men;  the  for¬ 
ward  gun  demands  14,  after  one  10;  but  I  will  go  in  and  attack  any 
battery  and  fight  my  guns  till  they  go  through  the  bottom.  This  ves¬ 
sel  has  not  been  at  the  yard  for  repairs  (or  fitting  up).  She  had  two 
guns  put  on  her  upon  her  arrival  there  from  New  York,  and  sent  down 
to  tow  a  lot  of  launches,  to  return  immediately;  that  was  on  the  20th 
of  August.  She  has  been  down  ever  since.  No  accommodations  for 
officers  or  men  for  the  coming  winter. 

I  have  the  honor,  sir,  to  be  your  obedient  servant, 

Edward  P.  McCrea, 

Lieutenant ,  Commanding,  and  Senior  Officer  Present. 

[Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy.] 

I  sent  Lieutenant  Sherburn[e]  to  the  commander  in  chief  per  tug 
Herbert. 


E.  P.  McC.

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that  this  morning  at  7  o’clock  a 
party  of  contrabands,  consisting  of  four  men  and  one  woman,  was 
picked  up  by  a  boat  from  this  ship  while  making  their  way  out  from

one  T.  B.  Robinson,  of  Ohio  Farm,  Virginia,  and  report  that  there  are 
in  [and]  about  that  vicinity  about  400  armed  men,  and  that  two  days 
since  they  commenced  erecting  a  battery  on  Freestone  Point,  about  4 
miles  from  our  present  anchorage,  and  that  200  men  with  two  heavy 
siege  guns  passed  through  their  place  yesterday.  They  tell  a  consistent 
story,  but  none  have  positix  ely  seen  the  aforesaid  battery. 

As  the  presence  of  the  woman,  from  want  of  accommodation,  is  rather 
embarrassing,  I  respectfully  request,  at  your  convenience,  instructions 
as  to  their  disposition. 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant,

Sir:  In  compliance  with  a  general  order  issued  by  Captain  Craven,

erty  for  safe-keeping,  viz :

penter  working  in  the  navy  yard.  It  was  in  care  of  a  Mr.  Posey,  noted 
for  secession  proclivities.  You  will  perceive  the  ground  of  seizure,  etc. 

No.  2.  A  wherry,  or  bateau,  owned  by  a  man  in  Alexandria.  Why  not 
keep  his  wherry  at  home? 

No.  3.  A  wherry,  or  bateau;  the  owner,  or  reported  owner,  is  a  slave; 
the  property  of  a  James  Milsted,  secessionist,  a  resident  of  Chicomuxen. 

The  above  doubtless  have  been  used  to  carry  night  mail  across  to 
Virginia,  and  in  order  to  suppress  the  business  as  far  as  practicable  I 
have  seized  the  above.  I  shall  hereafter  seize  all  boats  when  there  is 
just  room  for  suspicion,  and  send  them  to  the  navy  yard. 

Respectfully,  etc., 

Charles  Bentrick,  U.  S.  Navy. 

Captain  Dahlgren.

[Enclosure.] 

U.  S.  S.  Jacob  Bell, 

Indian  Head ,  Potomac  River ,  September  25,  1861. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  submit  the  following  report: 

This  morning  about  sunrise  I  discovered  men  at  work  digging,  etc., 
at  Freestone  Poiut.  I  got  underway  at  9.30  a.  m.  (having  satisfied 
myself  that  they  were  making  batteries)  in  company  with  the  Seminole , 
Lieutenant  Norton  in  charge.  I  ordered  her  to  follow  my  motions.  We 
proceeded  to  Freestone  Point,  and  I  went  in  and  fired  six  shells,  dis¬ 
persing  the  workmen.  Receiving  no  return  of  fire  I  stood  out.  At 
that  moment  the  Seminole  opened  fire  with  her  battery,  which  was 
immediately  answered  from  the  said  point  with  rifled  shots,  disclosing 
the  existence  of  a  battery  there.  The  Seminole  continued  her  fire  some 
time,  answered  continually  by  the  battery  on  shore.  After  she  fired 
sufficiently  long,  in  my  opinion,  I  ordered  her  to  cease  firing  and  return 
to  her  anchorage.  After  taking  a  curve  by  the  nature  of  the  channel, 
and  on  standing  up  the  river,  she  was  fired  upon  by  the  battery  on 
shore,  which  she  returned;  and  while  passing  the  Valley  City  she  was 
informed  that  a  shot  from  shore  had  passed  through  the  bows  of  the 
said  vessel;  and  not  having  sufficient  steam  to  make  any  progress  to 
get  out  of  the  reach  of  the  enemy’s  battery,  requested  Lieutenant  Norton 
to  tow  him  toward  Indian  Head,  which  was  done.  The  enemy’s  battery 
continued  their  fire  upon  all  vessels  and  steamers  passing  up  and  down 
until  3  ii.  m.  To  the  best  of  my  judgment  there  are  four  guns  at  said 
battery,  one  rifled  gun,  extreme  range,  as  many  of  their  shots  during 
their  firing  almost  touched  the  Maryland  shore.  No  one  was  injured 
during  the  action,  the  officers  and  men  firing  deliberately  and  coolly. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  your  obedient  servant, 

Edward  P.  McCrea, 
Lieutenant ,  Commanding ,  U.  S.  Navy. 

Commander  John  P.  Gillis, 

Commanding  Division  of  Potomac  Flotilla. 


Further  report  of  Lieutenant  McCrea,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Jacob  Bell. 

H.  S.  S.  Jacob  Bell, 

At  Anchor  off  Indian  Head ,  Potomac  River ,  September  26,  1861. 

Sir  :  I  herewith  submit  the  following  report  of  my  attack  upon  Free¬ 
stone  Point  yesterday.  I  have  already  written  one  and  forwarded  it 
to  Captain  [J.  P.j  Gillis,  of  the  Seminole,  who  arrived  at  this  point  last 
evening  after  the  affair.  Under  pressure  of  time  I  was  unable  to  keep 
a  copy  for  you  as  commander  in  chief  upon  your  arrival  here: 

At  sunrise  yesterday  morning  I  discovered  a  number  of  men  digging 
N  w  R — YOL  4 - 44 


690  OPERATIONS  ON  THE  POTOMAC  AND  RAPPAHANNOCK. 

and  throwing  up  earthworks  on  Freestone  Point.  After  having  satis¬ 
fied  myself  that  they  were  engaged  in  erecting  batteries  on  said  point, 
I  got  underway  in  company  with  the  Seminole ,  Lieutenant  Norton  in 
charge,  and  stood  close  to  the  point.  At  about  9:30  a.  m.,  I  got  close 
under  the  point  and  opened  my  guns  with  shell,  throwing  several 
among  the  workmen,  dispersing  them.  After  having  fired  sufficiently 
long  without  any  return  of  fire  I  stood  out  from  underneath  the  point. 
At  that  moment  a  shot  was  fired  at  me  from  the  point.  The  Seminole 
also  about  that  time  opened  her  guns  upon  the  discovered  battery, 
planting  her  shell  fairly.  After  thirty  minutes  continued  firing  on  both 
sides,  I  ordered  the  Seminole  to  cease  firing  and  return  to  her  anchor¬ 
age.  The  enemy  then  turned  their  fire  upon  the  Valley  City.  The 
Seminole ,  by  the  nature  of  the  channel,  could  not  turn  at  once,  in  obedi¬ 
ence  to  my  orders,  but  was  obliged  to  take  a  curve,  which  brought 
her  close  to  the  Valley  City ,  when  he  was  informed  by  Captain  Chaplin 
that  a  shot  had  passed  through  his  bows,  and  not  having  sufficient 
steam  to  get  quickly  out  of  the  enemy’s  line  of  fire,  he  requested  Lieu¬ 
tenant  Norton  to  take  him  in  tow  to  follow  me. 

All  the  vessels  of  this  division,  namely,  Seminole ,  Valley  City ,  Pen¬ 
guin ,  Satellite,  Murray ,  and  this  vessel,  anchored  here  at  about  meridian. 
The  enemy  continued  their  fire  on  all  the  vessels  passing  up  and  down 
the  river  until  about  3  p.  m.,  when  they  ceased.  I  judge  from  close 
observation,  only  three  guns  were  in  use  and  mounted,  though  they  no 
doubt  attempted  by  their  rapid  firing  to  deceive  us  in  the  idea  that 
they  had  more.  They  are  rifled  guns  and  of  long  range,  for  I  observed 
many  of  their  shot  striking  close  to  the  Maryland  shore.  No  one  was 
injured ;  the  officers  and  men  acting  deliberately  and  coolly  throughout. 

The  Murray ,  in  charge  of  Midshipman  McGlensey,  took  in  tow  a 
launch  that  was  anchored  in  front  of  the  enemy’s  batteries,  which  drew 
a  fire  upon  her,  but  she  accomplished  it  without  any  injury  to  herself 
or  those  on  board. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Edward  P.  McCrea, 

Lieutenant ,  Commanding ,  and  Senior  Commanding  Officer 

Of  this  Division  During  the  Engagement. 

Captain  T.  T.  Craven, 

Commanding  Potomac  Flotilla.

Report  of  Colonel  Wigfall,  C.  S.  Army,  commanding  First  Texas  Infantry. 


Dumfries,  September  25, 1861. 

The  fleet  lying  in  this  portion  of  the  river  sent  an  armed  tug  to  feel 
our  batteries.  She  fired  ten  shots  into  the  point  occupied  by  Hamp¬ 
ton’s  battery  before  they  were  returned.  The  battery  then  drove  her 
off.  The  war  steamers  then  opened.  We  fired  thirty  shots;  the  enemy 
twenty-two.  General  Whiting  ordered  the  firing  to  continue  after  they 
ceased  to  show  them  we  could  drive  them.  The  fleet  is  now  divided — 
part  above  Powell’s  Kun  and  part  below.  When  Stevens’s  batteries 
are  ready  they  will  stop  the  lower  detachment  of  the  fleet.  The  infan¬ 
try  supports  are  active  and  ready.  If  the  enemy  land  our  knowledge 
of  the  ground  will  make  us  equal  to  ten  times  our  numbers.  All  are 
cheerful,  and  the  army  will  send  you  its  congratulations  if  a  serious 
action  results. 

Your  friend, 

Louis  T.  Wigfael. 


President  Jefferson  Davis.

Report  of  Lieutenant  Haggerty ,  U.  8.  Navy,  commanding  U.  8.  brig 
Perry,  regarding  batteries  at  Freestone  Point ,  Va. 

U.  S.  Brio  Perry, 

Off  Alexandria,  September  26,  1861. 

Sir:  I  respectfully  make  known  to  you  tlie  following  intelligence: 
Acting  Master  Lelar,  attached  to  this  vessel,  while  performing  guard 
duty  last  evening,  boarded  two  vessels  on  their  passage  up  the  Potomac 
Kiver,  the  captains  of  which  informed  him  that  in  passing  a  place  on  the 
river  called  Freestone  Point,  they  were  tired  at  from  shore  batteries,  and 
subsequently  Acting  Master  French  boarded  several  vessels,  bound  up 
to  Washington,  the  captains  of  all  of  them  stating  that  while  passing 
the  same  place  their  vessels  were  fired  at,  and  that  men  were  employed 
on  shore  in  clearing  away  trees  and  other  obstacles  from  about  these 
batteries. 

I  remain,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

F.  S.  Haggerty, 
Lieutenant,  Commanding.

Instructions  from  the  Secretary  of  the  Navy  to  Captain  Craven,  U.  8. 
Navy,  commanding  Potomac  Flotilla ,  relative  to  contrabands  ( fugitive 
slaves). 

Navy  Department,  September  25,  1861. 
Sir  :  The  Department  finds  it  necessary  to  adopt  a  regulation  with 
respect  to  the  large  and  increasing  number  of  persons  of  color,  com¬ 
monly  known  as  contraband,  now  subsisted  at  the  navy  yards  and  on 
board  ships  of  war.  They  can  neither  be  expelled  from  the  sendee  to 
which  they  have  resorted,  nor  can  they  be  maintained  unemployed, 
and  it  is  not  proper  that  they  should  be  compelled  to  render  necessary 
and  regular  services  without  a  stated  compensation.  You  are  there¬ 
fore  authorized,  when  their  services  can  be  made  useful,  to  enlist  them 
for  the  naval  service,  under  the  same  forms  and  regulations  as  apply 
to  other  enlistments.  They  will  be  allowed,  however,  no  higher  rating 
than  boys,  at  a  compensation  of  $10  per  month  and  one  ration  a  day, 

I  am,  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy. 

Captain  Thomas  T.  Craven, 

Commanding  Potomac  Flotilla.

II .  S.  Steam  Sloop  Seminole, 

Off  Lndian  Head,  Potomac  River,  September  28,  1861. 
Sir:  William  O’Donohue,  orderly  sergeant  of  the  the  Sixty-ninth 
Regiment  of  New  York  Volunteers,  taken  x>risoner  at  the  battle  of  Bull 
Pun,  escaped  from  Richmond  on  the  18th  instant,  crossed  the  Potomac 
on  a  raft  from  bight  above  Freestone  Point  (Oecoquau  Bay),  left  two 


OPERATIONS  ON  THE  POTOMAC  AND  RAPPAHANNOCK.  695 

other  escaped  prisoners  in  an  old  fishing  house  at  same  place;  their 
names,  Kelly  and  James  Rorty,  of  the  Sixty-ninth. 

Officers  and  men,  prisoners  at  Richmond,  lie  says,  are  confined  in 
tobacco  warehouses,  without  any  conveniences;  not  even  a  blanket 
supplied. 

O’Douohue  reports  a  great  number  of  rifle  cannon  passing  through 
Richmond  toward  Yorktown,  and  some  fifty  army  wagons,  new  harness, 
and  tine  mules,  going  same  direction.  North  of  Richmond  are  two  forts, 
one  like  Fort  Corcoran.  Colonel  Corcoran  and  about  28  officers  and 
130  privates  sent  to  Charleston  10th  September.  Many  of  our  men 
attempted  to  escape,  but  were  brought  back.  All  citizens  of  the  country 
around  Richmond  and  in  other  parts  of  Virginia  act  as  police.  Negroes 
arrested  two  of  our  men.  He  further  states  that  1J  miles  from  Free¬ 
stone  Point  are  two  camps  of  the  rebels,  one  infantry,  the  other  cavalry. 
He  has  other  information  which  he  will  impart  on  arrival  at  Washing¬ 
ton.  WTill  send  him  to  Captain  Dahlgren,  commandant  of  navy  yard, 
for  your  disposal. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Jno.  P.  Gillis, 

Commander. 

Hon.  Gideon  Wtelles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy,  Washington.

[Enclosure.] 

U.  S.  Steam  Sloop  Seminole, 
Potomac  Flotilla,  off  Lndian  Head,  September  27,  1861. 

Sir:  I  beg  leave  to  lay  before  you  the  following  statement  with 
regard  to  the  collision  between  the  gunboat  Valley  City,  Captain 
Chaplin,  and  the  U.  S.  S.  Seminole  on  the  25th  instant: 

While  standing  down  the  river,  in  passing  the  Valley  City  I  saw  a 
shell  from  the  battery  go  through  her  bows  and  her  men  attempting  to 
lift  her  anchor  in  great  haste.  On  my  return,  in  about  fifteen  minutes 
after,  I  was  hailed  by  the  commanding  officer  of  the  Valley  City  and 
asked  to  take  his  hawser  and  tow  him  out  from  under  fire,  at  the  same 
time  waving  a  white  handkerchief,  which  1  took  to  be  a  signal  of 
distress. 

I  backed  in  toward  him  to  meet  his  boat  with  the  end  of  his  hawser, 
and  when  about  three  ship’s  lengths  off,  1  first  discovered  that  he  was 
underway  under  steam  and  had  considerable  headway. 

I  immediately  reversed  our  engines,  put  the  helm  hard  aport,  hailed, 
and  told  him  to  put  his  helm  to  starboard,  as  he  was  pointing  directly 
for  our  starboard  mizzen  chains. 

Before  we  could  overcome  our  sternway  and  start  her  ahead  the  stem 
of  the  Valley  City  struck  us  just  over  the  starboard  stern  port  (see 
enclosed  report  of  carpenter). 

There  was  an  abundance  of  time  and  space  for  the  Valley  City  to 
have  avoided  us  had  she  minded  her  helm,  nor  did  I  see  any  indica- 


OPERATIONS  ON  THE  POTOMAC  AND  RAPPAHANNOCK.  697 


tion  of  an  attempt  upon  tliat  vessel’s  part  to  reverse  tier  engines,  and, 
by  checking  lier  own  headway,  thus  avoid  collision. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

C.  S.  Norton, 
Lieutenant ,  U.  S.  Navy. 

Commander  John  P.  Gillis, 

Commanding  U.  8.  8.  Seminole. 


[Subenclosure.] 

U.  S.  Steam  SLOor  Seminole, 
Potomac  Flotilla,  off  Indian  Head,,  September  28,  1861. 

Sir  :  I  have  the  honor  to  make  the  following  report  of  defects  of  this 
vessel : 

The  head  is  started  to  starboard  some  2  inches,  from  the  effects  of 
the  collision  with  the  U.  S.  frigate  Wabash.  It  sways,  and  head  sail 
can  not  be  set  in  heavy  weather  when  at  sea. 

The  ship  usually  makes  from  16  to  18  inches  of  water  in  the  twenty- 
four  hours,  increasing  considerably  after  the  firing  of  guns. 

The  lower  boxes  of  the  main  pumps  have  to  be  drawn  almost  always 
after  pumping,  on  account  of  coal  choking  up  the  boxes.  This  can  not 
be  remedied  without  free  access  to  the  bottom  of  the  pipes,  which  can 
not  be  had  except  at  such  times  as  the  coal  bunkers  are  empty. 

The  bilge  water  is  very  bad,  which  I  judge  is  caused  by  the  decom¬ 
position  of  chips,  coal  dust,  and  drippings  of  oil  from  the  machinery 
between  the  timbers,  as  there  is  no  filling  in  the  ship. 

There  appear  to  be  no  limbers  under  the  engine,  as  the  water  can  not 
flow  aft.  The  limber  chain  runs  only  from  the  after  part  of  the  engine 
to  the  after  part  of  ship.  It  should  run  fore  and  aft. 

The  damage  sustained  by  our  collision  with  the  Valley  City  is  as  fol¬ 
lows:  Stove  in  the  main  rail  on  starboard  quarter  over  the  after  port; 
started  the  battery  [sic]  and  portion  of  plank  below  after  port,  and 
that  portion  of  plank  shear.  Both  the  battery  [sic]  and  rail  1  find  to 
be  rotten,  so  much  so  that  the  fastenings  will  be  very  insecure,  and  1 
have  no  means  of  repairing  it. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Jacob  M.  Dallas, 

Carpenter ,  U.  8.  Navy. 

Commander  John  P.  Gillis, 

Commanding  U.  8.  8.  Seminole.

Report,  of  commandant  navy  yard ,  Washington ,  of  the  readiness  of  the 
U.  S.  S.  Under  writer  for  service  in  the  Potomac  Flotilla. 

Commandant’s  Office,  Navy  Yard, 

Washington ,  October  1,  1861. 

Sir  :  The  Underwriter  has  been  made  fully  equal  to  any  service  and 
was  in  readiness  to  join  the  flotilla  last  night.  In  lifting  her  for  an 
armament  it  was  necessary  to  replace  the  slight  deck  beams  and  plank 
entirely,  so  as  to  endure  the  weight  of  the  heavy  guns.  The  bottom 
required  calking  and  was  also  coppered. 

These,  with  repairs  of  boiler  and  engine  and  a  renewal  of  the  joiner’s 
work,  are  estimated  to  have  cost  about  $9,000,  so  that  the  expense  of 
the  vessel  in  her  present  condition  has  been  $27,500. 

She  is,  however,  in  the  most  complete  order  except  the  boiler,  which 
may  last  six  months. 

The  frame  and  planking  were  found  to  be  strong  and  perfectly  sound, 
a  few  feet  of  stuff  replacing  all  the  unsound  plank  in  her  bottom. 

The  vessel  mounts  a  rifled  80-pounder  and  an  8-iuch  shell-gun  of  03 
hundredweight,  one  rifled  and  one  smooth  12-pounder. 

She  carries  also  more  than  two  months  provisions,  is  very  fast,  and 
of  light  draft. 

I  consider  her  the  best  vessel  of  the  class  that  has  been  at  this  yard, 
and  obtained  at  a  much  less  price  than  paid  for  vessels  much  inferior, 
if  I  am  correctly  informed. 

In  this  connection  I  may  mention  a  sample  of  quick  work  last  night. 
The  \R.  B.]  Forbes ,  which,  but  for  the  neglect  of  a  master  workman, 
would  have  been  launched  in  the  morning,  was  not  afloat  till  the  after¬ 
noon  tide,  about  4  p.  in.,  and  it  was  5  o’clock  before  she  was  under  the 
shears.  In  four  hours  her  masts  had  been  hoisted  in,  stepped,  and  the 
rigging  set  up,  the  armament  on  board,  powder,  shells,  etc.,  stowed, 
provisions  and  water  in,  steam  up,  men  aboard,  and  all  ready  to  join 
the  flotilla  and  go  into  action  by  9  p.  m.,  the  greater  part  of  the  work 
being  done  by  the  light  of  lanterns. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Jno.  A.  Daiilgren, 

Commandant ; 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Wavy.

Report  of  Captain  Craven ,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  Potomac  Flotilla , 

relative  to  collision  between  Ut  S.  S.  Yankee  and  schooner  Samuel  B. 

Grice. 

U.  S.  S.  Yankee,  October  3,  1861. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  ackowledge  the  receipt  of  your  letter  of 
the  2d  instant  asking  for  a  statement  of  the  circumstances  attending 
the  collision  between  this  vessel  and  the  schooner  Samuel  B.  Grice. 

On  Saturday  evening  at  about  8  o’clock,  the  night  being  quite  dark, 
the  pilots  suddenly  discovered  a  schooner  on  our  starboard  bow;  we 
were  then  hard  over  on  the  east  side  of  the  channel,  and  about  1J 
miles  below  Alexandria.  Immediately  upon  the  discovery  of  the 
schooner  (which  was  at  that  time  supposed  to  be  at  anchor)  the  engines 
were  stopped.  A  moment  thereafter  the  schooner  was  discovered  to  be 
underway  and  standing  directly  toward  our  starboard  bow.  The  ves¬ 
sel  was  hailed  and  ordered  to  put  his  helm  hard  down,  that  is,  astar- 
board,  which  he  failed  to  do,  and,  as  a  collision  was  inevitable,  our 
pilots,  very  properly,  to  avoid  being  struck  on  our  broadside,  put  our 
helm  hard  aport.  The  consequence  was  that  we  took  her  on  her  port 
bow,  starting  three  or  four  of  her  planks  and  carrying  away  her  bow¬ 
sprit.  The  damage  sustained  by  the  schooner  could  not,  in  my  opinion, 
amount  to  more  than  $150. 

When  the  Grice  was  first  discovered  this  vessel  was  going  at  the 
rate  of  about  7  knots,  or  at  half  speed;  the  schooner  had  shown  no 
lights,  and  from  the  discovery,  or  alarm,  to  the  moment  of  colliding  the 
time  was  scarcely  a  minute  and  a  half. 

We  towed  the  schooner  up  and  secured  her  to  a  wharf  at  Alexandria. 
V ery  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Thos.  T.  Graven, 
Commanding  Potomac  Flotilla. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy,  Washington,  I).  C.

Report  of  Captain  Craven,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  Potomac  Flotilla, 
regarding  increase  of  Confederate  force. 

IT.  S.  S.  Yankee,  October  3,  1861. 

Sir:  Lieutenant  Commanding  Magaw,  who  has  just  come  up  from 
Aquia  Creek  for  the  purpose  of  filling  up  his  water,  informs  me  that 
within  the  last  twenty-four  hours  there  has  been  a  large  increase  of 
rebel  forces  at  the  mouth  of  Potomac  Creek.  He  supposed  there  are 
about  three  regiments  now  encamped  at  that  place. 

I  noticed  this  morning  what  appeared  to  be  smoke  from  camp  fires 
extending  from  Powell’s  Creek  along  the  road  toward  Dumfries,  a  dis¬ 
tance  of  some  3  or  4  miles.  Excepting  these  indications  of  the  presence 
of  a  large  force  of  the  enemy  between  Occoquan  and  Aquia,  everything 
is  quiet  along  the  river. 

Yery  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Thos.  T.  Craven, 
Commanding  Potomac  Flotilla. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy,  Washington ,  D.  C.

Report  of  Acting  Master  Cash ,  U.  8.  Navy ,  of  an  expedition  under  his 
command  to  the  8t.  Marfs  River ,  Maryland. 

U.  S.  S.  Jacob  Bell, 
Potomac  River ,  October  7 , 1861. 

Sir  :  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that  in  obedience  to  your  orders  of 
the  5th  instant,  I  proceeded  with  ten  men  from  U.  S.  S.  Yankee ,  in 
this  vessel  to  Piney  Point,  and  there  taking  on  board  Acting  Master’s 
Mate  Gray,  commanding  U.  S.  schooner  Bailey ,  proceeded  to  an  anchor¬ 
age  in  St.  Mary’s  River,  where  we  arrived  at  7  a.  m.  yesterday. 

At  8  a.  in.,  with  Mr.  Gray  and  the  two  officers  accompanying  the 
expedition,  I  landed  at  the  residence  of  Mrs.  Booth,  from  whom  I 
obtained  information  regarding  the  different  localities.  I  then  pro¬ 
ceeded  to  the  post-office  at  Great  Mills,  distant  8  miles  from  our  anchor¬ 
age,  and  seized  all  the  mail  matter  then  in  that  office,  consisting  of 
fifty-five  letters,  giving  the  postmaster  a  receipt  for  the  same.  From 
the  postmaster,  who  appears  to  be  a  loyal  citizen,  I  received  valuable 
information  regarding  the  operations  of  a  Mr.  Allison,  a  merchant  and 
resident  of  Great  Mills;  it  appears  beyond  doubt  that  he  has  been 
engaged  in  aiding  the  enemy  in  many  ways;  forwarding  men  and  pro¬ 
visions  and  allowing  his  store  to  be  used  as  a  storehouse  for  goods  and 
rendezvous  for  men  en  route  to  Virginia.  I  am  of  opinion,  from  my 
conversation  with  the  postmaster,  that  the  majority  of  the  people 
in  that  section  of  the  country  are  engaged  in  the  same  business,  and 
do  not  hesitate  to  forward  men  and  provisions  to  Virginia  whenever 
the  opportunity  offers. 


See  p.  702. 


OPERATIONS  ON  THE  POTOMAC  AND  RAPPAHANNOCK.  705 


After  returning  to  the  vessel  at  6  p.  m.,  I  proceeded  to  the  residence 
of  Mr.  J.  Thomas  Travis  and  succeeded  in  arresting  him  without  diffi¬ 
culty,  and  transferred  him  to  officer  Thomas  E.  Williams,  thus  accom¬ 
plishing-  all  the  objects  of  the  expedition  with  the  force  under  my

Thos.  M.  Cash,

Off  Aquia  Creek,  October  7,  1861. 

Sir  :  I  fear  you  have  not  received  my  message  asking  for  instructions 
as  to  the  passage  of  vessels  up  the  river.  There  is  quite  a  little  fleet 
assembled  here  and  many  more  below.  Among  those  here  are  some 
half  dozen  with  Government  stores,  three  of  them  steamers,  one  having- 
on  board  a  company  of  soldiers  acting  as  escort.  I  will  thank  you  to  give

to  permit  them  to  pass  without  your  orders.  The  tugboat  Coeur  de  Lion , 
towing  a  small  sloop  belonging  to  the  Government,  has  just  anchored. 
She  is  without  armament  and  has  orders  to  proceed  to  the  navy  yard, 
Washington.  I  shall  permit  her  to  leave  during  the  night  if  you  do  not 
order  the  contrary.  Nothing  new  at  this  point.  Captain  Amos  P. 
Foster,  of  the  Resolute,  reports  that  he  saw  four  boats  under  the  bat¬ 
teries.  at  Shipping  Point. 

Your  obedient  servant, 

A.  D.  Harrell,

Report  of  Acting  Lieutenant  Budd,  U.  8.  Navy,  commanding  U.  8.  8. 

Penguin ,  of  the  collision  of  that  vessel  with  U.  8.  tug  Rescue. 

U.  S.  S.  Penguin, 
Rappahannock  River ,  October  8,  1861. 

Sir:  I  have  to  report  that  I  arrived  at  this  station  this  p.  m.  and 
relieved  Commander  Glisson  in  conformity  to  your  orders. 

In  consequence  of  the  inclemency  of  the  weather  and  darkness  of 
last  night  I  was  obliged  to  anchor  off  Maryland  Point,  previous  to  reach¬ 
ing  which,  this  vessel,  I  regret  to  state,  came  in  collision  with  the  tug 
Rescue.  She  was  first  discovered  on  the  starboard  bow.  I  slowed, 
stopped,  steered  well  clear  of  her,  and  started  ahead;  soon  after  which 
she  also  started  her  engine  and  ran  directly  athwart  my  bows,  regard¬ 
less  of  my  frequent  orders  to  back.  We  both  showed  lights.  The  only 


OPERATIONS  ON  THE  POTOMAC  AND  RAPPAHANNOCK.  707 

excuses  offered  by  her  officer  in  charge  were  that  he  took  us  to  be  the 
Resolute ,  which  he  knew  to  be  at  anchor  near  him.  As  I  had  uo  diffi¬ 
culty  in  determining  her  size  from  the  first,  I  can  not  conceive  how  he
