[Enclosure.] 

IT.  S.  S.  Union, 

Off  Aquia  Creek,  October  11,  1861. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  submit  the  following  report  for  your  infor¬ 
mation  : 

Being  informed  of  a  large  schooner  lying  in  Quautieo  (or  Dumfries) 
Creek,  knowing  also  that  a  large  number  of  troops  were  collected  at 
that  point  with  the  view  of  crossing  the  Potomac  Liver,  as  was  reported 
to  me,  I  conceived  it  to  be  my  duty  to  destroy  her.  With  this  object 
in  view  I  took  two  launches  and  my  boat  and  pulled  in  for  the  vessel 
at  half  past  2  this  morning.  One  of  the  launches  was  commanded 
by  Midshipman  W.  F.  Stewart,  accompanied  by  the  master,  Ed.  L. 
Haines,  of  the  Rescue,  and  the  other  by  Acting  Master  Amos  [P.] 
Foster,  of  the  Resolute.  1  took  with  me  the  pilot  of  this  vessel,  Lewis 
Penn. 

Some  little  difficulty  was  experienced  in  finding  the  entrance  to  the 
creek,  which  you  will  remember  is  very  narrow;  but  having  found  it 
we  pulled  up  this  crooked  channel  within  pistol  shot  of  either  shore 
until  we  discovered  the  schooner.  She  was  close  to  the  shore  in  charge 
of  a  sentry,  who  fled  at  our  approach  and  alarmed  the  camp.  She  had 
a  new  suit  of  sails,  and  all  the  furniture  complete  in  the  cabin,  which 
was  collected  together  and  fired,  producing  a  beautiful  conflagration, 
but  unfortunately  revealing  our  position  to  the  enemy,  who  commenced 


710  OPERATIONS  ON  THE  POTOMAC  AND  RAPPAHANNOCK. 

a  rapid  fire  from  both  banks  of  that  narrow  and  tortuous  stream  and 
kept  it  up,  intermingled  with  opprobrious  epithets,  until  we  were  beyond 
their  range. 

Our  crews  returned  a  random  fire  from  the  boats  and  two  steamers, 
gave  three  cheers,  and  pulled  for  their  vessels,  the  light  from  the  burn¬ 
ing  schooner  guiding  them  on  their  way.  Her  destruction  was  com¬ 
plete,  and  although  the  clothes  of  the  men  and  the  boats  were  perforated 
with  balls,  not  a  man  [was]  killed.  Officers  and  men  vied  with  each 
other  in  the  performance  of  their  duty.  Acting  Master  Foster  applied 
the  match  in  the  cabin  of  the  doomed  vessel.  Acting  Assistant  Sur¬ 
geon  W.  E.  Bonsall  accompanied  the  expedition,  ready,  should  his 
services  be  required. 

I  hope  what  I  have  done  will  meet  your  approbation,  notwithstanding 
I  have  acted  without  orders.  This  little  affair  will  show  the  enemy  at 
least  that  we  are  watching  him  and  ready  to  meet  and  destroy  his 
preparations  for  crossing  this  river  at  all  times. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  your  obedient  servant, 

A.  D.  Harrell, 

Lieutenant ,  Commanding. 

Captain  T.  T.  Craven, 

Commanding  Potomac  Flotilla. 


Letter  from  the  Secretary  of  the  Navy  to  Lieutenant  Harrell ,  U.  S.  Navy , 
commanding  (J.  S.  S.  Union ,  commending  him  and  the  officers  under 
his  command  for  the  destruction  of  the  schooner  in  Dumfries  Creek. 

Navy  Department,  October  12,  1861. 
Sir  :  The  gallant  achievement  performed  by  yourself  and  the  officers 
and  men  under  your  command  at  Dumfries  [Quantico]  Creek,  in 
destroying  the  schooner  which  the  insurgents  had  fitted  for  service, 
deserves  and  receives  the  approval  and  commendation  of  the  Depart¬ 
ment.  The  successful  result  under  great  disadvantages,  without  loss 
of  life,  demonstrates  the  daring  intrepidity  of  the  Navy,  which  only 
requires  a  field  whereon  to  prove  the  quality  of  those  who  serve  under 
its  banners.  The  Department  will  take  great  pleasure  in  assigning  you 
to  the  command  of  a  better  vessel  when  the  exigencies  of  the  service 
in  the  Potomac  will  permit  of  your  being  removed  from  the  sphere  of 
duty  where  you  have  proved  yourself  so  useful.  You  will  cause  this 
letter  to  be  read  to  those  who  took  part  with  you  in  the  expedition, 
and  express  to  them  the  thanks  of  the  Department  for  their  good 
conduct. 

I  am,  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Gideon  Welles. 

Lieutenant  Commanding  A.  D.  Harrell,  U.  S.  Navy, 

U.  S.  S.  Union ,  Potomac  Flotilla.

Report  of  Acting  Master's  Mate  Street ,  TJ.  S.  Nary,  commanding  U.  S. 
schooner  Dana,  of  engagements  with  Confederates  at  Stafford  Mills. 

U.  S.  Schooner  Dana,  October  11,  1861. 

Sir  :  While  cruising  close  along  the  Virginia  shore  on  the  7th  instant 
I  was  fired  into  by  the  rebels  with  riries  at  Stafford  [Stratford?]  Mills. 
I  fired  one  shot  at  them ;  the  second  jammed  in  the  gun.  It  being  near 
dark  I  withdrew.  On  the  10th  I  again  sailed  over  to  the  mills,  intend¬ 
ing  if  fired  upon  to  retaliate.  On  my  approach  horns  were  sounded 
around  the  country  and  in  a  few  minutes  I  could  see  men  on  the  bluffs 
(which  at  this  place  are  200  feet  high)  and  on  the  beach.  Those  on  the 
beach,  after  getting  behind  the  ood  piles  that  are  there,  fired  upon  us. 
I  fired  five  shrapnel  at  them,  being  all  the  dry  ammunition  I  had  on 
board,  each  of  which  went  on  shore  among  the  wood  and  bushes,  but 
with  what  effect  I  could  not  ascertain.  Those  on  the  bluffs  fired  con¬ 
stantly  at  us  while  we  remained  near  the  shore,  but  did  not  hit  anyone 
on  board. 

The  Island  Belle  came  down  the  river  shortly  afterwards  and  fired  a 
few  rounds  and  returned  up  the  river  again.  Sailing  down  the  river, 
and  when  near  the  mouth  of  Nomiui  Bay,  I  saw  a  man  on  the  hill  wav¬ 
ing  a  signal  attached  to  a  pole.  The  wind  being  offshore  1  worked 
in  toward  him  and  when  near  enough  he  halloed  to  us  that  he  wanted 
to  come  on  board.  I  told  him  to  go  down  to  a  long  sand  beach,  about 
300  yards  below,  and  I  would  take  him  on  board.  Finding  that  we  were 
as  near  to  the  shore  as  we  would  go,  a  fire  was  opened  on  us  from  the 
bushes  with  rifles.  Judging  from  the  number  of  shots  fired  the  first 
round,  there  were  from  fifteen  to  twenty  men.  Not  having  any  dry 
ammunition,  I  gave  the  order  for  the  men  to  lie  down  on  deck,  took  the 
helm  and  sheered  off  from  shore.  I  am  happy  to  state  that  no  one  was 
injured,  although  the  balls  fell  thick  around  us. 

I  remain,  very  respectfully,  your  most  obedient  servant, 

Wm.  T.  Street, 

Acting  Master's  Mate. 

Commander  T.  T.  Craven, 

Commanding  Potomac  Flotilla. 


Report  of  Acting  Master's  Mate  Harris,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  commanding  TJ.  S.  S. 
Island  Belle,  regarding  engagement  at  Stafford  Mills. 

U.  S.  S.  Island  Belle,  October  12,  1861. 
Sir:  Yesterday  evening  the  U.  S.  store  boat  Wyandank  came  steam¬ 
ing  down  the  river,  bound  to  Piney  Point.  I  got  underway  and  accom- 


712  OPERATIONS  ON  THE  POTOMAC  AND  RAPPAHANNOCK. 


panied  liim  to  Blakistone  Island,  wliere  I  discovered  a  schooner  under 
tlie  White  [Nomini]  Cliffs,  Va.,  directly  opposite,  firing  upon  some  per¬ 
sons  ashore.  1  immediately  directed  our  course  for  them  and  on  coming 
up  with  them  I  found  it  was  the  U.  S.  schooner  Dana.  I  enquired  the 
cause  of  his  firing.  He  said  they  were  recon noitering  along  the  shore 
when  a  party  of  men  ran  out  of  an  old  mill  and  fired  upon  his  vessel, 
the  balls  falling  all  around  him.  He  returned  their  fire  with  three 
shell  without  doing  any  execution,  so  I  steamed  along  within  half  a 
mile  of  the  beach  and  fired  a  rifle  shell  at  the  mill,  when  I  distinctly 
saw  some  thirty  men  running  from  different  hiding  places  and,  concen¬ 
trating  their  whole  force  behind  a  wood  pile,  they  commenced  a  deliber¬ 
ate  fire  at  us,  their  aim  being  either  too  high  or  too  low;  so  I  directed 
our  guns  for  the  wood  pile,  the  first  shell  passing  over  their  heads  and 
the  second  too  low;  the  third  exploded  in  their  very  midst,  scattering 
the  wood  in  every  direction  and  maimina-,  if  not  killing,  several  of 
them,  as  I  saw  some  of  them  assisting  others  to  get  away.  I  continued 
firing  as  long  as  I  could  see  them.  I  then  returned  to  my  station.  I 
sincerely  hope  this  will  not  meet  your  disapprobation,  for  I  acted  as  I 
thought  you  would  have  me  act  were  you  here. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Arnold  G.  Harris, 

Acting  Master’s  Mate. 

Commodore  Thomas  T.  Craven, 

Commanding  Potomac  Flotilla.

Headquarters  Army  of  the  Potomac, 

Washington ,  October  11,  1861. 

Sir:  The  following  report  has  been  received  from  a  very  reliable 
source. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

B.  B.  Marcy, 

Brigadier -General  and  Chief  of  Staff. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy. 

[Subenclosure.] 

I  left  Baltimore  Thursday  morning  and  landed  at  Millstone  Landing 
at  8  o’clock  p.  m.  I  left  there  Friday  morning  for  Herring  Creek.  I 
employed  a  negro  man  Friday  night  to  take  me  over  to  Bagged  Point. 
There  is  nothing  whatever  going  on  at  that  point. 


OPERATIONS  ON  THE  POTOMAC  AND  RAPPAHANNOCK.  713 


I  left  there  and  went  to  the  mouth  of  Machodoc  Creek  (under  the  plea 
of  delivering  some  letters  to  soldiers  from  Maryland).  An  old  man,  a 
farmer,  told  me  that  a  small  oyster  schooner  came  into  the  creek  about 
three- fourths  of  a  mile  up  with  200  kegs  of  powder  and  5,000  Minie  car¬ 
tridges.  He  told  me  that  nearly  every  week  some  one  or  more  vessels 
come  up  the  creek.  The  schooner  referred  to  received  her  cargo  at  or 
near  Newcastle,  Del.,  and  came  through  the  Chesapeake  and  Delaware 
Canal. 

I  went  back  to  the  creek  and  from  there  went  near  Port  Tobacco, 
and  at  night  (Sunday)  hired  a  man  to  take  me  to  Mathias  Point.  I 
landed  and  walked  fully  200  yards  before  I  met  a  rebel  soldier,  who  con¬ 
ducted  me  to  Captain  Edelin,  of  St.  Mary’s  County,  when  I  delivered 
five  letters  to  be  sent  to  Richmond.  He  told  me  that  there  are  two 
regiments  stationed  near  the  point.  One  is  commanded  by  Colonel  Bur¬ 
gess,  of  Virginia.  All  of  his  men  belong  to  the  eastern  part  of  Vir¬ 
ginia.  The  other  is  commanded  by  Colonel - ,  also  of  Virginia.  It 

is  composed  of  companies  from  Charles,  St.  Mary’s,  and  Calvert  coun¬ 
ties,  of  Maryland,  and  the  rest  of  Virginia. 

There  were  five  regiments  stationed  thereuntil  last  week,  Monday, 
when  three  left  to  go  in  the  neighborhood  of  Freestone  Point. 

They  have  no  battery  at  Mathias  Point,  but  two  8-pounder  cannon, 
mounted  on  four  wheels.  They  would  have  larger,  and  would  erect  a 
battery  at  the  point,  but  the  land  in  the  rear  of  the  point  is  swampy 
and  they  can  not  get  larger  cannon  there.  They  commenced  making  a 
battery  there,  but  abandoned  making  it. 

Edelin  also  told  me  that  they  wanted  the  Government  to  believe  that 
there  was  a  battery  there,  so  as  to  prevent  our  troops  landing  there  to  go 
to  Fredericksburg. 

He  says  there  is  not  less  than  10,000  men  between  Mathias  Point  and 
Aquia  Creek;  that  the  only  strong  batteries  that  they  have  on  the 
Potomac  are  at  Aquia  Creek.  He  also  says  that  on  nearly  every  point 
on  the  Potomac  they  have  brush  batteries  with  one  and  two  guns  each 
The  guns  are  not  exposed,  with  no  breastwork,  but  brush  in  front. 

He  also  says  they  are  going  to  erect  a  large  battery  at  the  White 
House,  5  to  8  miles  below  Mount  Vernon,  and  that  they  can  prevent 
the  navigation  of  the  Potomac  alone  at  that  point,  as  vessels  have  to 
come  within  200  yards  of  the  Virginia  shore  at  that  point. 

He  also  told  me  that  they  received  Washington  papers,  etc.,  every 
other  night;  that  every  week  three  men  come  over  to  the  point  sep¬ 
arately,  once  a  week ;  they  come  from  Washington,  and  report  to  Colonel 
Burgess. 

Two  of  them  are  named  Reynolds  and  Maxwell,  from  Maryland. 
When  they  want  to  go  over  to  the  point  a  small  red  lautern  is  hoisted 
in  a  cluster  of  trees  between  Port  Tobacco  and  Pope’s  Creek. 

He  says  these  men  go  to  Washington  by  an  old  road  to  Washington 
and  Baltimore  turnpike  road. 

The  men  are  stationed  about  400  yards  directly  in  the  rear  of  the 
point,  and  the  officers’  quarters  are  at  the  large  white  house,  which  is 
on  a  large  hill,  also  in  the  rear.

Navy ,  commanding  Potomac  Flotilla ,  regarding  volunteer  appointments. 

Navy  Department,  October  11, 1861. 
Sir:  In  this  great  emergency  the  Department  has  made  many 
appointments  from  outside  of  the  Navy  for  the  numerous  vessels  fitted 


714  OPERATIONS  ON  THE  POTOMAC  AND  RAPPAHANNOCK. 


out.  It  made  them  upon  the  best  recommendation^  possible  to  obtain, 
but  on  several  melancholy  instances  has  been  deceived. 

The  Department  relies  upon  the  vigilance  of  the  flag-officers  to  watch 
over  these  appointees,  instruct  them  carefully  in  their  duties,  perfect 
them  in  the  drill  at  the  great  guns  and  small  arms,  but  to  take  care 
that  no  movement  is  hazarded  by  being  confided  to  [incompetent 
hands. 

The  loss  of  one  of  our  useful  steam  tugs,  most  of  which  are  com¬ 
manded  by  persons  from  the  merchant  service,  would  be  felt  far  beyond 
its  pecuniary  value,  as  the  offensive  operations  of  the  Navy  thus  far 
have  been  skillful  and  successful.  You  will  make  such  changes  in  the 
commanders  of  these  vessels  and  the  subordinate  officers  as  shall  insure 
their  safety  and  efficiency. 

The  patriotism  of  the  merchant  service  gives  us  a  volunteer  force  of 
excellent  seamen,  brave  and  loyal,  and  yon  will  take  care  that  the 
inefficient  under  your  command  are  removed  immediately  from  positions 
of  trust,  reporting  action  in  all  cases  to  the  Department. 

I  am,  respectfully,  etc., 


Gideon  Welles. 


Captain  T.  T.  Craven, 

Commanding  Potomac  Flotilla ,  Washington ,  D.  C.

Report  of  Acting  Master1  s  Mate  Frank ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  commanding  U.  S. 
schooner  Howell  Cobb,  of  action  with  the  Confederates  on  Mathias 
Point. 

U.  S.  Schooner  Howell  Cobb, 

Mathias  Point ,  October  12 ,  1861. 

In  running  up  to  Pope’s  Creek  I  discovered  a  schooner  ashore  on 
Mathias  Point  and  ran  up  to  see  what  she  was.  I  came  to  anchor  about 
50  or  60  meters  off  and  I  manned  my  boat  with  four  men  and  myself,  and 
started  for  the  vessel  that  wTas  aground,  but  before  we  could  reach  the 
vessel  there  was  a  volley  of  musketry  tired  on  me  from  the  shore,  so  I 
had  to  retreat  to  my  vessel  again,  and  I  opened  fire  on  the  rebels  and 
kept  it  up  until  I  had  tired  thirty  rounds,  which  silenced  them.  This 
action  took  place  about  1  o’clock.  I  heard  our  shot  strike  very  dis¬ 
tinctly.  They  had  two  guns  that  would  reach  us  and  all  the  rest  fell 
short.  After  a  short  period  of  time  I  got  on  the  way  and  went  in 
search  of  the  Island  Belle  and  met  her,  and  she  took  the  Howell  Cobb 
in  tow  and  ran  up  to  Mathias  Point,  and  Captain  Harris  fired  a  few 
shells  in  those  pines,  and  the  rebels  ran  down  the  shore  like  wild  turkeys 
through  the  bushes.  I  lay  all  night  off  the  point  to  guard  the  schooner. 
They  seem  to  know  my  boat,  for  in  leaving  the  steamer  to  go  on  board 
they  tired  on  the  boat  from  down  the  beach  from  the  thicket. 

Since  I  last  saw  you,  sir,  I  have  paid  Port  Tobacco  Creek  three  visits 
and  making  [made]  strict  enquiry  of  the  said  Naley,  but  found  he  had 
gone  to  Virginia.  In  cruising  down  the  Virginia  shores,  I  find  there 


716  OPERATIONS  ON  THE  POTOMAC  AND  RAPPAHANNOCK. 


are  pickets  stationed  along  the  shore;  there  are  feonie  ten  or  twelve 
at  the  mouth  of  Pope’s  Creek  on  Virginia  shore.  I  see  them  very 
distinctly  through  the  glass. 

Yours  in  haste. 

Respectfully  yours,  A.  J.  Frank. 

Captain  T.  T.  Craven,  U.  S.  Navy, 

Commanding  Potomac  Flotilla.

regarding  disposition  of  some  of  the  vessels  of  his  command. 

U.  S.  S.  Yankee,  October  13,  1861. 

Sir  :  In  obedience  to  your  order  of  yesterday  to  have  the  steamer 
Penguin  relieved,  I  dispatched  the  Valley  City  last  evening  for  that 
purpose.

largest  vessels  from  the  flotilla  has  made  it  necessary  (for  the  want  of

yard. 

This  afternoon  Lieutenant  Commanding  E.  P.  McCrea,  whom  I  had 
sent  down  the  river  as  far  as  Aquia  Creek,  reported  on  his  return  that 
the  enemy  had  erected  a  battery  on  Shipping  Point  and  had  already 
several  guns  mounted  there.

Passage  of  U.  3.  steamers  Pocahontas  and  Seminole  by  the  Confederate 

batteries  on  the  Potomac  River. 


Report  of  Captain  Craven,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  Potomac  Flotilla. 

U.  S.  S.  Yankee, 

Off  Occoquan  Creek ,  October  15 ,  1861. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  inform  you  that  the  U.  S.  S.  Pocahontas 
passed  this  anchorage  at  about  9:40  this  morning.  At  about  10 : 30, 
when  abreast  of  Evansport,  she  commenced  firing. 

The  Seminole ,  which  was  at  that  time  abreast  of  me,  immediately 
started  on  her  way  down  the  river.  After  firing  some  eight  or  ten  shots 
the  Pocahontas  ceased  firing.  I  could  not  discover  that  her  fire  was 
returned  from  the  shore,  but  distinctly  saw  the  enemy  gather  in  large 
force  upon  the  river  bank,  cutting  and  clearing  away  trees.  At  about 
11 : 20,  the  Seminole  being  directly  abreast  of  Evansport,  the  rebels  com¬ 
menced  firing  upon  her  from  a  battery  of  at  least  ten  heavy  guns,  two 
or  three  of  which  were  rifled  and  of  large  caliber.  As  long  as  they 
were  within  range,  some  twenty  minutes,  the  Seminole  returned  their 
fire  with  great  spirit.  Some  thirty  or  thirty-five  shots  were  fired  from 
the  shore  and  some  tweuty  were  fired  from  the  Seminole. 

Since  the  engagement  the  rebels  have  been  amusing  themselves  by 
firing  at  a  small  schooner  which  is  at  this  timeout  of  reach  of  his  [their  J 
guns. 

At  the  time  of  this  engagement,  sir,  I  was  compelled  to  be  an  inactive 
and  useless  spectator,  the  engineers  being  at  work  upon  our  engine.  So 
long  as  that  battery  stands  at  Shipping  Point  and  Evansport  the  nav¬ 
igation  of  the  Potomac  will  be  effectually  closed.  To  attempt  to  reduce 
it  with  the  vessels  under  my  command  would  be  vanity.  Had  our  army 
occupied  the  points  opposite,  as  I  have  suggested  in  two  previous  com¬ 
munications,  this  insult  would  not  have  been  perpetrated. 

Very  respectfully ,  your  obedient  servant, 

Thomas  T.  Craven, 
Commanding  Potomac  Flotilla. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy. 


Report  of  Commander  Gillis,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Seminole. 

U.  S.  Steam  Sloop  Seminole, 

Potomac  River,  October  15,  1861. 

Sir:  Detained  yesterday  to  make  some  repairs  of  work  imperfectly 
done,  I  have  the  honor  to  report  to  you  that  we  proceeded  this  morn¬ 
ing  in  obedience  to  your  order  of  the  12th  instant,  Pocahontas  ahead. 


United  States  Steamer  Pocahontas. 


Y 


* 


■;  • 


OPERATIONS  ON  THE  POTOMAC  AND  RAPPAHANNOCK.  719 


We  discovered  a  short  distance  below  the  White  House  a  body,  say 
a  battalion,  of  men  on  the  hills  of  Virginia,  moving  up  the  river; 
between  Freestone  Point  and  Cockpit  another  body  of  Confederate 
troops  moving  in  same  direction. 

The  Pocahontas  being  some  distance  ahead,  was  seen  to  open  fire  on 
the  shore  below  Freestone  Point  and  at  Evansport  or  Shipping  Point, 
which  was  not  observed  to  be  returned  by  'the  Confederates. 

At  10 :  45  a.  m.,  as  the  Seminole  was  passing  majestically  slow  by  Evans¬ 
port,  three  batteries  opened  a  brisk  fire  of  rifled  shot  and  shell  upon 
us.  Two  of  these  batteries  were  on  the  bank  of  the  river;  the  other 
lies  a  short  distance,  say  400  yards,  inland.  We  returned  their  fire 
from  our  pivot  gun  and  two  medium  32-pounders  with  effect,  as  our 
shell  were  seen  to  fall  in  and  around  their  works,  keeping  steadily  on 
our  course,  as  a  matter  of  more  importance  to  take  our  vessel  to  her 
place  of  destination  uninjured. 

The  length  of  the  Seminole  and  her  very  slow  rate  of  speed  made  us 
a  fine  target  for  the  rebel  rifled  guns,  to  which  we  returned  fire  with 
interest. 

One  of  their  shot  crippled  our  mizzenmast  about  15  feet  below  cross- 
trees,  and  cut  away  starboard  after  mizzen  shroud;  another  carried 
away  mainstays  near  masthead;  another  passed  through  the  rail  near 
pivot  gun;  another,  amidships,  passed  through  both  hammock  nettings 
and  rail,  covering  the  deck  with  splinters;  a  heavy  shell  burst  close 
under  our  starboard  bow;  fragments  of  shell  taken  out;  waist  boat 
shot  through ;  a  rifled  shot  struck  obliquely  and  glanced  off  quarter 
seizing  of  after  swifter;  starboard  fore  rigging  shot  away,  and  some 
injuries  inboard. 

Several  persons  were  scratched  by  the  splinters,  but  providentially 
none  killed ;  officers  and  crew  did  their  duty  gallantly. 

I  shall  endeavor  to  have  damages  repaired  at  the  anchorage  desig¬ 
nated  in  your  order,  and  am,  respectfully,  sir,  your  obedient  servant, 

Jno.  P.  Gillis, 

Commander. 


Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  Navy ,  Washington. 


Unofficial  report  of  Commander  Gillis,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Seminole. 

[U.  S.  S.]  Seminole, 
Hampton  Roads ,  October  16 ,  1861. 

Hear  Craven:  Did  you  hear  the  row ?  We  had  quite  a  sharp  action 
with  the  rebel  batteries,  three  in  number,  as  we  passed  Evansport  yes¬ 
terday.  It  continued  about  forty  minutes,  as  the  u  old  wagon”  moved 
leisurely  down  the  river.  Two  of  the  forts  are  on  the  bank  of  the 
river,  the  other  lies  inland  300  or  400  yards.  They  poured  the  rifled 
shot  and  shell  into  us  in  a  lively  manner,  which  we  answered  briskly  so 
long  as  our  guns  could  be  brought  to  bear.  We  kept  steadily  on  our 
course,  deeming  it  a  matter  of  more  importance  to  take  the  vessel 
uninjured  to  her  destination  for  Avork  of  more  consequence  than  shell¬ 
ing  the  batteries  of  the  Potomac. 

The  Pocahontas  stirred  up  the  party  with  a  gun  or  two  as  she  steamed 
down  ahead  of  us,  which  the  batteries  did  not  rex>ly  to.  She  continued 
on,  leaving  us  to  do  battle  with  the  Dixie  boys.  They  did  us  some  dam¬ 
age.  The  u varmints”  shot  away  our  mizzenmast  and  mizzen  after

sliroud,  also  both  mainstays  near  masthead,  sent  two  shot  through  our 
rail  and  hammock  nettings,  and  doing  us  some  injury  inboard,  as  they 
passed  through  both  sides.  A  shell  or  two  burst  close  under  our  star- 
board  bow,  giving  us  a'fine  shower  bath  at  pivot  gun,  and  burying  some 
fragments  in  outside  planking,  etc.  Providentially  none  were  killed ;  a

How  are  you  getting  on?  Has  your  flagship  arrived  yet?  We  will

zenmast.  It  hung  by  a  thread  as  it  were,  the  shot  taking  effect  about 
15  feet  below  the  crosstrees.  Have  procured  a  spar  for  another,  an 
indifferent  stick,  7  feet  shorter  than  old  mast. 

Will  be  pleased  to  hear  from  you.  I  hurried,  or  hastened  away,  from 
your  vessel  to  assist  the  Pocahontas.  Did  she  come  back  to  mine? 
Yes,  some  thirty  or  forty  minutes  after  the  fight  was  over — well,  what 
of  it?  There  was  nobody  hurt. 

Sincerely  yours, 


Jno.  P.  G[illis]. 

Captain  Thomas  T.  Craven,  U.  S.  Navy,

Report  of  Lieutenant  Harrell,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Union. 

U.  S.  S.  Union, 

Off  Aquia  Creel',  October  15,  1861. 

Sir:  I  have  to  inform  you  that  while  passing  down  the  river  to-day 
the  Seminole  was  fired  upon  by  a  battery  from  the  Virginia  shore, 
located  at  the  mouth  of  Quantico  Creek.  The  Seminole  returned  the 
fire  with  shells,  many  of  them  bursting  in  the  enemy’s  batteries. 

I  boarded  her  as  she  passed  down,  and  Captain  Gillis  informed  me 
that  his  ship  had  been  struck  five  or  six  times.  His  mizzenmast  was 
nearly  cut  away;  he  was  then  fishing  it.  No  person  hurt.  There  is  a 
steamer  here,  which  I  have  detained,  loaded  with  Government  stores. 
Please  inform  me  whether  I  shall  permit  vessels  at  present  to  pass  up 
the  river. 

There  is  a  transport  steamer  on  shore  below  Maryland  Point.  She 
was  passing  down  the  river  when  she  took  the  ground.  I  have  noth¬ 
ing  to  send  to  her  assistance,  as  the  Freeborn  has  not  returned. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  your  obedient  servant, 

A.  D.  Harrell, 
Lieutenant,  Commanding. 

Captain  T.  T.  Craven, 

Commanding  Potomac  Flotilla.

Report  of  Captain  Craven ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  commanding  Potomac  Flotilla, 
transmitting  private  letter  of  Lieutenant  Wyman,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  command¬ 
ing  TJ.  S.  S.  Pawnee ,  regarding  the  passage  of  the  batteries  on  the  Potomac 
River. 

U.  S.  S.  Harriet  Lane,  October  17 ,  1861. 
Sir  :  I  have  the  pleasure  to  enclose  herewith  a  copy  of  a  private  let¬ 
ter  just  received  from  Lieutenant  Commanding  Wyman.  It  shows  that 
the  fire  from  the  rebel  batteries  was  much  more  effective  than  I  at  first 
supposed  it  to  be.  It  was  most  fortunate  that  Captain  Wyman  followed 
my  advice  “not  to  return  the  fire  of  the  enemy,”  for,  as  he  says,  had 
the  men  been  at  their  quarters  several  of  them  would  in  all  probability 
have  been  killed. 

Considering  the  improvement  of  their  gun  practice  I  would  respect¬ 
fully  suggest  that  until  the  enemy’s  batteries  be  silenced  or  removed 
that  there  shall  be  no  more  transportation  of  Government  stores  upon 
the  river. 

Yery  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Tiios.  T.  Craven, 
Commanding  Potomac  Flotilla. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy,  Washington,  L).  C. 


[Enclosure.] 

U.  S.  S.  Pawnee,  October  16,  [1861.] 
Dear  Sir:  We  have  received  no  damage  of  any  importance,  and  I 
believe  that  the  main  object  has  been  accomplished.  No  material  dam¬ 
age  to  hull  or  spars  and  no  one  hurt. 

After  having  the  guns  all  ready  I  sent  all  the  men  to  the  opposite  side 
of  the  deck,  protecting  them  by  hammocks,  etc.,  across  the  launch.  As 
agreed  upon,  I  had  determined  not  to  fire  unless  I  found  the  enemy’s 
fire  annoying  or  destructive,  and  as  it  was  neither,  not  a  gun  was  fired 
by  us.  I  am  glad  that  I  pursued  that  course,  as,  had  the  men  been 
at  the  guns,  several  of  No.  2  gun’s  crew  would  have  been  killed.  The 
shot  which  struck  or  passed  close  to  us  were:  One  through  nettings, 
starboard  and  port,  in  wake  of  No.  2  gun,  cutting  hammock  in  two; 
one  glanced  on  starboard  bow ;  one  shot  amidships,  2  feet  above  water 
line;  one  shot  through  dingy  and  into  side,  not  going  through,  lodged 
just  above  air  port  of  first  lieutenant’s  room  and  started  it;  one  knocked 
off  boat’s  rudder  abaft  starboard  gangway,  and  one  cut  away  fore  vang; 
another  or  perhaps  the  same  cutting  ridgerope  of  awning. 


OPERATIONS  ON  THE  POTOMAC  AND  RAPPAHANNOCK.  723 


I  think  there  are  live  or  six  guns — two  32-pounders,  one  heavy  rifle, 
say  6-inch,  two  or  three  small  rifles,  and  placed  in  two  batteries. 

I  am  now  waiting  at  Maryland  Point  merely  to  pack  our  engines  and 
shall  be  underway  as  quickly  as  possible  and  shall  Oe  glad  to  get  to  Old 
Point  and  get  rid  of  the  marines,  as  we  are  crowded  to  death. 
Respectfully,  and  truly,  yours, 


R.  H.  Wyman. 


[Captain  Thos.  T.  Craven, 

Commanding  Potomac  Flotilla.] 


The  Seminole  sustained  no  injury  excepting  a  shot  through  mizzenmast. 


[Telegram.] 

Navy  Yard  [Washington,  I).  C.],  October  17,  1861. 

I  sent  down  three  tugs  and  one  steamer  to  try  the  passage  last  night. 
Two  of  the  tugs  got  by  before  they  were  seen.  The  steamboat  would 
not  attempt  it,  and  the  other  tug  ran  into  a  propeller  coming  up  and 
disabled  her.  The  tugs  that  got  by  towed  back  two  loaded  vessels 
and  were  fired  at,  but  not  struck.  Some  measure  is  needed  to  lessen 
the  risk  of  the  passage,  and  even  if  counter  batteries  are  erected  I  think 
the  plating  of  the  Anacostia  will  contribute  very  much.  It  might  be 
done  in  two  weeks  from  order.  Lights  are  shown  on  the  Maryland  size 
to  give  notice  of  our  vessels  coming  and  should  be  seized.  Small  par¬ 
ties  of  troops  should  be  distributed  near  the  locality  to  observe  and 
check  communication  by  boats  between  the  shores.  The  Coeur  de  Lion 
arrived  last  night  from  New  York  with  a  sloop  in  tow;  was  not  hit  by 
the  batteries.  The  Harriet  Lane  went  down  about  half  an  hour  since. 

J.  A.  Dahlgren. 

Navy  Department.

seizing  a  boat  containing  tliree  men,  seen  crossing  from  Ship  [Shipping]

On  reaching  the  north  point  of  the  month  of  Chicomuxen  Creek  I

that  the  enemy  might  have  landed  a  small  force,  I  deemed  it  advisable 
not  to  land.  While  on  board  the  schooner  I  was  able  to  view  the  Vir¬ 
ginia  shore  from  the  mouth  of  Chopawamsic  Creek  to  Cockpit  Point,

Letter  from  the  Secretary  of  the  Wavy  to  Major-General  McClellan ,  TJ.  8. 
Army ,  commanding  Army  of  the  Potomac ,  regarding  the  navigation  of 
the  river. 

Navy  Department,  October  18,  1861. 
The  Department  is  advised  that  the  navigation  of  the  Potomac  River 
is  becoming  daily  and  almost  hourly  more  dangerous.  Commander 
Dahlgren  telegraphs  this  morning  that  “  some  measure  is  needed  to 


OPERATIONS  ON  THE  POTOMAC  AND  RAPPAHANNOCK.  727 


lessen  the  risk  of  the  passage.  Lights  are  shown  on  the  Maryland 
shore  to  give  notice  of  our  vessels  coming  and  should  be  seized.  Small 
parties  ol  troops  should  be  distributed  near  the  locality  to  observe  and 
check  communication  by  boats  between  the  shores.” 

Similar  views  are  expressed  by  Captain  Craven,  in  command  of  the 
flotilla.  The  Navy  has  exerted  itself  to  keep  open  this  important 
avenue  to  the  city,  and  thus  far  with  success,  but  the  erection  of  exten¬ 
sive  batteries  and  stationing  troops  to  the  amount  of  many  thousands 
in  their  vicinity,  imperatively  requires  the  action  of  the  Army,  unless 
communication  by  the  river  is  to  be  abandoned,  which  on  many 
accounts  would  be  unfortunate  and  almost  disastrous.  I  deem  it 
important  to  communicate  to  you  these  reports  and  suggestions  from 
the  officers  named  and  would  add  my  concurrence. 

I  am,  respectfully, 

Gideon  Welles. 

Major-General  George  B.  McClellan,  U.  S.  Army, 

Washington.

Sir  :  I  have  this  minute  received  your  letter  of  this  date  with  refer¬ 
ence  to  the  navigation  of  the  Potomac,  and  in  reply  have  the  honor  to

H.  S.  S.  Union,  October  19,  1861. 

I  have  just  learned  that  the  enemy  crossed  the  river  yesterday  morn¬ 
ing  during  the  fog  500  strong.  They  crossed  in  fishing  boats  and  scows. 
A  consultation  was  held  with  the  leading  men  of  the  neighborhood, 
conspicuous  among  whom  was  Mr.  Posey.  They  were  told  that  all  was 
ready  for  them  in  that  part  of  the  State;  they  then  returned,  with  the 
understanding  that  they  would  be  in  Maryland  immediately.  Mary¬ 
land  Point  is  to  be  fortified.  I  shall  keep  a  watch  upon  that  place,  and 
the  moment  I  see  a  movement  I  shall  at  once  destroy  certain  houses  and 
endeavor  to  keep  the  enemy  from  that  point.  As  they  have  command 
of  the  river  and  can  transport  artillery  across  at  pleasure,  I  fear  I  shall 
be  compelled  to  drop  farther  down  the  river.  To  add  to  my  unpleasant 
situation  I  have  only  two  days7  provisions.  I  may  be  able  to  get  some 
from  the  Ice  Boat ;  if  not,  I  must  depend  upon  the  shore.  Please  give 
me  some  general  instructions  as  to  my  course  should  the  Maryland 
shore  become  fortified,  which  most  assuredly  will  be  the  case  in  a  few 
days  unless  the  enemy  is  checked.  You  are  aware,  no  doubt,  that  they 
captured  two  schooners  during  the  fog.  I  permit  nothing  to  pass  and 
will  not  until  I  receive  orders  to  the  contrary.  The  man  I send  this  by 
is  a  most  trustworthy  person. 

Yours,  very  respectfully, 

A.  D.  Harrell. 

[Captain  Thos.  T.  Craven, 

Commanding  Potomac  Flotilla.] 

P.  S. — I  send  the  bearer  of  this  out  for  information  more  than  any¬ 
thing  else,  but  as  he  will  be  in  your  vicinity  I  avail  myself  of  the  oppor¬ 
tunity  to  communicate. 

[Endorsement.]

The  bearer  of  this  says  it  was  last  night  and  not  yesterday  that  the 
rebels  crossed  the  river.  This  note  was  written  this  morning  instead 
of  yesterday. 

Very  respectfully,  Tiios.  T.  Craven.

the  tugs  running  up  and  down  the  river  would  transmit  the  news.  I 
made  known  your  wish  in  reference  to  Mr.  Posey,  Mr.  Mason,  and  Mr. 
Ruuyea,  and  if  the  above  parties  were  arrested  to  let  you  know. 

Yery  respectfully, 

Charles  Bentrick,

Navy  Department,  October  21,  1861. 
Sir:  A  captain  of  one  of  the  vessels  which  came  up  the  river  yester¬ 
day  reported  to  General  Van  Vliet  that  over  forty  vessels  were  await¬

were  in  sight  to  protect  them  from  the  enemy.  The  Department,  of

erect  batteries  on  the  Maryland  shore.  In  the  meantime,  if  any  of  your 
heavy  rifled  guns  can  reach  the  works  of  the  enemy  without  exposing 
your  vessels  and  their  crews,  thereby  causing  an  expenditure  of  their 
ammunition,  you  are  requested  to  keep  up  at  your  discretion  a  fire  upon 
them.  You  will  take  prompt  and  severe  measures  with  any  parties  on 
the  Maryland  shore  who  shall  have  made  signals  to  the  Virginia  side. 
Yery  respectfully,  etc., 

Gideon  Welles.

Off  Aquia  Creek,  October  21,  1861. 

Sir  :  I  learned  last  night  through  a  trusty  channel  that  a  battery  at 
Mathias  Point  was  nearly  ready  to  open  fire.  Although  I  placed  full 
confidence  in  the  statement,  I  determined  to  wait  until  this  morning  to 
verify  it.  I  sent  the  Rescue  down  with  orders  to  Lieutenant  Magaw  to 
keep  a  sharp  lookout  upon  that  point.  Shortly  before  sundown  this 
evening  I  heard  firing  in  that  direction  and  immediately  dispatched 
the  Rescue  to  ascertain  what  it  meant.  She  met  a  schooner  close  to  the

Camp  Hooker,  near  Buddh  Ferry,  October  23,  1861. 
Sir:  The  steamer  Page ,  which  has  been  lying  in  Aquia  Creek,  made 
her  appearance  in  the  river  opposite  here  a  short  time  since,  and  is 
now  lying  under  the  guns  of  the  rebel  battery  at  Shipping  Point.  She 
has  thus  succeeded  in  eluding  the  U.  S.  S.  Union,  which  was  watching 
her*off  Aquia  Creek.  As  there  are  some  indications  on  the  other  side 
of  preparations  for  crossing  to  this  shore,  and  as  I  have  no  artillery 
and  would  be  unable  to  oppose  a  landing  by  them,  I  shall  this  evening 
move  my  encampment  to  some  point  upon  the  road  leading  from  here 
to  Washington,  and  near  where  I  encamped  last  Sunday  on  Mattawo- 
man  Creek. 

If  you  can  move  any  of  the  vessels  under  your  command  somewhat 
farther  down  the  river,  I  think  they  will  be  unable  to  land  above  the 
mouth  of  Mattawoman  Creek,  and  their  movements  from  Shipping 
Point  may  be  observed  if  not  prevented. 

Respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Nelson  Taylor, 

Colonel  Third  Regiment,  Excelsior  Brigade. 

Commodore  Craven,

Report  of  Captain  Craven ,  U.  S.  Wavy,  commanding  Potomac  Flotilla, 
regarding  affairs  on  the  Potomac  River. 

U.  S.  S.  Harriet  Lane,  October  23,  1861. 

Sir:  Last  night  I  received  a  message  from  Lieutenant  Commanding 
Harrell  informing  me  that  there  were  no  sailing  vessels  between  Smith’s 
and  Lower  Cedar  Points,  and  a  statement  that  by  to-morrow  morning 
there  would  be  four  additional  heavy  guns  mounted  at  Mathias.  In 
view  of  being  entirely  cut  off,  both  from  above  and  below,  he  requested 
permission  to  drop  down  under  cover  of  the  night  to  Lower  Cedar 
Point.  The  case  seemed  to  be  an  urgent  one,  and  taking  into  consid¬ 
eration  that  the  vessels  at  anchor  off’  Aquia  could  be  of  but  little  serv¬ 
ice  there,  I  sent  word  to  him  that  I  should  leave  him  to  act  altogether 
upon  his  discretion.  This  morning,  from  a  fishing  boat  just  up  from 
below,  I  learned  that  the  Union,  Ice  Boat,  Satellite,  and  Rescue  had  gone 
down  the  river,  and  that  the  rebel  steamer  George  Page  had  gone  up  to 
Quantico  Creek,  where  she  is  safe  under  the  batteries  of  Shipping  Point. 
Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Thos.  T.  Craven, 
Commanding  Potomac  Flotilla. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Wavy,  Washington,  I).  G.

Report  of  Captain  Craven ,  U.  8.  Wavy,  commanding  Potomac  Flotilla, 
requesting  to  be  detached  from  that  command,  in  view  of  its  uselessness 
for  the  protection  of  the  river. 

U.  S.  S.  Harriet  Lane,  October  23,  1861. 
Sir  :  In  view  of  the  utter  uselessness  of  the  Potomac  Flotilla  for  the 
farther  protection  of  the  river,  I  feel  it  my  duty  to  respectfully  suggest 
for  the  consideration  of  the  Department  that  the  guns  of  all  the  vessels 
be  landed  at  Mattawoman  Creek  and  mounted  upon  Stump  Neck.  In 
addition  I  would  propose  that  the  guns  of  the  Pensacola  be  also  mounted 
at  that  point;  then,  with  the  aid  of  as  many  heavy  siege  mortars  as  are 
available,  we  might,  by  concentrating  our  fire  upon  one  battery  at  a 
time,  be  enabled  to  drive  the  enemy  from  his  positions  on  the  opposite 
bank  of  the  river. 

I  must  confess,  sir,  that  I  am  wholly  ignorant  of  the  proper  manage¬ 
ment  of  such  an  operation,  but  if  intrusted  to  a  competent  officer  I 
have  no  doubt  that  it  would  result  to  our  advantage. 

Feeling  that  my  position  here  in  command  of  the  flotilla  can  be  of 
no  further  benefit,  I  most  respectfully  request  to  be  detached  from  the 
command  and  appointed  to  some  seagoing  vessel. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  sir,  your  obedient  servant, 

Tuos.  T.  Graven, 
Commanding  Potomac  Flotilla. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy ,  Washington ,  1).  C.

Instructions  from  the  Secretary  of  the  Navy  to  Captain  Craven ,  U.  S. 

Navy ,  commanding  Potomac  Flotilla ,  urging  continued  vigilance  in  coop¬ 
eration  with  the  Army. 

Navy  Department,  October  24,  1861. 

Sir:  Your  several  favors  of  the  23d  are  received,  stating  the  dis¬ 
membered  condition  of  the  flotilla  under  your  command,  the  withdrawal 
of  its  vessels  from  before  Aquia,  the  egress  of  the  George  Page  into  the 
Potomac,  and  the  further  demonstrations  by  the  batteries  of  the  insur¬ 
gents.  These  evidences  of  accumulated  force  in  that  quarter  may  for  a 
time  embarrass  your  command,  but  must  not  be  permitted  to  discour¬ 
age  you,  and  I  am  confident  will  cause  no  relaxation  of  your  vigilance 
or  exertion. 

I  notified  you  briefly  at  a  late  hour  last  night  that  General  Hooker’s 
division,  with  three  batteries,  would  commence  their  march  from 
Bladensburg  this  morning.  Such,  I  am  informed,  is  the  fact,  and  they 
go  with  a  view  of  cooperating  with  and  assisting  you  in  repelling  the 
enemy.  In  order  to  operate  effectually  against  the  batteries  on  the 
Yirginia  shore,  guns  of  a  larger  caliber  than  are  in  possession  of  either 
yourself  or  the  army  under  General  Hooker  will  be  necessary.  It  will 
not  be  advisable,  therefore,  to  land  the  guns  from  your  vessels,  as  sug¬ 
gested,  but  keep  them  prepared  for  active  use  on  board,  as  occasion  will 
soon  require. 

You  will  communicate  with  that  portion  of  the  flotilla  that  is  below 
you,  enjoining  upon  them  to  exercise  unremitted  vigilance  in  detecting 
and  preventing  all  hostile  movements  in  that  quarter  and  to  hold  them¬ 
selves  in  readiness  for  orders  to  proceed  up  the  river  when  you  shall 
require.  Great  firmness  and  resolution  are  expected  of  them  in  times 
like  these,  as  well  as  constant  watchfulness.  In  all  these  your  example 
and  counsel  will  have  their  effect,  and  in  you  the  Department  lias 
implicit  confidence. 

If  these  demonstrations  of  the  enemy  on  the  lower  Potomac  are  tem¬ 
porary,  and  designed  as  much  to  draw  attention  from  movements  in 
other  quarters  as  to  effect  the  lower  Maryland  counties,  it  is  none  the 
less  necessary  that  our  forces  and  vigilance  should  be  exercised. 

You  will  put  yourself  in  communication  with  General  Hooker  as  soon 
as  practicable  after  he  arrives  in  your  vicinity.  It  is  expected  he  will 
reach  Budd’s  Perry  or  some  point  in  that  neighborhood  to-morrow 
afternoon.  Communicate  freely  and  fully  with  that  officer,  who  will 
receive  similar  instructions  in  regard  to  yourself,  and  let  your  mutual 
counsels  produce  unity  of  action. 


OPERATIONS  ON  THE  POTOMAC  AND  RAPPAHANNOCK.  735 


Write  freely  and  fully  to  tlie  Department  by  every  opportunity  when 
you  have  anything  to  communicate,  and  keep  us  advised  of  the  condi¬ 
tion  of  affairs  as  thoroughly  as  possible. 

Very  respectfully,  etc.,  - 

Gideon  Welles.

Report  of  commandant  navy  yard ,  Washington,  regarding  means  for  pro¬ 
tecting  river  communication. 

Commandant’s  Office,  Navy  Yard, 

Washington ,  October  25,  1861. 

Sir  :  The  Potomac  is  now  so  far  obstructed  that  it  is  no  longer  used 
by  the  army  for  the  transportation  of  supplies,  and  the  sole  dependence 
for  that  purpose  and  for  the  supplies  of  the  inhabitants  of  this  city  is 
limited  to  the  railroads  alone. 

The  daily  consumption  of  the  Army  of  the  Potomac  is  about  700  tons, 
including  the  feed  for  the  horses.  The  travel  and  trade  of  the  city  will 
bring  the  total  to  nearly  1,000  tons  daily. 

The  capacity  of  the  railroad  is  stated  at  about  1,500  to  1,600  tons  per 
day.  This  would  seem  sufficient  to  meet  ordinary  wants  and  even  those 
of  an  unusual  description,  yet  some  days  since,  when  I  wished  to  obtain 
some  bales  of  hay  for  a  special  purpose  from  the  Quartermaster’s 
Department,  I  was  answered  by  Colonel  [D.  II.]  Bucker  that  he  had 
scarcely  more  than  one  day’s  provender  on  hand  for  the  horses,  and  up 
to  this  time  both  the  railroad  and  river  had  been  open  for  all  manner  of 
supplies. 

1 1  does  not  seem  advisable,  therefore,  to  permit  the  river  to  be  closed 
without  some  effort,  for  the  railroad  is  not  infallible,  but  is  liable  to 
interruption  from  severe  storms,  particularly  in  the  approaching  sea¬ 
son.  Moreover,  the  disposition  of  the  hostile  batteries  is  such  as  not 
only  to  separate  our  flotilla,  but  to  exclude  its  action  from  some  25  or 
30  miles  of  the  river  and  leave  this  extent  open  to  their  one  steamer 


736  OPERATIONS  ON  THE  POTOMAC  AND  RAPPAHANNOCK. 

and  other  facilities  by  water  for  communicating  with  the  Maryland 
shores  and  supply  their  forces  along  the  bank,  when  by  land  this  would 
be  tedious  and  uncertain. 

The  advance  of  the  army  will  undoubtedly  clear  the  Virginia  bank 
effectually,  and  even  cause  the  loss  of  the  cannon,  which  are  too  heavy  for 
withdrawal,  but  it  may  be  a  question  whether  it  is  not  better  to  relieve 
the  army  of  this  necessity  and  be  ready  to  assist  its  interim  operations 
as  well  as  to  open  an  important  avenue  for  its  supply.  To  this  end  we 
must  resort  to  counter  batteries,  which,  if  they  will  not  destroy  those 
of  the  enemy,  will  at  least  clear  the  river  of  his  craft,  and  probably 
cover  the  passage  of  our  own. 

I  assume  the  distance  across  as  3,500  yards,  and  propose  to  operate 
against  the  batteries  from  Cockpit  Point  to  Evansport  with  not  less  thau 
fifty  heavy  pieces. 

Of  these  there  are  now  disposable  here  (including  batterj^of  Pensa¬ 
cola)  27  of  IX-incli,  2  of  XI- inch,  1  50-pounder,  4  mortars  (10-inch),  3 
rifled  80-pounders;  total,  33  cannon  and  4  mortars.  Three  mortars  on 
their  way,  leaving  only  ten  cannon  to  be  provided,  which  can  no  doubt 
be  done  in  season. 

If  the  operation  is  to  be  performed  it  should  be  begun  in  twenty-four 
hours;  and  if  unlimited  means  be  placed  at  the  disposal  of  the  officer 
who  is  to  command,  the  batteries  should  be  ready  in  two  weeks  from  this 
date. 

Of  course  I  am  to  be  understood  to  speak  of  a  naval  affair  only, 
which  is  not  to  embarrass  the  army  or  to  divert  from  it  anything  neces¬ 
sary  to  the  particular  designs  of  the  commanding  general.  The  troops 
that  may  assist  in  throwing  up  the  entrenchments,  and  to  guard 
against  unfriendly  designs  in  the  rear,  will  be  most  convenient  for  cross¬ 
ing  to  the  opposite  shore  by  the  naval  forces  when  their  services  mav 
be  needed. 

Indeed,  if  we  are  able  to  silence  the  hostile  batteries,  an  opportunity 
may  be  found  for  attacking  in  good  force  when  the  advance  of  the  main 
army  may  render  it  advantageous. 

It  is  needless  to  enter  upon  technical  details.  These  must  be  left  to 
the  option  of  the  officer  in  command,  and  he  must  also  have  control  of 
the  flotilla. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Jno.  A.  Dahlgkren, 

Commandant. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy.

ting  information  regarding  Cockpit  Point  battery. 

Alexandria,  October  26,  1861. 

Dear  Sir  :  I  send  the  enclosed.  I  hope  it  may  be  of  some  service,  if 
[you  have]  any  intentions  of  dislodging  the  Confederates.  They  seem 
now  entirely  to  have  the  control  of  at  least  15  miles  of  the  river,  and  the

With  great  regard,  your  friend  and  servant, 

Lewis  McKenzie. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy.

[Enclosure.] 

Cockpit  Point  where  the  Confederates  have  a  battery,  is  in  some 
respects  a  remarkable  military  position.  It  commands  Freestone  Point 
on  the  north,  Ship  [Shipping]  Point  on  the  south,  being  distant  from 
either  about  2.J  miles.  The  land  is  higher  than  either  of  them  and  it 
projects  farther  into  the  Potomac.  In  the  rear  it  is  defended  by  Power’s 
[Powell’s]  Creek,  the  low  grounds  of  which  are  commanded  by  it. 

Opposite,  in  Maryland,  are  Stump  Neck  and  Budd’s  Ferry.  The 
height  of  the  land  at  Cockpit  above  the  river  is  from  40  to  50  feet, 
while  that  of  Stump  Neck  is  not  more  than  8  or  10  for  a  distance  of 
miles  back  from  the  river.  The  river  here  being  1^  miles  wide,  the  dis¬ 
tance  from  this  rebel  battery  to  high  ground  in  rear  of  Stump  Neck 
would  be  2f  miles;  to  the  heights  at  Budd’s  Ferry  not  more  than  2£ 
miles  at  most. 

A  vessel  lying  at  Six  Chimneys  (the  upper  point  of  Mattawoman) 
would  be  in  range  and  could  choose  her  position  anywhere  between  that 
point  and  Cockpit,  the  channel  being  deep  and  bold.

Report  of  Captain  Craven ,  TJ.  S.  Navy ,  commanding  Potomac  Flotilla, 
regarding  prisoners  captured  by  the  TJ.  S.  steamers  Island  Belle  and 
E.  H.  Herbert. 


U.  S.  S.  Harriet  Lane,  October  28,  1861. 

Sir  :  On  the  20tli  instant  a  person  calling  himself  Patrick  McCafferty 
was  picked  up  by  the  steamer  Island  Belle  while  in  the  act  of  crossing 
over  in  a  small  boat  from  the  Maryland  shore  toward  Mathias  Point. 

He  tells  a  very  lame  story  of  his  having  always  been  a  common  day 
laborer,  of  his  destitution  for  want  of  means  of  support,  and  that  he 
was  going  to  Fredericksburg  to  see  a  friend,  from  whom  lie  was  certain 
of  obtaining  assistance.  He  pretends  also  that  it  was  only  a  drunken 
spree  that  brought  him  to  this  trouble;  that  he  did  not  know  where  he 
was  or  where  he  was  going  to  when  he  was  taken  on  board  of  the 
Island  Belle.  A  day  or  two  after  he  was  received  on  board  of  this  ves¬ 
sel,  Acting  Master  Cash  recognized  him  as  a  person  who  had  been  in 
the  employ  of  Norris  Brothers,  of  Philadelphia,  where  he  held  the 
responsible  trust  of  timekeeper  at  a  salary  of  $1,000  per  annum.  Upon 
being  recognized  by  Mr.  Cash,  McCafferty  exhibited  a  considerable 
degree  of  uneasiness.  This  morning,  upon  further  questioning  by 
myself,  he  acknowledges  that  he  had  been  in  the  employ  of  Norris 
Brothers,  of  Philadelphia;  E.  S.  Norris,  Schenectady,  and  Richard 
Norris  &  Son,  of  Philadelphia.  E.  S.  Norris,  he  says,  has  recently  gone 
to  Europe.  Looking  upon  his  case  as  a  suspicious  one,  I  have  sent  him 
up  to  the  navy  yard  to  await  the  disposition  of  the  Department. 

This  morning  the  master  of  the  Herbert  took  a  man  from  the  beach 
at  Smoot’s  Landing.  This  person  pretends,  although  he  has  lived  all 
his  life  in  this  country,  that  he  can  not  talk  English;  says  his  name  is 
Albert  Jackson;  has  a  brother  living  in  Virginia,  where  he  left  him 
about  ten  or  twelve  days  ago.  Not  being  satisfied  with  his  account  of

Navy  Department,  October  28,  1861. 

Sir  :  The  Valley  City  and  Rescue  are  detached  from  the  flotilla  and 
now  form  part  of  the  North  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron.  As  they 
are  both  in  the  Bappahannock  River,  Flag-Officer  Goldsborough  has 
been  notified  of  the  fact  and  their  positions. 

The  steamer  Baltimore  has  been  ordered  to  remain  in  the  lower  part 
of  the  Potomac  River,  attached  to  your  force.  Should  the  senior  officer 
below  the  batteries  require  supplies  from  Hampton  Roads,  that  vessel 
can  be  used  for  the  purpose  of  obtaining  them. 

The  Stepping  Stones,  of  3  feet  draft,  left  New  York  for  the  Potomac 
a  week  ago. 

Direct  the  paymaster  of  the  flotilla  to  forward  to  their  proper  desti¬ 
nation  the  accounts  of  such  vessels  as  have  left  your  command. 

I  am,  respectfully, 

Gideon  Welles. 

Captain  Thomas  T.  Craven, 

Commanding  Potomac  Flotilla,  Washington.

on  steamer  George  Page. 

Headquarters  Hooker’s  Division, 

Six  Miles  from  Buddls  Ferry,  Md.,  October  29,  1861. 
Commodore  :  On  my  return  here  this  evening  I  found  the  dispatches 
referred  to  by  you.  On  conferring  with  Captain  [T.  H.]  Williamson, 
my  engineer,  who  has  been  down  to  the  ferry,  I  find  that  the  Page  is

able  to  defer  the  attack  until  she  presents  herself.  If  she  is  up  the 
creek  where  the  schooners  are  her  hull  is  completely  covered  by  the 
high  banks  of  the  river.  I  will  advise  you  when  an  opportunity  pre¬ 
sents  itself  for  opening  on  the  Page.

Joseph  Hooker, 

Brigadier-  General,  Commanding  Division.

Letter  from  Samuel  W.  Adams ,  esq.,  to  the  Secretary  of  the  Navy,  making 
statement  of  the  serious  loss  resulting  from  interrupted  communication 
by  the  river. 


Nanjemoy,  Charles  County,  Md.,  October  29,  1861. 

Dear  Sir:  I  have  to  call  your  honor’s  attention  to  tlic  subjoined 
statement  of  facts,  of  serious  import  to  myself  and  some  of  my  neigh¬ 
bors,  and  to  ask  your  favorable  consideration  of  the  same. 

The  facts  are  as  follows,  viz:  That  we  are  unable  to  get  our  grain 
to  market,  in  consequence  of  a  late  order  from  the  Navy  Department  to 
allow  no  vessel  or  sailing  craft  to  pass  up  the  Potomac  above  Mathias 
Point,  thereby  subjecting  many  of  us  to  great  inconvenience  and  pecun¬ 
iary  embarrassment  and  perhaps  loss.  If  we  can’t  get  our  produce  to 
market  we  have  not  the  means  to  purchase  supplies  of  stores  and  cloth¬ 
ing  for  our  families. 

Hence,  I  respectfully  ask  for  myself  and  neighbors  that  if  we  can  get 
vessels  from  below  to  carry  our  produce  to  market,  inasmuch  as  the 
flotilla  has  returned  to  Smith’s  Point,  that  an  order  may  be  given  to 
the  flotilla  below  Mathias  Point  to  allow  vessels  to  come  up  as  far  as 
Smith’s  Point  to  take  off  grain  and  produce  for  the  farmers  living 
between  those  points. 

I  would  further  state  to  your  honor  that  I  make  petition  at  the  sug¬ 
gestion  of  an  officer  of  the  flotilla  off  Smith’s  Point. 

I  would  also  state  that  it  bears  particularly  hard  upon  me,  as  I  was 
prevented  from  shipping  my  grain  by  an  order  for  arrest  from  your 
Department  in  the  case  of  Commander  Dove  and  detained  at  Washing¬ 
ton  with  my  entire  white  family  for  nearly  three  weeks,  and  I  had  made 
arrangements  to  commence  shipping  my  grain  the  day  following  the 
night  of  my  arrest,  and  hence  the  unfortunate  situation  in  which  I  am 
placed. 

Your  early  attention  to  and  favorable  consideration  of  the  above 
statement  will  greatly  oblige,  sir,  yours,  respectfully,' etc., 

Saml.  W.  Adams, 

Smith’s  Point,  Md. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  Navy,  TI.  S.  A.

[Enclosure.] 

II.  S.  S.  Union, 

Off  Aquia  Creek,  October  30,  1861. 

Sir  :  1  have  nothing  new  to  report  from  this  part  of  the  river,  except 
the  discovery  of  a  battery  of  rifled  guns  of,  I  think,  three  iu  number, 
about  1^  miles  below  any  that  have  been  fired  heretofore.  It  is  sit¬ 
uated  a  little  below  a  new  brick  house  which  you  may  remember 
stands  below  the  wharf  at  Evansport.  I  sent  the  Ice  Boat  up  to  try 
the  range  of  her  long  guns  upon  the  lower  battery  (as  I  supposed)  of 
the  enemy.  After  she  had  tired  several  times  the  new  battery  disclosed 
itself  within  easy  range.  In  fact  some  of  the  shot  went  entirely  across 
the  river.  She  was  struck  by  only  one  shot,  which  did  no  damage.  I 
have  sent  the  steamer  Baltimore  to  Old  Point  for  provisions  and  water. 
1  have  detained  two  coal  schooners,  which  will  supply  us  with  coal  for 
a  month  or  nearly. 

I  have  detached  the  Rescue,  by  order  of  Mr.  Pox,  and  sent  her  to  the 
mouth  of  the  Rappahannock. 

I  have  stationed  the  Island  Belle  at  Mathias  Point,  and  send  the 
Freeborn  down  every  day  to  shell  the  place.  As  there  are  no  troops  at 
that  point,  except  militia,  who  run  away  when  fired  at,  I  hope  to  delay 
if  not  entirely  put  a  stop  to  their  operations.  I  wish  much  to  establish 
a  signal,  which  can  only  be  done  by  rockets,  with  our  pickets  at  Budd’s 
Ferry  to  warn  me  in  case  the  Page  should  start  down  the  river.  I  am 
induced  to  believe  that  she  is  anxious  to  return  to  her  old  place  of 
refuge.  When  she  came  out  Aquia  Creek  she  supposed  we  had  aban¬ 
doned  this  part  of  the  river.  She  is  in  a  much  worse  position  now,  for 
her  own  safety,  than  she  was  before.

Letter  from  Brigadier -General  Hooker ,  U.  S.  Army,  to  Captain  Craven, 
U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  Potomac  Flotilla,  regarding  Confederate 
steamer  George  Page. 

Headquarters  Hooker’s  Divison, 

Six  Miles  from  Buddls  Ferry ,  Md.,  October  31,  1861. 
Commodore:  Yesterday  I  made  an  examination  of  the  enemy’s 
defenses  on  the  opposite  shore  of  the  Potomac,  and  found  them  with 
plenty  of  guns  in  position  and  actively  employed  in  establishing  addi¬ 
tional  ones.  The  Page  is  lying  up  Quantico  Creek,  and  so  much  shel¬ 
tered  by  the  high  bank  between  her  and  the  Potomac  as  to  expose 
only  about  two-tliirds  of  her  length  of  smoke  pipe  and  her  walking 
beam,  a  very  small  object  for  me  to  open  my  batteries  on  at  our  distance. 

Last  night  a  parapet  was  thrown  up  by  men  to  shelter  a  few  pieces, 
but  1  would  not  advise  the  use  of  it  until  the  Page  moves  from  her  pres¬ 
ent  moorings.  Under  the  most  favorable  circumstances  our  batteries 
will  be  exposed  to  a  much  heavier  fire  than  we  can  give,  as  regards 
calibers  and  number. 

I  have  written  to  Major-General  McClellan  to  this  effect. 

With  great  respect,  1  have  the  honor  to  be,  your  obedient  servant, 

Joseph  Hooker, 

Brigadier- General,  Commanding  Division. 

Commodore  Craven, 

Commanding  the  Fleet  of  the  Potomac. 


Report  of  Captain  Craven,  IJ.  S.  Navy,  commanding  Potomac  Flotilla, 

regarding  army  cooperation. 

U.  S.  S.  Harriet  Lane,  October  31,  1861. 
Sir  :  I  have  the  honor  to  acknowledge  the  receipt  of  your  letters  of 
the  24th,  28th,  and  29th  instant. 


OPERATIONS  ON  THE  POTOMAC  AND  RAPPAHANNOCK.  743 


In  accordance  witli  your  instructions,  I  called  upon  Brigadier-General 
Hooker  on  the  26th  instant,  and  was  gratified  to  find  that  he  was  ready 
and  willing  to  cooperate  with  me  at  all  times  in  repelling  the  enemy. 
On  the  29tli  instant  the  general  informed  me  that  the  rebels  had  sent  a 
small  boat  from  Quantico  Creek  over  toward  Budd’s  Ferry  bearing  a 
fiag  of  truce,  and  that  when  she  had  approached  within  200  or  300  yards 
of  tlieMaryland  shorea  barrel  with  something  attached  to  it  was  thro  wn 
overboard,  and  the  boat  immediately  turned  and  pulled  back  to  the  Yir- 
ginia  shore.  I  have  no  doubt  but  this  is  one  of  their  infernal  machines. 
If  this  is  the  use  to  which  the  enemy  is  to  put  flags  of  truce,  God  help 
us  from  Southern  chivalry. 

General  Hooker  thinks  with  me  that  for  the  present  any  demonstra¬ 
tions  on  the  part  of  the  flotilla  by  firing  upon  the  enemy  might  possibly 
embarrass  him  in  his  operations,  and  I  have  therefore  not  yet  fired  at 
him,  as  suggested  in  your  letter  of  the  21st  instant. 

The  Page  is  still  at  Quantico  Creek,  but  hauled  up  so  far  that  she  is 
not  discernible  from  the  Maryland  shore.  Three  small  oyster  pungies 
passed  up  last  night,  reporting  all  quiet  below. 

There  are  some  six  or  eight  Northern  schooners  now  lying  off  Indian 
Head  awaiting  a  fair  wind  and  dark  night  to  pass  down  the  river. 
Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Thos.  T.  Craven, 
Commanding  Potomac  Flotilla. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy,  Washington,  D.  C.

guns  ifc  Avas  necessary  to  discharge  them  at  an  angle  ofeight  or  nine

Report  of  Lieutenant  Harrell ,  U.  8.  Navy ,  Commanding  TJ.  S.  8.  Union , 
of  affairs  on  the  lower  Potomac. 

U.  S.  S.  Union, 

Off  Aquia  Creek,  November  1 ,  1861. 

Sir  :  I  have  given  permission  to  an  engineer  who  is  attached  to  the 
Ice  Boat  to  go  to  Washington  for  a  day  or  so,  if  it  meets  with  your 
approbation.  Lieutenant  Commanding  Pattison  says  he  can  spare 
him. 

I  have  nothing  new  to  report  on  this  part  of  the  river.  Men  occa¬ 
sionally  show  themselves  at  Mathias  Point,  but  retire  upon  the  approach 
of  our  vessels.  The  place  is  shelled  every  day,  and  I  keep  a  steamer 
there  always  at  night.  The  steamer  Baltimore  has  returned  with  all 
that  I  required. 

The  captain  of  that  vessel  reports  his  pilot,  Ransom  Brown,  as  hav¬ 
ing  deserted  his  ship  yesterday,  but  after  an  absence  of  some  hours 
returned,  having  changed  his  mind.  He  was  excessively  insolent, 

abusing  the  operations  of  the  llotilla,  and  saying  if  I  were  not  a  d - d 

coAvard  I  Avould  open  the  river,  and  much  more  infamous  language.  I 
had  him  put  in  irons.  The  captain  of  the  Baltimore  says  he  has  a 
man  on  board  who  is  a  good  pilot,  and  he  hopes  you  will  authorize  his 
appointment.  Most  assuredly  such  a  scoundrel  as  Brown  should  be 
dismissed  and  neA'er  permitted  to  reenter  the  service  in  any  capacity. 
He  has  forfeited  his  pay  by  desertion.  I  beg  you  to  excuse  my  earnest¬ 
ness  in  this  matter,  as  this  man  has  outraged  my  feelings  much  more 
than  I  have  expressed.  It  was  entirely  gratuitous  on  his  part,  too,  as 
I  had  never  seen  him  before. 

I  stretch  my  vessels  across  the  river  at  night,  so  that  the  Page  can 
not  escape  us  if  she  attempts  to  regain  her  old  anchorage. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  your  obedient  servant, 

A.  I).  Harrell, 
Lieutenant ,  Commanding. 

Captain  Thomas  T.  Craven, 

Commanding  Potomac  Flotilla ,  Potomac  River.

[Enclosure.] 


U.  S.  S.  Union, 

Off  Aquia  Creek,  November  8,  1861. 

Sir:  I  have  nothing  of  importance  to  communicate  in  relation  to  the 
enemy  at  this  point.  1  have  been  down  the  river  and  examined  Mathias 
Point;  found  everything  still  as  death.  The  talk  among  the  negroes, 
however,  is  that  a  battery  will  be  opened  there  soon  as  they  can  get 
soldiers. 

The  Island  Belle  picked  up  in  the  river  the  other  day  twenty-three 
negroes — men,  women,  and  children.  There  are  now  some  forty  or 
more  contrabands  on  board  the  different  vessels.  These  people  have 
all  to  be  rationed,  and  it  is  becoming  very  embarrassing  to  me,  short 
of  provisions  as  1  am.  The  last  party  of  twenty-three  have  not  been 
employed  on  any  military  works,  according  to  their  own  confessions, 
and  ran  away,  as  they  allege,  because  their  masters  did  not  give  them 
enough  to  eat,  which  their  appearance  by  no  means  indicates.  I  think  it 
would  be  a  good  strokeof  policy  to  return  these  negroes  to  their  owners. 
It  would  tend  to  put  a  stop  to  the  wholesale  desertion  that  is  now  going- 
on,  and  relieve  us  of  a  most  unpleasant  difficulty.  I  have  no  doubt  that 
many  of  them  are  from  Maryland,  notwithstanding  they  invariably  repre¬ 
sent  themselves  as  coming  from  Virginia.  Please  give  me  instructions 
astothe  disposition  to  be  made  of  these,  and  for  my  government  in 
future  similar  cases. 

The  Ice  Boat  is  becoming  more  rickety  every  day;  her  fires  are  now 
down  and  they  are  endeavoring  to  patch  her  boilers.  I  fear  every  day 
to  hear  of  her  breaking  entirely  down;  in  that  event  she  would  be  a 
source  of  great  trouble  to  us.  Should  you  have  any  vessels  above  that 
you  could  spare,  they  could  be  most  usefully  employed  below.  I  under¬ 
stand  there  is  communication  across  the  lower  part  of  the  river 
constantly. 

I  have  the  pilot  of  the  Baltimore  still  in  confinement,  awaiting  your 
decision. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

A.  13.  Harrell, 

Lieutenant,  Commanding. 

Captain  T.  T.  Craven, 

Commanding  Potomac  Flotilla.

Report  of  Lieutenant  Clary ,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Dawn,  of 
engagement  with  Confederate  battery  below  Maryland.  Point. 

U.  S.  S.  Dawn, 

Potomac  River,  November  10,  1861. 

Sir:  I  have  to  report  that  on  the  passage  down  the  river  this  p.  m. 
[we]  were  fired  upon  from  a  small  battery  of  two  or  three  guns  (rifled 
and  smoothbore),  none  of  which  struck  us.  We  returned  the  fire,  but 
ineffectually. 

This  battery  is  located  at  about  miles  above  Boyd’s  Hole,  3  miles 
below  Maryland  Point. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

A.  G.  Clary, 

Lieutenant,  Commanding  U.  S.  S.  Dawn. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy,  Washington,  D.  C.

U.  S.  S.  Union, 

Off  Aquia  C-reeTc,  November  11,  1861. 

Sir:  I  have  to  inform  you  that  I  learned  at  12  o’clock  last  night  that 
a  battery  was  ready  to  open  fire  from  Virginia  shore  nearly  opposite  to 
Maryland  Point.  I  sent  the  Freeborn,  Lieutenant  Commanding  Magaw, 
at  daylight  this  morning  to  ascertain  the  truth  of  the  information.  I 
herewith  enclose  his  report.  It  will  be  seen  by  an  inspection  of  the  chart 


750  OPERATIONS  ON  THE  POTOMAC  AND  RAPPAHANNOCK. 

% 

that  all  vessels  drawing  6  or  7  feet  of  water  will  have  to  pass  within 
less  than  three-quarters  of  a  mile  of  the  battery,  which  is  located  in  a 
ravine,  and,  with  pits  in  the  ground  for  the  men,  is  completely  sheltered 
from  our  guns. 

It  may  be  the  intention  of  the  enemy  to  cross  from  the  Potomac 
Creek.  Maryland  Point  should  be  occupied  immediately  by  our  troops. 
I  have  sent  an  officer  to  General  Hooker  to  inform  him  of  the  situation 
of  affairs. 

You  will  perceive  that  I  am  between  two  fires,  with  a  hostile  popula¬ 
tion  on  either  shore.  My  situation  is  by  no  means  enviable.  It  is  true 
I  can  pass  below  during  a  favorable  opportunity  and  escape.  If  I  do, 
however,  this  part  of  the  river  falls  into  the  enemy’s  hands  at  once. 
He  could  employ  the  steamer  Page  and  all  his  boats  for  such  purposes 
as  he  chooses;  in  short,  nothing  could  appear  upon  this  part  of  the 
river  except  with  his  consent.  I  shall  therefore  remain  here  until  other¬ 
wise  ordered.  I  have  more  than  fifty  contrabands  here.  I  must  dispose 
of  them  soon  or  I  shall  be  short  of  provisions.  I  have  a  schooner  of 
about  100  tons  loaded  with  coal.  When  that  is  gone  I  fear  I  can  get  no 
more  from  below. 

I  have  just  learned  that  the  Island  Belle  landed  a  party  of  men  from 
Colonel  [Charles  K.]  Graham’s  regiment  last  night  at  or  near  Mathias 
Point,  and  are  burning  houses,  etc.  I  have  not  learned  whether  they 
met  with  opposition  or  not. 

As  I  informed  you  in  my  last  we  are  much  in  want  of  clothes,  pea- 
jackets,  blankets,  shoes,  etc.  I  have  ordered  my  messenger  to  follow 
you  in  order  that  he  may  bring  back  your  orders  to  me.  I  think  the 
Resolute  could  pass  the  batteries  with  safety,  and  did  I  have  her  below 
I  could  communicate  with  you  with  ease;  now  it  is  difficult. 

In  great  haste,  I  remain,  your  obedient  servant, 

A.  D.  Harrell, 

Lieutenant ,  Commanding  Second  Division ,  Potomac  Flotilla. 

Captain  T.  T.  Craven, 

Commanding  Potomac  Flotilla. 

[Subenclosure.] 


U.  S.  S.  Freeborn, 

Off  Maryland  Point ,  November  11 — 8  a.  m. 

Sir  :  In  obedience  to  your  verbal  order,  I  made  an  examination  of  the 
Virginia  shore  in  this  vicinity  and  was  fired  on  by  a  battery  of  field- 
pieces,  I  think  four  in  number. 

This  battery  is  situated  about  200  yards  below  the  landing  at  Boyd’s 
Hole  and  is  protected  by  a  natural  embankment. 

The  enemy  threw  twelve  shell  over  and  around  us,  and  strange  to  say 
we  were  untouched  even  by  a  fragment.  I  fired  but  once,  throwing  an 
8-inch  shell;  the  morning  was  so  dark  I  could  see  nothing  but  the 
flashes.  At  7  a.  m.  the  house  of  Mr.  Grimes  and  others  in  that  vicinity 
on  Mathias  Point  were  in  flames. 

Yours,  respectfully, 

Samuel  Magaw, 

Lieutenant ,  U.  8.  Navy ,  Commanding. 

A.  D.  Harrell,  U.  S.  Navy, 

Commanding  Lower  Division ,  Potomac  Flotilla.

General  instructions  from  the  Secretary  of  the  Navy  to  Captain  Craven , 
U.  S.  Navy ,  commanding  Potomac  Flotilla. 

Navy  Department,  November  12, 1861. 

Sir:  Yours  of  tlie  lltli  instant,  enclosing  a  letter  from  Lieutenant 
Commanding  Harrell  and  also  one  from  Lieutenant  Commanding 
Magaw,  lias  been  received ;  also  your  dispatch  of  the  9th  instant. 

The  dismissal  of  the  pilot,  Brown,  is  approved,  and  I  congratulate  you 
on  the  favorable  termination  of  the  disease.  Cut  the  hatches,  as  you 
request,  as  early  as  practicable.  You  will  take  the  public  property  out 
of  the  Ice  Boat  aud  send  her  to  Philadelphia  under  charge  of  Acting 
Master  Parks  and  such  crew  only  as  are  necessary  to  carry  her  safely 
home,  where  she  will  be  turned  over  to  her  owners.  If  Acting  Master 
Parks  and  her  engineer  consider  her  unsafe  to  make  this  trip,  she  might 
be  temporarily  repaired  at  Baltimore.  The  shipped  men’s  accounts 
will  be  sent  with  them  to  Philadelphia.  Furnish  the  Department  with 
a  list  of  the  other  persons  who  leave  in  the  vessel. 

The  Department  presumes  that  you  will  have  no  difficulty  in  keeping 
open  communication  sufficient  for  transportation  of  stores,  etc.,  between 
your  vessels  with  the  light-draft  steamer  Stepping  Stones.  If  this  is 
impracticable  please  notify  the  Department,  as  it  will  involve  leaving 
the  river  above  Mathias  [Point],  according  to  the  dispatch  of  Lieutenant 
Commanding  Harrell.  This  must  be  avoided  if  possible.  The  Navy 
Department  has  some  200  tons  of  coal  at  Annapolis,  which  you  can  use 
if  necessary. 

The  ways  at  the  navy  yard  are  now  free  and  can  take  another  vessel 
for  repairs. 

I  am,  respectfully,  etc., 

Gideon  Welles. 

Captain  T.  T.  Craven, 

Commanding  Potomac  Flotilla. 


Report  of  Acting  Master  Street ,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  schooner 
Dana,  regarding  combined  reconnoissance  to  Mathias  Point. 

On  Board  the  U.  S.  Schooner  Dana, 

Off  Blakistone  Island,  November  12,  1861. 

Dear  Sir:  Having  received  information  from  Captain  Arnold  Har¬ 
ris,  of  the  steamer  Island  Belle,  that  Lieutenant  Commanding  Samuel 
Magaw,  of  the  steamer  Freeborn,  and  himself  had  arranged  au  expedi¬ 
tion  to  Mathias  Point,  in  conjunction  and  by  direction  of  Colonel  Charles 
K.  Graham,  Fifth  Regiment,  Excelsior  Brigade,  for  the  purpose  of  land¬ 
ing  a  military  force  and  making  a  reconnoissance,  and  as  the  commander 
of  the  Freeborn  was  prevented  by  circumstances  from  carrying  out  his 
intentions,  I  was  applied  to  to  furnish,  as  far  as  lay  in  my  power,  means 
of  transportation  in  lieu  of  that  vessel.  Judging  the  object  to  be 
attained,  viz,  the  ascertaining  the  positive  existence  of  the  presumed 
batteries  on  Mathias  Point  to  be  a  fact,  and  the  making  a  general 
inspection  of  the  country  to  be  a  sufficient  apology  for  leaving  my  sta¬ 
tion,  I  did  so  and  was,  on  the  evening  of  the  10th,  towed  up  by  the 
steamer  Island  Belle  opposite  Chapel  Point,  on  the  Port  Tobacco  Creek 
[River],  where,  at  10  o’clock  p.  m.,  I  embarked,  by  order  of  Colonel 
Graham,  about  200  men,  one-lialf  the  force  to  be  employed  on  the  expe¬ 
dition,  consisting  of  Companies  B,  C,  and  D  and  a  howitzer  squad. 


752  OPERATIONS  ON  THE  POTOMAC  AND  RAPPAHANNOCK. 

% 

During  the  afternoon  of  the  10th,  in  order  to  facilitate  matters,  I  seized 
boats,  such  as  I  deemed  suitable  for  the  purpose,  either  from  vessels  on 
the  river  or  fishing  boats  on  the  shores,  which,  in  connection  with  the 
launch  of  the  Island  Belle ,  furnished  adequate  means  for  embarking 
the  troops  in  perfect  good  order  and  without  confusion  in  about  three- 
quarters  of  an  hour. 

Arrived  at  Mathias  Point,  the  debarkation  was  superintended  by 
myself  and  was  successful,  as  was  in  fact  the  whole  expedition,  for  a 
detailed  account  of  which,  on  the  part  of  our  military  allies,  I  would 
respectfully  refer  you  to  Colonel  Graham’s  official  report  to  General  D. 
E.  Sickles. 

After  making  a  thorough  reconnoissance  and  seizing  and  destroying 
a  large  amount  of  rebel  property  and  skirmishing  with  the  enemy’s 
pickets,  killing  one  man  and  wounding  two  others,  the  troops  were 
withdrawn  and  reembarked  in  capital  order  about  9  o’clock  a.  m.,  and 
we  reached  Chapel  Point  at  12  in.,  finishing  an  affair  that  will  set  at 
rest  the  supposed  existence  of  heavy  artillery  on  that  point,  and  throw¬ 
ing  the  enemy  into  a  great  state  of  trepidation  for  their  unprotected 
coast  on  the  Potomac. 

It  was  the  original  intention  to  have  landed  from  the  Dana  the  how¬ 
itzer,  but  it  was  finally  decided  to  advance  without  it. 

I  can  not  close  this  report  without  referring  to  the  conduct  of  the 
regiment,  or  rather  detachment,  engaged  in  this  matter.  They  pre¬ 
served  the  most  perfect  order,  silence,  and  quiet  on  board  the  vessels 
employed,  and  while  engaged  ashore  evinced  the  coolness  and  determi¬ 
nation  of  veterans. 

There  are  on  the  point  partially  masked  and  unfinished  intrenchments 
in  three  places,  which  have  not  been  apparently  worked  upon  nor  occu¬ 
pied  for  some  time  and  are  of  no  particular  moment  in  their  present 
condition.  The  cord  wood  and  buildings  on  the  point  and  the  building 
known  as  Grimes’s  house  were  all  destroyed  by  fire,  thus  unmasking  to 
the  fire  of  passing  boats  the  only  earthworks,  as  spoken  above.  There 
were  also  numerous  attempts  made  to  fire  the  woods  upon  the  point,  but 
with  only  qualified  success,  on  account  of  the  dampness  from  the  recent 
storms  and  noniuflammable  nature  of  the  timber.  The  crew  of  the 
Dana  conducted  themselves  with  the  greatest  coolness  and  propriety 
during  the  affair,  and  merit  mention  for  their  general  demeanor  and 
prompt  obedience  to  orders. 

I  remain  with  great  respect,  your  obedient  servant, 

Wm.  T.  Street, 
Commanding  U.  S.  Schooner  Dana. 

Commodore  Thomas  T.  Craven, 

Navy  Yard ,  Washington ,  D.  C.
