Report  of  Lieutenant  Harr  ell,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Union , 

regarding  affairs  of  the  flotilla. 

U.  S.  S.  Union, 

Off  Aquia  Creek,  November  20,  1861. 

Sir:  I  avail  myself  of  the  opportunity  offered  by  the  Stepping  Stones 
to  report  all  quiet  on  the  lower  part  of  the  river  at  present.  The  ene¬ 
my’s  battery  at  Boyd’s  Hole  has  been  withdrawn.  Troops  are  numerous 
in  the  vicinity  of  Aquia  and  Potomac  creeks.  No  new  batteries  have 
been  discovered.  I  have  removed  all  the  public  property  from  the  Ice 
Boat,  as  directed,  and  will  send  her  to  Philadelphia  immediately.  I 
have  taken  fourteen  of  her  crew  to  fill  vacancies  on  board  this  vessel, 
and  respectfully  request  your  approval  of  the  same.  I  enclose  you  a  list 
of  the  men  thus  retained,  and  should  it  meet  your  approval,  please 
direct  the  transfer  of  their  accounts  to  this  ship.  I  enclose  also  a  list 
of  those  who  accompany  the  Ice  Boat;  also  of  those  I  send  to  you, 
together  with  a  list  of  contrabands  that  have  been  collected  by  the 
various  vessels  of  the  flotilla. 

Some  means  should  be  adopted  by  which  we  could  receive  a  regular 
supply  of  coal.  There  are  no  coal  vessels  in  the  river  except  one,  which 
is  partially  discharged.  We  require  about  100  tons  per  week,  and  have 
sufficient  for  nearly  three  weeks.  If  an  arrangement  could  be  made  by 
which  I  would  be  certain  to  receive  that  quantity  of  coal,  I  could  dis¬ 
pense  with  the  Baltimore  and  send  her  to  Washington.  The  pilot  of  the 
Island  Belle  has  run  that  vessel  ashore  repeatedly  and  is  entirely  unfit 
for  his  position.  He  wishes  to  be  discharged.  There  is  a  man  onboard 
the  U.  S.  schooner  Bailey  who  is  represented  to  be  an  excellent  pilot;  if 
you  will  authorize  his  employment  as  such,  I  will  give  him  the  order. 
If  he  proves  capable,  as  he  is  said  to  be,  he  should  receive  his  discharge 
and  be  rated  pilot. 

Yery  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

A.  D.  Harrell, 

Lieutenant ,  Commanding  Second  Division,  Potomac  Flotilla. 

Commodore  Thomas  T.  Craven, 

Commanding  Potomac  Flotilla. 


Order  from  the  commandant  navy  yard,  Washington,  to  Acting  Master 
Foster,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  TJ.  S.  S.  E.  B.  Hale,  regarding  trans¬ 
portation  of  ordnance. 

Commandant’s  Office,  Navy  Yard, 

Washington,  November  20,  1861. 

Sir:  Conformably  to  the  order  of  the  Bureau  of  Ordnance,  you  will

A  quia  Creek. 

U.  S.  S.  Union, 

Off  Aquia  Creek,  November  21,  1861. 
Sir:  Everything  tranquil  here.  The  enemy  has  been  engaged  dur¬ 
ing  the  last  three  days  in  throwing  up  works,  as  we  can  see  with  our 
glasses,  on  the  hills  about  1  mile  in  the  rear  and  a  little  above  the  lower 
battery.  It  must  be  intended  for  defense  of  the  river  battery  against  a 
flank  attack.  This  looks  very  much  like  a  determination  to  remain  on 
the  river  until  he  is  driven  away. 

I  have  a  contraband  on  board  this  vessel  who  is  a  good  cook,  and  I 
will  thank  you  for  permission  to  ship  him,  if  not  against  the  regulations.

A.  D.  Harrell,

Report  of  Captain  Craven ,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  Potomac  Flotilla , 
transmitting  report  of  Lieutenant  Harrell ,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding 
U.  S.  S.  Union ,  regarding  affairs  on  the  Potomac. 

U.  S.  S.  Harriet  Lane,  November  30,  1861. 
Sir  :  I  have  the  honor  to  enclose  herewith  a  report  which  I  received 
last  night  from  Lieutenant  Commanding  Harrell;  also  one  from  the 
engineer  of  the  Union.  I  would  respectfully  suggest  that  the  Union 
be  ordered  either  to  Baltimore  or  some  one  of  our  Northern  dockyards 
lor  repairs,  and  should  it  be  the  intention  of  the  Department  to  comply 
with  my  request  of  the  20th  instant,  to  be  detached  from  the  command 
of  this  flotilla,  which  I  earnestly  hope  for,  I  most  respectfully  recom¬ 
mend  Lieutenant  Commanding  Harrell  as  in  everyway  deserving  to  be 
my  successor. 

Excepting  on  the  occasion  alluded  to  in  Captain  Harrell’s  report,  the 
Page  has  not  been  outside  of  Quantico  Creek.  The  Island  Belle  was, 
as  is  usual,  cruising  during  the  night  that  the  Hale  passed  down,  and 
no  doubt  mistaken  by  the  latter  for  the  Page,  hence  the  ill-founded 
report,  which  I  have  observed  in  some  of  the  papers,  of  the  Page’s 
appearance  on  the  river. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Thos.  T.  Craven, 

Captain,  U.  S.  Navy. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy,  Washington ,  I).  C. 


[Enclosure.] 

U.  S.  S.  Union, 

Off  Aquia  Creel,  November  29, 1861. 

Sir:  Nothing  new  has  transpired  on  this  part  of  the  river  since  my 
last  report.  I  have  seen  it  stated  in  the  newspapers  that  there  is  a 
battery  5  or  0  miles  below  Aquia  Creek;  such  is  not  the  fact.  Since 
the  removal  of  the  guns  from  Boyd’s  Hole  none  have  been  seen  below 
Potomac  Creek. 

I  have  caused  a  strict  watch  to  be  kept  upon  the  Page,  and  have  never 
seen  her  outside  Quantico  Creek  until  last  night.  The  guard  boat  of 
this  vessel  found  her  at  10  o’clock  last  night  in  the  middle  of  the  river 
opposite  Budd’s  Ferry.  She  was  lying  across  the  stream,  evidently 
waiting  for  something  to  pass.  The  guard  boat  pulled  close  to  her,  so 
close  as  to  see  [a]  great  many  men  on  board.  She  hailed  and  said  she 
was  the  Penguin  and  had  important  dispatches,  and  desired  the  boat 


OPERATIONS  ON  THE  POTOMAC  AND  RAPPAHANNOCK.  759 

to  come  and  get  them.  The  boat,  however,  knowing  that  the  Penguin 
was  not  in  the  river,  thought  it  advisable  to  pull  in  another  direction. 
I  suppose  she  was  afraid  to  fire  upon  the  boat,  lest  she  should  draw  the 
fire  of  our  batteries  upon  herself. 

The  Ceeur  de  Lion  has  arrived  here  from  Fortress  Monroe,  and  I 
thought  it  best  to  detain  her  under  the  circumstances  until  I  hear  from 
you.  Should  she  fall  in  with  the  Page  her  capture  would  be  almost 
certain.  Please  inform  me  whether  I  shall  permit  other  vessels  to 
pass  up. 

1  have  refrained  from  reporting  the  condition  of  this  vessel  until  I 
can  defer  it  no  longer.  She  has  been  leaking  very  badly  for  a  long 
time  past  and  it  is  increasing  daily,  and  has  now  reached  from  9  to  10 
inches  per  hour.  As  we  have  no  means  of  freeing  her  except  by  the 
hand  pumps,  the  crew  are  now  employed  nearly  half  their  time  in 
keeping  the  water  below  the  floor  of  the  engine  room.  We  have  lost  a 
quantity  of  powder,  and  have  no  secure  place  to  store  it  below  the 
water  line. 

Her  boilers  and  machinery  also  are  much  out  of  order.  I  enclose  the 
report  of  the  engineer  for  your  information  in  that  department. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

A.  E>.  Harrell, 

Lieutenant ,  Commanding  Second  Division ,  Potomac  Flotilla. 

Captain  Thomas  T.  Craven, 

Commanding  Potomac  Flotilla ,  Potomac  River. 


[Subeuclosure.] 

U.  S.  S.  Union,  November  28 ,  1861. 

Sir  :  I  take  this  method  of  informing  you  of  the  condition  of  the 
engines  and  boilers  of  this  vessel. 

In  the  first  place  the  engines  are  an  old  pair,  and  are  considerably 
out  of  order  and  want  repairing  in  many  places;  the  packing  bolts  in 
the  steam  cylinder  are  completely  gone,  and  is  the  cause  of  our  using 
a  greater  amount  of  fuel  than  we  should  do.  One  of  the  air  pump  rock- 
shaft  arms  is  cracked  and  bent  and  is  liable  to  give  out  at  any  moment. 

Both  of  the  boilers  are  in  a  very  bad  condition,  especially  the  star¬ 
board  boiler;  there  are  thirty-two  of  the  tubes  entirely  stopped  up  and 
entirely  useless,  and  the  others  are  leaking  badly  and  getting  worse 
every  day.  And  by  having  no  auxiliary  power  for  pumping  up  the 
boilers  while  lying  at  anchor,  we  have  to  blow  off  steam  and  pump  up 
by  hand,  which  is  a  great  injury  to  them. 

John  F.  McCittoheon, 

Senior  Fngineer  in  Charge. 

Lieutenant  A.  D.  Harrell.

costia,  of  duty  performed  by  that  vessel. 

U.  S.  S.  Anacostia,  December  1,  1861. 

Sir:  I  have  to  report  that  I  proceeded  down  the  river  as  you 
ordered;  arrived  off  Quantico  Creek  at  7:30;  found  all  quiet.  At 
9:30  a  boat  came  from  Maryland  shore  with  three  of  the  members  of 
the  Fifth  Massachusetts  Regiment.  They  stated  that  the  batteries  had 
fired  on  a  schooner  yesterday,  and  a  shell  from  them  had  burst  in  their 
camp.  At  4 : 25  ran  up  to  Stump  Neck  and  spoke  the  steamer  Herbert. 
At  4 :  50  heard  six  musket  shots  on  Virginia  shore.  Started  up  at  7 :  55. 

Respectfully,  your  obedient  servant,

Report  of  Acting  Master  Street,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  schooner 
Dana,  regarding  need-ed  repairs  to  that  vessel. 

IT.  S.  Cutter  Dana, 

Wade's  Bay  \Md.],  December  3,  1861. 

Sir  :  I  arrived  here  on  the  1st  instant,  out  of  provisions  and  with  my 
mainsail  split.  Having  no  canvas  or  twine,  I  could  not  mend  it  until  I 
arrived  here. 

My  sails,  sir,  are  very  old  and  tender,  and  should  I  get  caught  in  a 
squall  I  have  no  canvas  to  mend  them.  I  also  require  a  large  anchor. 

Should  I  not  get  a  new  set  of  sails  soon  the  vessel  will  be  rendered 
ineffectual.  She  is  also  in  need  of  other  repairs. 

Hoping  you  will  permit  me  to  go  to  the  yard,  I  remain,  very  respect- 
fully,  your  most  obedient  servant, 

W.  T.  Street, 

Acting  Masters  Mate ,  Commanding  Dana. 

Captain  Thomas  T.  Craven, 

Commanding  Potomac  Flotilla.

Abstracts  of  log  boolcs  of  vessels  serving  in  the  Potomac  Flotilla  during 
the  period  from  April'to  December  7,  1861. 

Abstract  log  of  R.  S.  S.  E.  B.  Hale,  September  4  to  November  22,  1861. 

September  4 , 1861. — At  2  p.  in.  tlie  vessel  was  put  in  commission,  navy 
yard,  New  York. 

September  28. — At  8  a.  m.  got  underway  for  Washington. 

October  1. — At  3:45  a.  in.  arrived  at  navy  yard,  Washington. 

October  7. — At  11  a.  m.  got  underway  to  proceed  down  to  the  flagship 
for  further  orders. 

October  10. — At  G  a.  m.  went  up  river.  Received  orders  to  board 
every  vessel  bound  out. 

October  11.— At  3  a.  m.  we  heard  the  report  of  guns  and  saw  the  flash 
in  the  direction  of  Quantico  Greek. 

October  15. — At  9:20  a.  m.  the  U.  S.  S.  Pocahontas  passed  down  the 
river.  When  off  Shipping  Point  heard  the  report  of  three  guns  fired 
from  a  battery  on  the  point.  At  10:15  the  IT.  S.  S.  Seminole  passed 
down  the  river.  When  off  Shipping  Point,  11  : 10,  two  shots  were  fired 
from  the  battery,  the  Seminole  returning  the  compliment.  Kept  firing 
till  11  :30;  niueteen  shots  were  fired  from  the  battery  and  eleven  from 
the  Seminole. 

October  16. — At  4 : 40  a.  m.  IT.  S.  S.  Pawnee  passed  down  with  two  boats 
in  tow.  When  the  boats  were  down  toward  Shipping  Point  the  battery 
opened  fire  upon  them.  Kept  on  till  6:25;  twenty-seven  shots  were  fired. 
At  6  p.  m.  three  shots  were  fired  from  Shipping  Point  battery;  niueteen 
shots  were  fired  from  the  battery  toward  the  Mount  Vernon ,  as  reported 
by  the  Pusey. 

October  17. — At  6  a.  m.  sixteen  shots  were  fired  from  the  battery, 
Shipping  Point,  and  fifteen  at  8:25. 

October  18. — From  1:45  till  12:10  midnight:  Fourteen  shots  were 
fired  from  the  rebel  battery  toward  the  U.  S.  S.  Columbia ,  which  passed 
us  during  the  time  up  river.  From  1:57  to  2:20  a.  in.  six  shots  were 
fired  from  the  battery.  At  10  Captain  Foster  and  Chief  Engineer 
Harrington  went  in  the  starboard  boat,  all  armed  with  small  arms,  in 
company  with  the  Reliance’s  boat,  up  Chicomuxen  River  [Creek],  and 
returned  at  1  p.  m.,  each  with  a  skiff.  At  5  p.  m.  three  shots  were  fired 
off  Aquia  Creek  from  the  IT.  S.  S.  Satellite. 

October  19. — At  12:40  a.  m.  six  shots  were  fired  from  the  rebel  battery. 
At  2 : 10  three  shots  were  fired ;  at  9  seventeen  shots  fired.  At  10  a.  m. 
commenced  firing,  continuing  until  10:55;  in  that  time  fired  152  shots 
from  the  rebel  battery  toward  the  towboat  Resolute,  with  two  schooners, 

and  the  towboat - ,  with  two  schooners  in  tow  alongside.  At  noon 

towboats  passed  with  three  schooners ;  the  Resolute  let  one  schooner 
go,  which  the  rebels  took  into  Aquia  Creek.  From  1:30  p.  m.  five 
shots  were  fired  from  Shipping  Point. 

October  20. — From  8  until  11  a.  m.  thirty  shots  were  fired  from  rebel 
battery  at  passing  vessels. 

October  22. — At  9:15  p.  m.  the  IT.  S.  S.  Rescue  came  with  dispatches 
from  Commodore  Craven;  reported  a  new  battery  erected  on  Mathias 
Point,  mounting  eighteen  guns. 

October  23. — At  11  a.  m.  saw  a  steamer  off  the  rebel  battery  going  up 
Quantico  Creek. 

October  28. — At  7:30  a.  m.  dropped  anchor  off  Indian  Head.  During 
the  afternoon  twenty-nine  shots  were  fired  from  the  rebel  battery  at

Abstract  log  of  the  TJ.  S.  S.  Pawnee,  May  20  to  August  21,  1861. 

May  20 ,  1861. — Off  Alexandria  from  8  to  meridian.  The  steamer 
Thomas  Freeborn  passed  up  the  river  to  Washington  with  several 
prizes  in  tow. 

May  24. — Making  preparations  to  land  troops.  At  4:20  a.  m.  an 
officer  was  sent  ashore  by  the  commanding  officer  to  demand  the  sur¬ 
render  of  the  city  (Alexandria).  Before  negotiations  were  concluded 
the  steamers  Baltimore  and  Mount  Vernon  arrived  with  troops  and  took 
possession  of  the  place.  Manned  and  armed  boats  and  took  out  from 
the  dock  the  steamers  Thomas  Collyer  and  Gipsy.  From  meridian  to  4 
p.  m. :  Prisoners  in  charge  of  Lieutenant  Chaplin  were  sent  up  to  navy 
yard  (Washington)  in  the  Baltimore  and  delivered  to  Commander 
Dahlgren. 

June  1. — At  10:20  a.  m.  came  in  sight  of  Aquia  Creek;  steamed  in. 
At  11:40  the  batteries  on  shore  opened  fire  with  rebel  flag  up. 
Returned  fire.  At  12 : 30  p.  m.  ceased  firing.  At  1  p.  m.  beat  to  quar¬ 
ters  and  opened  with  e fleet  with  shell.  Continued  firing  until  4:05 
p.  m.,  when,  having  been  within  1,700  yards,  after  an  action  and  hot  fire 
of  four  hours  and  twenty-five  minutes,  in  which  this  ship  expended  196 
shell,  and  155  hollow  shot,  hauled  off  at  4 : 30,  having  completely  silenced 
their  batteries.  The  enemy  at  an  early  stage  of  the  action  set  fire  to 
the  railroad  wharf  and  bridge.  Received  eight  shot,  one  in  pipe,  one 
in  maintopsail  yard,  one  in  forecastle  deck,  one  through  first  cutter, 
one  port  quarter,  one  through  mizzen  topmast,  one  cut  ridgerope,  star¬ 
board  side,  and  one  cut  lead  off  after  air  port,  starboard  side. 

June  2.- — Commences  and  till  4  a.  m. :  At  anchor  off  Aquia  Creek. 
From  8  to  midnight:  Lights  moving  along  the  beach  at  Aquia  Creek. 

June  3. — From  8  to  meridian:  Rebels  throwing  up  earthworks. 

June  4. — From  meridian  to  4:  Boarded  several  vessels  bound  up  and 
down  and  warned  them  off  the  blockade  coast. 

June  5. — At  4:30  a.  m.  got  up  anchor  and  steamed  down  the  river. 
At  6:30  anchored  off  Mathias  Point.  At  8  a.  m.  sent  armed  party  of 
marines  and  seamen  on  shore,  under  command  of  Master  Blue,  to  pro¬ 
tect  surveying  party.  At  5 : 30  p.  m.  completed  survey.  Got  underway 
and  steamed  up  to  Aquia  Creek.  At  8  anchored  in  old  position. 

June  6. — At  5  a.  m.  got  underway  and  stood  up  the  river,  with  Cap¬ 
tain  Palmer  and  surveying  party  on  board.  Stopped  several  times  to 
overhaul  crafts.  At  10 : 30  stopped  off'  White  House.  Sent  40  marines 
and  seamen,  under  command  of  Lieutenant  Chaplin,  to  protect  survey-

June  24. — From  4  to  S  a.  m.:  The  West  Hill  battery  fired  two  shots 
at  a  sailing  vessel  beating  up  the  river;  both  shots  fell  short. 

June  25. — Off  Mathias  Point.  At  2 : 45  a.  in.  got  underway  and  stood 
down  the  river.  At  5 : 30  discovered  armed  troops  in  ambush  along 
Mathias  Point.  Opened  lire  with  shell.  Armed  and  sent  on  shore  under 
charge  of  Lieutenant  Chaplin,  Master  Blue,  Midshipman  Snell,  Engineer 
Trilley,  sixty  men,  all  armed,  under  command  of  Captains  Palmer  and 
Woodbury,  U.  S.  Army.  Boats  landed  and  men  scouted  about  the 
secession  forces.  At  8  the  party  returned,  having  captured  two  horses 
with  their  equipments.  Reported  driving  in  the  enemy  with  a  fire  of 
musketry.  Discovered  a  camp  and  supposed  the  forces  were  500  men. 
Fired  forty-eight  shell,  grape  and  shot.  A  man,  Kelly  Jackson,  came 
to  our  boat  and  gave  himself  up.  At  10  stood  up  the  Potomac. 

June  26. — Off  Aquia  Creek.  At  9  p.  m.  Lieutenant  Chaplin  left  the 

ship  in  command  of  first  and  third  cutters,  consisting  of -  men, 

armed  and  equipped,  to  be  towed  by  the  tug  Reliance  to  the  Freeborn , 
near  Mathias  Point,  there  to  report  to  Commander  Ward,  in  obedience

Ward,  a  bale  of  waste,  4  gallons  tar,  1  gallon  spirits  turpentine,  axes, 
hatchets,  and  coal  bags. 

June  27. — At  9  p.  m.  the  Thomas  Freeborn  came  up  river  and  hailed

in  the  expedition  at  Mathias  Point.”  The  Reliance  came  up  with  the

ing  from  the  point  the  boats  left  behind  them  200  coal  bags,  1  spyglass, 
several  shovels,  and  one  Sharps  rifle.

October  16. — Steaming  down  the  Potomac  with  tugs  alongside.  At  5

struck  by  a  32-pounder  shot  abreast  mizzenmast,  the  shot  passing 
through  dingey  and  lodging  in  ship’s  side.  The  enemy  fired  twenty

ting,  others  through  the  rigging,  carrying  away  the  forward  vang,  the 
ridgerope,  starboard  after  guy,  rudder  to  third  cutter.  Ship  did  not 
return  the  fire.  Came  to  anchor  above  Maryland  Point.  Mount  Vernon 
came  alongside,  when  we  reembarked  troops. 


Abstract  log  of  the  U.  S.  S.  Pocahontas,  April  25  to  October  15,  1861,  Commander  John  P. 

Gillis,  Commanding. 

April  25,  1861. — In  the  Potomac  River.  Passed  near  the  White 
House,  below  Mount  Vernon,  to  ascertain  if  any  batteries  were  there. 
At  11  discovered  two  large  schooners  at  Aquia  Creek  landing.  Stood 
down  for  them;  everything  looking  quiet,  hauled  off  and  stood  down 
the  river.  From  8  to  midnight:  Point  Lookout  bore  E.  N.  E.  f  E.,  dis¬ 
tant  about  1  mile.  Saw  a  fire  bearing  S.  by  W. 

May  2. — From  8  to  midnight:  Discovered  a  steamer  standing  up  the 
[Chesapeake]  Bay.  At  8:45  got  up  steam  and  gave  chase;  fired  a 
rocket  and  howitzer,  but  failed  to  heave  her  to. 

May  12. — At  noon  spoke  the  schooner  Sally  Frances ,  of  Accomac,  Va. 
From  12  to  4  p.  m. :  Sent  a  boat  on  board  the  schooner  Sally  Frances ; 
found  she  had  neither  pass  nor  flag  on  board;  sent  a  prize  crew  in  com¬ 
mand  of  Lieutenant  Howison  on  board. 

May  15. — Mouth  of  the  Rappahannock  River.  The  Mount  Vernon 
came  alongside  and  reported  that  she  had  spoken  a  schooner  from  up 
the  river,  which  reported  a  fortification  about  35  miles  up  the  river.  At 
9:30  p.  m.  discovered  a  steamer  passing  down  the  bay.  The  Mount 
Vernon  got  underway  and  gave  chase,  and  at  10:20  returned  without 
being  able  to  speak  her. 

May  21. — At  10  a.  m.  stood  in  Aquia  Creek,  beat  to  quarters;  discov¬ 
ered  a  battery  on  shore  and  the  steamer  George  Page  at  anchor  off  the 
wharf. 

May  26. — Captain  Dove  came  on  board  and  relieved  Captain  Gillis  of 
the  command  of  this  ship.

to  be  two  officers,  who  had  been  captured  at  Manassas  and  escaped. 
Eeceived  a  launch  and  howitzer,  with  six  cases  of  fixed  ammunition. 

August  23. — At  4:  30  p.  m.  the  gunboat  [Jacob]  Bell  and  tugs  Reliance 
and  Resolute  came  down  for  the  purpose  of  driving  away  new  encamp¬ 
ment  of  the  rebels  south  of  Potomac  Creek  on  the  highland.  The  Ice 
Boat  accompanied  them  over.  After  some  very  ineffectual  wild  firing 
the  first  three  returned  on  signal  from  this  vessel.  The  Ice  Boat 
engaged  at  long  range,  with  her  rifle  gun  and  IX-inch,  the  Potomac 
Creek  battery,  which  fired  briskly  at  her  but  without  effect;  nobody 
hurt. 

August  28. — At  12:15  p.  m.  the  launch,  in  charge  of  Midshipman 
Stewart,  was  dispatched  to  destroy  all  boats  found  on  the  Maryland 
shore  in  this  vicinity.  Prom  0  to  8  p.  m. :  Launch  returned,  having 
destroyed  three  small  boats  and  one  scow  belonging  to  George  Carpen¬ 
ter,  and  three  small  boats  and  one  scow  below  him. 

August  30. — At  9  a.  m.  sent  launch  to  destroy  small  boats.  At  11 : 30 
launch  returned  with  two  small  boats;  destroyed  them  alongside  the 
ship;  having  destroyed  one  large  fishing  boat,  one  scow,  and  five 
small  boats,  valued  in  all  at  about  $350,  belonging,  it  is  said,  to  James 
Perguson,  of  Baltimore. 

August  31. — The  enemy  fired  a  gun  from  a  battery  at  the  mouth  of 
Aquia  Creek. 

September  3. — Lieutenant  P.  G.  Watmough  took  command  of  this 
ship. 

September  10. — At  9.  p.  m.  sent  out  the  cutter  to  observe  the  move¬ 
ments  of  the  enemy  at  Aquia  Creek. 

September  20. — Boats  returned  from  expedition  to  Virginia  shore. 

September  24. — Prom  G  to  8  p.  m. :  Steamer  Island  Belle  passed  down 
the  river,  throwing  a  few  shell  in  the  direction  of  Aquia  Creek. 

September  30.— Lieutenant  A  I).  Harrell  was  placed  in  command  of 
this  vessel. 

October  10. — Prom  4  to  6  p.  m. :  Prepared  launch  for  immediate 
action.  At  8  our  launch  and  the  Release's  shoved  off.  At  9  an  expedi¬ 
tion  for  the  purpose  of  destroying  a  schooner  called  the  Martha  Wash¬ 
ington,  lying  up  Dumfries  [Quantico]  Creek,  left  this  anchorage.  It 
consisted  of  two  launches,  with  howitzers,  each  of  17  men;  one  in 
charge  of  Midshipman  Stewart,  accompanied  by  Master  E.  L.  Haines 
and  Assistant  Engineer  McCutcheon;  and  the  other  of  Acting  Masters 
Palmer  and  Poster;  and  the  gig  and  four  men  and  pilot,  containing 
Lieutenant  Commanding  Harrell,  in  command  of  the  expedition. 
These  boats  were  towed  off  the  mouth  of  the  creek  by  the  steamers  Res¬ 
cue  and  Resolute. 

October  11. — At  2:30  a.  m.  the  boats  pulled  into  the  creek  and  reached 
the  schooner,  which  was  effectually  fired.  In  coming  out  the  enemy 
fired  several  volleys  of  musketry,  which  were  replied  to,  but  fortu¬ 
nately  nobody  hurt.  The  steamers  then  fired  several  shell  where  the 
firing  was  seen.  At  3  got  underway  for  our  station.  Observed  two 
rockets  ascend  and  burst  up  the  river,  supposed  from  the  expedition. 
Soon  after  saw  the  flash  of  powder,  and  soon  heard  the  report  of  can¬ 
non  at  intervals  of  five  minutes.  Directly  after  saw  flames  ascend  from 
what  proved  to  be  a  vessel  fired  by  the  expedition.  At  4 : 15  a.  m.  the 
expedition  returned,  having  burned  the  schooner  in  Dumfries  Creek 
without  losing  a  single  man.

October  15. — At  10  a.  m.  heard  firing  from  a  steamer  coming  down ; 
slie  proved  to  be  the  Pocahontas.  At  10:45  heard  heavy  firing  in  the 
neighborhood  of  Dumfries  [Quantico]  Creek;  it  proved  to  be  from  on 
shore  and  the  steamer  Seminole.  From  12  to  4:  Orders  given  to  stop 
all  vessels  bound  up. 

October  16. — At  5:30  a.  m.  the  batteries  on  Quantico  Creek  opened 
fire  on  the  steamer  Pawnee  as  she  was  coming  down.  As  she  passed  us 
she  reported  “no  damage  done;  struck  only  six  times.”  At  9  p.  m.  the 
battery  on  Dumfries  [Quantico]  Creek  opened  fire  on  the  steamer  Reso¬ 
lute  and  fired  nine  shots. 

October  17. — From  12  to  4  a.  m. :  Flashes  as  if  from  guns  were  occa¬ 
sionally  seen  in  the  direction  of  Quantico  Creek,  but  heard  no  reports. 
From  4  to  8  a.  m. :  Transport  steamer  William  Whildin  arrived  from 
upper  Potomac  with  mail  for  Commodore  Craven ;  reports  a  heavy  bat¬ 
tery  and  large  caliber  guns  mounted  upon  the  Virginia  side.  Several 
schooners  passed  down  and  were  fired  on,  but  were  not  injured,  though 
near.  At  10:30  two  schooners  arrived  from  up  river;  were  fired  on 
from  batteries  at  Dumfries  [Quantico]  Creek,  none  of  the  shots  injur¬ 
ing  the  vessels.  From  3:15  p.  m.  to  midnight:  Shots  were  frequently 
fired  from  the  batteries  at  Quantico  Creek  at  vessels  going  up  and  coming 
down  the  river. 

October  18. — At  5  p.  m.  discovered  a  battery  in  process  of  erection  on 
the  Virginia  shore;  sent  the  Resolute  and  Satellite  to  reconnoiter. 

October  19. — At  2  a.  m,  the  steamer  Murray  arrived  from  above  and 
was  fired  on  by  the  batteries  at  Dumfries  [Quantico]  Creek.  From 
8  a.  m.  to  12  m. :  Dispatched  boats  for  the  purpose  of  intercepting  any 
movements  up  the  river.  At  1 : 30  p.  m.  steamer  Satellite  ran  in  under 
the  Virginia  shore  to  reconnoiter;  threw  two  shot  by  firing  ashore  and 
was  recalled.  At  3  p.  m.  discovered  a  schooner  off  Dumfries,  a  prize 
to  the  enemy.  Steamer  Satellite  dispatched  to  watch  Aquia  Creek 
movements. 

October  20. — At  6  a.  m.  dispatched  the  cutter,  well  armed,  to  notify 
every  sailing  vessel  to  get  underway  and  go  down  the  river  below 
Mathias  Point.  From  8  to  12  meridian :  A  few  shots  were  fired  by  the 
batteries  at  Quantico  Point  at  vessels  passing  down,  none  taking  effect. 

October  28. — At  2  p.  m.  Release  went  up  to  exchange  shot  with  bat¬ 
teries  ;  discovered  one  gun  below  any  before  opened. 

November  1. — At  3  p.  m.  three  small  sailing  vessels  came  down  from 
upper  Potomac  and  were  saluted  by  the  batteries  by  three  shot,  but 
passed  unscathed.  From  4  to  6  p.  m. :  Two  schooners  in  passing  down 
were  fired  upon  by  the  batteries  at  Quantico. 

November  11. — At  10  a.  m.  steamer  Freeborn  arrived  from  Maryland 
Point;  reported  a  battery  at  Boyd's  Hole,  which  opened  fire  upon  her 
while  passing,  the  missiles  passing  over  and  beyond  some  150  yards, 
sustaining  no  damage.  From  12  to  4  p.  m. :  Steamer  Satellite  passed 
down  the  river  to  reconnoiter  near  Boyd’s  Hole.  At  12 : 30  p.  m.  heavy 
firing  at  Quantico  Creek  upon  sailing  vessels  passing. 

November  12. — From  8  to  12  midnight :  Steamers  Freeborn  and  Release 
left  for  reconnoissance. 

November  13. — At  2  p.  m.  heard  heavy  firing  in  the  direction  of  Poto¬ 
mac  Creek  and  saw  several  shots  strike  the  water  about  the  middle  of 
the  river.  At  2 :  50  p.  m.  steamer  Satellite  arrived  from  Maryland  Point; 
reports  troops  crossing  Potomac  Creek  in  large  numbers  in  launches 
toward  Aquia  Creek.

Report  of  Major  Williamson ,  Virginia  army ,  and  Lieutenant  Lewis ,  Vir¬ 
ginia  navy ,  regarding  reconnoissance  in  Aquia  Greek  with  a  view  to 
fortifying  it. 

Fredericksburg,  Va.,  April  24, 1861. 
[Sir:]  By  your  orders  I  proceeded  to  Aquia  Creek  and  examined 
the  place  with  the  view  of  fortifying  it  for  the  purposes  indicated  by 
your  verbal  directions  of  this  date,  viz,  to  secure  the  railroad  iron,  the 
timber,  two  vessels,  and  a  small  steamer  at  that  point  from  the  enemy. 
I  was  joined  in  the  evening  by  Lieutenant  Lewis,  of  the  Virginia  navy, 
at  your  request,  and  we  reviewed  the  ground  together.  After  examin¬ 
ing  the  topography  of  the  ground  and  the  character  and  position  of 
the  channel,  we  are  of  the  opinion  that  the  best  place  to  put  a  battery 
is  on  the  Split  Bock  Bluff  [Va.],  as  the  channel  can  be  commanded  from 
that  point  by  guns  of  sufficient  caliber.  A  battery  on  Cream  Point 
[Va.]  would  invite  attack  and,  being  separated  from  the  landing  by 
Aquia  Creek,  would  be  difficult  to  hold.  W e  do  not  think  the  place  worth 
fortifying,  and  would  respectfully  recommend  that  a  small  force  of  ten  or 
twenty  men  be  kept  there  to  keep  off  any  boats  that  might  attempt  to 
land  there,  and  be  employed  in  loading  cars,  which  should  be  sent  to 
remove  the  iron  and  timber  to  Fredericksburg  at  once;  that  the  cap¬ 
tain  of  the*vessels  be  allowed  to  sail  with  their  vessels  at  their  jdeas- 
ure.  While  the  enemy  holds  the  Potomac  the  steamer  is  of  no  value 
to  us,  and  we  have  not  the  slightest  idea  that  the  enemy  will  make  the 
attempt  to  possess  themselves  of  it.  The  men  kept  there  should  be 
required  to  give  information  to  headquarters  of  any  attempt  of  the 
enemy  to  land  there  in  force,  which  would  be  indicated  by  the  number 
of  vessels  in  the  offing,  and  not  allowed  to  harass  the  inhabitants  by 
reporting  every  vessel  they  see  in  the  river. 

Very  respectfully  submitted  by 

Thomas  H.  Williamson, 

Major  of  Engineers ,  Virginia  Army. 

H.  H.  Lewis, 

Lieutenant ,  Virginia  Navy. 

Brigadier-General  Buggles. 

P.  S. — William  H.  Kerr,  brigade  inspector,  concurs  in  this  report.

Headquarters  Potomac  Department, 

Culpeper  Court-House ,  May  2 ,  1861-^-7  a.  m. 

[Sir:]  After  consultation  with  Lieutenants  Maury  and  Smith,  of  the 
Navy,  I  find  the  time  is  not  yet  when  we  should  unmask  our  designs 
upon  a  certain  point,  or  when  we  are  in  force  sufficient  to  enter  fully 
upou  that  enterprise,  in  the  very  face  of  the  enemy,  now  probably 
50,000  strong  at  Washington,  Annapolis,  and  the  Potomac  Biver.  The 
heavy  guns  should  doubtless  be  held  ready  in  yonr  rear  and  in  mine 
until  we  shall  be  ready  ou  both  lines  of  operations  to  converge,  unmask, 
and  force  on  that  enterprise  in  the  face  of  any  odds  that  can  be  brought 
against  us.  Strengthen  your  position,  therefore,  with  men,  munitions, 
and  heavy  ordnance,  while  I  shall  do  the  same.  As  to  your  front,  cover 
it  with  the  “eyes  and  ears  of  an  army” — cavalry — as  best  you  may. 
Observe  the  enemy;  gather  intelligence;  keep  at  your  outposts  lines  of 
vedettes  and  couriers;  gather,  therefore,  all  the  cavalry  you  can  in 
your  district  without  infringing  on  mine;  strengthen  yourself  in  infan¬ 
try  and  field  artillery;  drill,  organize,  equip,  discipline,  and  generally 
get  ready  to  converge  with  me  when  the  time  shall  come;  keep  yourself 
in  regular,  prompt,  and  speedy  communication  with  my  headquarters 
through  all  media — rail,  wire,  and  courier.  Beport  to  Assistant  Adju¬ 
tant-General  Jones  from  time  to  time  the  numbers,  description,  and 
general  condition  of  all  forces  under  your  command  and  how  located 
or  distributed. 

Very  respectfully,  your  most  obedient, 

Philip  St.  Geo.  Cocke, 

Brigadi er-  Genera  l,  Com  manding. 

General  Buggles, 

Fredericksburg,  Ya. 


Culpeper  Court-House,  April  29,  1861. 

Sir:  In  obedience  to  your  order,  we  have  conferred  upon  the  subject 
of  placing  a  battery  at  the  point  indicated  in  your  instructions,  and 
have  the  honor  to  make  the  following  report: 

To  place  this  battery  a  large  supporting  force  will  be  necessary,  and 
as  the  Federal  Government  has  now  in  Washington,  as  we  believe, 
20,000  or  25,000  troops,  and  means  of  transporting  4,000  or  5,000  in  a

few  Lours  to  any  point  on  the  Potomac,  we  consider  a  movement  of  that 
kind  at  present  injudicious.  We  would  respectfully  suggest  tLat  the 
two  8  inch  guns,  ammunition,  etc.,  now  in  Alexandria,  be  removed  to 
this  or  some  other  point  on  the  railroad,  where  they  would  be  in  a  safer

We  are,  respectfully,  your  obedient  servants, 

Wm.  L.  Maury,

Letter  from  Colonel  Garnett, adjutant-general, volunteer  forces  of  Virginia, 
to  Brigadier- General  Ruggles,  commanding  Virginia  volunteers,  regard¬ 
ing  cooperation  with  the  Navy. 

Headquarters  Virginia  Forces, 

Richmond,  Va.,  May  6,  1861. 

Colonel:  Captain  Lynch,  of  the  Navy,  has  been  instructed  to  use 
the  four  guns  first  intended  for  Mathias  Point  to  protect  the  approaches 
to  Fredericksburg  from  the  Potomac.  You  are  instructed  so  to  dispose 
of  the  force  under  your  command  as  to  aid,  to  the  extent  of  your  power, 
in  this  purpose.  Measures  must  be  taken  to  destroy  the  railroad 
approach  to  wharf,  etc.,  if  our  troops  should  be  driven  by  force  from  its 
terminus,  in  such  an  effectual  manner  that  they  can  not  be  opened  again 
by  the  enemy  without  great  delay. 

,  I  am,  sir,  etc., 

B.  S.  Garnett, 

Adjutant-  General. 

Colonel  D.  Buggles, 

Virginia  Volunteers,  Fredericksburg,  Va.

Extract  of  letter  from  Captain  Ingraham ,  Virginia  navy ,  to  Captain 
Lynch,  Virginia  navy ,  regarding  erection  of  batteries  at  Mathias  Point. 

I  am  given  to  understand  that  the  intention  of  erecting  a  battery 
at  Mathias  Point  is  not  abandoned.  Although,  after  sounding  the 
channel  off  that  point,  I  expressed  in  my  report  the  opinion  that  a 
cross  fire  from  it  upon  a  steamer,  at  a  distance  1J  miles,  for  the  space 
of  about  five  minutes,  would  be  a  waste  of  ammunition,  yet  I  am  ready 
to  obey  any  order  upon  the  subject;  and  in  pursuance  of  the  information 
I  have  received,  respectfully  ask  what  guns  can  be  furnished  for  that 
position?  It  was  originally  designed  to  mount  twelve  8-inch  guns 
there  and  a  like  number  at  the  White  Mouse  [Ya.,  Potomac  River],  To 
the  latter  place  I  gave  the  preference. 


Instructions  from  Major-General  Lee  to  Brigadier -General  Buggies,  com¬ 
manding  Virginia  volunteers ,  regarding  measures  for  defense  of  Vir¬ 
ginia. 


Headquarters  Virginia  Forces, 

Richmond ,  Va .,  May  8 ,  1861. 

General  :  I  am  instructed  by  Major-General  Lee  to  acknowledge 
the  receipt  of  communications  from  Major  T.  H.  Williamson,  engineer 
Virginia  army,  Lieutenant  H.  H.  Lewis,  Virginia  navy,  and  W.  H. 
Kerr,  brigade  inspector  Virginia  volunteers,  in  relation  to  fortifying 
Aquia  Creek.  The  general  commanding  desires  me  to  say  that  the 
object  in  view  is  the  defense  of  the  avenues  of  approach  to  the  terminus 
of  the  railway,  rather  than  the  protection  of  the  few  vessels  at  Aquia 
Creek ;  that  the  instructions  given  by  him  with  reference  to  this  matter 
were  based  upon  the  report  of  Captain  Lynch,  Virginia  navy.  You 
will  therefore,  being  on  the  spot  and  in  possession  of  the  facts  requisite 
to  a  proper  disposition  of  the  works  and  the  troops  under  your  com¬ 
mand,  exercise  your  judgment,  in  connection  with  that  of  Captain 
Lynch,  with  reference  to  the  defense  of  the  avenues  of  approach  to  the 
terminus  of  the  railroad  and  the  general  protection  of  that  country. 

The  importance  of  erecting  batteries  at  Mathias  Point  is  apparent; 
but  from  the  report  of  Captain  Lynch,  which  represents  the  necessity 
of  supporting  such  a  movement  by  a  larger  force  than  you  had  at  your 
disposal,  it  was  considered  advisable  to  employ  the  guns  originally 
intended  for  that  point  in  the  defense  of  the  approaches  to  Fredericks¬ 
burg  by  rail  or  river. 

Very  respectfully, 


Brigadier-General  Buggles, 

Commanding ,  Fredericksburg ,  Va. 


J.  M.  Brooke. 


Report  of  Brigadier- General  Ruggles ,  commanding  Virginia  volunteers , 
regarding  erection  of  battery  at  Aquia  Creek  Railroad  Landing. 

Headquarters,  Fredericksburg ,  Va.,  May  8,  1861. 
Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  for  the  information  of  the  command¬ 
ing  general  that  I  located  a  battery  at  the  Aquia  Creek  Railroad 
Landing  this  morning  and  placed  it  under  the  charge  of  Major  T.  H. 
Williamson,  engineer,  for  completion. 


OPERATIONS  ON  THE  POTOMAC  AND  RAPPAHANNOCK.  775 


In  tlie  absence  of  Captain  Lynch,  of  the  Navy,  for  whom  I  have  dis¬ 
patched  a  messenger,  I  have  directed  Captain  Tliorbnrn  to  put  the  guns 
in  position  and  make  the  necessary  preparation  for  service.  It  is  my 
expectation  that  the  battery  will  be  in  a  measure  completed  within 
forty-eight  hours.  Measures  will  be  taken  to  give  the  requisite  protection. 

I  respectfully  recommend  that  a  battery  of  four  32-pounders  be  estab¬ 
lished  on  the  Rappahannock  River  at  Bristolmines  [Brisco  Mines?]  or 
Rappahannock,  with  as  little  delay  as  is  practicable. 

I  transmit  a  memorandum  of  a  statement  made  yesterday  by  Messrs. 
John  T.  Washington  and  John  H.  Stuart,  of  King  George  County,  Ya. 
Measures  were  taken  immediately  by  dispatching  mounted  men  to 
intercept  and  recover  the  slaves  supposed  to  have  escaped,  but  thus 
far  without  satisfactory  results. 

Repeated  applications  have  been  made  to  me  from  counties  bordering 
on  the  Rappahannock  on  both  sides,  along  the  Northern  Neck,  for 
iustructions  preliminary  to  enrollment  as  volunteers,  from  the  fact, 
doubtlessly,  that  they  were  within  my  original  jurisdiction.  I  am 
instructed  by  General  Cocke  to  embrace  my  original  limits  until  further 
orders. 

Yery  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Daniel  Ruggles, 

Brigadier- General  Volunteers ,  Commanding  Forces. 

Colonel  R.  S.  Garnett, 

Adjutant- General  Volunteer  Forces,  Richmond,  Va. 


Report  of  Commander  Kennedy ,  C.  S.  Vary,  of  a  reconnoissance  of  the 

Potomac  River. 


Richmond,  July  8,  1861. 

Sir:  I  have  returned  from  the  exploration  of  the  river  Potomac  at 
Evansport.  The  activity  of  the  enemy’s  cruisers  on  the  river,  the 
method  and  importance  of  keeping  the  secret  from  the  enemy,  neces¬ 
sarily  caused  much  delay.  I  lost  also  much  time  by  endeavoring  to 
measure  the  angles  for  the  determination  of  the  distance  across  the 
river  with  a  worthless  quadrant  that  would  not  stay  in  adjustment,  and 
I  was  at  last  compelled  to  borrow  a  surveyor’s  compass  in  order  to 
measure  the  angles.  I  found  the  nearest  measured  distance  from  shore 
to  shore  to  beH2,ol3  yards.  There  are  two  channels  and  a  middle  ground 
between  them,  with  3£  fathoms  of  water  on  it.  The  Virginia  edge  of 
this  middle  ground  lies  about  GOO  yards  from  the  shore.  From  this  edge 
the  water  gradually  shoals  to  3J  fathoms  and  then  deepens  again  to  5 
fathoms  on  the  Maryland  edge  of  the  bank,  the  width  of  the  bank 
being  about  300  yards.  The  main  ship  channel  runs  on  the  Virginia 
shore,  and  1  learned  from  a  fisherman,  who  professed  to  know  the  river 
well,  that  the  course  of  ships  of  heavy  draft  is  on  a  line  connecting 
Sandy  Point  with  Possum  Nose,  a  point  on  the  Virginia  shore  about 
three-fourths  of  a  mile  above  Ship  [Shipping]  Point,  the  southern 
point  Quantico  Creek.  He  also  informed  me  that  a  kettle  bottom  shoal 
makes  out  about  600  yards  from  the  Maryland  shore  below  Budd’s 
Ferry,  with  channels  between  the  knolls,  and  that  another  shoal  makes 
out  from  the  Maryland  shore  about  2  miles  from  Stump  Point  [Neck], 
the  northern  point  of  Chicomuxen  Creek.  I  was  not  able  to  verify  this 


776  OPERATIONS  ON  THE  POTOMAC  AND  RAPPAHANNOCK. 

* 

statement,  nor  to  measure  the  width  of  the  Virginia  channel.  I  went 
out  in  a  crazy  skiff  for  this  purpose,  and  having  narrowly  escaped  cap¬ 
ture  by  one  of  the  enemy’s  tugs  I  did  not  attempt  it  again.  Ship  [  Ship¬ 
ping]  Point  is  a  bluff  of  clay  formation  and  about  25  feet  in  height. 
Prom  it  the  land  slopes  away  gradually  to  Mulberry  Point,  and  a  little 
distance  therefrom  dips  suddenly,  forming  a  depression ;  thence  it  rises 
again  to  a  height  of  8  or  10  feet,  and  slopes  away  to  the  edge  of  the 
marsh  in  rear  of  the  wharf.  Through  this  marsh  runs  a  very  small 
stream,  emptying  into  the  river  near  the  wharf.  Ship  [Shipping]  Point 
is  thickly  wooded  with  a  growth  of  cedar  trees,  extending  nearly  or 
quite  to  Mulberry  Poiut,  but  thinner  there.  How  far  the  middle  ground 
extends  up  or  down  the  river  I  was  unable  to  ascertain.  I  was  informed 
that  vessels  of  12  feet  draft  could  not  pass  over  the  shoal  that  makes 
out  from  Stump  Neck  without  difficulty,  the  channel  being  very  narrow 
and  winding  among  the  knolls  comprising  the  shoal.  My  opinion  is 
that  9-inch  guns  will  command  the  channel,  and  with  the  aid  of  one 
rifled  12-pounder  will  close  the  river  in  the  day  time.  During  the  night 
tugs  and  vessels  of  light  draft  may  pass  by  hugging  the  Maryland 
shore.  I  was  assisted  in  the  work  by  Mr.  Holmes,  of  Prince  William 
County,  and  the  other  surveyors. 

Respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

C.  H.  Kennedy, 

Commander ,  <7.  S.  Navy. 

Captain  S.  Barron, 

Officer  of  Ordnance  and  Detail ,  Richmond ,  Va.
